Also, as Robert Merton has discussed, technological developments and financial innovation are having a profound impact on how the financial system functions. As a result, the boundaries between banking and non-banking institutions are blurring. This is likely to have an impact on the way central banks conduct monetary policy. It will also have consequences for the scope of supervision and for the assessment of financial stability. Finally, the trend towards increasing internationalisation, reinforced by technological progress, will bring challenges for central banks. Having summarised what I think are the major trends that may have a bearing on the role of central banks, I would now like to discuss them in more detail and assess their impact. Technological development in payment systems It may sometimes be difficult to explain to the uninitiated public what central banks actually do. However, mentioning banknotes as an important product is almost always a means of getting instant recognition. It has been argued that, in the future, this most tangible product of central banks is very likely to face severe competition. As observed in previous years, the use of physical cash is diminishing rapidly. In the face of the cash change-over to the Euro, the banknote circulation in the Euro-area has declined by approximately 20% since the end of 2000. Alternatives such as debit/credit cards, electronic purses and e-cash have gained wider public acceptance. Ultimately, the extent to which notably electronic cash will replace its physical  central bank supplied  rival, will depend on whether such currency can provide finality of payment and anonymity and whether it generates sufficient trust as to its stability and acceptance. In the end, however, the banknote circulation is likely to be substantially reduced. For central banks this would imply shrinking balance sheets and the loss of seigniorage income. This will prompt them to enhance the efficiency of their operations. After all, financial independence is a necessary precondition for sufficient independence in performing their tasks. Banknotes in circulation make up only one part of the central bank liabilities used for final settlement. Even if banknotes would totally disappear, other central bank liabilities  bank reserves - would still be used for final settlement in wholesale payment systems. It has been suggested, however, that the use of central bank reserves as a means of ultimate settlement is not likely to remain unchallenged. For instance, netting systems or clearing houses could play a role in the final settlement of wholesale balances. In such systems, central bank reserves would then be substituted with interbank credit. Therefore, hypothetically, central banks could become obsolete as far as final settlement in wholesale payment systems is concerned. This would then hamper their ability to influence price formation in the money market, i.e. their ability to conduct monetary policy. It can be argued, however, that - as long as their credibility is intact - central banks would still be able to influence interest rates by providing borrowing and lending facilities, albeit without as much leverage as is currently the case. In practice, in a competition for final settlement status in payment systems, central banks are likely to have advantages that will make such competition difficult for any contender. First and foremost, there is the track record of central banks in providing a stable currency that is unlikely to be matched by any contender. Additionally, the reserves of central banks - being public institutions - involve no default risks and central banks have the capacity and willingness to lend clearing funds in case of need. Finally, it should not be forgotten that  as long as central banks are considered to contribute to the welfare of the economy at large  their position is likely to be legally protected. Such protection may include legal tender provisions, reserve requirements, the right for the central bank to act as the sole cashier or banker to the government, and regulations restricting final settlement to base money or requesting convertibility of all moneys into base money. Financial intermediation Technological and financial innovation is not restricted to payments but also affects the financial sector in other areas. By enhancing transparency and lowering transaction costs, financial innovation has eroded margins in the financial services industry and has contributed to increased competition in financial markets. As a result, financial institutions will be forced to re-assess their business models. Some of them may be prompted to concentrate on specialised high margin niche markets; others may seek to maintain revenues in an increasingly competitive environment by cutting costs and increasing market share, thus contributing to further consolidation in the financial sector. This development may affect systemic risk in the financial sector and will have a direct impact on the supervisory, regulatory and oversight activities of the central bank. Also, financial innovations have blurred the traditional boundaries between bank and non-bank financial institutions. Nowadays, in attracting funding, banks compete with insurers and asset managers for investors money. Moreover, traditionally illiquid bank assets can increasingly be traded and managed today using instruments such as credit derivatives. At the same time, corporates tend to increasingly bypass the banking system by funding themselves directly in the capital market. As a result, traditional credit-related banking risks increasingly end up on the balance sheet of non-bank institutions. Banks are likely to continue to play a role in the origination of loans and in the distribution of credit risk within the economy, but it will be more difficult to distinguish them from non-banking institutions by looking at their balance sheet. The changing structure of the financial system may influence the conduct of monetary policy. Typically, central banks influence financing conditions by setting the price of base money to which only banks have access. If other institutions start to behave more like banks, it makes sense to treat them as such for the purposes of conducting monetary policy. Against this background, money market mutual funds and institutions issuing e-money are nowadays regarded as credit instititutions in Europe for the purpose of monetary policy. Moreover, because of disintermediation and other changes in the structure of the financial sector, the transmission of monetary policy is undergoing changes. Consequently, financial markets and the expectations in these markets nowadays play an important role in the conduct of monetary policy. For central banks, this implies tighter requirements as to the transparency and clarity of monetary policy. With the boundaries between banks and non-banks blurring and in view of the resulting close links between institutions in both categories, safeguarding financial stability is likely to be a far greater challenge for central banks than it used to be. As far as systemic financial stability is concerned, central banks remain the natural candidate for safeguarding financial stability as they continue to be the nexus of payment systems and the ultimate source of liquidity in times of stress. In the future , this will require central banks to bolster their knowledge and understanding of the functioning of financial markets beyond what is going on in the banking sector. The developments that I have just sketched will have a particular impact on the supervisory role of central banks. The blurring of the borders between banking, insurance and security market activities will continue to bring challenges for supervisory activities. In the Netherlands, financial conglomerates offering integrated financial services exist for nearly a decade. Consequently, co-operation between banking and insurance supervision has strengthened over time. This has resulted in a new supervisory model, which is operational since early 2002. This model involves an integrated risk based approach to supervising financial conglomerates; it also enables pooling of resources in prudential supervision of both banks and insurance companies, involving both the Dutch central bank and the Pensions and Insurance Supervisory Authority. Market- and conduct of business supervision is performed on a cross sector basis by a separate supervisor. As a result, systemic stability and cross-sector prudential supervision will be closely associated with the central bank, recognising the close link between both. This is particularly relevant for a country like the Netherlands, where the banking system is highly concentrated. In such an environment, problems within individual institutions are very likely to directly translate into systemic issues. Finally, on the topic of supervision and regulation in general, I would like to remark that regulators should be careful not to obstruct - and where possible even encourage - market discipline and that they should aim for consistent supervisory approaches, avoiding both arbitrage and overlap. Herein lies a major challenge for central banks and financial regulators. Internationalisation Another element of the rapidly changing financial markets is the increasing internationalisation, resulting from technological changes as well as deregulation over the past few decades. The continuing cross-border link-ups and consolidation in the financial sector are bound to have consequences for central banks. Today already this trend is reflected most clearly in the pooling of central bank resources within the European System of Central Banks. One can argue that such consolidation is likely to intensify in the coming years. This may increase competition between central banks, perhaps prompting them to specialise in certain areas. On this issue, it can be argued that subsidiarity  doing locally what can be done locally, doing centrally what must be done centrally  tends to work well in practice and that the central banking system as a whole could benefit from the competition between participating institutions. Moreover, subsidiarity ensures that country-specific factors can be taken into account in decision-processes and it may help increasing public confidence in the policies of the system. The major challenges stemming from internationalisation will be in the area of financial stability, supervision and regulation. In the future, strengthening international co-operation in these areas  in global platforms, such as the FSF, the BIS and the IMF  will be essential for central banks. In the Netherlands, having a very international banking system (in some cases half of the assets and profits of Dutch banks are related to overseas activities), we are most aware of the need of upholding high and consistent supervisory standards worldwide. Therefore, we feel that there is a continuing need to actively engage in designing, maintaining and promoting such standards. Conclusion So let me wrap up. Although financial markets are in flux and central banks are not likely to remain unaffected, central banks are likely to continue to play a useful role in these markets. Their source of income may erode as banknotes loose popularity in favour of other (electronic) means of payment. However, the role of central banks at the heart of payment systems, providing the funds for ultimate settlement, is likely to remain unchallenged; the same holds for the ability of central banks to conduct monetary policy, although they may have to re-evaluate some operational aspects. The biggest future challenges for central banks will stem from the safeguarding of financial stability in an increasingly complex and global marketplace. To deal with such challenges, central banks will be required to invest in their knowledge of the structure and functioning of financial markets. For central banks there are important synergies to be exploited in this area, as they are involved in market operations, monetary policy, financial supervision and financial stability issues and participate in various policy discussions. So much for discounting the future. Albert Einstein once said that he never thought much of the future as it tends to come too quickly. Likewise, as I mentioned earlier, discounting the future involves translating its implications into present actions. To be able to continue to play an important role in financial markets we will have to face the challenges ahead and work hard on what needs to be done to overcome them. Thank you very much for your attention.

Title: Social exclusion and the financial system
Subtitle: 1 Introduction I would like to thank the organising committee for the invitation to participate in this conference. Its main theme is so-called social exclusion. This is defined as a situation in which people are not willing or not able to participate and/or not allowed to participate in social or economic systems. I have been requested to talk about social exclusion and economics. In order to do so, I will discuss some aspects of social exclusion in the Netherlands. Next, I will talk about the global financial system and how central banks and financial sector supervisors may contribute in preventing exclusion from this system.
text: Social exclusion and the financial system Speech Datum 27 juni 2002 Tijd 11:35 uur Lokatie the 30th International Conference on Social Welfare in Rotterdam Spreker prof dr Arnold Schilder, directeur van De Nederlandsche Bank 1 Introduction I would like to thank the organising committee for the invitation to participate in this conference. Its main theme is so-called social exclusion. This is defined as a situation in which people are not willing or not able to participate and/or not allowed to participate in social or economic systems. I have been requested to talk about social exclusion and economics. In order to do so, I will discuss some aspects of social exclusion in the Netherlands. Next, I will talk about the global financial system and how central banks and financial sector supervisors may contribute in preventing exclusion from this system. But first let us consider the main theme of the conference: what is social exclusion, or how does it come about? Social exclusion manifests itself in entirely different ways in the western world and in developing countries. It is a problem of not being able, willing or allowed to join in with the rest of society. On an individual level, the socially excluded person is exceptional. He or she is set apart from society and prevented from returning to the fold. The exceptional nature of it is a feature of social exclusion as we see it in developed countries, such as the Netherlands. In the developing world, however, social exclusion is a problem of groups of people, the poor, who are excluded from opportunities to improve their conditions. 2 Social exclusion in the Netherlands As is evident in and around this conference building, the Netherlands is a wealthy country. It is prosperous, and it also has an elaborate safety net of public social services. For that reason, it seems that no-one should have to want for anything. Yet, somehow, some people are slipping through the net. This problem has not been diminished by the economic boom in recent years rather on the contrary. The Salvation Armys annual report for 2000, for example, records a worrying development. The annual number of people who turn to the Salvation Army for help, because they are homeless or have run into other problems which they themselves are unable to solve, has almost doubled in a few years, from some 9,000 in early 1996 to some 16,000 in late 2000. So the question is: why has the problem of social exclusion grown in this country? Research into the relationship between money and happiness has shown that attaining and holding on to social status is an important behavioral motive. At times when others are doing well, people who are less successful may feel powerless and, eventually, abdicate their willingness to participate, for example in the labor process. Similar studies in Europe and the United States have revealed that unemployment is a major source of unhappiness for many people. The social contacts on the job, the sense of recognition, the opportunity to perform well, in other words, social inclusion, appear to be the major assets of having a job. Exclusion from the labour market, on the other hand, leads to the destruction of human capital, in the sense that people loose their work experience and technical expertise. But social exclusion goes a step further. One loses all that is dear to one, both in a material and in an immaterial sense. Destruction of physical and emotional capital is most visible when a person is evicted on account of high debts and his or her possessions are subsequently auctioned off. Sometimes, the amount owed is insignificant compared to the damage done to the individual and, similarly, to the effort needed to repair it  if indeed it can be repaired. Prevention of eviction is therefore extremely important. For the Netherlands, this might be one step to turn the curve. Let me give you a practical example. The Netherlands has a highly efficient and all-inclusive financial sector. The very fact that our financial sector is so sophisticated, however, means that those who have been denied access to the financial system have also ceased to count  in a very literal sense. They are excluded from the banking system, which is an essential system. Unfortunately, this happens to people who have a negative track record with their bank, due to not paying off their debts. The underlying mechanism, however, is that this track record also is recorded in a central register, so other banks also refuse these people a new bank account. This way, individual people and households are excluded from the banking system, which severely limits their opportunities in life. I do not exaggerate when I say that in Western Europe, participation in the banking system has become one of the economic rights which, according to Section 22 of the Universal Declaration on Human Rights, are "indispensible for ones dignity and for the free development of ones personality". In order to help the people excluded from the banking system, the Salvation Army requested De Nederlandsche Bank some years ago for an allowance to administer individual bank accounts for them, so as to safeguard their access to financial services. This would be an adequate approach, thanks to an institution which enters into direct contact with the people who have disappeared from the view of private firms and public agencies. De Nederlandsche Bank fully supported this initiative and granted the Salvation Army the necessary bank license, at fair conditions, of course. Moreover, we discussed the issue with the Netherlands Bankers Association. The banks representative organisation recognised the importance of being included in the financial system and banks responsibility in this respect. Last year, it has agreed to a covenant to guarantee access, for every single individual in the Netherlands, to an individual bank account. This is just one example of preventing social exclusion. It illustrates that such prevention needs three elements. First, signalling the specific issue. The Salvation Armys intervention was a key factor here. Second, recognising the need for action by relevant authorities. Third, effective and constructive action by the responsible agencies. The Dutch central bank stimulates such actions to its best efforts. 3 Social exclusion and the global financial system Let me now turn to social exclusion and the global financial system. Globalisation of the financial system has favourable effects. In short, a more sophisticated financial system fosters economic growth and may contribute to poverty alleviation. Recent studies confirm this view. But recent crises have shown that globalisation poses risks as well. In 1997, emerging Asia was struck by a severe financial crisis which originated in Thailand, but quickly spread to Indonesia, Malaysia and Korea. In the subsequent years, Russia, Brazil, Turkey and Argentina also had to contend with financial upheaval. The common denominator is that in all of these countries the turmoil took a heavy toll, both in social and economic terms. It also raised questions about whether, and under what conditions, capital account liberalisation and subsequently increasing international capital flows are beneficial, rather than harmful for developing countries. Some take the view that the potential hazards outstrip the benefits, and tend to reinstate restrictions, for instance by introducing a tax on all international currency transactions. Others argue that these risks should primarily be addressed by increasing countries resilience by improving macro-economic and financial policies, and not by reneging on liberalisation. As a matter of fact, the Asia crisis hit some countries much harder than others, irrespective of their degree of openness to international capital flows. In 1998, Russia was forced into default within days, but Poland was hardly affected. Chile hasnt experienced negative spillovers from Argentinas woes, while neighbouring Brazil and Urugay did. Experience suggest that especially countries with misguided macroeconomic policies, unsustainable debt burdens and financial system inadequacies are prone to the so-called vagaries of financial markets. They also experience deeper recessions and slower recoveries than countries implementing sound policies. After all, there is a growing consensus that the best way to benefit from unrestricted capital mobility while minimising the concommittant risks is by conducting, among others, sound macro-economic policies, good supervision and corporate governance in the financial sector Indeed, an important role is to be played by sound policies. These should aim for monetary and financial stability, as this is one of the necessary conditions for efficient financial development and poverty reduction. Stable monetary conditions favour credit assessment and enhance financial intermediation and benefit the poor. If a financial crisis would occur, the poor bear a disproportionally large share of the negative effects of monetary and financial instability, since they usually have only limited possibilities to protect themselves against inflation. Moreover, if a crisis occurs, the number of poor people increases rapidly. Let me once again give some examples on how central banks and banking supervisors contribute to financial stability and sound financial policies. First, technical assistance to the financial authorities in developing and transition countries. Assistance at a technical level in banking supervision is an instrument that fosters a stable and efficient global financial system at the basis in individual countries. De Nederlandsche Bank provides this kind of assistance regularly amongst others to central banks of selected countries, among others to those that aspire to become members of the European Union. Moreover, assistance is provided at the request of international organisations, like IMF and Worldbank. For instance, at the request of the World Bank, we provided assistance to supervisors in Asian countries in the aftermath of the Asian crisis. Second, the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision has issued its Core Principles for effective banking supervision, dealing, among others, with sound risk management and corporate governance by banks. Also, the standards for adequate capital holdings by banks are being substantially improved, ultimately ending up in a new so-called Basel Capital Accord. The Committee consults and discusses these issues through its Core Principles Liaison Group with banking supervisors all over the world. The International Banking Supervisors Conference, which will be held in September, in Cape Town, South-Africa, will be devoted to these subjects and will bring delegates from over 100 countries together. Macro-economic policies, technical assistance, banking supervision. These subjects are rather abstract and may seem remote to the urgent needs of people socially excluded today. However, I want to emphasize that a financially stable economy and a solid banking system are key factors to allow better chances for social inclusion of the poor, thereby again turning the curve. If there is no such stability, only the rich will safeguard their economic interest, often to the detriment of the poor. 4 Concluding remarks Ladies and gentlemen, in every society, there are individuals or groups that can be defined in the terms of the famous Mahatma Gandhi: the least, the last, the lost and the latest. They are, very unfortunately, excluded. Today, I have explained that social exclusion can take various forms. In any event, however, given the immense damage caused by exclusion, it is better to prevent it than to cure it, for individuals, groups or countries. I hope that this conference will contribute to prevention and reduction of social exclusion worldwide.

Title: 'The Dutch retail payment system: the law of the inhibiting head start?'
Subtitle: Als er wereldkampioenschappen betalingsverkeer zouden worden georganiseerd, zou Nederland het beter doen dan op het voetbalterrein. De Nederlandse betaalmarkt laat al jaren doelmatige resultaten zien. Toch zijn er geluiden dat het niveau van de nationale competitie te laag is omdat bepaalde spelers te veel en andere te weinig invloed hebben. Gaat het spelpeil hierdoor omlaag of wordt het buitenland beter? Soms ook zijn er fluitconcerten van het publiek, dat echter wel massaal blijft toestromen. Moeten scheidsrechters ingrijpen?
text: 'The Dutch retail payment system: the law of the inhibiting head start?' Speech Datum 18 september 2002 Time: 11:12 a.m. Location farewell meeting of Regional Director North/East drs. P.J.G. Baselaar, in Zwolle Speaker J. Koning, Director of Payments at the Dutch Central Bank If the World Championships were to be organised, the Netherlands would do better than on the football field. The Dutch payments market has been showing effective results for years. However, there are rumours that the level of the national league is too low because certain players have too much influence and others too little. Will this lower the level of play or will foreign countries improve? Sometimes there are also flute concerts by the audience, which continues to flock to the audience. Should referees intervene? Today I don't want to talk to you about football, but about the current state of affairs in Dutch retail payments. About efficiency and market forces, about possible improvements and about the influence of Europe. High efficiency rate Every year, more than 3 billion cashless payments and another half a billion cash withdrawals are processed in the Netherlands, which amounts to about 115 cashless transactions per second. In order to cope with this volume of transactions, processing processes have been highly standardised, automated and centralised. The Dutch payment market has achieved a high degree of efficiency. Both in terms of time and in comparison with other countries. On the supply side, in processing and product innovation, and on the demand side, in the use of efficient payment products. Giralization The payment system is more efficient due to the greater use of scriptural money. Transferring bank balances makes remote payments easier and safer. We know that better than anyone in the Netherlands. As early as the Golden Age, Amsterdam was a world trade center where the Amsterdam Exchange Bank could thrive, because domestic and foreign merchants held funds there to settle their accounts. However, it was not until the middle of the last century that the 'homo giralicus' made its appearance, when the advent of the computer made mass processing possible and consumers and businesses started using payment accounts on a large scale. And at the end of the century, cashless financing will be given new impetus by far-reaching 'front-office applications': information technology will make cashless credit accessible from the living room, the office, in retail situations and from anywhere where a computer or mobile phone can connect to the bank. Paying and receiving becomes easier, safer, faster and .... more and more cashless. In 1900 the share of cash in the total money supply was still 80%, in 2001 the share of this cash ratio has fallen to 5% (slightly distorted downwards by the depotting effects of the euro exchange). These good market results are partly the result of good cooperation between banks, businesses and consumers in setting up and implementing campaigns to encourage tailor-made payments, among other things. Electronization Front-office applications make it possible to automate the entire processing chain of a cashless payment, also known as 'straight through processing' in Drenthe. An indicator of the degree of electronisation is the share of written orders in the total number of cashless payments. This 'paper ratio' will drop to 10% this year, compared to 50% ten years ago. Most striking is the growth of debit cards in shops and the like, from 30 million transactions in 1992 to more than 1 billion this year. Initially mainly at the expense of cheques, now mainly of cash. Another significant factor is the increased popularity of authorization  orders that are processed fully automatically  the number of which more than doubled in ten years to almost 900 million this year, mainly at the expense of the acceptance giro. In addition, banking and payments via the computer have increased rapidly in recent years. International perspective Worldwide, too, there is a migration movement in retail payments from the use of cash and paper payment instruments to scriptural money and electronic instruments. An international comparison of eleven countries shows that between 1990 and 1999 the cash and paper ratios in general fell considerably. If we combine both indicators, we see that most countries are moving in the direction of the 'most efficient quadrant', which combines a high degree of cashless conversion (low cash ratio) with a high degree of electronisation (low paper ratio). The Netherlands is at the forefront of this. Internationally, too, the use of debit cards, such as our debit card, is the big driver, at the expense of cheques and cash, as well as the increasing use of mandates. Fee structure What do we pay for paying? The sun rises for nothing. Commercial companies are used to paying for their payment services. Through transactional rates for incoming and outgoing payments, commissions on deposited funds, debit card authorization rates, tariffed account statements, and also through differences in interest and book dates. Consumers, on the other hand, still often have the idea that payment transactions cost them nothing. They are not used to paying for every transaction. Banks do charge fixed amounts for debit card, credit card or telephone banking, but these are independent of use. There are also indirect costs in the form of lost interest income that are a result of low or no interest payment on the checking account. Because these costs are invisible, the payment system is only optically free. The Dutch Central Bank is in favour of a more transparent fee structure, by charging transactions in combination with, for example, higher interest rates. Moreover, to the extent that these rates correspond to the cost price of the payment service, more control can be taken towards even more efficient use. The direct tariffs paid by users of payment products and distribution channels generally compare favourably with those abroad. Comparisons are complicated by the fact that there are many different models, such as package accounts with price tags above a certain discretionary base or a standard commission for holding an account. Just as in the Netherlands, business users in other countries are also extensively charged for their payment and receipts. However, there are larger differences in the level of tariffs and in product use. A well-known example is France, where cheques are still widely used which, according to a legal provision, may not be tariffed. When it comes to debit cards, Dutch rates are also often lower than elsewhere. Indirect costs also exist in other countries, but are often combined with some form of direct pricing in both the private and business markets. In short, from this point of view, the Dutch payment system is efficiently organised, innovative and has good market outcomes, which on average results in a very reasonable price-quality ratio, especially from an international perspective. 3. Efficiency Opportunities One of the main tasks of the Dutch Central Bank is to promote the smooth operation of the payment system. In the light of what I have just said, the idea might arise that we can sit down with our arms folded. However, nothing could be further from the truth, it can be even better! Demand Because good market results have been achieved, the opportunities for improvement due to changes in payment behaviour seem to be approaching their limits. In the Netherlands, electronisation and cashless payments are highest in the payments initiated remotely by account holders from home or the office, such as salary payments and payments of telephone and energy bills. Here cash payments are very rare, the cashless payment is almost 100%. As far as electronization is concerned, the paper ratio in business traffic is already so low that the possibilities for efficiency improvements are limited. Consumers still use the majority of forms, but here too the limits are coming into view, especially since not everyone is able or willing to use electronic distribution channels or authorizations. In cashless counter transactions, electronization is almost 100%, now that the cheques are off the market. However, there is still room for further cashing here. According to a rough estimate, about 80% of the total number of point-of-sale transactions will be paid in cash this year, compared to about 50%. Pinning is still showing ample growth rates and chipping seems to be growing out of its infancy this year. The Dutch will pay 80 million times with their chipknip this year, two and a half times as much as in 2001. Interestingly, the development of chipping currently shows the same characteristics as that of pinning in the similar product life stage. As a result, the share of cash point-of-sale payments is declining in favour of electronic forms of payment. In fact, it seems that the number of cash payments has recently decreased in absolute terms. Will this be the century of the cashless society? This question was also asked at the beginning of the last century. I'm not a seer, I don't know what's going to happen next. What I do know is that cash still clearly meets a need, and not just in the somewhat dark-colored circuits. After all, you can use it to pay directly, quickly and anonymously. Butter with the fish. But I didn't come here to advertise our own product. For the Bank, the efficiency of retail payments is paramount. Advantages of cashless processing lie in higher security and less manual processing. So it may well become a less cash society. However, we do not have sufficient insight into the nature and extent of the substitution possibilities and into what is most efficient for society. Supply-side The opportunities for improvement on the supply side include product innovation. For example, options for offline debit card transactions, which do not require a telephone connection to a bank computer. And the contactless chip for public transport, internet payment methods and the standardisation of electronic and mobile banking. More advanced identification techniques, such as iris, finger profile or voice recognition, could increase security and also accessibility of electronic services. In principle, the market determines what the commercially viable options are, taking into account requirements of safety and reliability. The Dutch payment market scores well in international comparisons from the point of view of product use, but scores less in many studies if only the use of the technologies is considered. Other countries, for example, score better because electronic banking packages are more standardized and because more chip technology is used. However arbitrary such studies may be - comparing apples and oranges often cannot be ruled out - there is of course the danger that the full exploitation of successful, i.e. mature, applications will hold back investment in new technologies. Furthermore, it is inevitable that countries that are lagging relatively behind will be more inclined to adopt the latest technologies, because the fruits are greater and mature more quickly. The law of the inhibiting lead or the law of stimulating disadvantage, therefore. 4. Tensions and market forces Despite demonstrably good results from the payment market, there is a lot of criticism. Retailers complain about excessive debit card rates and poor communication, and consumers complain about the reduced service level and rate increases. Banks, for their part, complain that the payment system is still loss-making. Complaining about the abuses fits in with the image of the 'dissatisfier' that is supposed to be a payment system. But it can also mean that the market is not transparent enough, that the market parties do not have a sufficient picture of each other's wishes and motivations. The payment market is a peculiar one. The core product only satisfies a derived need, it serves to settle the sale of goods and services. Another special feature is that a single cashless payment can involve as many as five or six parties: two offering banks, a telecom company, a processing centre and two different customers, often a consumer and a company. Moreover, the provision of services in the payment system has characteristics of public interest, while the providers are mainly commercial market players. In the payment system, there is a natural tension between competition and cooperation. Interbank agreements and centralization of processing are essential for an efficient design of the payment market. There may be a danger that too much power will be vested in one or a few parties. For example, there is a feeling among point-of-sale institutions that the banking subsidiary Interpay is the only provider of network services for debit card payments that sets excessively high rates and does not sufficiently inform users about the nature and necessity of software adjustments. Too much together  and too little market forces? It has been said that competition is hampered because it is cumbersome to change banks because customers cannot take their account number with them. This requires more infrastructural cooperation and standardization in accounting and control systems. Before putting pressure on the market to do so, I believe that a careful cost-benefit analysis is required. 5. How can it be improved? In the spring, the research report of the Wellink Working Group was published. Commissioned by the Minister of Finance, the Bank has carried out a study into the tariff and infrastructure in retail transactions in collaboration with the banks and in consultation with user groups. The conclusion was that the Dutch payment infrastructure has led to satisfactory outcomes, but that as a secondary aspect there is a high dependence on a small number of providers. In the opinion of the Dutch Central Bank, such a situation requires that sufficient checks and balances are in place. In this context, and in view of the tensions identified, the Bank made recommendations for further improvement of efficiency and the functioning of the market. These have generally been well received, so that work is now underway on implementation. Given the quantity and heterogeneity of the players, it will come as no surprise that good communication and openness are key. In the payment system, you simply need the cooperation of all parties involved in order to achieve adequate improvements. What's going to happen? The Ministry of Finance has set up a 'Social Consultation on the Payment System' (MOB) with the aim of contributing to a socially efficient organisation of the Dutch retail payment system. Participants are representatives of numerous relevant civil society groups, who consult twice a year on social efficiency and on important developments - such as accessibility. Mapping costs When we talked about the costs in cash transactions, our outgoing regional director used to remark that 'the money is paid dearly'. Society is not sufficiently aware of the costs of the payment system. To increase this insight and transparency, a study has been launched into the social costs of the point-of-sale means of payment cash, debit cards, chips and credit cards. Banks, Interpay, DNB and representative organisations of businesses and consumers are participating in this. Once the cost ratios are known, it is possible to steer towards even greater efficiency in counter traffic. Bringing users and providers together In order to improve communication in electronic payments, an advisory group will be set up, in which the parties involved can exchange views in a structured manner on matters of mutual interest, such as new future applications and standards. More competition In order to increase transparency and competition in electronic payments, the banks themselves will no longer conclude debit card contracts with retailers. Banks purchase the transport services from Interpay and offer point-of-sale institutions the terms and conditions for the total product. This creates more room for negotiation and gives the customer more options. In addition, the Bank is in favour of more competition in the provision of transport services for the authorisation of debit card transactions, if this is beneficial to social efficiency. In order to increase access to the payments market, DNB is also prepared to allow players other than banks involved in the settlement of payment transactions to access its own payment infrastructure. However, it is subject to the condition that it will contribute to improvements in efficiency in the financial infrastructure and that it does not contravene European regulations. Finally, the Bank itself is also giving substance to its task by constantly striving to improve the efficiency of its own cashless and cash processing processes. In this context, exploratory talks were started with the banks last month to see what efficiency improvements are still possible in the logistics of the banknotes. 5. European dimension So far, you have not heard me talk about the European dimension. I have saved that for last, because I do not think it is enough to be satisfied with the results achieved at home and improvements in the pipeline. In fact, precisely because we score well in the Netherlands on a large number of points and are approaching the limits of major improvements, it is more important than ever to look beyond the border. There is still a lot to be done there. It is difficult for the average European citizen to understand that we pay and calculate with the same currency in twelve countries, while cross-border payments between those countries are many times more expensive and take longer to travel. Distances can be bridged easily and quickly with the help of today's communication technology. Why not in the European payment system? The main reason for this is that there are still large differences in product handling standards across euro area countries. As a result, orders often still have to be processed manually. Cooperation is therefore required. For some years now, the Eurosystem, the ECB and the central banks of the euro area have been urging banks to increase the efficiency of this cross-border traffic. The banks have also started working on this. This year, however, the European Commission has thrown the bat into the hen house by decreeing that rates for cross-border payments within the euro area must not be higher than rates for similar domestic payments. In response, banks have accelerated plans to create a uniform payment space. This involves uniformity of all payments in the twelve countries, which means that the boundaries between domestic and cross-border within the euro area must disappear. Of course, this requires close consultation between the banks themselves and between banks and their customers in order to align standards and processing processes. Banks expect the first results in 2005. It is no longer a question of having a technical advantage, but rather of contributing to joint technical improvements, aimed at higher European efficiency. More and more, the focus will have to be on the efficiency of the entire current national and cross-border payment system of all euro countries. That will be the new domestic European efficiency. The aim is for the costs of payment transactions within the single payment area to be lower than the sum of the current costs of national and cross-border payments. 6. Conclusions The Dutch certainly don't have to be ashamed of the quality of their payments. The payments market is showing great dynamism, with plenty of room for process and product innovation. Consumers and businesses have contributed to the widespread use of efficient means of payment, which has led to a high degree of efficiency, for which they pay reasonable rates from an international perspective. The downside may be that the introduction of more advanced techniques in efficient countries such as the Netherlands will take place at a later date. After all, the potential for improvement is smaller in the countries that are in the lead than in the countries that are less advanced. This is where the law of the inhibiting head start could come into play. However, from the point of view of the desired integration and efficiency of the European payments market, product and processing standards will become the same in all euro area countries. In the uniform payment area, the integration of the payment system of twelve countries, there are still interesting efficiency opportunities. On the basis of the national offer, it can be expected that the Dutch banks will be strong players in the increased competition in the uniform euro payment market. A prerequisite for a strong role in the European competition is that the players in the payment system are also kept sharp in a national competition. Improvements are being worked on through numerous initiatives. The extent to which efficiency can be further increased by further book-entry in point-of-sale transactions is the subject of a study carried out by the Bank in cooperation with the market parties. However, the cashless society still seems a long way off, so our new regional director can still work in cash in these parts.
text_original: Het Nederlands retailbetalingsverkeer: wet van de remmende voorsprong? Speech Datum 18 september 2002 Tijd 11:12 uur Lokatie afscheidsbijeenkomst van Regiodirecteur noord/oost drs. P.J.G. Baselaar, te Zwolle Spreker drs. J. Koning, directeur Betalingsverkeer van de Nederlandsche Bank Als er wereldkampioenschappen betalingsverkeer zouden worden georganiseerd, zou Nederland het beter doen dan op het voetbalterrein. De Nederlandse betaalmarkt laat al jaren doelmatige resultaten zien. Toch zijn er geluiden dat het niveau van de nationale competitie te laag is omdat bepaalde spelers te veel en andere te weinig invloed hebben. Gaat het spelpeil hierdoor omlaag of wordt het buitenland beter? Soms ook zijn er fluitconcerten van het publiek, dat echter wel massaal blijft toestromen. Moeten scheidsrechters ingrijpen? Vandaag wil ik het niet met u over voetbal hebben, maar over de huidige stand van zaken in het Nederlandse retailbetalingsverkeer. Over efficiency en marktwerking, over mogelijke verbeteringen en over de invloed van Europa. Hoge efficiencygraad Jaarlijks worden er in Nederland ruim 3 miljard girale betalingen en ook nog eens een half miljard kasopnames verwerkt, wat neer komt op zon 115 girale transacties per seconde. Om deze transactieomvang aan te kunnen, zijn verwerkingsprocessen vergaand gestandaardiseerd, geautomatiseerd en gecentraliseerd. De Nederlandse betaalmarkt heeft een hoge graad van efficiency bereikt. Zowel in de tijd bezien als in vergelijking met andere landen. Aan de aanbodzijde, in verwerking en productvernieuwing, en aan de vraagzijde, in het gebruik van doelmatige betaalproducten. Giralisering Het betalingsverkeer is doelmatiger door het groter gebruik van giraal geld. Het overboeken van banktegoeden maakt het betalen op afstand gemakkelijker en veiliger. Dat weten we in Nederland als geen ander. Al in de Gouden Eeuw was Amsterdam een wereldhandelscentrum waar de Amsterdamse Wisselbank kon gedijen, omdat binnen- en buitenlandse kooplieden er tegoeden aanhielden om hun rekeningen te vereffenen. Toch deed pas midden vorige eeuw de homo giralicus zijn intrede, toen de komst van de computer massale verwerking mogelijk maakte en consumenten en bedrijven op grote schaal betaalrekeningen gingen gebruiken. En aan het einde van de eeuw krijgt de giralisering nieuwe impulsen door vergaande front-officetoepassingen: de informatietechnologie maakt het girale tegoed toegankelijk vanuit de huiskamer, het kantoor, in winkelsituaties en vanaf elke plek waar een computer of mobieltje een verbinding met de bank kan leggen. Betalen en ontvangen wordt gemakkelijker, veiliger, sneller en . steeds meer giraal. In 1900 bedroeg het aandeel van het chartale geld in de totale geldhoeveelheid nog 80%, in 2001 is het aandeel van deze contantgeldquote afgenomen tot 5% ( iets neerwaarts vertekend door ontpottingseffecten van de euro-omwisseling). Deze goede marktresultaten zijn mede een gevolg van goede samenwerking tussen de banken, bedrijven en consumenten bij onder meer het opzetten en uitvoeren van campagnes om het betalen op maat te stimuleren. Elektronisering Front-officetoepassingen maken het mogelijk de hele verwerkingsketen van een girale betaling te automatiseren, in goed Drents ook wel straight through processing geheten. Een indicator voor de mate van elektronisering is het aandeel van schriftelijke opdrachten in het totale aantal girale betalingen. Deze papierquote daalt dit jaar naar 10%, terwijl die tien jaar geleden nog 50% bedroeg. Meest opvallend is de groei van het pinnen in winkels en dergelijke van 30 miljoen transacties in 1992 naar ruim 1 miljard dit jaar. Aanvankelijk vooral ten koste van cheques, nu vooral van contant geld. Een factor van betekenis is ook de gestegen populariteit van het machtigen  opdrachten die volledig automatisch worden verwerkt -, waarvan het aantal in tien jaar meer dan verdubbelde naar bijna 900 miljoen dit jaar, ten koste vooral van de acceptgiro. Bovendien neemt de laatste jaren het bankieren en betalen via de computer snel toe. Internationaal perspectief Ook wereldwijd is een migratiebeweging in het retailbetalingsverkeer gaande van het gebruik van contant geld en papieren betaalinstrumenten naar giraal geld en elektronische instrumenten. Uit een internationale vergelijking van elf landen blijkt dat tussen 1990 en 1999 de contantgeld- en de papierquote in het algemeen behoorlijk zijn gedaald. Combineren we beide kengetallen, dan zien we dat de meeste landen zich bewegen in de richting van het meest efficinte kwadrant, dat een hoge mate van giralisering (lage contantgeldquote) paart aan een hoge mate van elektronisering (lage papierquote). Nederland bevindt zich hier in de voorhoede. Ook internationaal is het gebruik van debitcards, zoals onze pinpas, de grote aanjager, ten koste van cheques en contant geld, alsook het toenemend gebruik van machtigingen. Tariefstructuur Wat betalen we voor betalen? Voor niks gaat de zon op. Commercile bedrijven zijn gewend om te betalen voor hun betaaldiensten. Via transactiegebondentarieven voor inkomende en uitgaande betalingen, provisies over afgestort geld, pinautorisatietarieven, getarifeerde rekeningafschriften en ook via verschillen in rente- en boekdatum. Consumenten daarentegen hebben nog vaak het idee dat betalingsverkeer hen niets kost. Zij zijn niet gewend om voor elke transactie te betalen. Banken berekenen weliswaar vaste bedragen voor bankpas, creditcard of telebankieren, maar die zijn onafhankelijk van het gebruik. Ook zijn er indirecte kosten in de vorm van gederfde rente-inkomsten die een gevolg zijn van een lage of geen rentevergoeding op de betaalrekening. Omdat die kosten onzichtbaar zijn, is het betalingsverkeer slechts optisch gratis. De Nederlandsche Bank is voorstander van een meer transparante tariefstructuur, door transacties te tariferen in combinatie met bijvoorbeeld hogere rentevergoeding. In de mate waarin die tarieven corresponderen met de kostprijs van de betaaldienst, kan bovendien meer sturing plaatsvinden naar een nog efficinter gebruik. De directe tarieven die de gebruikers van betaalproducten en distributiekanalen betalen, steken in het algemeen gunstig af bij die in het buitenland. De vergelijkingen worden bemoeilijkt doordat er tal van verschillende modellen worden gehanteerd, zoals pakketrekeningen met prijskaartjes boven een bepaalde vrije voet of een standaardprovisie voor het aanhouden van een rekening. Net als in Nederland worden zakelijke gebruikers ook in andere landen op uitgebreide schaal voor hun betalings- en ontvangstenverkeer getarifeerd. Wel doen zich hier op onderdelen grotere verschillen voor in de hoogte van de tarieven en in het productgebruik. Bekend voorbeeld is Frankrijk waar nog op grote schaal cheques worden gebruikt die volgens een wettelijke bepaling niet mogen worden getarifeerd. Ook wat het pinnen aangaat zijn de Nederlandse tarieven veelal lager dan elders. Indirecte kosten bestaan ook in andere landen, maar worden zowel in de particuliere als de zakelijke markt vaak gecombineerd met een vorm van directe tarifering. Kortom, vanuit deze optiek is het Nederlands betalingsverkeer efficint georganiseerd, innovatief en kent het goede marktuitkomsten waardoor zeker in internationaal perspectief gemiddeld een alleszins redelijke prijs-kwaliteitverhouding ontstaat. 3. Efficiencymogelijkheden Een hoofdtaak van de Nederlandsche Bank is het bevorderen van de goede werking van het betalingsverkeer. Gelet op mijn betoog van zojuist, zou de gedachte kunnen ontstaan dat we met de armen over elkaar kunnen gaan zitten. Niets is echter minder waar, het kan nog beter! Vraagzijde Doordat goede marktresultaten zijn behaald, lijken de verbetermogelijkheden door veranderingen in het betaalgedrag hun grenzen te naderen. In Nederland is de elektronisering en giralisering het grootst bij de betalingen die rekeninghouders op afstand vanuit huis of kantoor initiren, zoals salarisbetalingen en betalingen van telefoon- en energienotas. Hier wordt zeer zelden contant betaald, is de giralisering vrijwel 100%. Wat de elektronisering aangaat, is de papierquote in het zakelijke verkeer al dusdanig laag, dat de mogelijkheden voor efficiencyverbeteringen beperkt zijn. Consumenten gebruiken nog de meeste formulieren, maar ook hier komen de grenzen in zicht, temeer daar niet iedereen in staat of bereid is elektronische distributiekanalen of machtigingen te gebruiken. In het girale toonbankverkeer is de elektronisering vrijwel 100%, nu de cheques van de markt zijn. Hier ligt echter nog ruimte voor verdere giralisering. Volgens een ruwe schating zal dit jaar ongeveer 80% van het ntal toonbanktransacties contant worden betaald, terwijl dit naar wrde ongeveer 50% bedraagt. Het pinnen vertoont nog ruime groeicijfers en het chippen lijkt dit jaar uit de kinderschoenen te groeien. De Nederlanders zullen dit jaar 80 miljoen maal met hun chipknip betalen, tweeneenhalf maal zoveel als in 2001. Interessant is dat de ontwikkeling van het chippen momenteel dezelfde karakteristieken vertoont als die van het pinnen in de vergelijkbare productlevensfase. Gevolg is dat het aandeel van de chartale toonbankbetalingen afneemt ten gunste van elektronische betaalvormen. Het lijkt er zelfs op dat het aantal contante betalingen sinds kort in absolute zin afneemt. Wordt dit de eeuw van de cashless society? Deze vraag werd ook al gesteld aan het begin van de vorige eeuw. Ik ben geen ziener, ik weet niet wat er nog aan innovaties gaat plaatsvinden. Wat ik wel weet is dat cash nog duidelijk in een behoefte voorziet, en echt niet alleen in de wat donker gekleurde circuits. Je kunt er nu eenmaal direct, snel en anoniem mee betalen. Boter bij de vis. Maar ik ben hier niet gekomen om reclame te maken voor ons eigen product. Voor de Bank staat de doelmatigheid van het retailbetalingsverkeer voorop. Voordelen van giralisering zijn gelegen in hogere veiligheid en in minder handmatige verwerking. Het mag dus best een less cash society worden. We hebben echter onvoldoende inzicht in aard en omvang van de substitutiemogelijkheden en in wat maatschappelijk de meeste efficintie oplevert. Aanbodzijde De verbetermogelijkheden aan de aanbodzijde liggen onder meer in productinnovatie. Hierbij kunt u denken aan mogelijkheden voor offline pintransacties, waarbij geen telefoonverbinding met een bankcomputer nodig is. En aan de contactloze chip voor het openbaar vervoer, aan internetbetaalmethoden en aan standaardisatie van elektronisch en mobiel bankieren. Meer geavanceerde identificatietechnieken, zoals iris-, vingerprofiel- of stemherkenning, zouden veiligheid en ook toegankelijkheid van elektronische diensten kunnen verhogen. De markt bepaalt in principe wat de commercieel verantwoorde mogelijkheden zijn, rekeninghoudend met eisen van veiligheid en betrouwbaarheid. De Nederlandse betaalmarkt scoort goed in internationale vergelijkingen vanuit de optiek van het productgebruik, maar scoort in menig onderzoek minder als louter naar het gebruik van de technologien wordt gekeken. Andere landen scoren bijvoorbeeld beter doordat electronic banking pakketten meer zijn gestandaardiseerd en doordat meer chiptechnologie wordt toegepast. Hoe arbitrair dergelijke onderzoeken ook zijn - het vergelijken van appels met peren is vaak niet uit te sluiten - is er natuurlijk het gevaar dat het volledig uitnutten van succesvolle, dus volrijpe, toepassingen de investeringen in nieuwe technologien tegenhoudt. Voorts is het nu eenmaal onontkoombaar dat landen met een relatieve achterstand sneller geneigd zijn de nieuwste technologien toe te passen, omdat de vruchten groter zijn en sneller tot wasdom komen. De wet van de remmende voorsprong dan wel de wet van stimulerende achterstand, derhalve. 4. Spanningsvelden en marktwerking Ondanks aantoonbare goede resultaten van de betaalmarkt, is er veel kritiek. Retailers klagen over te hoge pintarieven en slechte communicatie, en consumenten over het afgenomen serviceniveau en tariefsverhogingen. Banken klagen op hun beurt dat het betalingsverkeer nog altijd verlieslatend is. Klagen over de misstanden past in het beeld van de dissatisfier die betalingsverkeer heet te zijn. Maar het kan ook betekenen dat de markt niet transparant genoeg is, dat de marktpartijen onvoldoende beeld hebben van elkaars wensen en beweegredenen. De markt voor het betalingsverkeer is een eigenaardige. Het kernproduct voorziet slechts in een afgeleide behoefte, het dient om de verkoop van goederen en diensten af te wikkelen. Bijzonder is ook dat bij n girale betaling wel vijf of zes partijen betrokken kunnen zijn: twee aanbiedende banken, een telecombedrijf, een verwerkingscentrale en twee verschillende afnemers, vaak een consument en een bedrijf. De dienstverlening in het betalingsverkeer vertoont bovendien trekjes van algemeen nut, terwijl de aanbieders vooral commercile marktpartijen zijn. In het betalingsverkeer bestaat een natuurlijk spanningsveld tussen concurrentie en samenwerking. Interbancaire afspraken en centralisatie van verwerking zijn essentieel voor een efficinte inrichting van de betaalmarkt. Gevaar kan zijn dat teveel macht bij n of enkele partijen komt te liggen. Zo bestaat bij toonbankinstellingen het gevoel dat bankendochter Interpay als enige aanbieder van netwerkdiensten voor het pinnen te hoge tarieven vaststelt en de gebruikers onvoldoende informeert over aard en noodzaak van softwareaanpassingen. Teveel samen  en te weinig marktwerking? Men hoort wel beweren dat de concurrentie wordt belemmerd omdat het omslachtig is van bank te veranderen doordat klanten hun rekeningnummer niet kunnen meenemen. Dit vereist juist meer infrastructurele samenwerking en standaardisatie in rekening- en controlesystematiek. Voordat hiertoe druk op de markt wordt gezet, lijkt me een zorgvuldige kosten-batenanalyse geboden. 5. Hoe kan het nog beter? In het voorjaar kwam het onderzoeksrapport van de Werkgroep Wellink uit. De Bank heeft - in opdracht van de Minister van Financin  in samenwerking met de banken en in consultatie met gebruikersgroepen onderzoek gedaan naar de tarief- en infrastructuur in het retailverkeer. Conclusie was dat de Nederlandse betaalinfrastructuur tot bevredigende uitkomsten heeft geleid, maar dat als nevenaspect een grote afhankelijkheid bestaat van een klein aantal aanbieders. Een dergelijke situatie vereist naar het oordeel van de Nederlandsche Bank dat er voldoende checks and balances aanwezig zijn. In dit verband en gelet op de gesignaleerde spanningsvelden, deed de Bank aanbevelingen ter verdere verbetering van de doelmatigheid en de marktwerking. Deze zijn in het algemeen in goede aarde gevallen, zodat inmiddels gewerkt wordt aan de uitvoering. Gegeven kwantiteit en heterogeniteit van de spelers zal het u niet verbazen dat goede communicatie en openheid centraal staan. In het betalingsverkeer heb je nu eenmaal medewerking van alle betrokken partijen nodig om op adequate wijze verbeteringen te bewerkstelligen. Wat staat er te gebeuren? Het Ministerie van Financin heeft een Maatschappelijk Overleg Betalingsverkeer (MOB) ingericht dat ten doel heeft bij te dragen aan een maatschappelijk efficinte inrichting van het Nederlandse retailbetalingsverkeer. Deelnemers zijn vertegenwoordigers van tal van betrokken maatschappelijke groeperingen, die twee maal per jaar overleggen over de maatschappelijke efficiency en over belangrijke ontwikkelingen - zoals toegankelijkheid. Kosten in kaart brengen Als we het over de kosten in het chartale verkeer hadden placht onze scheidende regiodirecteur wel op te merken dat het geld duur wordt betaald. Te weinig is de maatschappij zich ervan bewust wat het betalingsverkeer kost. Ter verhoging van dit inzicht en van de transparantie is een onderzoek gestart naar de maatschappelijke kosten van de toonbankbetaalmiddelen contant geld, pinnen, chippen en creditcard. Banken, Interpay, DNB en vertegenwoordigende organisaties van bedrijven en consumenten werken hier aan mee. Als de kostenverhoudingen bekend zijn, kan er gerichter worden gestuurd naar nog meer doelmatigheid in het toonbankverkeer. Gebruikers en aanbieders samenbrengen Ter verbetering van de communicatie in het elektronisch betalingsverkeer zal een adviesgroep worden ingesteld, waarin de betrokken partijen gestructureerd van gedachten kunnen wisselen over zaken van wederzijds belang, zoals nieuwe toekomstige toepassingen en standaarden. Meer concurrentie Ter verhoging van de transparantie en concurrentie in het elektronisch betalingsverkeer zal niet langer Interpay maar zullen de banken zelf de pincontracten met de retailers gaan afsluiten. Banken kopen de transportdiensten bij Interpay in en bieden toonbankinstellingen de voorwaarden voor het totale product aan. Hierdoor ontstaat meer ruimte voor onderhandelingen en verkrijgt de afnemer meer keuzemogelijkheden. Voorts is de Bank voorstander van meer concurrentie bij het aanbieden van de transportdiensten voor het autoriseren van pintransacties, indien dat de maatschappelijke efficintie ten goede komt. Ter vergroting van de toegang tot de betaalmarkt is DNB bovendien bereid ook andere spelers dan banken die betrokken zijn bij de afwikkeling van het betalingsverkeer toe te laten tot haar eigen betaalinfrastructuur. Voorwaarde is wel dat het zal bijdragen tot verbeteringen van de efficintie in de financile infrastructuur en dat het niet in strijd is met Europese regelgeving. Tenslotte geeft de Bank ook zelf inhoud aan haar taak door een continu streven de efficiency van de eigen girale en chartale verwerkingsprocessen te verbeteren. In dit kader zijn vorige maand orinterende gesprekken met de banken gestart om te bezien welke efficiencyverbeteringen er nog mogelijk zijn in de logistiek van de bankbiljetten. 5. Europese dimensie Tot dusver hebt u mij niet over de Europese dimensie gehoord. Dat heb ik voor het laatst bewaard, want ik denk dat we niet kunnen volstaan met tevredenheid over in het binnenland bereikte resultaten en op stapel staande verbeteringen. Sterker nog juist omdat we in Nederland op een groot aantal punten goed scoren en de grenzen van majeure verbeteringen naderen, is het meer dan ooit zaak over de grens te kijken. Daar moet nog veel gebeuren. Het is voor de gemiddelde Europese burger nauwelijks te begrijpen dat we in twaalf landen betalen en rekenen met dezelfde munt, terwijl grensoverschrijdende betalingen tussen die landen vele malen duurder en langer onderweg zijn. Afstanden kunnen met behulp van de hedendaagse communicatietechnologie eenvoudig en snel overbrugd worden. Waarom niet in het Europese betalingsverkeer? De reden is vooral dat in de landen van het eurogebied nog grote verschillen bestaan in standaarden voor verwerking van producten. Vaak moeten opdrachten daardoor nog handmatig worden verwerkt. Samenwerking is dus geboden. Al enige jaren spoort het Eurosysteem, de ECB en de centrale banken van het eurogebied, de banken aan de efficintie van dit grensoverschrijdende verkeer te verhogen. De banken zijn hiermee ook aan de slag gegaan. De Europese Commissie heeft dit jaar echter de knuppel in het hoenderhok gegooid door te verordonneren dat tarieven van grensoverschrijdende betalingen binnen het eurogebied niet hoger mogen zijn dan tarieven van soortgelijke binnenlandse. Banken hebben in reactie hierop plannen versneld om te komen tot een uniforme betaalruimte. Daarbij gaat het over uniformiteit van alle betalingen in de twaalf landen, dat houdt in dat binnen het eurogebied de grenzen tussen binnenlands en grensoverschrijdend moeten verdwijnen. Om dat te bewerkstelligen is uiteraard nauw overleg vereist tussen de banken onderling en tussen banken en hun afnemers om standaarden en verwerkingsprocessen op elkaar af te stemmen. Banken verwachten de eerste resultaten in 2005. Het gaat er dan niet meer om een technische voorsprong te hebben, maar eerder om bij te dragen aan gemeenschappelijke techniekverbeteringen, gericht op een hogere Europse efficiency. Meer en meer zal de focus gericht moeten zijn op de doelmatigheid van het gehele huidige nationale en grensoverschrijdende betalingsverkeer van alle eurolanden. Dt wordt de nieuwe binnenlandse Europese efficiency. Doel is dat de kosten van het betalingsverkeer binnen de uniforme betaalruimte lager zijn dan de som van de huidige kosten van nationaal en grensoverschrijdend betalingsverkeer. 6. Conclusies Nederlanders hoeven zich zeker niet te schamen voor de kwaliteit van hun betalingsverkeer. De betaalmarkt laat een grote dynamiek zien, met veel ruimte voor proces- en productinnovatie. Mede doordat consumenten en bedrijven op grote schaal efficinte betaalmiddelen gebruiken, is er een hoge graad van efficiency bereikt, waarvoor zij in internationaal perspectief bezien redelijke tarieven betalen. Keerzijde kan zijn dat invoering van geavanceerder technieken in efficinte landen als Nederland later zal plaatsvinden. Immers het potentieel voor verbetering is in de landen die voorop lopen kleiner dan in de landen die minder ver gevorderd zijn. Hier zou de wet van de remmende voorsprong opgeld kunnen doen.Vanuit het oogpunt van de gewenste integratie en doelmatigheid van de Europese betaalmarkt zullen product- en verwerkingsstandaarden echter in alle eurolanden dezelfde worden. In de uniforme betaalruimte, de integratie van het betalingsverkeer van nu twaalf landen, liggen dan ook nog interessante efficiencymogelijkheden. Op basis van het nationaal gebodene mag worden verwacht dat de Nederlandse banken sterke spelers zullen zijn in de verhoogde competitie op de uniforme eurobetaalmarkt. Voorwaarde voor een sterke rol in de Europese competitie is, dat de spelers in het betalingsverkeer ook in een nationale competitie scherp gehouden worden. Via tal van initiatieven wordt aan verbetering gewerkt. In welke mate de doelmatigheid nog kan worden vergroot door verdere giralisering in het toonbankverkeer is voorwerp van een onderzoek dat de Bank in samenwerking met de marktpartijen uitvoert. De cashless society lijkt echter nog ver weg, zodat onze nieuwe regiodirecteur nog volop chartaal aan de slag kan in deze contreien.

Title: Financial Stability
Subtitle: Let me start by telling you the good news: over the last year the international financial system has proven to be remarkably resilient to many challenges. We have witnessed the terrorist attacks in September, Argentinas financial collapse, Enrons bankruptcy, a long list of corporate governance scandals, a strong stock market downturn, and mounting financial tensions in South America. Still, financial stability has been broadly preserved. This may be called quite an achievement, especially if one considers that linkages between countries, financial institutions and between the various segments of financial markets have never before been so close. These interlinkages are particularly visible in the banking sector, where cross-border and cross-sectoral integration has lead to a rapidly increasing number of systemically important financial institutions.
text: Financial Stability Speech Datum 20 september 2002 Tijd 11:05 uur Lokatie CEPR/ESI annual conference "Regulatory Challenges for European Financial Markets", Vienna Spreker drs. H.J. Brouwer, directeur van De Nederlandsche Bank Let me start by telling you the good news: over the last year the international financial system has proven to be remarkably resilient to many challenges. We have witnessed the terrorist attacks in September, Argentinas financial collapse, Enrons bankruptcy, a long list of corporate governance scandals, a strong stock market downturn, and mounting financial tensions in South America. Still, financial stability has been broadly preserved. This may be called quite an achievement, especially if one considers that linkages between countries, financial institutions and between the various segments of financial markets have never before been so close. These interlinkages are particularly visible in the banking sector, where cross-border and cross-sectoral integration has lead to a rapidly increasing number of systemically important financial institutions. The absence of internationally systemic crises reflects the strength of the underlying regulatory and supervisory framework, and its capacity to keep up with the rapidly changing financial landscape. This framework has been broadly effective in improving and refining risk management, and it has also adequately dealt with the increasing administrative complexities  notably the growing importance of cooperation between supervisors and central banks. But uUnfortunately  and this is the bad news  no matter how hard we try to prevent them, we can at best only minimise the probability of crises; in a market economy, crises can not be banished altogether. Therefore, the absence of systemic crises should provide little reason for complacency. Policy makers should always look ahead, and anticipate future challenges to financial stability. In this context, there is a certain analogy with geologists. Geologists shouldnt draw too much comfort from the absence of major earthquakes in the recent past. Rather, they should be mindful of the effects of todays fault lines for tomorrows earthquakes. And if crises do occur, policy makers should stand ready to act quickly, and should have the right instruments at their disposal. Fortunately, most policy makers engaged in supervisory and regulatory activities are as forward-looking as the best geologists. And unlike geologists, they can do their utmost to prevent major disasters from happening. Not only does this room to manoeuvre make the policy makers profession far more exciting than that of a geologist, it has also spurred a lively debate about the modalities of a regulatory framework that best suits our supervisory needs. This is especially visible in Europe, where the debate focuses on crisis prevention and to a lesser extent on crisis management. In the following half-hour I intend to touch upon the major controversies, and explain my own position. A changing financial landscape: where do we stand? The international financial landscape has changed substantially over the past two or three decades, and will undoubtedly continue to do so in the foreseeable future. More recently, linkages between financial markets and financial institutions, both across borders and across sectors, have been intensifying at an unprecedented pace. Consolidation and internationalisation would not have been possible without advances in information technology (which have significantly lowered transaction costs), and the creation and use of new financial vehicles for risk sharing, like derivatives. In the euro area, the absence of exchange rate fluctuations and the establishment of a pan European payment system are also important factors promoting cross-border and cross-sector integration. The consequences for financial stability are not clear-cut. On the one hand, better risk management, and improved product and geographical diversification make financial institutions less vulnerable to sectoral or national business cycles, which adds to their resilience to asymmetric shocks. This reduces the likelihood of mishaps. On the other hand, consolidation and internationalisation leads to the creation of an increasing number of large financial institutions. Their failure can pose systemic risks to the overall stability of the financial system, and can facilitate the multiplication of risks and contagion effects. Consequently, today a problem in one segment of the euro-area can have more severe repercussions on the euro area-wide market and beyond. Crises are especially rapidly transmitted through the banking channel. This derives from the maturity mismatch in the balance sheets of banks, the prominent role banks play in payment and settlement systems, and their substantial interbank exposures. In other words, while financial integration tends to reduce the likelihood of financial crises, it also increases their potential magnitude. Discussions on new arrangements in the sphere of crisis prevention What are the implications of these developments? In general, there is broad consensus among authorities and financial institutions that the EU regulatory process needs to keep pace with the rapidly changing financial system. In this context, traditional EU legislative procedures are perceived to be excessively lengthy and cumbersome. Some contend that the perceived shortcomings of the current procedures are best addressed by extending specific comitology arrangements for financial regulation to the banking, insurance and pension industries. These arrangements, which have already been implemented in the area of security supervision, are based on the four-level Lamfalussy approach, in which each subsequent level is responsible for furthering the practical elaboration. According to this approach, the usual EU procedures apply to the initial stages of legislation. That is, proposals are made by the Commission for codecision by the Council of Ministers and the European Parliament. These first decisions define the general regulatory framework, and are taken at the so-called first level. The framework regulation is then elaborated in subordinate regulation by the Commission and a committee of representatives of member states at the second level. In this process, the Commission is advised by a level 3 committee of national experts in the official sector. The level 3 also consults the private sector about the intended regulation and ensures that level 1 and 2 legislation is consistently and equivalently transposed into practice in the different member states, because the actual supervision takes place on a national level. Finally, level 4 secures strengthened enforcement, notably with more vigorous action by the European Commission to enforce Community law, underpinned by enhanced cooperation between the Member States, their regulators, and the private sector. First, let me state that I underscore the potential benefits of applying the Lamfalussy approach to the banking sector. However, the arrangements for the banking sector need to take account of its different nature being far more prone to systemic risks. AlsoHowever, in the discussion about the institutional set-up of regulatory arrangements other elements have crept up as well and we should be careful to avoid that reform becomes an end in itself. This would be detrimental to the overall objective of creating a framework that can better accommodate the regulatory needs of the rapidly changing international financial environment. More specifically, I have three major worries about current proposals for reform. One is related to the optimal organisation of supervisory tasks in view of the blurring of cross-sector and cross-border boundaries. The second concerns the representation of central banks in the new system. The third is related to the use of political accountability as an argument for change. As to my first concern, the optimal organisation of supervisory tasks, the debate revolves around two issues. The first one relates to the question whether or not to take a blueprint approach for intrasectoral integration between the three spheres of supervision (for banking, insurance and securities supervision). Let me start by noting that various European countries are in the process of changing the division of labour between the traditionally separated sectors of prudential supervision. This will however not lead to the emergence of a uniform, pan-European framework. While some European countries have moved towards full integration of supervisory responsibilities into a single agency, others prefer creating intrasectoral committees, or partially consolidating responsibilities. Indeed, while reform is not prompting a common pattern across Europe, such uniformity is not desirable and should not be sought. In my view, a blueprint approach to institutional reform should be avoided, as such an approach lacks the flexibility to deal adequately with the considerable sectoral differences of financial activities throughout the European Union and to cater for specific supervisory needs. Let me illustrate this point on the basis of the experience of my own country. Until recently, we had a sectoral model of supervision in which the type of financial institution determined which supervisor was responsible. The central bank was charged with supervising banks, investment firms and money exchange offices, while the Pensions and Insurance Supervisory Authority supervised pensions and insurance companies, and the Securities Board supervised securities firms and exchanges.
