Economic Developments in the Antilles The Antillean economy has struggled for some time now. In part, this reflects the weak global business cycle. Its geographical location in a region of the world where political turmoil is nearby, such as in Venezuela , serves as an extra obstacle to growth. Recent economic developments have been more favourable though. With the upturn in the United States and presumably Europe , the Antilles can hopefully consolidate the nascent economic growth in the coming years. It has to be clear that economic growth is a function of structural adjustment efforts and the current upturn in the economy is still too fragile. Therefore, the challenges that face the Netherlands Antilles are no smaller than those elsewhere. As in Europe , structural weaknesses stand in the way of a truly robust economic recovery. Liberalisation of labour markets and consolidation of public finances are necessary prerequisites to lift the economy towards higher growth. As in Europe , opposition to such measures is fierce. Public debate focuses on the urgency and necessity of spending cuts. As in Europe , this tends to be a drawn out process. But recognition has grown among policy makers and the wider public that corrective measures are necessary. Apart from the parallels, there are also some important differences. As a small and open island economy, the Antilles are vulnerable to external shocks. This is because its small economic size limits the scope for diversification. Moreover, the benefits from economies of scale are limited. This vulnerability increases the importance of economic flexibility, including in terms of macroeconomic policies. Apart from these economic characteristics, another difference stands out. As I said earlier: you should repair your roof when the sun is shining. Given weather conditions here, it would seem there is ample opportunity to fix the roof. Nevertheless, the necessary construction work has not progressed in recent years, to put it mildly, even though the urgency for budgetary reform is arguably greater on the Antilles than elsewhere. Public debt is already nearing 100% of GDP. Though public finances have not yet deteriorated as far as in Japan , the debt dynamics are at least as worrisome, given the Antilles  lower savings rate, less diversified economy and its less-developed financial sector. The report of the commissie schuldenproblematiek estimated that in absence of corrective action, public debt will rise to 250% of GDP in 2010. This is unsustainable and would lead to financial instability. I would echo the warning given by the report of the commission on debt difficulties in the Antilles and urge the authorities to draw up -- and implement -- a plan on fiscal consolidation. I would also like to echo the message from the first president of the European Central Bank, Mr. Duisenberg. In his speech earlier this year, he also stressed the need for budgetary reforms. In doing so, he also emphasised the importance of doing so in a medium term fiscal framework. This should smooth the fiscal impact of measures to restore sustainability of public finances. It would prevent a re-occurrence of the damaging impact of past stop-and-go fiscal adjustment policies. Moreover, it would inspire confidence in the debt servicing capabilities of the government. Needless to say, this is a difficult challenge as it limits the policy options available to politicians. The recent difficulties regarding the implementation of the Stability and Growth pact in Europe provide ample illustration of this. The Antillesand the European Union Given these challenges, it is perhaps inevitable that discussions have flared up about the political and financial relationship between the Antilles and the Netherlands . On both sides of the Atlantic , there is a willingness to review the current relationship and to work towards a different association of the members of the Kingdom. Currently, there is a feeling that we are drifting apart. While the Netherlands is moving towards ever-closer integration with Europe , the Antilles wonder about their place in the world and within the Kingdom. It is not surprising then, that among the proposals for reform is the possible entry of the Antilles to the European Union. This could be achieved through the so-called, ultra periphery area status for the islands. In short: the UPG-status. Current examples of extra-European areas that have such a status are: the Azores , Madeira , the Canary Islands and the French overseas departments. To review the options and issues concerning EU-entry of the Antilles , it is perhaps enlightening first to explain the present institutional arrangement. Currently, the relationship between the Antilles and the Netherlands is governed by the so-called Statuut. The Statuut covers all common responsibilities and competencies for the members of the Kingdom of the Netherlands . The three countries or constituent parts of the Kingdom -- the Antilles , Aruba and the Netherlands -- are of equal status. This gives the Antillean islands a fair amount of autonomy. In light of its distinct geographical location, and the distinct set of policy issues and challenges it faces, such policy autonomy is desirable. To give just an example: there is an independent central bank for these islands, the Bank Nederlandse Antillen. The Antilles consequently have their own currency and banking supervision. However, this contrasts sharply with the current UPG-members of the European Union. Their status also brings with it many obligations. All UPG-members have ceded considerable autonomy to their capitals or Brussels . In this sense, the UPG-entry of the Antilles would be unique, as it is without precedent that such an autonomous region would enter under this regime. In principle, the entire body of European law would have to be incorporated in the Antilles . Exemptions from this principle would have to be negotiated between the Antilles , the Netherlands and the other member states. Consequently, it remains to be seen whether and how policy authority has to be shared between the Antilles , the Netherlands and Brussels in case of EU entry. In all, much is still uncertain regarding the terms and policy consequences of a possible formal closer relationship to the European Union. It is for politicians and ultimately the people of the Antilles to decide whether and how they would like to proceed with EU-integration and whether this is feasible in the existing frameworks. Nevertheless, I can highlight some issues that are relevant for the context of this discussion. First, there are clear benefits attached to closer relations with the EU. It would allow the Antilles better access to European markets, and would upgrade legislation concerning a wide range of topics. Furthermore, EU-entry would allow for peer pressure and reviews on economic issues, promoting responsible government. That said, apart from the discussions regarding policy autonomy, it is important to also highlight the possible monetary consequences. For example, all present UPG-members now have the euro as their currency. It is therefore uncertain whether the Antilles would be able to keep their current monetary arrangement after EU-entry. In light of the theory of optimal currency areas, it is not self-evident that pegging to the euro is optimal for the Antilles. This depends on the present and future trade relations with euro or dollar-oriented economies. Therefore, the benefits and drawbacks of switching to the euro would have to be weighed carefully. Conclusion Ladies and gentlemen, let me conclude. I have offered you a broad picture of the global economic environment. As you have seen, these broad global developments touch us all. Furthermore, policy challenges are not very different for many countries. In the Antilles , as well as in the US , Japan and Europe , the common thread is the deterioration of public finances in a difficult economic climate. Finally, I have touched upon the issue of the closer links with the European Union for the Antilles . I am confident that the Antilles will find a comfortable and suitable new framework within the Kingdom and possibly also in the EU. I thank you all for your attention.

Title: President Wellink's speech on 'Does ageing lead to impoverishment?'
Subtitle: Aanleiding: vergrijzing vereist welvaartsgroei In een zaal vol mensen van in de twintig lijkt het niet echt voor de hand te liggen om te gaan praten over ouderdom. Dit hoort een vergezicht te zijn op uw leeftijd, iets waar andere mensen last van hebben maar u pas in een heel ander tijdsgewricht. Helaas geldt dit voor uw generatie niet meer. Mijn generatie stevent af op haar pensioen en u stevent af op een werkzaam leven waarin u niet alleen voor uzelf moet zorgen, maar ook voor vele mensen in de AOW en bedrijfspensioenregelingen. In 2015 zijn er een kleine 3 miljoen mensen boven de 65 jaar tegen ruim 2 miljoen vorig jaar. Als over 35 jaar de vergrijzing op zijn hoogtepunt is, staan tegenover elke bejaarde slechts iets meer dan 2 personen in de werkende leeftijd. Doordat een steeds kleinere beroepsbevolking het inkomen moet verdienen voor een steeds grotere groep afhankelijken, neemt het inkomen per hoofd van de bevolking af. Pensioen- en zorgkosten zullen bovendien sterk stijgen, ondanks de grote pensioenbesparingen die ons land gelukkig kent. Als de bevolking een bepaalde levensstijl wil handhaven, is het nodig dat de welvaart blijft groeien. Vandaag wil ik daarom met u van gedachten wisselen over de vragen wat de determinanten zijn van economische groei en hoe we, maar vooral u allen, er voor kunnen zorgen dat de totale economische koek blijft groeien.
text: President Wellink's speech on 'Does ageing lead to impoverishment?' Speech Date: February 26, 2004 Time: 00:00 hrs Location: Study association for general economics Creative Destruction on February 26, 2004 in Groningen Speaker Dr. A.H.E.M. Wellink, President, De Nederlandsche Bank Reason: ageing requires growth in prosperity In a room full of people in their twenties, it doesn't really seem obvious to start talking about old age. This is supposed to be a distant prospect at your age, something that other people suffer from but you only have at a completely different time. Unfortunately, this is no longer the case for your generation. My generation is heading towards retirement and you are heading for a working life in which you not only have to take care of yourself, but also many people in the state pension and occupational pension schemes. In 2015, there were just under 3 million people over the age of 65, compared to more than 2 million last year. When the ageing population is at its peak in 35 years' time, there will be only slightly more than 2 people of working age for every elderly person. Because an ever-shrinking working population has to earn the income for an ever-larger group of dependents, per capita income is decreasing. Pension and healthcare costs will also rise sharply, despite the large pension savings that our country is fortunate to have. If the population wants to maintain a certain lifestyle, it is necessary that prosperity continues to grow. Today, therefore, I would like to exchange views with you on the questions of what the determinants of economic growth are and how we, but especially all of you, can ensure that the overall economic pie continues to grow. Prosperity can only be increased by the largest possible production, assuming that all externalities are reflected in prices, such as pollution and other nuisances. The two variables that determine the level of production are labor productivity and labor force participation. I will start with the issue of employment rates. Labour force participation and productivity The labour participation rate in the Netherlands is still lagging behind the rest of Europe and the US. There is an average of 1325 working hours per year, which is the lowest number of hours worked in the euro area. Elsewhere in Europe, this number is at least 100 hours higher. In the US, a person works an average of 1900 hours, so just under 600 hours more. There is a clear explanation for this backlog: There is a large, partly 'enforced' preference for leisure time in the Netherlands. As a result, not only are more than 40% of jobs filled part-time, especially those of women, but full-time jobs also have relatively fewer hours than abroad due to holidays and short-time working. Another typical phenomenon in the Netherlands is that large groups of people will definitely never work again. The Netherlands still has a very large group of disabled people, almost one million people. In addition to these typical Dutch phenomena, inactivity is also high among older people over the age of 55. Only 40% of this group is still working. Other European countries also have the latter problem, but that does not make the problem any less urgent. Labour productivity is a more difficult concept. Not the definition, which is the total output divided by the total labour input, i.e. the value added per unit of labour. But there is a measurement problem on several levels. First of all, there is the problem of what you measure and how you compare the outcome. Most countries measure the level of labour productivity per person employed. The Netherlands will then be in the middle of the European rankings. This method of measurement gives an indication of the contribution to production per employed person. Measured per hour, the Netherlands, on the other hand, leads the way. This difference is, of course, due to the high number of part-time jobs. These figures say something about the Dutchman: he likes to work for a short time, but efficiently. Because he works so little, the per capita prosperity is very average, place 8 in the EU ranking. The US is many thousands of euros richer per capita, although we are now catching up with them unnoticed by the appreciation of the euro. What the U.S. is also better at is labor productivity growth. Since the second half of the 1990s, the US has outpaced Europe's productivity growth rates. Why is that? It is difficult to give a precise answer to that question. Figures do show which sectors are doing better in the US: the ICT manufacturing industry and the ICT-using services sector. Given the size and enormous growth in the size of the ICT manufacturing industry in the US, a strong positive effect on the productivity figures of the overall economy is not surprising. There is, however, a caveat to this. In the US, the productivity of ICT production is measured differently than here. There, the production of a faster computer than last year means correspondingly higher production and therefore higher productivity. In Europe, so to speak, only the boxes are counted as production, regardless of the quality improvement of the contents. So there is a distortion in the figures. In the ICT-using services sector, retail trade is particularly important. ICT applications in, for example, inventory management and logistics have been implemented far and widely. Another measurement problem is the measurement of changes in labour productivity. In a world that should be familiar to you from your early years of study, namely that with a Cobb-Douglas production function with the factors of production labor and capital, an increase in labor productivity is a reflection of a higher capital commitment, ceteris paribus. But of course, reality is not so static and straightforward. Productivity can be increased by deploying relatively more capital, but also by making better use of existing capital and labour. Examples are, respectively, making better use of long-standing ICT solutions and organising work differently so that employees can perform their tasks more efficiently. Improving the quality of capital and labour, innovation and training will also increase labour productivity. However, attributing a signalled increase in productivity to one of these factors presents enormous estimation problems. What is the effect of one percent more R&D spending? This measurement problem also has policy implications: there is no panacea for the lagging productivity growth in the Netherlands by aiming for just one of these determinants of productivity growth. The market itself will find the right mix of We need to make more use of the factors of production labour and capital, make better use of the factors of production and improve quality, with the government playing a supporting role. I will discuss this role in more detail in the future. But first, the market must have a reason to invest in productivity improvements. There is a relationship here with market forces. Competition constantly forces companies to improve efficiency and innovate products. Therefore, in principle, a country's productivity can best develop in an economy that is as open as possible with flexible markets and sufficient competition. The most productive and innovative companies will then displace the less well-functioning companies because they can produce more cheaply. This gives companies sufficient incentive to constantly invest in their production factors, labour and capital and encourages starting entrepreneurs to find a niche in the market for their product. The well-known economist Schumpeter called this process creative destruction. In a less efficient economy such as ours, this process of 'survival of the fittest' is rudely disrupted by the presence of market imperfections such as cartels and government intervention. Such intervention is usually motivated by non-economic considerations such as a fair distribution of income. However valid these considerations may be, a consequence is also that less productive firms can continue to exist, meanwhile wasting factors of production that could have been better used elsewhere. A much-quoted, but little-supported solution to force creative destruction is a wage wave. A wage wave means that wage costs rise much faster than labour productivity justifies, causing less innovative companies to die. In principle, this is correct. The disadvantage of such a medicine is that such a deviation from the balance evokes counterforces that are worse than the disease. Thus, capital intensity will increase sharply. If, as a result of the unemployment that has finally arisen, wages fall again, the new equilibrium will have achieved a lower level of employment than would have been possible in the absence of a wage shock. This is because in the first instance, research will be explicitly shifted to labour-saving technology. In the new equilibrium, with lower wages again, the relatively high cost of capital will cause research to move in the other direction. This is inefficient, which means that, in addition to the level of employment, the level of technology will ultimately be lower than it would be without an artificial wage increase. In addition to these countervailing forces, a wage wave will worsen the position vis-a-vis the rest of the world, because companies there will not have to deal with the same cost increase. The question is whether domestic companies will be able to innovate in time to maintain their position and not be immediately pushed out of the market by foreign competition. A third point is that a wage wave causes a disruption of the employment relationship. This can continue to work for a long time, even after reaching a new equilibrium after the shock. Companies will be reluctant to make new investments, for fear of being held hostage by high wage demands from their employees immediately after those investments. Another way in which companies are encouraged to innovate more is if the currency appreciates. Competition with countries outside the euro area is intensifying, but unlike a wage shock, there are also some advantages to this that soften the process. First of all, raw materials and capital goods become cheaper, including foreign R&D such as software. Imported goods for consumers are also becoming cheaper. In part, this has a negative effect on domestic producers due to a shift in the consumption basket. On the other hand, these lower prices increase consumer disposable income, which can increase demand for non-tradables. A final benefit of an appreciation is more psychological. An external shock can give politicians a good argument to implement electorally sensitive reforms. This is how rules coming from 'Europe' work, for example on fiscal policy, and so does an appreciation. Internal shocks such as a wage wave are less clearly identifiable and also of our own making, so it is more difficult to cite as a reason for unpleasant decisions. What can the government do? As mentioned earlier, future prosperity is generated by a simultaneous increase in labour supply and labour productivity. Looking at the conditions in which labour productivity grows, there is a clear task for the government: to remove barriers, including international barriers, that can distort competition and to remove rigidities in the labour market that hinder rapid adaptation to technological innovation. Such structural reforms, they cannot be repeated often enough, are desperately needed if we are to maintain or raise our standard of living. These are partly in the area of product markets, such as tightening competition supervision and reducing the administrative burden. To some extent, the labour market must be relieved of restrictive regulations in the field of dismissal law and working hours. In addition to structural reforms, a well-educated workforce is essential. There, too, there is a clear public task when it comes to the initial education of young people, from primary school to university. The first thing that often comes to mind is the training of many researchers, but at least as important is the training of people who can handle new techniques, make better use of technology and are able to apply R&D. Furthermore, companies in a competitive environment also need good managers and entrepreneurs, and they too start their careers in primary school. Companies then have the task of building on the knowledge of their employees with training and courses. There is a danger in the aforementioned difficulties in attributing productivity growth to specific sub-factors. While structural reforms are often painful and met with resistance, other measures seem to have the same effect without the pain. Soon there will be policies such as increasing public R&D or incentive programs for companies. Public R&D is not the only instrument for increasing labour productivity growth. Government incentives for private R&D are also difficult. Is such public money being used in the most effective way? After all, the companies themselves make clearly profitable investments in research, which means that the government either wrongly funds certain research or only helps 2nd best projects to set up. The companies themselves must be encouraged to make better use of their factors of production and to innovate more. This is only possible if they are no longer shielded from market forces due to a lack of domestic and foreign competition, or if the savings of change are dwarfed because it turns out to be impossible to lay people off. Policy aimed at the other determinant of prosperity, participation, is not an easy subject either. Reform of the WAO and social assistance and raising the effective retirement age is necessary for higher participation, but increases the risk of political and social tensions. Nevertheless, this is also an important policy challenge. For example, raising the retirement age by three years could make sufficient financial space available to finance indexation of pension entitlements. In addition, utilising people's individual productivity, even if it is not high, is always profitable. It is also a very cynical way of dealing with people to write off large groups with the message 'no thank you, we don't need you'. Everyone can do something and has something to add to society, for an appropriate salary. Making use of this is a major policy challenge for the coming years. It is clear that social security should only accommodate people who have no other option due to illness or other misfortune. Due to the ageing population, the government will be confronted with lower revenues and higher costs. This reality is incompatible with a deactivating social security system. Outside of social security, the role of the government in stimulating participation is rapidly diminishing. The participation of women with a family is still lagging behind, especially in terms of hours. Where this is a conscious choice by these women, there is little the government can do. If the choice not to work or to work little is motivated by, for example, a shortage of childcare or too high costs, that is a shame and the government certainly has a major role to play in creating the right conditions for this group. This also applies to the number of hours worked. If working Dutch people en masse opt for lower prosperity in exchange for more free time, that's fine. However, if it turns out that people would like to work more but are held back by regulations, the government must also intervene here. My message to you is clearly not devoid of any self-interest. In a few years' time, my contemporaries, including me, will be retiring en masse. While we are enjoying our well-deserved rest, you are just starting your working life to help pay for it. So you have to participate. But participation alone is not enough. In order to have some free time, you also have to work better and smarter, start new businesses, motivate your people well as a manager and create the conditions for such a productive climate as a politician or policy official. I wish you every success in this, but I also have firm faith that you will succeed.
text_original: Speech president Wellink over 'Leidt vergrijzing tot verarming?' Speech Datum 26 februari 2004 Tijd 00:00 uur Lokatie Studievereniging voor algemene economie Creative Destruction op 26 februari 2004 in Groningen Spreker Dr. A.H.E.M. Wellink, President, De Nederlandsche Bank Aanleiding: vergrijzing vereist welvaartsgroei In een zaal vol mensen van in de twintig lijkt het niet echt voor de hand te liggen om te gaan praten over ouderdom. Dit hoort een vergezicht te zijn op uw leeftijd, iets waar andere mensen last van hebben maar u pas in een heel ander tijdsgewricht. Helaas geldt dit voor uw generatie niet meer. Mijn generatie stevent af op haar pensioen en u stevent af op een werkzaam leven waarin u niet alleen voor uzelf moet zorgen, maar ook voor vele mensen in de AOW en bedrijfspensioenregelingen. In 2015 zijn er een kleine 3 miljoen mensen boven de 65 jaar tegen ruim 2 miljoen vorig jaar. Als over 35 jaar de vergrijzing op zijn hoogtepunt is, staan tegenover elke bejaarde slechts iets meer dan 2 personen in de werkende leeftijd. Doordat een steeds kleinere beroepsbevolking het inkomen moet verdienen voor een steeds grotere groep afhankelijken, neemt het inkomen per hoofd van de bevolking af. Pensioen- en zorgkosten zullen bovendien sterk stijgen, ondanks de grote pensioenbesparingen die ons land gelukkig kent. Als de bevolking een bepaalde levensstijl wil handhaven, is het nodig dat de welvaart blijft groeien. Vandaag wil ik daarom met u van gedachten wisselen over de vragen wat de determinanten zijn van economische groei en hoe we, maar vooral u allen, er voor kunnen zorgen dat de totale economische koek blijft groeien. Welvaartsstijging kan alleen door een zo groot mogelijke productie, er van uitgaand dat alle externaliteiten in de prijzen tot uitdrukking komen zoals vervuiling en andere overlast. De twee variabelen die het niveau van de productie bepalen zijn arbeidsproductiviteit en arbeidsparticipatie. Ik zal beginnen met de arbeidsparticipatie. Arbeidsparticipatie en arbeidsproductiviteit De arbeidsparticipatie in Nederland loopt nog steeds achter op de rest van Europa en op de VS. Een jaar kent hier gemiddeld 1325 arbeidsuren, dat is het laagste aantal gewerkte uren van het eurogebied. Elders in Europa ligt dit aantal ten minste 100 uren hoger. In de VS werkt een persoon gemiddeld 1900 uur, dus een kleine 600 uur meer. Deze achterstand heeft een duidelijke verklaring: Er is een grote, voor een deel afgedwongen, preferentie voor vrije tijd in Nederland. Hierdoor wordt niet alleen ruim 40 % van de banen in deeltijd vervuld, vooral die van vrouwen, maar kent ook een voltijdbaan relatief minder uren dan in het buitenland door vakantie en arbeidsduurverkorting. Een volgend typisch verschijnsel in Nederland is dat er grote groepen definitief nooit meer werken. Nederland kent nog steeds een heel grote groep arbeidsongeschikten, bijna n miljoen mensen. Naast deze typisch Nederlandse verschijnselen is ook hier onder ouderen boven de 55 jaar de inactiviteit groot. Nog maar 40% van deze groep werkt. Andere Europese landen kennen dit laatste probleem ook, maar dat maakt het probleem niet minder urgent. Arbeidsproductiviteit is een lastiger begrip. Niet de definitie, dat is de totale productie gedeeld door de totale arbeidsinzet, oftewel de toegevoegde waarde per eenheid arbeid. Maar er is op verschillende niveaus een meetprobleem. Allereerst is er het probleem wat je meet en hoe je de uitkomst vergelijkt. De meeste landen meten het arbeidsproductiviteitniveau per werkende. Nederland komt dan uit in de Europese middenmoot. Deze manier van meten geeft een indicatie van de bijdrage aan de productie per werkend persoon. Per uur gemeten loopt Nederland daarentegen voorop. Dit verschil komt natuurlijk door het hoge aantal deeltijdbanen. Deze cijfers zeggen dus iets over de Nederlander: hij werkt graag kort, maar wel efficint. Omdat hij zo weinig werkt is de welvaart per hoofd van de bevolking zeer gemiddeld, plaats 8 in de EU ranglijst. De VS zijn per capita vele duizenden euros rijker, hoewel we hen door de appreciatie van de euro nu ongemerkt hard inlopen. Waar de VS ook beter in zijn is de arbeidsproductiviteitsgroei. Sinds de tweede helft van de jaren negentig overtreffen de VS de productiviteitsgroeicijfers van Europa. Hoe komt dat? Het is moeilijk een precies antwoord te geven op die vraag. Uit cijfers blijkt wel welke sectoren het beter doen in de VS. Dat is de ICT producerende industrie en de ICT gebruikende dienstensector. Gezien de omvang en de enorme groei in omvang van de ICT producerende industrie in de VS is een sterk positief effect op de productiviteitscijfers van de totale economie niet verwonderlijk. Hier is wel een kanttekening bij te plaatsen. In de VS wordt de productiviteit van de ICT productie anders gemeten dan hier. Daar betekent de productie van een snellere computer dan vorig jaar een navenant hogere productie en dus een hogere productiviteit. In Europa worden bij wijze van spreken alleen de dozen geteld als productie, ongeacht de kwaliteitsverbetering van de inhoud. Er zit dus een vertekening in de cijfers. In de ICT gebruikende dienstensector is vooral de retail trade belangrijk. ICT toepassingen in bijvoorbeeld voorraadbeheer en logistiek zijn daar ver doorgevoerd. Een volgend meetprobleem is het meten van veranderingen in de arbeidsproductiviteit. In een wereld die u bekend zou moeten voorkomen vanuit uw eerste studiejaren, namelijk die met een Cobb-Douglas productiefunctie met de productiefactoren arbeid en kapitaal, is een stijging van de arbeidsproductiviteit een reflectie van een hogere kapitaalinzet, ceteris paribus. Maar natuurlijk is de werkelijkheid niet zo statisch en rechtlijnig. De productiviteit kan stijgen door relatief meer kapitaal in te zetten, maar ook door een betere benutting van het bestaande kapitaal en van de bestaande arbeid. Voorbeelden zijn respectievelijk het beter benutten van al langer bestaande ICT-oplossingen en het anders organiseren van het werk waardoor werknemers hun taken efficinter kunnen uitvoeren. Ook door een verbetering van de kwaliteit van kapitaal en arbeid, door innovatie en scholing, stijgt de arbeidsproductiviteit. Het toewijzen van een gesignaleerde productiviteitsstijging aan n van deze factoren geeft echter enorme schattingsproblemen. Wat is het effect van n procent meer R&D uitgaven? Dit meetprobleem heeft ook consequenties voor het beleid: er bestaat geen panacee voor de achterblijvende productiviteitsgroei in Nederland door te mikken op slechts n van deze determinanten voor productiviteitsgroei. De markt zal zelf de juiste mix van meer inzet van de productiefactoren arbeid en kapitaal, een betere benutting van productiefactoren en van kwaliteitsverbetering moeten vinden, waarbij de overheid een ondersteunende rol heeft. Over deze rol kom ik in het vervolg nog uitvoeriger te spreken. Maar eerst moet de markt wel een aanleiding hebben om te gaan investeren in productiviteitsverbetering. Hier ligt een relatie met de marktwerking. Concurrentie dwingt bedrijven constant tot efficintieverbetering en productvernieuwing. Daarom kan in principe de productiviteit van een land zich het beste ontwikkelen in een zo open mogelijke economie met flexibele markten en voldoende mededinging. De meest productieve en innovatieve bedrijven zullen dan de minder goed functionerende bedrijven verdringen omdat zij nu eenmaal goedkoper kunnen produceren. Dit geeft bedrijven voldoende prikkel om constant te blijven investeren in hun productiefactoren arbeid en kapitaal en stimuleert startende ondernemers om een niche in de markt te vinden voor hun product. De u welbekende econoom Schumpeter noemde dit proces creative destruction. Dit proces van survival of the fittest wordt in een minder efficinte economie zoals de onze ruw verstoord door de aanwezigheid van marktimperfecties als kartels en overheidsingrijpen. Zulk ingrijpen is meestal ingegeven door niet-economische overwegingen als een rechtvaardige inkomensverdeling. Hoe valide deze overwegingen ook zijn, een consequentie is ook dat minder productieve bedrijven kunnen blijven bestaan, intussen productiefactoren verspillend die beter ergens anders hadden kunnen worden aangewend. Een veel geciteerde, maar weinig gesteunde oplossing om de creative destruction toch te forceren is een loongolf. Een loongolf houdt in dat de loonkosten veel sneller stijgen dan de arbeidsproductiviteit rechtvaardigt, waardoor minder innovatieve bedrijven het loodje leggen. In principe klopt dit. Nadeel van zon medicijn is dat een dergelijke afwijking van het evenwicht tegenkrachten oproept die erger zijn dan de kwaal. Zo zal de kapitaalintensiteit sterk toenemen. Wanneer door de uiteindelijk ontstane werkloosheid de lonen weer dalen, is in het nieuwe evenwicht een lager werkgelegenheidspeil bereikt dan mogelijk was geweest zonder loonschok. Dit komt doordat in eerste instantie onderzoek nadrukkelijk zal worden verlegd naar arbeidsbesparende technologie. In het nieuwe evenwicht, met weer lagere lonen, zullen de relatief hoge kapitaalkosten het onderzoek weer een beweging naar de andere kant doen maken. Dit is inefficint waardoor naast het niveau van de werkgelegenheid ook het technologisch peil uiteindelijk lager zal liggen dan zonder een kunstmatige loonsverhoging. Naast deze tegenkrachten zal een loongolf de positie ten opzichte van het buitenland verslechteren, omdat bedrijven daar niet te maken hebben met dezelfde kostenstijging. Het is de vraag of binnenlandse bedrijven op tijd kunnen innoveren om hun positie te handhaven en niet meteen van de markt worden gedrukt door buitenlandse concurrentie. Een derde punt is dat een loongolf een verstoring van de arbeidsrelatie met zich meebrengt. Deze kan lang doorwerken, ook na het bereiken van een nieuw evenwicht na de schok. Bedrijven zullen huiverig zijn om nieuwe investeringen te doen, uit angst gegijzeld te worden door hoge looneisen van hun werknemers vlak na die investeringen. Een andere manier waarop bedrijven tot meer innovatie worden aangezet is als de valuta apprecieert. De concurrentie met landen buiten het eurogebied verhevigt, maar in tegenstelling tot een loonschok zitten hier ook enkele voordelen aan die het proces verzachten. Zo worden allereerst de grondstoffen en kapitaalgoederen goedkoper, inclusief buitenlandse R&D zoals software. Ook importgoederen voor de consument worden goedkoper. Deels werkt dit negatief voor de binnenlandse producenten wegens verschuiving in het consumptiepakket. Aan de andere kant verhogen deze lagere prijzen het besteedbaar inkomen van de consument, wat de vraag naar non-tradables kan verhogen. Een laatste voordeel van een appreciatie is meer psychologisch. Een externe schok kan politici een goed argument geven om electoraal gevoelige hervormingen toch door te voeren. Uit Europa komende regels werken zo, bijvoorbeeld op het begrotingsbeleid, en een appreciatie ook. Interne schokken als een loongolf zijn minder duidelijk aanwijsbaar en ook van eigen makelij, dus moeilijker op te voeren als reden voor onaangename beslissingen. Wat kan de overheid doen? Zoals eerder gezegd wordt toekomstige welvaart gegenereerd door een gelijktijdige stijging van het arbeidsaanbod en de arbeidsproductiviteit. Kijkend naar de omstandigheden waarin arbeidsproductiviteit groeit, ligt daar een duidelijke taak voor de overheid: het wegnemen van barrires, ook internationaal, die mededinging kunnen verstoren en het weghalen van rigiditeiten op de arbeidsmarkt die een snelle aanpassing aan technologische vernieuwing hinderen. Dergelijke structurele hervormingen, het kan niet vaak genoeg herhaald worden, zijn broodnodig om onze levensstandaard te kunnen handhaven dan wel verhogen. Deze liggen deels op het gebied van de productmarkten, denk aan verscherping van het mededingingstoezicht en terugdringing van de administratieve lastendruk. Voor een ander deel moet de arbeidsmarkt worden verlost van knellende regelgeving op het gebied van ontslagrecht en arbeidstijden. Naast structurele hervormingen is een goed opgeleide beroepsbevolking essentieel. Ook daar ligt een duidelijke publieke taak waar het gaat om de initile scholing van jongeren, van basisschool tot universiteit. Hierbij wordt vaak als eerste gedacht aan het opleiden van veel onderzoekers, maar tenminste even belangrijk is het opleiden van mensen die met nieuwe technieken kunnen omgaan, techniek beter kunnen benutten en in staat zijn R&D toe te passen. Verder hebben bedrijven in een concurrerende omgeving ook behoefte aan goede managers en ondernemers en ook zij beginnen hun carrire op de basisschool. Bij bedrijven ligt vervolgens de taak voort te bouwen op de kennis van hun werknemers met trainingen en cursussen. In de eerder genoemde moeilijkheden bij het toewijzen van productiviteitsgroei aan specifieke deelfactoren schuilt een gevaar. Waar structurele hervormingen vaak pijnlijk zijn en op verzet kunnen rekenen, lijken andere maatregelen hetzelfde effect te sorteren zonder die pijn. Al snel komt er dan beleid als verhoging van de publieke R&D of stimuleringsprogrammas voor bedrijven. Publieke R&D is niet het enige instrument tot verhoging van de arbeidsproductiviteitsgroei. Stimulering door de overheid van private R&D is ook lastig. Wordt dergelijk publiek geld wel op de meest effectieve manier aangewend? Duidelijk renderende investeringen in onderzoek doen de bedrijven tenslotte zelf ook, waardoor de overheid f ten onrechte bepaald onderzoek financiert f alleen 2nd best projecten helpt op te zetten. De bedrijven moeten zlf aangezet worden tot een betere benutting van hun productiefactoren en meer innovatie. Dit kan alleen als zij niet langer worden afgeschermd van marktwerking door te weinig binnen- en buitenlandse concurrentie of als de besparingen van verandering in het niet vallen omdat het onmogelijk blijkt om mensen te ontslaan. Beleid gericht op de andere determinant van welvaart, participatie, is ook geen gemakkelijk onderwerp. Hervorming van de WAO en bijstand en het verhogen van de effectieve pensioenleeftijd is nodig voor een hogere participatie, maar geeft een verhoogde kans op politieke en maatschappelijke spanningen. Niettemin ligt daar ook een belangrijke beleidsuitdaging. Zo zou met het verhogen van de pensioenleeftijd met drie jaar voldoende financile ruimte beschikbaar kunnen komen om indexatie van pensioenaanspraken te financieren. Hiernaast is het benutten van de individuele productiviteit van mensen, ook als die niet hoog is, altjd winst. Het is bovendien een heel cynische manier van omgaan met mensen om grote groepen af te schrijven met de boodschap `nee dank u, aan u hebben we geen behoefte. Iedereen kan iets en heeft iets toe te voegen aan de samenleving, tegen een daarbij aangepast salaris. Daar gebruik van maken is een grote beleidsuitdaging voor de komende jaren. Het is duidelijk dat de sociale zekerheid alleen plaats moet bieden aan mensen die niet anders kunnen door ziekte of ander ongeluk. De overheid zal zich door de vergrijzing geconfronteerd zien met lagere inkomsten en hogere kosten. Deze realiteit rijmt niet met een deactiverend sociale zekerheidsstelsel. Buiten de sociale zekerheid wordt de rol van de overheid in het stimuleren van participatie al snel kleiner. De participatie van vrouwen met een gezin loopt nog steeds achter, zeker in uren gemeten. Waar dit een bewuste keuze is van deze vrouwen kan de overheid weinig doen. Als de keuze om niet of weinig te gaan werken is ingegeven door bijvoorbeeld een tekort aan kinderopvang of te hoge kosten is dat zonde en heeft de overheid zeker een grote rol om de juiste voorwaarden te scheppen voor deze groep. Zo ook in het aantal gewerkte uren. Als werkende Nederlanders en masse kiezen voor een lagere welvaart in ruil voor meer vrije tijd is dat prima. Als echter blijkt dat mensen meer zouden willen werken maar worden tegengehouden door regelgeving moet ook hier de overheid ingrijpen. Mijn boodschap aan u is duidelijk niet gespeend van enig eigenbelang. Over een aantal jaar gaan mijn generatiegenoten en dus ik ook, massaal met pensioen. Terwijl wij genieten van onze welverdiende rust, begint u net aan uw arbeidsleven om daaraan mee te betalen. U moet dus participeren. Maar participatie alleen is niet genoeg. Om ook nog wat vrije tijd over te houden moet u ook beter en slimmer werken, nieuwe ondernemingen starten, als leidinggevende uw mensen goed motiveren en als politicus of beleidsambtenaar de voorwaarden scheppen voor een dergelijk productief klimaat. Ik wens u daarbij veel succes, maar heb ook een rotsvast geloof dat dat u gaat lukken.

Title: Paying costs money: how much actually and can it be cheaper?
Subtitle: Voor iedereen die regelmatig kranten leest, moge het duidelijk zijn wat het afgelopen jaar een van de belangrijkste onderwerpen in het financieel-economische debat is geweest: de pensioen- problematiek. De financile perikelen van pensioenfondsen, noodzakelijke hervormingen van de pensioenregelingen en de op ons afkomende vergrijzingsgolf: de kranten stonden er bol van. Voor velen kwam al dit onheil als een donderslag bij heldere hemel. Echter niet voor degenen die voormalig DNB- en ECB-president Duisenberg een beetje hebben gevolgd. Reeds in de jaren tachtig van de vorige eeuw waarschuwde hij keer op keer voor de financile gevolgen van de vergrijzing en maande hij overheid en sociale partners om tijdig adequate maatregelen te nemen.
text: Paying costs money: how much actually and can it be cheaper? Speech Date: March 10, 2004 Time: 3:45 p.m. Location Congress Payments: the balance Speaker Drs J. Koning, Director of Payments at the Dutch Central Bank For anyone who regularly reads newspapers, it should be clear what one of the most important topics in the financial and economic debate has been in the past year: the pension issue. The financial vicissitudes of pension funds, necessary reforms of pension schemes and the ageing wave that is coming our way: the newspapers were full of them. For many, all this calamity came as a bolt from the blue. However, not for those who have followed former DNB and ECB President Duisenberg a bit. As early as the 1980s, he repeatedly warned of the financial consequences of the ageing population and urged the government and social partners to take adequate measures in good time. It is not for nothing that I am bringing Mr Duisenberg to the stage. In his long career, he has given many messages worth giving. One of them is close to my heart and often succinctly expressed by him with the slogan: 'Paying costs money'. I would like to thank the organisers of this day for inviting me to speak to you about the efficiency of the payment system. 'Payment costs money'. Many outside this Chamber are unaware of this, particularly those who are not faced with the cost of paying. An important question is, of course, how much that payment actually costs and which means of payment are cheaper or more expensive. I will tell you this afternoon. This is the first theme of my story. If we know which payment products are more expensive than others, the logical question arises as to how we can ensure that the more efficient payment products will be used more. This is the second theme I will deal with. The question of how to steer brings me more or less automatically to the discussion on the organisation of the market. More focused on the subject of payments: the well-known discussion of market forces versus cooperation. I will deal with this as my final theme. Paying costs a lot of money Unfortunately, I cannot tell you how much we all spend for all the payments we make. I do not know the costs for cashless payments by bank transfers, direct debits, authorizations and the like. What I do know is the amount involved in paying for all point-of-sale payments, i.e. paying in shops, restaurants, etc. In 2002, we spent just under 3 billion euros on this in our country, 2.9 billion euros to be precise. A considerable amount: it amounts to more than half a percent of our GDP or more appealing 400 euros per household. This amount has been calculated in a joint project carried out within the framework of the Social Consultation on the Payment System by representatives of the banks and Interpay, point-of-sale institutions, the Consumers' Association and DNB. Central bankers, as is well known, are somewhat subdued by nature, and that is how it should be. However, I would like to say that this is a unique project. I know of no precedent in our country and I am not aware of any examples abroad. The uniqueness of the study is that the costs for the entire payment system are considered: the costs of DNB, the banks, Interpay and the point-of-sale institutions. In the study, the so-called social costs were calculated for the most common means of payment: cash, debit card, chipknip and credit card. A special aspect of this cost project is that the parties involved themselves have inventoried and supplied the costs for their sector, and have also jointly discussed the progress of the project and the outcomes. Some means of payment are more expensive than others It is interesting to know what all those payments in stores cost us. What I find more interesting, however, is how the means of payment differ in terms of their costs. This question is particularly relevant to discussions about how we can all improve the efficiency of the payment system. In the past, this question has often been the subject of a Babylonian confusion of tongues, because everyone has their own ideas about the content of the concepts to be used. Even among people of good will, this can quickly lead to a conversation between deaf people. As you know, the strength of the arguments is not directly proportional to the volume with which they are put forward. Rather inversely proportional, I would say. Discussions often benefit from better listening. A point-of-sale transaction costs an average of 35 cents. The cost of a chipknip payment is more than 90 cents and is therefore significantly higher. This is because the number of chipknip transactions is still low, despite the fact that there has been a sharp increase in recent years. The infrastructure is therefore still severely underutilised. For the question of how we can best promote efficiency, it is therefore better to look at the costs involved in carrying out one extra transaction. After all, the costs for the payment infrastructure have already been incurred and if one means of payment is replaced by another, these are the variable costs. An additional chipknip payment costs only 3 cents, which is considerably less than with the other payment methods. The study shows that the chipknip scores best from a cost point of view (see table). When choosing between debit card and cash, transaction amounts below 12 euros are best paid with currency and amounts above 12 euros with debit card. The credit card, regardless of the transaction amount, turns out to be the most expensive. So the message is clear: more must be paid with the chipknip. If people don't want to do that or if the choice between currency and debit card is limited in the store, we have to use debit card for amounts larger than 12 euros and for amounts smaller than 12 euros we have to use currency. The credit card is not a suitable means of payment for our home, garden and kitchen payments (see figure). Significant savings possible How much could we save if we were to pay more efficiently? We assume a scenario in which 1.5 billion cash payments are replaced by electronic payments. In this scenario, the number of debit card payments doubles and the number of chipknip payments increases fivefold. All in all, this yields more than 100 million euros. It should be noted that only the effects on the variable costs of the payment products have been taken into account. Cost savings will be higher if even more drastic changes in payment behaviour occur, because then the fixed costs will also have to be included in the calculations. The scenario mentioned here is therefore one of the possible variants and others should also be considered. In my opinion, the cost report is a fruitful starting point for the discussions to be held about possible ways of making payments more efficient. I think it would be a good thing if research such as the one that has just been completed should be carried out on a regular basis. I can imagine that this cost study will be repeated every two or three years. This gives us insight into the developments over time and we can also measure the extent to which the follow-up actions to be taken yield the desired results, not only in terms of the number of transactions paid for with chipknip and debit cards, but also in terms of the cost savings achieved. Ease of use and security are also important Within the framework of the Social Consultation on the Payment System, discussions will take place with the parties involved about the desired follow-up actions to stimulate more efficient payment products. In addition to the costs that have now been identified, aspects such as ease of use and safety will also play an important role. Of course, I do not want to and cannot anticipate the results of these consultations. In the light of the heated discussions about the euro falsifications and all the grumbling about the 1 and 2 euro cents, I do have the impression that the electronic payment products do not score badly in terms of security and ease of use. At this stage of the discussions, I will confine myself to a few more general qualifications and observations. First of all, a note about ease of use and security. It is clear that these are important aspects, especially for the consumer because he has not yet been directly confronted with the costs of using the payment products, or only to a limited extent. At the end of the day, of course, it is the consumers who pay the bill. Costs of payment products must be factored into the selling prices by banks, retailers, etc. Where this is not possible, efforts will be made to recoup the costs through cross-subsidisation. This, in turn, has distortive effects in the subsidizing markets. In the end, consumers pay the bill together and they have little or no incentive to pay consciously through tariffs. This, in my opinion, leads to the fact that the overall cost can be lower and every consumer could benefit from that. This brings me to the second topic I would like to address here: the management of payment behaviour. In any case, it is necessary for the public to be aware of the costs associated with his behaviour so that he has a fair chance to make a conscious choice. Good information is therefore in order. This is where all parties active in the payment chain come into play. In the past, joint campaigns such as Pay on Demand have proven their worth. Once again, a joint campaign is a serious option. Incentives for efficient payment The question of how best to reward desirable behaviour is essentially about how best to shape the incentives for efficient payment behaviour. These incentives have not been the subject of a study, also because the social costs of the payment products have been examined. From an economic perspective, however, the application of pricing is a logical steering mechanism. I believe that market forces could also do a good job here. The problem, of course, is that consumers are not used to pricing for their payment services. Of course, as I said, they will pay the bill together. For merchants or more generally for business users, transaction-related pricing is common. In our country, consumers are, as it were, steered through the retailer. After all, it is in the interest of his customers to pay efficiently, and he will do his best to persuade them to choose the cheap payment products. In doing so, he will steer in the direction of payment products that are cheap for him. However, the cheapest payment products for the retailer do not necessarily have to be the cheapest for society as a whole. Indirect control by the retailer does not necessarily have to lead to a socially optimal result. It seems to me that the chances of disruptive processes occurring are the smallest if all parties pass on their costs to their customers. In any case, this should be the starting point for the policy. The chances that the overall costs will be reduced and that the good payers will not suffer from the losses seem to me to be the greatest with this strategy. This would be a major change for consumers. Judging by the large scale with which retailers charge a fee for debit cards for small transaction amounts, at least some consumers will be accustomed to pricing. The shopkeeper incurs costs and it seems logical to me that he passes them on to the customer. It is better to do this through a tariff than through the selling prices. Another example of consumer pricing by the retailer is the so-called cash-back, i.e. the use of a larger amount than that of groceries, so that the customer has access to cash. Cash-back saves the consumer a visit to the ATM and thus offers him ease of use. In the eyes of many, this convenience may well come at a price in the form of a tariff. For the shopkeeper, it is a double-edged sword, which shows a clever merchant's mind. After all, in addition to the income from cash-back pricing, the costs of depositing excess cash can be reduced. It should be avoided that retailers have to keep extra cash in-house to meet the demand for cash-back. This would not be in the interests of safety. However, discussions held by DNB with market parties suggest that things will not go that fast. A director of a large retail chain indicated that only if the percentage of debit card payments were to rise to 80% of the total number of payments, the available cash could be too limited to meet the demand for cash-back. By the way, it would be best if everyone would pay with the chipknip. Retailers could encourage the use of the chipknip and perhaps the banks could come up with something nice to further increase the ease of use of the chipknip. I often hear the complaint that people don't know what balance is on their chipknip. In the case of cash, a quick glance in the wallet is sufficient, and it would perhaps be useful if the possibilities for reading the balance could be extended for the chipknip. This would also be an incentive to stimulate more efficient payment behaviour. Market forces are the starting point The payments market needs effective market forces. However, market forces are not an end in themselves. For DNB, it is ultimately about the security and efficiency of the payment system. We do, however, take the view that market forces are the primary vehicle for achieving these objectives. After all, market parties themselves are best placed to respond to new technologies and social developments. This is the best way to serve, certainly in the longer term, the smooth functioning of the payment system. A safe and efficient payment system therefore requires effective market forces, in which supervisory authorities have an important role to play. In this context, DNB therefore supervises payment systems, in which matters such as security, operational reliability and efficiency are assessed. It is necessary to take account of a number of specific characteristics of this market in the conduct of policy. For example, many parties are usually involved in a payment: the payer and recipient of the money, the banks of both parties, Interpay which processes the interbank information and DNB which finalises the interbank settlements in its books. A cheap and fast settlement of transactions therefore requires that those involved make specific agreements with each other, including with regard to the necessary standards and coordination of the mutual systems. This cooperation is also necessary because network and scale effects are important. Network effects occur, for example, if a consumer can pay with their debit card in many places. The usefulness he derives from his debit card increases when many retailers facilitate this payment product. In addition, investments in the payment infrastructure are often only profitable if the payment services are used on a large scale. In order to be able to take full advantage of the resulting economies of scale, it is important to ask how a sufficiently large critical mass of transactions to be processed can be achieved. Standardization is also one of the key words here. In all sectors where network effects play an important role, agreements between providers are needed on standards and the like. Otherwise, products may not be able to get off the ground. Of course, care must be taken to ensure that this does not curtail market dynamics and make prices artificially high. A secure and efficient payment system requires a good infrastructure. The roles and responsibilities of the various parties must therefore be clearly defined. In this context, for example, the transfer of debit card contracts from Interpay to the banks will improve market transparency. It is also clear that the aforementioned scale and network effects require close cooperation between banking parties in order to make optimal use of the common payment infrastructure. At the same time, the banks are each other's competitors in offering financial services. This is necessary to keep the service provision and the organisation of internal processes optimal. Competition must also be such that the profits realised by banks through more efficient organisation of their processing processes also accrue to consumers and business end-users. In addition, there must be sufficient incentives to develop and implement technological innovations. A particular point of attention is that new financial service providers should be able to enter the market without creating unacceptable risks for payment systems and participants. Interpay's new organisational structure for debit cards and chipknips can be useful here. By clearly describing the product characteristics, requirements for participating parties, etc., in the Brands and Licences, clarity is provided to potential new entrants. Effective market forces also place demands on the tariff structure. I have already raised this issue this afternoon. In general terms, I would also like to say that, in my opinion, there must be sufficient incentives to encourage the efficient use of payment products. In any case, this must also apply to the quality and price of the payment products. This transparency is a necessary ingredient for effective market functioning. Balance between competition and cooperation The foregoing discussion indicates that there is no unambiguous answer to the question of what the right balance between competition and cooperation in the payment market is. Of course, it will be interesting to see how the Dutch payment market is performing. In its report, the Wellink Working Group has concluded that this market has shown great dynamism and that our country can be placed in an efficient quadrant due to the implemented process and product innovations. We have a relatively efficient use of products and efficient processing processes. This image is in line with my experience that at international meetings other countries often appear to judge the Dutch market with a certain jealousy. All this has led to Dutch users being offered a secure payment system at a, in my opinion, modest price. I would also like to mention Interpay's contribution. It has not escaped my notice that it is subject to criticism, but I would also like to take this opportunity to remind you that Interpay has played  and continues to play  an indispensable role in the development of the common payment infrastructure in our country. And I don't say this because Interpay is one of the organizers of this day and has been kind enough to invite me. Today's theme is balance. I think this theme also applies to the discussion about competition versus cooperation. I am convinced that a balanced assessment is necessary because both aspects are important. Because social and technological developments exert an important influence, it is not possible to determine unambiguously where the balance between competition and cooperation lies. In general terms, I would like to say that competition must be the starting point and that cooperation should only take place if it is beneficial to efficiency and safety. Collaboration will be needed in the processing of payment transactions rather than in the front-office activities. It is important to be able to respond quickly and adequately to changing circumstances. The developments of the past decade have been very turbulent and I expect that major changes will also occur in the coming years. For example, through the design of the uniform, common European payment area. It is a major challenge for all parties involved to manage these changes. The Wellink Working Group concluded that we are in a favourable starting position, which offers good prospects for responding to the future challenges in the field of technological innovation, the development of payment infrastructures, also in international terms, and the implementation of product innovations. I agree with this and wish all parties great wisdom in making the right decisions. Thank you for your attention.
