text: Globalization and international migration Speech Datum 12 maart 2004 Tijd 00:00 uur Lokatie Lunch meeting of the Rotterdam Japan club. Spreker Dr. A.H.E.M. Wellink, President, De Nederlandsche Bank Introduction Good afternoon ladies and gentlemen. Let me begin by saying that it is a great pleasure to be here. Speaking before such a reputable international audience, in a city that boasts having the worlds largest harbor, the subject of my talk today  globalization  may be considered highly appropriate. Indeed, you are all active witnesses and participants in the process of international economic integration. Half of the members of the  Japan club are from a country on the other side of the world. They have come here to profit from the advantages of international economic specialization. Japanese companies have seen opportunities to do business in this faraway country. In doing so, they have also sent employees here to capture a very specialist niche in the Dutch labor market: that of Japanese speaking managers that can bridge the gap between cutting-edge companies in Japan and their Dutch subsidiaries. Today I would like to talk about three flows that are important for economic integration. These are: international flows of capital, international flows of goods and services; and international flows of labor. Whereas the first two flows are relatively free, the latter is still subject to many restrictions. On the latter front, I will present some considerations. Global trade and capital flows are beneficial But first, let me say something about global trade and capital flows. Economic theory tells us that the exchange of capital and goods is beneficial. You may recall the line of reasoning from your study books. For trade of goods and services, this rests on the theory of comparative advantage. The theory goes back to the famous early nineteenth century economist David Ricardo. Basically it boils down to international specialization. If every country produces what it does best and trades what it produces, we are all better off. For example, neither Japan nor the Netherlands would probably benefit from producing labor-intensive products such as textiles and shoes. This is because companies in China or India can do such things relatively better. It is in our interest to focus on more high-tech products such as developing new medicines or the next generation of DVD-players. And we can trade the proceeds of our specialization to our mutual benefit. Of course, we should also always stick to producing cheese and flowers and Japan should never give up making sushi. Turning to capital, the liberalization of flows increases the opportunities for intertemporal savings and investment decisions. Surplus aggregate savings can be directed towards the internationally most profitable investment opportunities. This allows some countries to accumulate assets for later consumption, while others with large investment needs can import capital. For example, spendthrift Americans are able to sustain their consumption and investment by borrowing from foreigners, while Japan can accumulate savings to take care of its rapidly ageing population. As a result, the Japanese economy as a whole is accumulating substantial claims on future US production. Foreign capital can also foster technological spillovers. Many developing nations profit from foreign direct investment as they learn international best practices. For example, China s rapidly expanding economy has benefited enormously from international expertise by opening the country up to foreign investment. For developed nations, the efficiency enhancing effect of foreign competition is also important. An example is the car market, where Japanese companies have boosted production efficiency in both Europe and the US when they entered these markets. Over the past decades the world has reaped the benefits I have just mentioned. We have seen a tremendous increase in global trade flows, at about twice the rate of global production. Furthermore, in the past decade we have seen an explosion in global FDI and portfolio flows. Strikingly, these have risen even faster than trade flows. Governments around the world have recognized the potential for greater welfare and have launched various liberalization initiatives to reap the rewards. Particularly in the last decade, many of these initiatives have taken form at the regional level. Allow me to highlight the developments in the three major trading blocs. Regional examples of increased integration A good starting point is the enactment of NAFTA in 1994, which removed many restrictions on trade and capital flows between the economies of the United States , Canada and Mexico . This agreement was highly controversial in all three countries. Many feared stiffer competition, increased unemployment and downward pressure on wages. Agricultural interest groups secured various exemptions and lengthy tariff phase-out periods. Despite the remaining agricultural restrictions, trade flows between the three countries almost tripled once NAFTA was signed. Capital flows have also surged. American companies have invested nearly 250 billion to profit from lower labor costs in Mexico . This increased integration has generated substantial benefits. This can be illustrated by pointing to the fact that in Mexico , those regions with the greatest exposure to globalization registered a higher increase in wages. Moreover, the shift of manufacturing jobs to Mexico did not lead to overall job losses in the US . In fact, the US unemployment rate dropped substantially in the 1990s. Indeed, between 1994 and 2000 the US economy created more than 2 million new jobs a year even as productivity accelerated. Virtually all economists and businessmen now consider NAFTA to be a success. Turning to Europe , we have also seen an intense drive towards economic integration both within the EU and with countries that will be joining the union in the near future. Since 1993, the annual export growth of the accession countries towards the EU has averaged close to 15%. In addition, since 1990 more than 100 billion in FDI flowed eastwards to benefit from cheaper labor and specialization. These flows have triggered drastic changes in export and import structures. For the current EU-members, the accession countries have now developed into the largest export market after the United States . In May, this economic integration process will culminate in EU-entry for ten accession countries. I do not doubt that most of you have been taken a close look at these developments, have felt their economic impact, and are considering the economic opportunities. Indeed, this may have been the very reason for companies to operate from the Netherlands . Our economy has traditionally been very open, in contrast to some other European countries, which allows companies to profit from these developments. Moreover, in the past years we have been one of the most dynamic economies in Europe . And while we are currently experiencing some economic difficulties, I do not doubt that our economic future is bright. I now turn to the region where perhaps the greatest strides towards economic integration have been made: in Asia . Japan is lucky to be situated in the most dynamic economic area of the world, which will turn into a center of global economic activity in the coming decades. Large capital and trade flows have facilitated this development and will continue to do so in the future. This is triggered for a large part by the booming Chinese economy. Last year alone, China attracted more than 50 billion in foreign direct investment. Moreover, its blistering pace of growth has been accompanied by an ongoing integration into the world economy. China is rapidly developing into the hub for intra-Asian trade through vertical specialization. Regional semi-products are exported to China , processed, and re-exported to developed markets. Japan has benefited tremendously from this development. The improved profitability of its manufacturing companies and its latest economic upturn are firmly supported by robust exports to China , which increased by almost 40% in 2003. I do not know if there already exists a Shanghai-Japan club, but I do not doubt there will be one in the future. International labor migration remains restricted despite benefits So far, I have talked about the great progress that has been made in important parts of the world in liberalizing capital and trade flows. While the policy dynamics driving liberalization have often been regionally oriented, they have been underpinned by global trade and capital liberalization efforts through organizations as the WTO and OECD. In contrast, the international flow of labor remains fairly restricted. This is regretful because international labor migration has substantial benefits too. According to the economist Dani Rodrik, global welfare can be greatly improved by lifting immigration restrictions. He argues that this will bring more benefits than further trade or capital market integration. Greater international labor mobility would allow economies to balance shortages and surpluses of labor at the aggregate level, and to solve labor mismatches at the micro level. The economic consequences of global ageing spring to mind as an important example. On a somewhat smaller scale, the shortage of Japanese speaking managers in the Netherlands I referred to earlier is another example. Despite the obvious benefits, international labor mobility remains restricted. Arguably, labor is also considerably less mobile than it used to be in the past. This is especially true, if we compare today with the end of the nineteenth century. At that time, large numbers of Europeans and Asians headed towards the United States in search of a better future. The world has been witness to the results. Today, the pressures for international labor migration have risen in line with the greater mobility of goods, capital and information. They are also spurred on by sustained disparities in the global income distribution. Nevertheless, in this day and age, countries are reluctant to liberalize migration flows. This generally stems from concerns related to a countrys social cohesion and, in a more economic sense, the sustainability of social security systems. This is especially true if immigrants skills do not meet the demands of the labor market, creating the risk of a heavy burden on state benefit schemes. A flexible economy and labor market can serve to limit these risks. The argument can then be turned on its head: if integration is successful, immigrants add to the tax base and help sustain social security systems. Beside the common concerns about welfare programs, another worry among many is that immigrants cause downward pressure on domestic wages. However, economic studies suggest that this effect is small at best. Some studies even find positive wage effects. A drawback is that these benefits were realized mainly by highly-educated workers, which could lead to greater income inequality. International migration policy I now turn to reflect on those labor policy initiatives and migration challenges that are particularly relevant for Europe , Japan and the United States . A good starting point is the reluctance to open the EU labor market for accession countries. Already some 400 thousand workers from central Europe work legally within the EU. Estimates from the CPB Netherlands Bureau suggest that over the longer term almost 2 million immigrants from the accession countries could head to join the nearly 380 million people that currently reside in the EU. This potential migration of a host of Eastern European workers is seen as a threat, rather than as an opportunity. Many current member states, including the Netherlands , have therefore decided to maintain restrictions on laborers from accession countries, even after the formal EU-entry. In Japan , the story is much the same. Historically, it has always been relatively closed to foreigners. Although it now has one of the fastest ageing populations, and immigrants could add to the local economic dynamics, Japan continues to restrict its labor market for foreign workers. For a different approach to immigration we can turn to the United States , which has a long tradition of using permissive immigration policies to stimulate economic growth. But also there, fears of labor migration are prevalent. Especially when NAFTA was enacted, Mexican immigration was seen as a direct threat for US jobs. In practice, an estimated 1.3 million Mexicans have actually migrated to the US since 1994 in search of a better future. And the flexible US labor market has managed to absorb these newcomers. They are contributing substantively to American production. Moreover, the influx of foreign labor has lessened the burden of ageing in the US , which may provide an important example for Europe and Japan . Conclusion Ladies and gentlemen, let me conclude. International integration through increased trade and capital flows has progressed rapidly in the last decades. The global economy has profited from this development. However, policy makers have shied away from liberalizing the international labor market, especially in Europe and Japan . In the United States , we can see that a sufficiently flexible economy can profit handsomely from immigration. In Europe , the fear of foreign labor has led to restrictions on workers from the accession countries, even though this old continents population will age faster in the coming years, causing labor shortages. In Japan , we can already see that there is a continuing debate on possible innovative migration policies to limit the economic burden of an ageing population. In Europe , this debate will continue to surface as well. I thank you for your attention.

Title: Speech by President Wellink on 'Vision on economic developments in the Netherlands and Europe'
Subtitle: Ik wil met u van gedachten wisselen over de internationale economische ontwikkelingen en in het bijzonder in Nederland. Ik wil beginnen met een blik op de wereld en daarna de focus verleggen naar Europa. Vervolgens ga ik in op Nederland en tenslotte op de ontwikkeling in het noorden van ons land. Daarbij zal ik ook de rol van banken in de regionale ontwikkeling aan de orde stellen. Dat geldt in het bijzonder voor de Rabobank Sneek-Zuidwest Friesland, die ik erkentelijk ben voor deze uitnodiging. Dat ik pas aan het einde van mijn betoog in het Noorden aankom betekent niet dat ik dit minder belangrijk vind. Dat hoop ik u in het vervolg duidelijk te kunnen maken.
text: Speech by President Wellink on 'Vision on economic developments in the Netherlands and Europe' Speech Date: March 22, 2004 Time: 00:00 hrs Location On the occasion of the Spring Meeting of Rabobank Sneek-Zuidwest Friesland in Joure Speaker Dr. A.H.E.M. Wellink, President, De Nederlandsche Bank I would like to exchange views with you on international economic developments and in particular in the Netherlands. I want to start with a look at the world and then shift the focus to Europe. Next, I will discuss the Netherlands and finally the development in the north of our country. In doing so, I will also raise the issue of the role of banks in regional development. This applies in particular to Rabobank Sneek-Zuidwest Friesland, to which I am grateful for this invitation. The fact that I am only arriving in the North at the end of my speech does not mean that I consider this to be any less important. I hope to be able to make that clear to you in the future. I International economic development America, Japan and China The U.S. economy is growing strongly. Last year, gross domestic product (GDP) increased by more than 3%, with growth of 4% in the fourth quarter compared to the previous quarter (year-on-year). Continued high productivity growth, profit recovery and balance sheet restructuring have improved the financial basis of companies. I am therefore optimistic about the US economy and expect GDP growth of 4.5-5% this year. However, the current account deficit of 5% of GDP is a medium-term imbalance that hangs like a shadow over the US economy and is not sustainable in the long term. In Japan, too, the outlook is better. Due to a pick-up in exports and investments, the economy has started up again. Last year, GDP grew by 2.7%. The increasing orientation of the Japanese economy towards the expanding China plays an important role in this. The conditions for a sustainable recovery have improved: the capital position of companies has been strengthened and there has been a lot of restructuring in the banks, although they remain vulnerable. However, the problem that the country has been struggling with for years - deflation - is still there. Last year, the price level of private consumption fell by 0.3% and this continued to the same extent in January this year. China is developing economically at a rapid pace. Since 1994, China's economy has been growing at a rate of about 8% per year, doubling its production volume in nine years. The country is becoming a world-class player. Given the rapid expansion and strong domestic demand, there is a risk of an overheating of the economy, which is reflected in an acceleration of inflation to around 3%. One problem is that China's banks, which are largely state-owned, are not healthy because of the large number of non-performing loans. This poses a risk to financial stability, not only to China but to the whole of South-East Asia. Euro area Next, I would like to turn my attention to Europe. The favourable development of the US economy is a major stimulus for the European economy. Cautiously, it has taken its way up. In the third quarter of last year, the economy grew by 0.4% compared to the previous quarter and in the fourth quarter it grew by 0.3%. A moderate growth rate, but a plus. In Germany, the growth rate was 0.2% in the fourth quarter, in France 0.5% and in Italy 0%. In our eastern neighbours, as in other countries in Europe, it is mainly private consumption that is struggling, which can be attributed to weak consumer confidence. It is essential that consumption gets back on track. Is the economic environment for European consumers worse now than in other periods of economic recovery? I have compared the current economic conditions for the euro area with the previous periods of early economic recovery, namely 1982 and 1993. Although consumer confidence is low now, it is at a somewhat higher level than it was then. Employment has continued to grow in the past two years, in contrast to the previous year, and unemployment is now at the average of the two previous periods. And last but not least, interest rates are lower now than they were then. Important characteristics of the current economic situation are therefore better for consumers than before. On the other hand, there is now more and more uncertainty about pensions in almost all countries. This can be a reason to start saving more for old age, which in itself is a good goal. In addition, the cost of health care is placing an increasing burden on consumers' budgets in many countries. These more structural developments may put consumption on a lower growth path, but in the short term this will not have a strong impact. I therefore expect a further recovery for the European economy, led by exports and supported by consumption. For this year, I estimate GDP growth of around 11/2% is possible for the euro area and next year of around 21/2%. Appreciation of the euro At the moment, the rise in the exchange rate of the euro is receiving a lot of attention. This appreciation of the euro comes at a time when it is exports that are pulling the European economy out of the doldrums. When the euro was introduced in 1999, the rate was set at 1.17, now it hovers around 1.23. Such an appreciation of the euro has some effect on the economic recovery, but it does not reverse this, as euro area exports are benefiting from the international economic recovery, which is stronger than previously anticipated. It would be more worrisome if the euro exchange rate were to fluctuate sharply, because that would create uncertainty among exporters and importers. I have already reminded you that when the euro was introduced in 1999, the exchange rate was set at USD 1.17. It has since fallen to a low of around 0.82 in mid-2001. This was a positive development for euro area firms. But the fact is that they have not benefited sufficiently from this with their exports and have not increased their market share. It's not entirely clear why not. Apparently, the advantage of the falling euro exchange rate was offset by other negative effects. It may be that the composition and quality of the European export package has become less technologically up-to-date and innovative than that of our competitors. Some studies give an indication of this, with all caution. The underlying cause may be that the adaptability of the European economy has been reduced and that we are not keeping up with technology and are not innovative enough. If that is the case, it would be a bad thing now, because on top of the disadvantage of the increased euro exchange rate, there will be a technologically backward export package, making it difficult for European exports to act as an engine for economic recovery. III Development of the Dutch economy Climbing out of the valley Having made these reflections on Europe, I would like to make a few remarks about economic development in the Netherlands. The Dutch economy contracted by 0.8% last year. Within the euro area, only Portugal performed worse. Last year, the volume of private consumption fell by 1%, the first time since 1982. But the Dutch economy is also cautiously climbing out of the valley. In the last quarter of last year, GDP grew by 0.3% compared to the third quarter, for the better. According to recent figures, consumer confidence has improved, which is an encouraging sign. Another bright spot is that exports are picking up. It increased by 0.8% in the third quarter and by 1.7% in the fourth quarter. This shows that our country is able to join the international economic recovery. As a small open economy, our country is largely in line with international economic developments. The Netherlands has a distribution function within Europe and earns a large part of its national income from international trade. Our economy will follow Europe's further recovery, but at a slower pace because of its weakened competitive position. The recovery will also not be strong due to the loss of impulse in government spending. For this year and next year combined, I foresee GDP growth of about 23/4% for our country, assuming a somewhat slower initial recovery than the Netherlands Bureau for Economic Policy Analysis. Setbacks could result from a rise in the value of the euro, a disappointing recovery in the United States and a higher oil price. Unfortunately, unemployment will not fall next year, as it reacts to the economic recovery with a delay. In view of the number of bankruptcies and applications for dismissal, the current restructuring process has not yet been completed. Structural problems of the Dutch economy What needs to be done to improve the economy of the Netherlands? I would like to mention a few points briefly. Firstly, our competitive position, which has weakened in recent years due to high wage growth and low growth in labour productivity. It is therefore necessary to strengthen the competitive position through moderate wage developments. The zero line for wages that was agreed in the Social Agreement last autumn is a contribution to this. Increasing labour force participation in general is desirable in order to maintain growth potential and thus ensure the sustainability of pensions and health care. The low proportion of older people in work and the high number of people unable to work are worrying. The government's plans to slow down the influx into the WAO therefore deserve support, although other choices are conceivable in certain areas. In order to maintain a solid system of pensions, it is necessary to cut back on the schemes. An important element in this is an extension of working life. In addition, a transition to an average pay system could be considered, in which the pension is based on the salary during the entire period that one has worked and no longer on the final salary. Finally, health care, where spending is skyrocketing. More market forces and more use of ICT can reduce costs in this sector. In addition, there is no escaping the fact that more is at your own expense and less is provided through the collectivity. IV Development of the economy of the Northern Netherlands North: unfavourable sector structure Finally, I would like to talk about the economy of the North. The globalisation of the economy has also affected the north of our country. Companies are much less tied to a particular region than before and are more likely to relocate their activities to, for example, Eastern Europe. Location factors play an important role in retaining existing businesses and attracting new ones. Regions compete with each other in this way, which promotes the vitality of the regional economy. Economic growth in the northern provinces has been lower than in the Netherlands as a whole for a number of years. In 2002 there was almost zero growth in the Netherlands, but GDP fell by 1% in Friesland and Drenthe. The gross regional product per capita, a rough measure of prosperity, has lagged behind the rest of the Netherlands for years. If we set the gross regional product per capita in the Netherlands at 100, it is about 90 in the three northern provinces. Employment growth is lower in the north and unemployment is higher. In 2003 unemployment was over 8% in Groningen and over 6% in Friesland. For the Netherlands as a whole, this was 5.3%. The lower growth in output and employment can be explained by the disadvantageous sector structure. The agricultural sector, manufacturing and construction are more strongly represented in the north than in the rest of the Netherlands. However, the growth of output and employment in these sectors is relatively low. Financial and business services, on the other hand, are underrepresented, and it is precisely this sector that has a high growth rate and creates a lot of jobs. This sector structure also means that there are relatively few jobs for highly educated people and that many young people are moving away. Targeted regional policy freezes economic relations In order to make up for the lack of development, targeted regional policy is being pursued. To this end, 2.3 billion will be made available for the North in the period 2000-2006, of which 1.9 billion will come from the national budget and 400 million from the European Union's structural funds. These so-called 'Langman funds' are intended to strengthen the spatial-economic structure of the North and to create new jobs. This is coordinated by the Northern Netherlands Partnership (SNN), in which the three northern provinces have combined their administrative forces. Under the title 'Compass for the North', the SNN has formulated a strategy aimed at the development of economic core zones, investments in urban centres and development of rural areas. Companies and local authorities can submit projects to the SNN for funding. As I understand it, the granting of grants and the implementation of the projects are well on track. Further decisions will be taken on the period after 2006. Despite this regional policy, it is proving difficult for the north to catch up with the rest of the Netherlands. This may have something to do with the fact that targeted regional policy is based too much on existing economic relations. As a result, these proportions are kept intact and freeze, as it were. But in a dynamic economic environment, regions are changing and their pace of development is different. It would be better to pursue a policy based on the dynamism of the regions. For example, more regional wage differentials could be allowed in collective agreements. Where there is a high demand for workers, wages should rise more sharply than in regions with high unemployment. Because wage formation takes place decentrally, there is in principle room to respond to the position of certain regions in collective bargaining. More generally, I believe that the best way to improve the general conditions for economic development in the Netherlands as a whole is to improve the general conditions for economic development in the Netherlands as a whole. A strong and flexible national economy is essential in this respect, as it promotes economic dynamism. I have already mentioned what needs to be done for this, such as an improvement in the competitive position of our country. The North can benefit from this, exploit its strengths and benefit from its location advantages such as space, low land prices for industrial sites and an attractive living environment. The more profitable projects will then be tackled, even without subsidies. This requires entrepreneurs who follow new developments and seize opportunities. Without going into further detail, I would like to mention in this context the accession of Poland and the Baltic States to the European Union. This can offer new sales opportunities for the Northern Netherlands, which will increase as these countries become more prosperous and are able to link up with the economic development of the EU. Regional role of banks Banks have an essential role to play in the development of the regional economy. Because of lending and business advice, banks have close links with companies and are well placed to assess promising projects. In practice, this is particularly important for small and medium-sized enterprises. Large companies can also enter the capital market by issuing shares and bonds, but smaller companies usually have to rely on bank credit for further expansion. As such, banks play an important role in the proper functioning of a region's economy, which certainly also applies to the north of our country. V Lock This is particularly important for the Rabobanks, because they have traditionally played an important role in the local economy and society. This is also the case at Rabobank Sneek-Zuidwest Friesland. Your bank has acquired a prominent place in the North, which it fully deserves. After the merger with Rabobank Bolsward on 1 January of this year, your bank will be the fourth Rabobank in the Netherlands, with 19 branches and approximately 400 employees. I would like to congratulate you on this. I hope that your bank will be able to make an important contribution to the further development of the economy of the North and that of 'Fryslan' in particular for a long time to come.
text_original: Speech president Wellink over 'Visie op de economische ontwikkelingen in Nederland en Europa' Speech Datum 22 maart 2004 Tijd 00:00 uur Lokatie Ter gelegenheid van de Voorjaarsbijeenkomst van de Rabobank Sneek-Zuidwest Friesland te Joure Spreker Dr. A.H.E.M. Wellink, President, De Nederlandsche Bank Ik wil met u van gedachten wisselen over de internationale economische ontwikkelingen en in het bijzonder in Nederland. Ik wil beginnen met een blik op de wereld en daarna de focus verleggen naar Europa. Vervolgens ga ik in op Nederland en tenslotte op de ontwikkeling in het noorden van ons land. Daarbij zal ik ook de rol van banken in de regionale ontwikkeling aan de orde stellen. Dat geldt in het bijzonder voor de Rabobank Sneek-Zuidwest Friesland, die ik erkentelijk ben voor deze uitnodiging. Dat ik pas aan het einde van mijn betoog in het Noorden aankom betekent niet dat ik dit minder belangrijk vind. Dat hoop ik u in het vervolg duidelijk te kunnen maken. I Internationale economische ontwikkeling Amerika, Japan en China De Amerikaanse economie groeit flink. Vorig jaar nam het bruto binnenlands product (bbp) toe met ruim 3%, met in het vierde kwartaal zelfs een groei van 4% ten opzichte van het kwartaal ervoor (op jaarbasis). Een continu hoge productiviteitsgroei, winstherstel en herstructurering van balansen hebben de financile basis van de bedrijven verbeterd. Ik ben dan ook optimistisch over de Amerikaanse economie en verwacht een bbp-groei van 4,5  5% voor dit jaar. Wel vormt het tekort op de lopende rekening van de betalingsbalans van 5% bbp, op middellange termijn een onevenwichtigheid die als een schaduw over de Amerikaanse economie hangt en op lange termijn niet houdbaar is. Ook in Japan zijn de vooruitzichten beter. Door een aantrekken van de export en de investeringen is de economie weer op gang gekomen. Vorig jaar groeide het bbp met 2,7%. De toenemende orintatie van de Japanse economie op het expanderende China speelt daarbij een belangrijke rol. De voorwaarden voor een duurzaam herstel zijn verbeterd: de vermogenspositie van bedrijven is versterkt en bij de banken is veel gesaneerd, al blijven deze kwetsbaar. Het probleem waarmee het land al jaren worstelt - deflatie - is er echter nog altijd. Vorig jaar daalde het prijspeil van de particuliere consumptie met 0,3% en dit zette zich in januari van dit jaar in dezelfde mate voort. China ontwikkelt zich economisch in een onstuimig tempo. Sinds 1994 groeit de economie van China met zon 8% per jaar, waardoor het productievolume in negen jaar is verdubbeld. Het land is een speler van wereldformaat aan het worden. Gezien de snelle expansie en de grote binnenlandse vraag dreigt een oververhitting van de economie, tot uitdrukking komend in een versnelling van de inflatie naar zon 3%. Een probleem is dat de Chinese banken, die grotendeels in handen zijn van de staat, vanwege de vele oninbare leningen niet gezond zijn. Dit vormt een risico voor de financile stabiliteit, niet alleen voor China maar voor heel Zuid-Oost Azi. Eurogebied Vervolgens wil ik de blik richten op Europa. De gunstige ontwikkeling van de Amerikaanse economie vormt een belangrijke stimulans voor de Europese economie. Voorzichtig heeft deze de weg omhoog ingeslagen. In het derde kwartaal van vorig jaar groeide de economie met 0,4% ten opzichte van het kwartaal ervoor en in het vierde kwartaal kon een groei van 0,3% worden genoteerd. Een matig groeitempo, maar wel een plus. In Duitsland was het groeicijfer in het vierde kwartaal 0,2%, in Frankrijk 0,5% en in Itali 0%. Bij onze oosterburen, evenals in andere landen van Europa, is het vooral de particuliere consumptie die kwakkelt, wat is toe te schrijven aan een zwak consumentenvertrouwen. Van essentieel belang is dat de consumptie weer op gang komt. Is het economische klimaat voor de Europese consument nu slechter dan in andere perioden van economisch herstel? Ik heb voor het eurogebied de economische omstandigheden van nu, eens vergeleken met de vorige perioden van pril economische herstel, namelijk 1982 en 1993. Het consumentenvertrouwen is nu weliswaar laag, maar ligt op een wat hoger niveau dan toen. De werkgelegenheid groeide in de afgelopen twee jaar nog, in tegenstelling tot destijds en de werkloosheid ligt nu op het gemiddelde van beide vorige perioden. En niet het minst belangrijk: de rente is nu lager dan toen. Belangrijke karakteristieken van de huidige economische situatie zijn voor de consument dus beter dan voorheen. Daar staat tegenover dat er nu in vrijwel alle landen meer en meer onzekerheid is rond de pensioenen. Dit kan een reden zijn om meer te gaan sparen voor de oude dag, op zich een goed streven. Daarnaast leggen de kosten van de gezondheidszorg in veel landen een toenemend beslag op het budget van de consument. Deze meer structurele ontwikkelingen kunnen de consumptie op een lager groeipad brengen, maar op de korte termijn zal dit zijn invloed niet sterk doen gelden. Ik verwacht dan ook een verder herstel voor de Europese economie, dat door de export wordt geleid en door de consumptie wordt ondersteund. Voor dit jaar is naar mijn inschatting voor het eurogebied een bbp-groei van rond 1% mogelijk en volgend jaar van rond 2%. Appreciatie van de euro Momenteel krijgt de stijging van de koers van de euro veel aandacht. Deze appreciatie van de euro komt op een moment dat het de export is die de Europese economie uit het dal moet trekken. Bij de invoering van de euro in 1999 werd de koers vastgesteld op $ 1,17, nu schommelt deze rond $ 1,23. Een dergelijke appreciatie van de euro werkt enigermate remmend op het economisch herstel, maar maakt dit niet ongedaan, want de export van het eurogebied profiteert van het internationale economische herstel dat sterker is dan eerder werd voorzien. Meer zorgelijk is het als de eurokoers sterk zou fluctueren, want dat geeft onzekerheid bij exporteurs en importeurs. Ik memoreerde al dat bij de invoering van de euro in 1999, de koers werd vastgesteld op $ 1,17. Nadien is deze gedaald naar een dieptepunt van circa $ 0,82 medio 2001. Dit was voor bedrijven in het eurogebied een gunstige ontwikkeling. Maar een feit is dat zij hiervan met hun export onvoldoende hebben geprofiteerd en hun marktaandeel niet hebben vergroot. Het is niet helemaal duidelijk waarom niet. Kennelijk stonden er tegenover het voordeel van de dalende eurokoers, andere negatieve effecten. Het zou kunnen zijn dat de samenstelling en kwaliteit van het Europese exportpakket in technologisch opzicht minder up-to-date en innovatief is geworden dan dat van onze concurrenten. Sommige studies geven hiervoor, met alle voorzichtigheid, een indicatie. Achterliggende oorzaak kan zijn dat het aanpassingsvermogen van de Europese economie is verminderd en dat wij technologisch niet goed meekomen en te weinig innovatief zijn. Als dat zo is dan zou dat nu slecht uitkomen, want bij het nadeel van de gestegen eurokoers komt dan nog een technologisch achtergebleven exportpakket, waardoor het voor de Europese export moeilijk wordt om als motor voor het economisch herstel te fungeren. III Ontwikkeling van de Nederlandse economie Klimmend uit het dal Na deze beschouwingen over Europa wil ik enkele opmerkingen maken over de economische ontwikkeling in Nederland. De Nederlandse economie liet vorig jaar een krimp zien van 0,8%. Binnen het eurogebied presteerde alleen Portugal slechter. Vorig jaar daalde het volume van de particuliere consumptie met 1%, de eerste keer sinds 1982. Maar ook de Nederlandse economie klimt voorzichtig uit het dal. Het laatste kwartaal van vorig jaar groeide het bbp met 0,3% ten opzichte van het derde kwartaal, een keer ten goede. Volgens recente cijfers is het consumentenvertrouwen toegenomen en dat is een bemoedigend teken. Een ander lichtpuntje is dat de export aantrekt. In het derde kwartaal nam deze toe met 0,8% en in het vierde kwartaal met 1,7%. Hieruit blijkt dat ons land weet aan te haken bij het internationale economische herstel. Als kleine open economie deint ons land in belangrijke mate mee met de internationale conjuncturele ontwikkelingen. Nederland heeft een distributiefunctie binnen Europa en verdient een groot deel van zijn nationale inkomen met de internationale handel. Onze economie zal het verdere herstel van Europa volgen, maar vanwege de verzwakte concurrentiepositie wel in een trager tempo. Ook door het wegvallen van de impuls in de overheidsbestedingen zal het herstel niet krachtig zijn. Voor dit jaar en volgend jaar tezamen voorzie ik voor ons land een bbp-groei van zon 2%, waarbij ik van een wat trager initieel herstel uitga dan het Centraal Planbureau. Tegenvallers kunnen voortvloeien uit een koersstijging van de euro, een tegenvallend herstel in de Verenigde Staten en een hogere olieprijs. Helaas zal de werkloosheid volgend jaar nog niet verminderen, want deze reageert met een vertraging op het economische herstel. Gezien het aantal faillissementen en ontslagaanvragen is de huidige saneringsslag nog niet voltooid. Structurele problemen van de Nederlandse economie Wat moet er worden gedaan om de economie van Nederland te verbeteren? Ik wil kort enkele punten noemen. In de eerste plaats onze concurrentiepositie, die de laatste jaren is verzwakt vanwege een hoge loonstijging en een geringe groei van de arbeidsproductiviteit. Versterking van de concurrentiepositie door een gematigde loonontwikkeling is daarom nodig. De nullijn voor de lonen die afgelopen herfst in het Sociaal Akkoord is afgesproken vormt hiertoe een bijdrage. Verhoging van de arbeidsparticipatie in den brede is wenselijk om het groeipotentieel in stand te houden en daarmee de betaalbaarheid van de pensioenen en de gezondheidszorg veilig te stellen. Zorgelijk is het lage aandeel van de ouderen dat werkt en het hoge aantal arbeidsongeschikten. De regeringsplannen om de instroom in de WAO af te remmen verdienen dan ook steun, al zijn op onderdelen andere keuzes denkbaar. Om een solide stelsel van pensioenen in stand te houden is versobering van de regelingen nodig. Een belangrijk element hierbij is een verlenging van het werkzame leven. Daarnaast is te denken aan een overgang naar een middelloonstelsel, waarbij het pensioen is gebaseerd op het loon gedurende de hele periode dat men heeft gewerkt en niet meer op het eindloon. Tenslotte de gezondheidszorg, waar de uitgaven explosief stijgen. Meer marktwerking en meer toepassing van ICT kan in deze sector de kosten verminderen. Daarnaast is er niet aan te ontkomen dat meer voor eigen rekening komt en minder via de collectiviteit wordt verstrekt. IV Ontwikkeling van de economie van Noord-Nederland Noorden: ongunstige sectorstructuur Tenslotte wil ik ingaan op de economie van het Noorden. De globalisering van de economie laat ook het noorden van ons land niet onberoerd. Bedrijven zijn veel minder dan voorheen aan een bepaalde regio gebonden en verplaatsen hun activiteiten gemakkelijker naar bijvoorbeeld Oost-Europa. Vestigingsplaatsfactoren spelen een belangrijke rol bij het vasthouden van bestaande bedrijven en het aantrekken van nieuwe bedrijven. Regios beconcurreren elkaar hiermee en dat bevordert de vitaliteit van de regionale economie. De economische groei is in de noordelijke provincies al een aantal jaren lager dan in Nederland als geheel. In 2002 was er ongeveer een nulgroei in Nederland, maar daalde het bbp in Friesland en Drenthe met 1%. Het bruto regionale product per hoofd van de bevolking, een ruwe maatstaf voor de welvaart, blijft al jaren achter bij de rest van Nederland. Als we het bruto regionale product per hoofd in Nederland op 100 stellen, dan bedraagt dit in de drie noordelijke provincies ongeveer 90. De groei van de werkgelegenheid is in het noorden lager en de werkloosheid is hoger. In 2003 was de werkloosheid in Groningen ruim 8% en in Friesland ruim 6%. Voor Nederland als geheel was dit 5,3%. De lagere groei van productie en werkgelegenheid zijn te verklaren uit de nadelige sectorstructuur. De agrarische sector, de industrie en de bouwnijverheid zijn in het noorden sterker vertegenwoordigd dan in de rest van Nederland. De groei van productie en werkgelegenheid is in deze sectoren echter relatief gering. De financile en zakelijke dienstverlening is daarentegen ondervertegenwoordigd en juist deze sector kent een hoge groeivoet en creert veel werkgelegenheid. Deze sectorstructuur brengt bovendien met zich mee dat er relatief weinig banen zijn voor hoogopgeleiden en dat veel jongeren wegtrekken. Gericht regionaal beleid bevriest economische verhoudingen Om de achterstand in ontwikkeling in te halen wordt gericht regionaal beleid gevoerd. Hiertoe komt voor het Noorden in de periode 2000-2006  2,3 miljard ter beschikking, waarvan  1,9 miljard uit de Rijksbegroting en  400 miljoen uit de structuurfondsen van de Europese Unie. Deze zogenoemde Langman-gelden dienen om de ruimtelijk-economische structuur van het Noorden te versterken en nieuwe arbeidsplaatsen tot stand te brengen. Een en ander wordt gecordineerd door het Samenwerkingsverband Noord-Nederland (SNN), waarin de drie noordelijke provincies hun bestuurlijke krachten hebben gebundeld. Het SNN heeft onder de titel Kompas voor het Noorden een strategie geformuleerd gericht op de ontwikkeling van economisch kernzones, investeringen in stedelijke centra en ontwikkeling van landelijke gebieden. Bedrijven en lokale overheden kunnen aan het SNN projecten ter subsidiring voordragen. Naar ik heb begrepen liggen de verstrekking van subsidies en de uitvoering van de projecten goed op schema. Over de periode na 2006 zal nadere besluitvorming plaatsvinden. Ondanks dit regionale beleid blijkt het voor het noorden moeilijk de inhaalslag met de rest van Nederland te realiseren. Mogelijkerwijs heeft dit ermee te maken dat gericht regionaal beleid te veel uitgaat van de bestaande economische verhoudingen. Daardoor houdt men deze verhoudingen intact en bevriest ze als het ware. Maar in een dynamische economische omgeving veranderen de regios en loopt hun ontwikkelingstempo uiteen. Het is dan beter een beleid te voeren dat de dynamiek van de regios als vertrekpunt kiest. Zo zou men bijvoorbeeld in de caos meer regionale loonverschillen kunnen toelaten. Waar veel vraag is naar werknemers zouden de lonen sterker mogen stijgen dan in regios met veel werkloosheid. Omdat de loonvorming decentraal plaats vindt is er in beginsel ruimte om in de cao-onderhandelingen in te spelen op de positie van bepaalde regios. Meer algemeen is het Noorden mijns inziens het beste geholpen met het verbeteren van de algemene voorwaarden voor de economische ontwikkeling in Nederland als geheel. Hierbij is een sterke en flexibel werkende nationale economie essentieel, want dit bevordert de economische dynamiek. Wat hiervoor moet gebeuren noemde ik al, zoals een verbetering van de concurrentiepositie van ons land. Het Noorden kan hiervan zijn graantje meepikken, zijn sterke punten uitbuiten en profiteren van zijn vestigingsplaatsvoordelen als ruimte, lage grondprijzen voor bedrijfsterreinen en een aantrekkelijk woon- en leefklimaat. De meer rendabele projecten zullen dan worden aangepakt, ook zonder subsidies. Dit vraagt om ondernemers die nieuwe ontwikkelingen volgen en kansen grijpen. Zonder dit verder uit te werken wil ik in dit verband de toetreding van Polen en de Baltische staten tot de Europese Unie noemen. Dit kan voor Noord-Nederland nieuwe afzetmogelijkheden bieden, die ruimer worden naarmate deze landen welvarender worden en bij de economische ontwikkeling van de EU weten aan te haken. Regionale rol van banken Voor de ontwikkeling van de regionale economie is een essentile rol weggelegd voor de banken. Vanwege de kredietverlening en bedrijfsadvisering hebben banken nauwe banden met bedrijven en zijn zij goed in staat kansrijke projecten te beoordelen. Dat is in de praktijk vooral van belang voor bedrijven in het midden- en kleinbedrijf. Grote bedrijven kunnen ook op de kapitaalmarkt terecht door uitgifte van aandelen en obligaties, maar kleinere bedrijven zijn voor verdere expansie meestal aangewezen op bankkrediet. Daarmee spelen de banken een belangrijke rol in het goed functioneren van de economie van een regio, wat zeker ook geldt voor het noorden van ons land. V Slot Voor de Rabobanken speelt dat wel in het bijzonder, omdat zij vanouds een belangrijke plaats in de lokale economie en samenleving innemen. Dit is ook bij de Rabobank Sneek-Zuidwest Friesland het geval. Uw bank heeft zich een prominente plaats in het Noorden verworven, die zij ten volle verdient. Na de fusie op 1 januari van dit jaar met de Rabobank Bolsward is uw bank de vierde Rabobank van Nederland, met 19 vestigingen en circa 400 medewerkers. Ik wil u hiermee hartelijk gelukwensen. Ik hoop dat uw bank nog lange tijd een belangrijke bijdrage mag leveren aan de verdere ontwikkeling van de economie van het Noorden en die van Frysln in het bijzonder.

Title: Recent economic developments
Subtitle: Speech van dr. A.H.E.M. Wellink , president van de Nederlandsche Bank, ter gelegenheid van de Voorjaarsbijeenkomst van de Rabobank Sneek-Zuidwest Friesland op 22 maart 2004 te Joure
text: Recent economic developments Speech Date: March 23, 2004 Time: 11:39 a.m. Location Spring Meeting of Rabobank Sneek-Zuidwest Friesland Speaker Dr. A.H.E.M. Wellink, President, De Nederlandsche Bank Speech by Dr. A.H.E.M. Wellink, President of the Dutch Central Bank, on the occasion of the Spring Meeting of Rabobank Sneek-Zuidwest Friesland on 22 March 2004 in Joure I Introduction 1. First of all, I would like to discuss with you this evening international economic developments. I will then discuss Europe and the Netherlands and finally the development in the north of our country. The fact that I am only arriving in the North at the end of my speech does not mean that I consider this to be any less important. I hope to be able to make that clear to you in the future. II International economic development America, Japan and China 2. The U.S. economy is growing strongly. Last year, gross domestic product (GDP) increased by more than 3%, in the second half of the year by as much as 6% year-on-year. Continued high productivity growth, profit recovery and balance sheet restructuring have improved the financial basis of companies. I am therefore optimistic about the US economy and expect GDP growth of 4.5-5% this year. However, the current account deficit of 5% of GDP is an imbalance that hangs like a shadow over the US economy and is not sustainable in the long term. In my opinion, the so-called 'jobless recovery', which is politically sensitive in the US in this election year, is unjustifiably viewed negatively. It is the result of a better utilization of the available amount of labour and capital at this economic stage and of the rapid restructuring of the American economy. With some delay, the number of jobs will also start to grow again. 3. In Japan, the outlook is better than it has been in a long time. With the pick-up in exports and investment, the economy has restarted. Last year, GDP grew by 2.7%. The increasing orientation of the Japanese economy towards the expanding China plays an important role in this. The conditions for a sustainable recovery have improved: the capital position of companies has been strengthened and there has been a lot of restructuring in the banks, although they remain vulnerable. However, the problem that the country has been struggling with for years  deflation  is still there, albeit to a less threatening degree. 4. China is developing economically at a heady pace. This country accounted for 40% of world GDP growth in 2003. Since 1994, China's economy has grown at an average rate of about 8% per year, doubling its production volume in nine years. The country is becoming a world-class player. Given the rapid expansion and strong domestic demand, there is a risk of an overheating of the economy, which is reflected in an acceleration of inflation to around 3%. An appreciation of the currency against the dollar will provide some relief. One problem is that the Chinese banks, which are largely owned by the state, are not healthy because of the many non-performing loans. The Chinese government has recognised this point and has embarked on a drastic restructuring of the banking system. Euro area 5. Let me now turn my attention to Europe. The favourable development of the American and Asian economies is an important stimulus for the European economy. Cautiously, it has taken its way up. In the third quarter of last year, the economy grew by 0.4% compared to the previous quarter and in the fourth quarter it grew by 0.3%. A moderate growth rate, but a plus. In Germany, the growth rate was 0.2% in the fourth quarter, in France 0.5% and in Italy 0%. In our eastern neighbours, as in other countries in Europe, it is mainly private consumption that is struggling, which can be attributed to weak consumer confidence. 6. Is the economic environment for European consumers worse now than in other periods of economic recovery? I have compared the current economic conditions for the euro area with the previous periods of early economic recovery, namely 1982 and 1993. Although consumer confidence is low now, it is at a somewhat higher level than it was then. Employment has continued to grow in the past two years, in contrast to the previous year, and unemployment is now at the average of the two previous periods. And last but not least, interest rates are lower now than they were then. Important characteristics of the current economic situation are therefore better for consumers than before. 7. On the other hand, there is now quite a bit of uncertainty about pensions in almost all European countries. This can be a reason to start saving more for old age, which in itself is a good goal. In addition, the cost of health care is placing an increasing burden on consumers' budgets in many countries. However, I still expect a further recovery of the European economy, which is led by exports and supported by consumption. For this year, I estimate GDP growth of around 11/2% is possible for the euro area and next year of around 21/2%. Appreciation of the euro 8. At the moment, the rise in the exchange rate of the euro is receiving a lot of attention. This appreciation of the euro comes at a time when it is exports that are pulling the European economy out of the doldrums. When the euro was introduced in 1999, the rate was set at 1.17, now it hovers around 1.23. This increase is not very spectacular, but we have to forget about the intervening course. 9. I have already recalled that when the euro was introduced in 1999, the rate was set at 1.17. It has since fallen to a low of around 0.82 in mid-2001. This was a positive development for euro area firms. But the fact is that they have not benefited sufficiently from this with their exports and have not increased their market share. It's not entirely clear why not. Apparently, the advantage of the falling euro exchange rate was offset by other negative effects. It may be that the composition and quality of the European export package has become less technologically up-to-date and innovative than that of our non-European competitors. Some studies give an indication of this, with all caution. The underlying cause may be that the European economy is too incapable of adapting and that we are not keeping up with technology and are not innovative enough. If that is the case, it would be a bad thing now, because on top of the disadvantage of the increased euro exchange rate, there will be a technologically backward export package, making it difficult for European exports to act as an engine for economic recovery. Fortunately, in the current economic phase, the very rapid pick-up in world trade is counterbalanced. III Development of the Dutch economy Climbing out of the valley 10. Let me now make a few remarks on economic developments in the Netherlands. The Dutch economy shrank by 0.8% last year. Within the euro area, only Portugal and Germany also showed negative growth rates. In 2003, the volume of private consumption fell by 1%, the first time since 1982. But the Dutch economy is also cautiously climbing out of the valley. In the last quarter of last year, GDP grew by 0.3% compared to the third quarter, for the better. According to recent figures, consumer confidence has risen sharply, which is an encouraging sign. Another bright spot is that exports are picking up. It increased by 0.8% in the third quarter and by 1.7% in the fourth quarter. This shows that our country is gradually joining the international economic recovery. 11. Our economy will follow Europe's further recovery, but probably at a slower pace due to its weakened competitive position. The recovery will also be less powerful due to the loss of the stimulus in government spending. For this year and next year combined, I foresee GDP growth of around 23/4% for our country, with DNB assuming a somewhat slower initial recovery than the Netherlands Bureau for Economic Policy Analysis, but it must be admitted that the estimated uncertainties are relatively high at this stage of the recovery. Setbacks could result from a rise in the value of the euro, a disappointing recovery in the United States and a higher oil price. Unfortunately, unemployment will not fall next year, as it reacts to the economic recovery with a delay. In view of the number of bankruptcies and applications for dismissal, the current restructuring process is apparently not yet complete. Structural problems of the Dutch economy 12. What needs to be done to improve the economy of the Netherlands? I would like to mention a few points briefly. Firstly, our competitive position, which has weakened in recent years due to high wage growth and low growth in labour productivity. It is therefore necessary to strengthen the competitive position through moderate wage developments. The zero line for wages that was agreed in the Social Agreement last autumn is a contribution to this. Increasing labour force participation in general is desirable in order to maintain growth potential and thus ensure the sustainability of pensions and health care. The low proportion of older people in work and the high number of people unable to work are worrying. The government's plans to slow down the influx into the WAO therefore deserve support. In order to maintain a solid system of pensions, it is necessary to cut back on the schemes. An important element in this is an extension of working life. In addition, a transition to an average pay system could be considered, in which the pension is based on the salary during the entire period that one has worked and no longer on the final salary. Finally, health care, where spending is skyrocketing. More market forces and more use of ICT can reduce costs in this sector. In addition, there is no escaping the fact that more is at your own expense and less is provided through the collectivity. IV Development of the economy of the Northern Netherlands North: unfavourable sector structure 13. Finally, I would like to turn to the economy of the North. The globalisation of the economy has also affected the north of our country. Companies are much less tied to a particular region than before and are more likely to relocate their activities to, for example, Eastern Europe, India or China. Location factors play an important role in retaining existing businesses and attracting new ones. Regions compete with each other in this way, which promotes the vitality of the regional economy. 14. Economic growth in the northern provinces has been lower than in the Netherlands as a whole for a number of years. In 2002 there was almost zero growth in the Netherlands, but GDP fell by 1% in Friesland and Drenthe. The gross regional product per capita, a rough measure of prosperity, has lagged behind the rest of the Netherlands for years. If we set the gross regional product per capita in the Netherlands at 100, it is about 90 in the three northern provinces. Employment growth is lower in the north and unemployment is higher. In 2003 unemployment was over 8% in Groningen and over 6% in Friesland. For the Netherlands as a whole, this was 5.3%. 15. The lower growth in output and employment can be explained by the disadvantageous sectoral structure. The agricultural sector, manufacturing and construction are more strongly represented in the north than in the rest of the Netherlands. However, the growth of output and employment in these sectors is relatively low. Financial and business services, on the other hand, are underrepresented, and it is precisely this sector that has a high growth rate and creates a lot of jobs. This sector structure also means that there are relatively few jobs for highly educated people and that many young people are moving away. Targeted regional policy freezes economic relations 16. In order to make up for the lack of development, targeted regional policies are being pursued. To this end, 2.3 billion will be made available for the North in the period 2000-2006, of which 1.9 billion will come from the national budget and 400 million from the European Union's structural funds. These so-called 'Langman funds' are intended to strengthen the spatial-economic structure of the North and to create new jobs. This is coordinated by the Northern Netherlands Partnership (SNN), in which the three northern provinces have combined their administrative forces. Under the title 'Compass for the North', the SNN has formulated a strategy aimed at the development of economic core zones, investments in urban centres and development of rural areas. Companies and local authorities can submit projects to the SNN for funding. As I understand it, the granting of grants and the implementation of the projects are well on track. Further decisions will be taken on the period after 2006. 17. In spite of this regional policy, it is proving difficult for the north to catch up with the rest of the Netherlands. This may have something to do with the fact that targeted regional policy is based too much on existing economic relations. As a result, these proportions are kept intact and freeze, as it were. But in a dynamic economic environment, regions are changing and their pace of development is different. It would be better to pursue a policy based on the dynamism of the regions. 18. More generally, I believe that the best way for the North to do so is to improve the general conditions for economic development in the Netherlands as a whole. A strong and flexible national economy is essential in this respect, as it promotes economic dynamism. I have already mentioned what needs to be done for this, such as an improvement in the competitive position of our country. The North can benefit from this, exploit its strengths and benefit from its location advantages such as space, low land prices for industrial sites and an attractive living environment. The more profitable projects will then be tackled, even without subsidies. This requires entrepreneurs who follow new developments and seize opportunities. Without going into further detail, I would like to mention in this context the accession of Poland and the Baltic States to the European Union. This can offer new sales opportunities for the Northern Netherlands, which will increase as these countries become more prosperous and are able to link up with the economic development of the EU. Regional role of banks 19. Banks have an essential role to play in the development of the regional economy. Because of lending and business advice, banks have close links with companies and are well placed to assess promising projects. In practice, this is particularly important for small and medium-sized enterprises. Large companies can also enter the capital market by issuing shares and bonds, but smaller companies usually have to rely on bank credit for further expansion. As such, banks play an important role in the proper functioning of a region's economy, which certainly also applies to the north of our country. V Lock This is particularly important for the Rabobanks, because they have traditionally played an important role in the local economy and society. This is also the case at Rabobank Sneek-Zuidwest Friesland. Your bank has acquired a prominent place in the North, which it fully deserves. After the merger with Rabobank Bolsward on 1 January of this year, your bank will be the fourth Rabobank in the Netherlands, with 19 branches and approximately 400 employees. I would like to congratulate you on this. I hope that your bank will be able to make an important contribution to the further development of the economy of the North and that of 'Fryslan' in particular for a long time to come.
