Title: Speech by director Witteveen: 'Steering ability requires good glasses'
Subtitle: Het thema van dit seminar luidt: Pensioen anders bekeken. De logische vraag is dan: hoezo anders? Vanuit welk perspectief kijk je normaal gesproken aan tegen pensioen? De organisatoren hebben gekozen voor een financile invalshoek. U krijgt vandaag inzicht in de ontwikkelingen op de financile markten en hoe u daar als bestuurslid mee om kunt gaan, gegeven de doelstelling van uw fonds. Daarbij komen ook de ervaringen in de praktijk aan bod.
text: Speech by director Witteveen: 'Steering ability requires good glasses' Speech Datum 27 september 2005 Time: 00:00 hrs Location Interpolis Pensions in the Congress Building in Amstelveen Speaker: mr. D.E. Witteveen The theme of this seminar is: Pension viewed differently. The logical question then is: what do you mean different? From what perspective do you normally view retirement? The organisers have opted for a financial approach. Today you will gain insight into the developments in the financial markets and how you can deal with them as a board member, given the objective of your fund. Practical experience is also discussed. I have been asked to approach the theme from the perspective of the regulator. I do this on the basis of three core concepts: risk-aware, responsive and realistic. At the heart of my argument are three messages that are in line with this: As a pension fund board, you have the task of guaranteeing the commitments made. This requires good risk management. The emphasis is on the steering capacity of your fund. To be a responsive organization, you need to be critical and open. Understand what you are doing, do it and explain what you have done. Be realistic and think about a fallback position for the moment that a negative scenario becomes reality. Risks and risk management. Every year, at the end of winter, the Dutch have such a question. Summer is coming. What is it going to be this year, hot and dry or cold and wet? You need to be prepared for both. Otherwise, you're not doing it right. And if you assume the "average" summer, then you are almost certain that you are really wrong. Every Dutch person knows how to deal with that. So risk management can't be that difficult. Structural trends First of all, I would like to say a few words about today's theme. The seminar will focus on the following question: how can a pension fund respond to uncertain developments in the external environment? From the perspective of the financial markets, it is obvious to think about interest rates and returns. At a higher level of abstraction, three structural trends are important. Firstly, an ageing population. By 2040, there are expected to be 4.4 million pensioners. Our society will look quite different then. There will be two and a half workers per pensioner, now it is one in five. The dependency ratio doubles. As a result, negative shocks to the assets of pension funds are less and less able to be absorbed by means of contribution adjustments. Other control mechanisms are needed. This indicates the importance of risk awareness and, by extension, the steering capacity of your fund. Secondly, technological development and financial innovation. Advancing insight and deepening of knowledge make it possible to make increasingly sophisticated analyses. Financial markets offer an almost unprecedented number of opportunities for risk management appropriate to your fund-specific situation. The new techniques help you to paint a more realistic picture of the risks you run and the possibilities of absorbing blows. Thirdly, a social trend. There is an increasing need for transparency and accountability. This requires responsive organisations: an open organisation that communicates clearly and takes a critical stance. In order to keep our beautiful Dutch pension system afloat in the long term, we need to respond to these structural developments. This applies not only to you, but also to supervision. A lot is happening in this area. There is an increasing emphasis on a transparent, consistent and risk-based approach by the supervisor. The need for such an approach is not a typically Dutch phenomenon. Internationally, there is an increasing trend towards risk-based supervision of financial institutions. Basel II as a global standard for the supervision of banks and the Solvency II project for the supervision of insurers within the European Union are in the pipeline. With regard to pensions, it can be said that the Netherlands leads the leading group internationally. On 1 January 2007, the Financial Assessment Framework will be mandatory for all pension funds, with up-to-date valuation and risk-based supervision as the core components. By providing a realistic understanding of the value of liabilities and assets and the associated uncertainties, the risks can be properly managed and confidence in the pension system can be guaranteed. Risk awareness and insight into steering ability Trust is the pillar of the stability of a financial system. But this trust cannot be taken for granted. For example, the pension sector has been under great pressure in recent years due to the deteriorating financial position of funds. This deterioration has its origins in the 1990s. I said a lot about this two weeks ago in Apeldoorn. There was the threat of skimming off alleged surplus assets by the government. But there was also the influence of the interest rate gap, as a result of the so-called duration mismatch between investments and liabilities, insufficiently visible in the development of the funding ratio. And very substantially less was deposited than the cost-covering premium, which both gave a silent wage cost subsidy at the wrong time and affected the pension assets. And finally, the shift from fixed income to equities was not, or not sufficiently, accompanied by the build-up of buffers to cover the increased equity risks. Since 2002, the course has changed considerably. Social partners and pension fund managers have made strong efforts to restore the solid financial position of funds. Let's be honest with each other. Around 1990, the Dutch pension funds were more or less covered and buffered in real terms, nominally it was even better. Less than 15 years later, after another of the best investment periods, we see, in real terms, under-coverage. Of course, no matter how easy it is to explain, that is not a result to write home about. We still have a fine and rich pension system, but not as rich as it was. Looking back, it is striking that it was precisely in the 1990s, when a lot of energy was invested in ALM studies, that these developments took place uninhibited. However, the stochastic future projections may have placed too much emphasis on the 'average path'. This was often a positive path and negative scenarios were dismissed as unrealistic. This created a certain degree of false security among pension fund managers and other relevant players: the unilateral use of advanced  and in itself fine  techniques made it appear  wrongly  that the risks were relatively small. Relying on the adage "retirement is a long-term thing, and everything will be fine in the long run" is not risk management. No misunderstandings. Knowing risks and keeping them manageable is not the same as not taking risks. On the contrary, the essence of pensions is that nothing is certain due to the long term, which by definition means that risk is incurred. Within the FTK, pension fund boards have the freedom to make their own choices and considerations in dealing with these risks. It is up to the board to determine whether the investment policy is appropriate to the nature and extent of the pension obligations. The regulator does not take the place of the board and does not provide investment advice, let alone investment regulations. However, the quality of the financial set-up is examined. This must be done in a careful and targeted manner, whereby the pension fund knows and must be able to bear the investment risks in relation to the obligations. Admittedly, it's easy to talk afterwards. Don't get me wrong. My message is not not to use ALM studies. The technology has improved enormously and can make a powerful contribution to a good risk assessment. We are able to perform very complex calculations, which allow us to clearly map out the accrual of pension provisions. This is a positive development. My warning lies in the use of these techniques, reading the map. It is not the sophistication that leads to better risk management, but the extent to which and the way in which the models are used. In contrast to the past, the focus should not be one-sidedly on the probability of a risk, but also on the impact of this risk. The FTK provides better insight into both elements. A certainty measure of 97.5 percent for the unconditional liabilities means that from the equilibrium situation, 25 scenarios out of 1000 may show a situation of undercoverage. The degree of undercoverage will differ in those 25 scenarios. The starting point is that recovery should be possible within one year. And not, of course, by cutting back on nominal duties. Since many of you have a little more technical expertise in this area, and since there was also such a well-known point cloud in the slides just now, I would like to say the latter a little more technically. It means that if you run another 1000 simulations on those 25 scenarios, all 1000 simulations will be positive. However, even if you were to apply a 97.5% certainty measure, there should still be a situation of full coverage of liabilities in 975 simulations. As a director, you will therefore have to have insight into your bad chances: what does a scenario that occurs with a probability of 2.5 percent mean for your financial position? Simulations may show that the degree of underfunding is so substantial that you, as a fund, have virtually no options left to recover. Of course, you don't want to end up in a situation where you can't possibly get out of the pit. That is why it is so important to focus on the steering capacity of your fund: what are the consequences of a negative scenario and how can and do you want to deal with it as a board, given the nature of your fund's obligations? The recent past has taught us that negative scenarios can become reality and that the impact on the financial position of a pension fund can be substantial. That is why the FTK makes it possible to shift the emphasis in management and supervision from an assessment of the past to a flexible view of the future. The key elements of the FTK that make an important contribution to this are the continuity analysis, the cost-covering premium and the premium discount limit. An assessment of your fund's management capacity will soon play a much more important role than an assessment of the state of affairs at one time. This avoids a semantic discussion. After all, many of the critics of the FTK who are now calling for political intervention are basing their criticism on the current transition problems. But as Nout Wellink recently pointed out, we did not hear a similar criticism in the 1990s when too few premiums were paid in an economy tending to overheating. Therefore, let us look ahead in order to manage such risks as well as possible. Responsiveness requires a critical attitude and crystal-clear communication The risks taken by a pension fund have consequences for pension participants. They depend on the performance of a pension fund for a significant part of their future income. They therefore have a right to information, and they expect it. This brings me to my second core concept: responsiveness. A good pension fund is a responsive organization. To me, this is an organization that is open to signals and suggestions from outside, that converts these into actions and policies in a timely and adequate manner, and communicates about them. To stay in terms of today's organizer, crystal clear communication about risks, considerations made and choices. People expect quite a lot in this area. They want concrete and quick solutions, understandable conditions and clarity about coverage. Of course, I see that as an aim in the host's advertisements. But I also see a clear parallel with the indexation matrix, for example. This gives you policy leeway to make a choice that is in line with the wishes of your participants (the concrete solution), indicating how you index rights and what financing structure fits in with this (the understandable conditions), and what the participants can reasonably expect (clarity about the coverage). Responsiveness is not just receiving signals from and communicating with third parties. It also requires a critical attitude from you as a director and asking the right questions. I say this because at the moment a 'search for yield' is visible, due to the low interest rates. Understandable, but is this focus the right answer to the questions that the future will ask us? It is best to answer this question for your fund; You know the nature of the obligations and the expectations of your participants. The regulator pays attention to proportionality: higher returns go hand in hand with higher risks. Or, let me put it a little more simply, a higher risk does not make a pension cheaper, just as good supervision requirements do not make a pension more expensive. By now, you understand that there is a relationship between the generous 15-year period to restore buffers and the 1-year period in the event of under-coverage. With this 15-year term, the much-desired co-breathing buffer is de facto introduced. In 15 years, many of the well-known economic waves also fit. At the same time, it is appropriate to manage the risk of a reserve shortage. It should be a buffer that may move with you, not a deficit that occurs for a longer period of time and deepens when the tide is against us. Simply put, we have to make sure that there is little chance that someone will get so long or so deep under water that he cannot come up again. And for that, the one-year term  as long as there is room for customization  is a sensible approach. Realism requires thinking about a fallback position This brings me to the third key concept in my argument: realism. It is important that you have a realistic picture of the risks you run, but also the risks your participants can and want to run with regard to their pension assets. The average Dutch person is risk-averse when it comes to pensions. In that respect, he or she not only seems to be a bit more conservative than the average pension fund manager. The average Dutch person also wants to see their own risk profile reflected in their pension fund. This is clear from surveys conducted by the Dutch Central Bank. It shows that almost half of the respondents are willing to pay a higher pension contribution for more certainty about the final pension payment. The great social importance of pension funds and the conservative risk profile of the participants require careful management. Before all efforts are focused on achieving a high return, it must always be assessed to what extent the investments are in line with the structure of the liabilities. There are many possibilities for this. For example, new forms of investment can be used to match liabilities and investments. An overlay strategy makes it possible to add a certain exposure to a portfolio very precisely, without radically changing the portfolio itself. This makes it possible to steer the risk profile of the pension balance sheet in the desired direction. An example of this is a long duration overlay, which extends the duration of the investments and reduces the interest rate risk. I am sure you will see a number of examples of this this afternoon. However, some asset managers also focus on adding extra returns to their overlay strategies. Through active management, the aim is to beat the market with these products. I can imagine that this higher return is an attractive prospect, especially now that the expected returns on traditional investments no longer reach the sky. But how realistic is it to count on a structurally higher return than the market? By definition, it is impossible for everyone to do better than the market average. At the end of the day, it's just a redistribution of investment returns and it's just a penny change. You can't afford the fundamental costs of an ageing population. This is not to conclude that active management cannot have added value. The key question that must always be asked is whether a financial product is sufficiently in line with the characteristics of a fund. It can be a wise investment. For example, an asset manager may focus on outperformance relative to the nominal liabilities of the fund in question. This contributes to the indexation possibilities. At the same time, the fund must be able to bear the associated risk. Whereas in the past the focus was mainly on return and risk, we now know that the combination of return, risk and their relationship to the liabilities must be central. In other words, as a fund, you can take risks if you have sufficient buffers to absorb those risks. Ultimately, the cost of retirement is determined by the 'pension deal' in combination with the degree of security, and not by the financing set-up with any innovative financial instruments. We also have to face up to the fact that the bill cannot be passed on to the future indefinitely. A good pension costs money. When it comes to pensions, people seem to be much less aware of value for money. Everyone would like to pay the lowest possible pension contribution, and rightly so. And in the past, no one was surprised by long-term premium reductions or even exemptions. But then one must also accept the other side of the coin. It is not realistic to count on an indexed, reliable retirement provision without paying the corresponding bill. That is why Minister De Geus calls on you to focus your policy on ensuring that your fund is structurally at and above balance. We don't have to go far from home to find examples of how not to do it. In the United Kingdom, pension funds are faced with such large funding shortfalls that many DB schemes have now been converted to DC schemes. Future generations will be careful not to foot the bill for deficits that have arisen in the past. Coverage shortages are also commonplace in the United States. There are many examples of stamped pension rights there. Here, too, the DNB survey has indicated that the Dutch prefer DB to DC. In the Netherlands, we see that the social partners are taking different paths to strengthen the financial position of the funds. In doing so, it is sometimes decided to shift all risks to participants and pensioners. If this has been jointly chosen, then this may be very legitimate  even under the obligation  but it makes transparency all the more important. After all, in fact, a different pension system with a different type of risk-sharing is chosen. This cannot be attributed to the FTK; The supervisory framework does make the risks of the agreed pension contract visible. Of course, the FTK can be criticized. What is perfect? An open and robust debate is healthy and makes things better. But the rules of openness and transparency apply there too. What I would find unfortunate is that proposals to radically overhaul the Dutch pension system are wrapped up in a jacket of 'The FTK is no good'. After all, in doing so, we are doing each other and the (political) debate a disservice. Completion I will conclude. It is clear that risk management is an extremely important core activity for your pension fund. You need to be prepared for a bad outcome. A lawyer can't have a strategy that he never loses. At the same time, I have tried to make it clear that knowing and managing risks is not the same as not taking risks. Your freedom to invest is also not curtailed by rigid rules. But you will need to be able to make an adequate trade-off between risk and return, in relation to the liabilities. And you will have to demonstrate that where you run this, you can actually bear the risk. In doing so, you also contribute to the necessary confidence in pension schemes. That is your challenge. And I think you can succeed in doing so, given the successful efforts you have made in recent years to get the pension system back on its feet. At the same time, there is a challenge for market parties, including your host. I said earlier that financial instruments can help, for example, to hedge all or part of the interest rate risk. Of course, this comes at a price, but it does not increase the cost of retirement. Above all, it means that the risk is reduced. By using various financial products, tailored to your fund-specific situation. And by using various forms of expertise that help you to gain insight into the financial instruments and to arrive at a well-considered policy judgment. Together, we can give the Dutch pension system a good and transparent future.

D.E. Witteveen Het thema van dit seminar luidt: Pensioen anders bekeken. De logische vraag is dan: hoezo anders? Vanuit welk perspectief kijk je normaal gesproken aan tegen pensioen? De organisatoren hebben gekozen voor een financile invalshoek.
