The main sources of growth are export and investment, while private consumption lags behind. The export of China now represents about 7% of world export, a doubling since the turn of the century. With an export ratio of 35% gdp and an inflow of foreign direct investment of 60 billon last year, China is a very open economy. But it is also a dual economy: the developed eastern and southern coastal areas are an open economy, whereas the other areas are underdeveloped and closed. Measured in dollar gdp, China is the fourth-largest economy in the world, leapfrogging over France and the United Kingdom. Only the United States, Japan and Germany are larger. When China is able to maintain its high economic growth, it will overtake these countries in the first half of this century. A simple tentative calculation may illustrate things (Chart 1 China catching up). When China s real gdp grows at a yearly rate of 8%, Germany and Japan at 2% and the United States at 3%, China will have overtaken Germany in 2010, Japan in 2020 and the United States in 2042. Of course this is just a simple arithmetic extrapolation and future reality might turn out very different. In order to assess China s future economic development, I shall now discuss the main strengths and weaknesses of its economy. The first element contributing to high economic growth is the high investment of the private and the public sector of some 40% gdp. The government stimulates the development of new technology, high grade foreign investment and R&D. The second growth factor is the abundant supply of labour. In the rural areas, where some 500 million persons are employed, people switch from low tech agriculture to more productive industrial activities and services. This process will continue in the next decades. Last but not least, economic reforms such as the restructuring of state companies and banks go on, which raise productivity of labour and capital. But China has also problems, which are to some degree interrelated. Market incentives are still weak and dont sufficiently feed back into economic decisions. The financial sector is stronger than a few years ago,but the banks remain under control of the central and local government. There are pressures to allocate credit on the basis of political conditions, particularly at the local level. Becauselow interest rates do not reflect economic risks, cheap and easy financing leads to overinvestment. The resulting overcapacity in many sectorsdoes not trigger lower investment, so overcapacity and imbalances tend to continue, putting downward pressure on prices. Because p rivate consumption growth is sluggish as households save due to the lack of social security, pension provisions and health care, enterprises shift to export to keep up capacity utilization. The outcome is unbalanced economic growth, with a high growth of investment and export, and private consumption lagging behind. Another, related problem is growing regional income disparity. The rural areas of China, where 60% of the population lives, benefit less from the economic boom in the east and south. In the urban areas, average per capita income is three times as high as in the rural areas (Chart 2 Real disposable income per capita in China). This means a low consumption capacity in rural areas. Moreover, it leads to social unrest, which is aggravated by the forced acquisition of farming land for cities and factories and by the corrupt and capricious way of acting of local officials. Last year 87.000 public order disturbances were officially recorded. Eventually, this may threaten stable economic growth. In all, China has a high growth capacity, besides serious problems such as a weak financial sector, overcapacity, high savings and growing regional income inequality. These problems are to a certain extent interlinked. When the country manages to solve these problems, the abundant sources of economic growth will make their influence felt. But when the problems are not solved and are getting worse, there is a chance that the economy will stagnate, maybe for a long time. My own guess is that the authorities of China will be able to solve the problems or at least can control them. Helpful is the fact that the Chinese leadership has shown an pragmatic attitude to economic issues and not an ideological one. Global current account imbalances Now, I turn to the next topic, global imbalances, which is closely related to China's development and problems. The United States has a high and growing deficit on its current account and China, Russia and the Middle East area have a surplus. In the last few years, both surpluses and deficits have widened, largely due to higher oil prices. As an illustration I present some figures (Table 1 Current account balance ( billions) and (Chart 3 Current account balance (% gdp). In 2005 the United States had an all-time high deficit on current account of 800 billion, corresponding to 6% gdp. Now, May 2006, it has reached 7% gdp already. Chinas surplus on current account doubled to 160 billion last year, corresponding to 7% gdp, with international reserves exceeding 800 billion, the highest of any country. Due to higher oil prices, the surplus on the current account of the Middle East tripled in two years, from about 60 billion in 2003 to nearly 200 billion in 2005, corresponding to 19% gdp. One of the most important drivers in the development of global imbalances has been the decline of savings in the United States. In recent years house prices have increased, thereby raising households net wealth, providing more capacity to borrow and spend. This boosted private consumption and lowered household savings. In recent years, accommodative monetary policy in the US has contributed to a low long-term rate of interest, thereby adding to the price increase of houses. Besides, the rise of the budget deficit of the United States has lowered public savings. Another important driver in global imbalances is the exchange rate policy of China and the Middle East surplus countries. China stabilizes its currency, the renminbi, within a narrow range against the US dollar by intervening in the market and investing the dollar reserves largely in American government bonds. In this way it prevents the appreciation of the renminbi, which would exert a downward pressure on its trade surplus after some time. Due to this exchange rate policy, the imbalance continues and the stockpiling of dollar reserves goes on. The Middle East surplus countries also invest part of their petrodollars in American government bonds. Altogether, the demand for American bonds contributes to a low long term interest rate of the United States and simulates private consumption, reducing household saving and widening the deficit on current account. Global rebalancing necessary The most apparent fact characterizing global imbalances is the size and the resilience of the current account deficit of the United States of 7% gdp. This leads to an accumulating stock of liabilities, with a growing risk of disorderly unwinding, damaging economic development. A market driven adjustment would involve a depreciation of the dollar, which boosts exports and lowers imports. Besides, a market driven decrease in house prices would reduce the growth of consumer spending, raising household savings and narrowing the deficit on current account. When the adjustment proceeds orderly and gradually, the world economy can absorb the drop in demand and the risks to the financial system can probably be contained. So far, the United States has had little trouble in funding the current account deficit, with international investors willing to buy great quantities of US assets, among others Asian central banks. A more risky scenario, however, unfolds when international investors lose confidence in the dollar and reduce their dollar assets. Asian central banks might stop buying US government bonds by diversifying their reserves away from the dollar. The resulting lower value of the dollar carries a risk of downward overshooting, entailing a higher interest rate, resulting in a recession in the United States with global repercussions. Because of these risks, policy actions are necessary to facilitate an orderly adjustment of excessive current account deficits and surpluses. Global rebalancing requires commitment and cooperation of main global economic players. As to the United States, this policy would include fostering household savings, by way of - among others - a higher long-term interest rate. Just as much a reduction of the government budget deficit seems necessary. The euro area can contribute by enhancing the resilience of its economy to external negative shocks that may entail a global adjustment. In this respect, more flexibility of the European markets and improvement of the competitive position are essential. China and the Middle East countries can contribute to global rebalancing by allowing for a more flexible exchange rate of their currency to the dollar, as well as switching to more domestic expenditure. Last month, I attended the IMFs annual meeting where global imbalances were discussed. In order to resolve trade imbalances, it was agreed that the IMF will organise multilateral consultations and procedures between the countries with the largest imbalances. I welcome this decision as a step forward to address the problem of global imbalances. The best way countries can contribute is, in my view, when they adjust their economic policy mix in a way that is also necessary for the rebalancing of their own domestic economy and implement reforms that they should have carried out anyway. This brings me to the topic of Chinas contribution to global rebalancing, which I will discuss next. Chinas contribution to global rebalancing In the United States, many blame the high current account deficit and, especially the bilateral trade deficit with China, on that country pegging its currency at an artificially low level. Last year, the bilateral trade deficit of the Unites States with China amounted to 200 billion, nearly a quarter of the US deficit on current account. About a year ago the peg of the renminbi exchange rate to the dollar was replaced by a basket of the dollar, the euro and some Asian currencies, which was allowed to fluctuate by 0,3% in daily trading. The change in regime was accompanied by a revaluation of the renminbi by 2,1% against the dollar. Since this revaluation, however, the Chinese currency has only risen by a further 1% or some more. The Chinese authorities are reluctant to move rapidly to a substantial revaluation because of the risks involved. In their view, a strong revaluation of the renminbi has two risks for China. The first risk is the weakening of the agricultural sector. Revaluation makes imported agricultural products cheaper and agricultural export more expensive. The fall in income and economic activity of farmers in the rural areas would widen the growing gap between rural and urban incomes, which might make social unrest even worse. Second, a strong revaluation will diminish the value of the dollar assets of banks, thereby weakening their balance position, which is already vulnerable due to the still high non-performing loans. This illustrates that China s problems are interrelated and that especially the regional inequality limits the authorities scope for monetary policy. The high surplus on the current account of China reflects the high national savings, which exceed 40% gdp. Due to a low level of social security, pensions and public health, households save a quarter of disposable income to cope with unexpected expenditure for sickness, job loss and old age. In the rural areas the potential for consumption is low because of poverty and the low level of consumption related infrastructure such as roads, electricity and water. Business savings are high as state companies do not pay dividend to the state and retain their profits for making investment. On account of the underdeveloped capital markets, private enterprises are thrown back on own savings when they cannot get bank loans. The external imbalance of China thus reflects its internal imbalance, such as overcapacity, high savings and regional income disparity. For China, reducing the internal imbalance is the best remedy to reduce external imbalance. It is a necessary condition for the country to move towards a more flexible exchange rate system. Improvement of social security and pensions and better public health service will lower household precautionary savings and reduce the surplus of saving over investment, thereby contributing to diminishing global imbalances. In order to counter inequality and stimulate private consumption, the government will raise spending on social security, pensions, public health and education, especially in rural areas. In the recently accepted Eleventh Five-Year Plan, this policy of a New Socialist Countryside was explicitly laid down. Two weeks ago, the central bank of China increased bank-lending interest rate by 27 basis points, leaving deposit rates unchanged. This reflects a policy of curbing overinvestment and heading off overheating of the economy, while shielding consumption at the same time. It signals the governments goal to redirect growth towards consumption and away from exports and investment. It may also illustrate that China is willing to let markets play a role, and not only relies on administrative measures. The aim of the Chinese authorities is, ultimately, to move to more flexibility in the exchange rate system. But China will carry this out in a gradual and controllable manner, when the financial system is strong enough, regional disparities have fallen and social tensions have lessened. Because this policy seizes at the fundamental features of China internal imbalance, it is a sustainable and appropriate contribution of China to global rebalancing. Sequencing of capital account liberalisation, more flexibility of the exchange rate, reform of the financial sector and a rise in private consumption should be chosen in such a way, that imbalances within China do not grow further. In this way China can contribute to an orderly unwinding of global imbalances. Apart from that, a large and abrupt rise in the renminbi is not desirable because this could possibly entail unpredictable and destabilizing effects on the main currencies. Therefore, any adjustment of the renminbi should be spread over some years, gradually accommodating market forces by widening the band within which it fluctuates. Conclusion To conclude, all parties involved should step up their efforts to resolve global imbalances. For the United States , this would include tightening of monetary and fiscal policy to increase private and public saving. China will not strongly raise the exchange rate of its currency in the short run, because that would damage the agricultural sector, as well as the fragile banking system. The surplus on current account of China reflects its internal imbalance. Reducing this is the best remedy for China to improve its external balance. Economic policy is acting in this direction by reforming the financial system, reducing income inequality and improving social security provisions and pensions, which stimulates household consumption and reduces the need for precautionary saving. In the end, the world economy will benefit from a high and balanced economic growth of China. Consumers profit from the lower prices of goods imported from China and for global business there is a growing export market. China is a chance, not only a threat. The rise of the country challenges us to renovate, revitalize and adjust our economies, in particular the labour market. Only then we will reap the fruit of a rising China. Title: President Wellink's speech on 'The future of the Dutch welfare state'
text: President Wellink's speech on 'The future of the Dutch welfare state' Speech Date: May 19, 2006 Time: 11:00 a.m. Location Anniversary celebration of the Study Society for Economic Policy Speaker Dr. A.H.E.M. Wellink When I was still a member of the study group for Economic Policy, I didn't have to travel far from my home to the meetings in De Wittenburg Castle, and for this anniversary celebration I only had to walk out of my office. The study group is therefore very close to me, both literally and figuratively, and I would therefore like to congratulate you on the 75th anniversary. You have asked me to give a speech on the theme 'now', which I consider to be a testimony to the undiminished enthusiasm with which the study group studies the world around us. In order to leave time for the other festive activities today, I will limit the theme to the question of what reforms are needed now to keep the Dutch welfare state social and affordable in the future. Compared to many other countries, the Netherlands has an extensive and largely publicly funded welfare state. A welfare state has at least three possible functions: redistribution from rich to poor, redistribution over the life course and insurance of labour market risks. The Dutch welfare state fulfils all these functions, for example through social assistance, state pension and benefits in the event of unemployment and disability. These schemes are often universal in nature and are largely publicly funded, which means that in the Netherlands we spend about a quarter of our national income on public social schemes. In this respect, the Netherlands resembles many continental European countries and Scandinavia, while other industrialised countries, such as the UK, the US and OECD countries outside Europe, have significantly lower social public spending. The differences between the industrialised countries are less pronounced if we take into account the fact that not all social expenditure is financed by public funds. Some functions of the welfare state are fulfilled by private arrangements between employers and employees, and are not reflected in public spending. An example is the pension system, or the WAO gap insurance with which the reduction in the WAO benefit in the 1990s was repaired. These schemes are sometimes stimulated by tax breaks, which is also not visible in public spending. On the other hand, the government also taxes public social spending, for example by taxing benefits or indirectly by levying VAT. A better measure of the size of the welfare state is therefore total social spending, both privately and publicly funded and adjusted for taxation and tax exemptions. A study by the OECD shows that in 2001 total social spending in the United States was about the same as in the Netherlands, mainly because American health care costs are largely privately financed. Incidentally, an important difference is that many schemes in the US do not cover the general economy. For example, despite high health care expenditures, many Americans are not insured for health care. In recent years, the Dutch welfare state has undergone a radical reform, in which the role of the government in several areas has been replaced by private provision within legal frameworks. An example of this is the recent reform of health insurance. The Dutch ambition to insure everyone against health care has not changed  insurance is now even compulsory  but private insurers and former health insurance funds are now competing with each other in its implementation. As a result, the knowledge that insurers have about the medical sector can lead to a more efficient care offer. In the design of the welfare state, therefore, we must choose not only how much redistribution and insurance is desirable, but also how it is offered. Public services create a high tax burden, which has a negative effect on potential growth. Private provision combined with few legal frameworks leads to incomplete coverage, especially for people with lower incomes. The recent reforms of the welfare state in the Netherlands have mainly been driven by problems with specific arrangements, and have been taken in economically difficult times. In addition to the introduction of the new health care system, this government has also reformed the WAO and abolished the pre-pension. The distortive effect of both schemes had increased over time. In 2003, for example, nearly one million people received disability benefits, an increase of almost 350% compared to 1970. In a recession, the will for reform sometimes seems greater than in good times, perhaps because the inefficiencies of existing schemes are more visible and the public budget has less room for manoeuvre. Of course, this does not mean that reforms are popular. It is precisely in a disappointing economic situation that reforms hurt more  for example, people returning to the labour market have a better chance of finding a job in a tight labour market than when unemployment rises. In the Netherlands, there is strong and constant support for the welfare state, and it is therefore not surprising that recent reforms have led to increased dissatisfaction with socio-economic policies for years. In a 2004 survey by the Netherlands Institute for Social Research, only 15% of respondents gave their socio-economic policy a satisfactory rating, compared with 50% in 2000 (Note 1). This higher dissatisfaction is related to a general decline in trust in the government, but cannot be attributed to that alone. In other policy areas, such as education, the environment, childcare and culture, twice as many people were positive in 2004 than in 2000. In the same survey, two-thirds of those surveyed in 2004 indicated that income differences in the Netherlands were too large, and 55% mentioned maintaining social security as an important policy priority for politicians. Over a longer period of time, support for the welfare state has remained high and constant, according to a survey of opinion polls conducted by the Netherlands Institute for Social Research since 1970 (Note 2). When the economic environment deteriorates, support for parts of the welfare state, for example for public services, decreases but remains at a high level. The strong support for the welfare state in the Netherlands is in line with our views on the determinants of social success. International comparative research shows that the Dutch relatively often attribute social success to "luck", while "bad luck" is seen as an important cause of poverty. A comparative analysis of public social spending in 59 countries, carried out here at DNB, shows that public opinion about the causes of poverty is an important explanation for international differences in the size of the welfare state. The greater the percentage of residents who see "bad luck" as the main cause of poverty, the greater the public social spending. Another striking outcome is a negative correlation between income inequality and redistribution. The higher the pre-tax income inequality, the lower public social spending as a percentage of GDP. This connection, which is in line with recent academic studies, is linked to people's belief that they can influence their own destiny. People are more likely to accept the market's income distribution if they are more convinced that it is the result of individual effort rather than luck. Support for the welfare state seems to be a reason to pause new reforms, but it is precisely in an improving economy that adjustments are less painful. From the constant and strong support of a large part of the Dutch population for the welfare state, you could draw the conclusion that further reforms are undesirable, or at least electorally unwise. I do not do so for the following reasons. First of all, people are often more likely to speak out in surveys for extra spending than for their funding. In the 2004 survey by the Netherlands Institute for Social Research, 63% of respondents wanted to see an increase in spending on public services, and 66% wanted government spending to remain the same or decrease. Reconciling these desires implies austerity or, more likely, rising budget deficits. Second, Dutch society is changing due to various trends, namely globalisation, individualisation and ageing, which may undermine solidarity and increase the inefficiencies of current schemes. It is precisely in order to preserve the good and social aspects of the welfare state in this force field that new reforms are needed. The current favourable economic climate offers an important opportunity to implement these reforms with relative ease, and we should not miss it. I will now turn to the ways in which globalisation, individualisation and ageing affect the welfare state. Globalisation can put pressure on funding for the welfare state and lead to increasing income inequality, reducing support for social spending. Greater international competition between companies is incompatible with Dutch taxes that are much higher than our neighbouring countries or inefficient regulations that drive up companies' wage costs. In addition, globalisation may lead to a larger pay gap between low- and high-skilled workers in the future. The increase in international trade is leading to the specialisation of developed countries such as the Netherlands in the production of knowledge-intensive goods and services. Work is becoming more complex due to the intensive use of new machines with advanced applications, which is likely to increase the demand for higher-skilled workers more than the demand for lower-skilled workers. The DNB Household Panel, a periodic survey of 1500 households, shows that Dutch people with a high income are more likely to think that people should take care of themselves than people with a low income. Greater income disparities could thus lead to greater acceptance of income inequality, and thus less to solidarity. In addition, the level of education of people with a foreign background lags behind that of native Dutch people, partly due to their relatively high drop-out rate in secondary education. Increasing income disparities in a partially segregated labour market can put pressure on the willingness to contribute to a collectively organised social security system. Social and cultural changes are leading to an increasing individualization of Dutch society, to which we have to adapt the organization of the welfare state. In the 1960s and 1970s, Dutch society was still a breadwinner society, with a relatively equal distribution of education and income. Social services, which had a high degree of uniformity, covered the income risks for the largest group of people. The breadwinner model has now been replaced by a one-and-a-half-income model, but there are also more single men and women, with or without children. The variety of employment contracts has also increased, with more temporary contracts and part-time employees. Our welfare state does not respond sufficiently to this new situation. The Netherlands, for example, has become the international champion of part-time work, partly due to the incentives provided by our welfare state. The high marginal tax on labour for the second earner in a household, usually the woman, discourages full-time work. Other bottlenecks to greater participation in the labour market are the relatively expensive childcare for high incomes, school hours that do not match working hours and the lack of affordable after-school care. Some of these bottlenecks also hamper the participation of single parents in the labour market. Partly as a result of this, dependence on benefits is concentrated in a limited number of groups, and this concentration is expected to increase rather than decrease in the future. The ageing of the Dutch population necessitates measures to maintain the affordability of the welfare state. Currently, there are five employees for every pensioner in the Netherlands, but in the next three decades this ratio will change to two to five. In the same period, revenues from the Dutch gas bubble will fall sharply. The Netherlands Bureau for Economic Policy Analysis (CPB) recently published a report in which the consequences for public finances up to 2040 are calculated (Note 3). Because spending on the state pension and health care will rise sharply and income will not increase sufficiently, unchanged policy will lead to an increasing national debt and unsustainable public finances. According to the CPB calculations, saving for the ageing population means that the next government will have to create a substantial structural surplus in the government budget, which will then have to be held for years until the government debt is turned into a positive asset. Both doing nothing and the savings variant ultimately amount to austerity, in anticipation of the ageing population or enforced when public finances become unsustainable. Preventing public finances from becoming unsustainable is better than cure, which is why the next government should both save and take measures to reduce the costs of an ageing population. Globalisation, individualisation and ageing are trends that are surrounded by uncertainties, but in all scenarios an increase in labour participation in the Netherlands is necessary. Higher labour force participation, in terms of people but also in hours, improves the affordability of the welfare state and helps to prevent long-term inactivity among certain groups. Forced adjustment in bad economic times is more painful and possibly less equitable than a deliberate gradual adjustment, which allows people to prepare for change in a timely manner. In addition, uncertainty about the sustainability of our welfare state undermines trust in the government, and thus people's confidence in economic development. The question of how big the role of the government should be in the provision of collective insurance and income redistribution in the future is mainly a political choice. In a recent study, the Netherlands Bureau for Economic Policy Analysis (CPB) outlined several possible future directions for the Dutch welfare state, with their advantages and disadvantages (Note 4). One variant, the targeted welfare state, is based on the flexibilisation of the labour market and a retiring government, and thus goes in the direction of the Anglo-Saxon model. Lower benefits and taxes increase employment, but so does income inequality. The main risk is the creation of a group of people left behind who remain dependent on social services due to the poverty trap. Another variant, the universal welfare state, is also based on the flexibilisation of the labour market, but in combination with extensive redistribution and collective schemes aimed at increasing participation. The preservation, or even increase, of public social spending is exchanged for less privacy and freedom of choice, because a strict and activating government policy is needed to keep labor participation high. In this variant, the Netherlands is moving towards the Scandinavian model, which seems to be very popular these days. Incidentally, these models also conceal large differences between countries. Therefore, a discussion on models cannot replace a discussion on specific measures. The Dutch rightly attach great importance to our welfare state, which will come under pressure from globalization, individualization and an aging population. In order to preserve the good and social aspects of our system, reforms are necessary. The reforms that I am proposing are mainly about increasing the employment rate, which will not happen overnight. Because of this, and in order to enable people to prepare for the reforms, now is the time to decide on new reforms. My preference is for measures that are mainly aimed at increasing labour market participation. Note 1: Netherlands Institute for Social Research, The Social State of the Netherlands 2005, September 2005. Note 2: SCP, 2005, Support for the welfare state in public opinion, 1970-2002, SCP publication 2005/3. Noot 3: CPB, Ageing and the Sustainability of Dutch Public Finances, 2006. Noot 4: Centraal Planbureau, Reinventing the welfare state, 2006.
text_original: Speech president Wellink over 'De toekomst van de Nederlandse verzorgingsstaat' Speech Datum 19 mei 2006 Tijd 11:00 uur Lokatie Lustrumviering van het Studiegezelschap voor Economische Politiek Spreker Dr. A.H.E.M. Wellink Toen ik nog lid was van het studiegezelschap voor Economische Politiek hoefde ik niet ver te reizen van mijn huis naar de bijeenkomsten in Kasteel De Wittenburg, en voor deze lustrumviering hoefde ik alleen maar mijn werkkamer uit te lopen. Het studiegezelschap staat mij dus letterlijk en figuurlijk zeer na, en ik wil u daarom van harte feliciteren met het 75-jarig bestaan. U heeft me gevraagd een speech te houden met als thema nu, wat ik beschouw als een getuigenis van het onverminderd grote enthousiasme waarmee het studiegezelschap de wereld om ons heen bestudeert. Om nog tijd over te houden voor de andere feestelijke activiteiten vandaag, zal ik het thema beperken tot de vraag welke hervormingen nu nodig zijn om de Nederlandse verzorgingsstaat in de toekomst sociaal en betaalbaar te houden. In vergelijking met veel andere landen heeft Nederland een uitgebreide en grotendeels publiek gefinancierde verzorgingsstaat. Een verzorgingsstaat heeft tenminste drie mogelijke functies: herverdeling van rijk naar arm, herverdeling over de levensloop en verzekering van arbeidsmarktrisicos. De Nederlandse verzorgingsstaat vervult al deze functies, bijvoorbeeld door de bijstand, AOW en uitkeringen bij werkloosheid en arbeidsongeschiktheid. Deze regelingen hebben vaak een universeel karakter en worden grotendeels publiek gefinancierd, waardoor we in Nederland ongeveer een kwart van ons nationaal inkomen uitgeven aan publieke sociale regelingen. Nederland lijkt in dit opzicht op veel continentaal-Europese landen en Scandinavi, terwijl andere gendustrialiseerde landen, zoals het VK, de VS en OESO-landen buiten Europa, aanmerkelijk lagere sociale publieke uitgaven hebben. De verschillen tussen de gendustrialiseerde landen zijn minder groot wanneer we rekening houden met het feit dat niet alle sociale uitgaven worden gefinancierd met publieke gelden.Sommige functies van de verzorgingsstaat worden ingevuld door private regelingen tussen werkgevers en nemers, en komen niet in de publieke uitgaven tot uiting. Een voorbeeld is het pensioenstelsel, of de WAO-hiaatverzekering waarmee de verlaging van de WAO-uitkering in de jaren 90 is gerepareerd. Deze regelingen worden soms gestimuleerd door belastingvoordelen, wat ook niet zichtbaar is in de publieke uitgaven. Aan de andere kant heft de overheid ook belasting op de publieke sociale uitgaven, bijvoorbeeld door uitkeringen te belasten of indirect door BTW te heffen. Een betere maatstaf voor de omvang van de welvaartstaat zijn daarom de totale sociale uitgaven, zowel privaat als publiek gefinancierd en gecorrigeerd voor belastingheffing en belastingvrijstellingen. Uit een studie van de OESO blijkt dat in 2001 de totale sociale uitgaven in de Verenigde Staten ongeveer gelijk waren aan de Nederlandse, vooral doordat de Amerikaanse zorgkosten grotendeels privaat worden gefinancierd. Overigens is een belangrijk verschil dat veel regelingen in de VS niet algemeen dekkend zijn. Ondanks de hoge zorguitgaven zijn bijvoorbeeld veel Amerikanen niet verzekerd voor ziektekosten. De afgelopen jaren is de Nederlandse verzorgingsstaat ingrijpend hervormd, waarbij de rol van de overheid op meerdere terreinen is vervangen door privaat aanbod binnen wettelijke kaders. Een voorbeeld daarvan is de recente hervorming van de ziektekostenverzekeringen. De Nederlandse ambitie om iedereen tegen ziektekosten te verzekeren is onveranderd  verzekering is tegenwoordig zelfs verplicht  maar bij de uitvoering concurreren particuliere verzekeraars en voormalige ziekenfondsen tegenwoordig met elkaar. Hierdoor kan de kennis die de verzekeraars hebben over de medische sector leiden tot een efficinter zorgaanbod. Bij de inrichting van de verzorgingsstaat moeten we dus niet alleen kiezen hoeveel herverdeling en verzekering wenselijk is, maar ook hoe die wordt aangeboden. Publieke voorziening zorgt voor een hoge belastingdruk, wat een negatief effect op de potentile groei heeft. Private voorziening in combinatie met weinig wettelijke kaders leidt tot onvolledige dekking, vooral bij mensen met lagere inkomens. De recente hervormingen van de verzorgingsstaat in Nederland zijn vooral gedreven door problemen met specifieke regelingen, en zijn genomen in economisch moeilijke tijden. Naast de invoering van het nieuwe zorgstelsel, heeft dit kabinet ook de WAO hervormd en het prepensioen afgeschaft. Het verstorende effect van beide regelingen was in de loop van de tijd steeds groter geworden. Zo ontvingen in 2003 bijna een miljoen mensen een arbeidsongeschiktheidsuitkering, een stijging van bijna 350% ten opzicht van 1970. In een recessie lijkt de wil tot hervorming soms groter dan in goede tijden, misschien omdat de inefficinties van bestaande regelingen zichtbaarder zijn en de overheidsbegroting minder ruimte heeft. Dit betekent natuurlijk niet dat hervormingen populair zijn. Juist in een tegenvallende conjunctuur doen hervormingen meer pijn  zo hebben herintredende WAO-ers meer kans op een baan in een krappe arbeidsmarkt dan wanneer de werkloosheid stijgt. In Nederland bestaat een grote en constante steun voor de verzorgingsstaat, en daarom is het niet verwonderlijk dat de recente hervormingen jaren hebben geleid tot meer ontevredenheid over het sociaal-economische beleid. In een onderzoek door het Sociaal en Cultureel Planbureau gaf in 2004 slechts 15% van de ondervraagden het sociaal-economische beleid een ruime voldoende, tegen 50% in 2000 (Noot 1). Deze grotere ontevredenheid hangt samen met een algemene daling van het vertrouwen in de overheid, maar kan niet alleen daaraan worden geweten. Over andere beleidsgebieden, zoals onderwijs, milieu, kinderopvang en cultuur oordeelden in 2004 twee keer zoveel mensen positief dan in het jaar 2000. In hetzelfde onderzoek gaf tweederde van de ondervraagden in 2004 aan de inkomensverschillen in Nederland te groot vinden, en 55% noemde handhaving van de sociale zekerheid als belangrijke beleidsprioriteit van de politiek. Over een langere periode bekeken is de steun voor de verzorgingsstaat groot en constant gebleven, zo blijkt uit een overzicht van opiniepeilingen van het Sociaal en Cultureel Planbureau sinds 1970 (Noot 2). Wanneer het economische klimaat verslechtert daalt steun voor onderdelen van de verzorgingsstaat, bijvoorbeeld voor openbare voorzieningen, maar blijft op een hoog niveau. De grote steun voor de verzorgingsstaat in Nederland sluit aan bij onze opvattingen over de determinanten van maatschappelijk succes. Uit internationaal vergelijkend onderzoek blijkt dat Nederlanders relatief vaak maatschappelijk succes toeschrijven aan geluk, terwijl pech als een belangrijke oorzaak van armoede wordt gezien. Bij een vergelijkende analyse van de publieke sociale uitgaven in 59 landen, die hier op DNB is uitgevoerd, blijkt dat mening van de bevolking over de oorzaken van armoede een belangrijke verklaring is voor internationale verschillen in de omvang van de verzorgingsstaat. Hoe groter het percentage inwoners dat pech als belangrijkste oorzaak van armoede ziet, hoe groter de publieke sociale uitgaven. Een andere opvallende uitkomst is een negatief verband tussen inkomensongelijkheid en herverdeling. Hoe groter de inkomensongelijkheid vr belastingen is, des te lager zijn de publieke sociale uitgaven als percentage van het bbp. Dit verband, dat in lijn is met recente academische studies, hangt samen met de overtuiging van mensen dat ze hun eigen lot kunnen benvloeden. Mensen accepteren de inkomensverdeling waar de markt op uitkomt sneller, naarmate ze er sterker van overtuigd zijn dat die het resultaat is van individuele inspanningen in plaats van geluk. De steun voor de welvaartstaat lijkt een reden om een pas op de plaats te maken met nieuwe hervormingen, maar juist in een aantrekkende economie doen aanpassingen minder pijn. Uit de constante en grote steun van een groot deel van de Nederlandse bevolking voor de verzorgingsstaat zou u de conclusie kunnen trekken dat verdere hervormingen onwenselijk zijn, of op zijn minst electoraal onverstandig. Ik doe dat niet, en wel om de volgende redenen. Ten eerste spreken mensen zich in enqutes vaak makkelijker uit voor extra uitgaven dan voor hun financiering. In de enqute van het Sociaal en Cultureel Planbureau uit 2004 wilde 63% van de ondervraagden een stijging van de uitgaven voor de openbare voorzieningen, en 66% dat de overheidsuitgaven gelijk zouden blijven of dalen. Het verenigen van deze wensen impliceert bezuinigingen of, waarschijnlijker, oplopende begrotingstekorten. Ten tweede verandert de Nederlandse samenleving door verschillende trends, namelijk globalisering, individualisering en vergrijzing, die de solidariteit kunnen ondergraven en de inefficinties van de huidige regelingen vergroten. Juist om de goede en sociale aspecten van de verzorgingsstaat in dit krachtenveld te behouden, zijn nieuwe hervormingen nodig. Het huidige, gunstige economische klimaat biedt een belangrijke kans om deze hervormingen relatief gemakkelijk in te voeren, en die moeten we niet laten lopen. Ik zal nu ingaan op de manieren waarop globalisering, individualisering en vergrijzing invloed hebben op de verzorgingsstaat. Globalisering kan de financiering voor de verzorgingsstaat onder druk zetten en zorgen voor toenemende inkomensongelijkheid, waardoor het draagvlak voor sociale uitgaven afneemt. Grotere internationale concurrentie tussen bedrijven verdraagt zich niet met Nederlandse belastingen die veel hoger zijn dan ons omringende landen of inefficinte regelingen die de loonkosten van bedrijven opdrijven. Daarnaast kan globalisering in de toekomst leiden tot een groter beloningsverschil tussen laag- en hoog opgeleiden. De toename van het internationale handelsverkeer leidt tot specialisatie van ontwikkelde landen als Nederland in de productie van kennisintensieve goederen en diensten. Werk wordt complexer door het intensieve gebruik van nieuwe machines met geavanceerde toepassingen, waardoor de vraag naar hoger opgeleide werknemers waarschijnlijk sterker zal stijgen dan de vraag naar lager opgeleide werknemers. Uit het DNB Household Panel, een periodieke enqute onder 1500 huishoudens, blijkt dat Nederlanders met een hoog inkomen vaker vinden dat mensen voor zichzelf moeten zorgen dan mensen met een laag inkomen. Grotere inkomensverschillen zouden op die manier kunnen leiden tot grotere acceptatie van inkomensongelijkheid, en daarmee minder tot solidariteit. Daarbij blijft het opleidingsniveau van allochtonen achter bij dat van autochtone Nederlanders, onder andere door hun relatief grote schooluitval in het voortgezet onderwijs. Toenemende inkomensverschillen op een gedeeltelijk gesegregeerde arbeidsmarkt kunnen de bereidheid om mee te betalen aan een collectief georganiseerde sociale zekerheid onder druk zetten. Sociale en culturele veranderingen zorgen voor een toenemende individualisering van de Nederlandse maatschappij, waarop we de organisatie van de verzorgingsstaat moeten aanpassen. In de jaren zestig en zeventig was de Nederlandse samenleving nog een kostwinnersmaatschappij, met een relatief gelijke spreiding van opleiding en inkomens. De sociale voorzieningen, die een grote mate van eenvormigheid kenden, dekten voor de grootste groep mensen de inkomensrisicos goed af. Inmiddels is het kostwinnersmodel vervangen door een anderhalfverdienersmodel, maar er zijn ook meer alleenstaande mannen en vrouwen, al dan niet met kinderen. Ook de variteit aan arbeidscontracten is toegenomen, met meer tijdelijke contracten en part-time werknemers. Onze verzorgingsstaat speelt niet voldoende in op deze nieuwe situatie. Nederland is bijvoorbeeld internationaal kampioen part-time werken geworden, mede door de prikkels die onze verzorgingsstaat geeft. De hoge marginale belasting op arbeid voor de tweede verdiener in een huishouden, doorgaans de vrouw, ontmoedigt voltijds werken. Andere knelpunten voor grotere participatie op de arbeidsmarkt zijn de relatief dure kinderopvang voor hoge inkomens, schooltijden die slecht aansluiten op werktijden en het gebrek aan betaalbare naschoolse opvang. Sommige van deze knelpunten belemmeren ook de participatie van alleenstaande ouders op de arbeidsmarkt. Mede hierdoor concentreert de afhankelijkheid van uitkeringen zich bij een beperkt aantal groepen, en naar verwachting wordt deze concentratie in de toekomst eerder groter dan kleiner. De vergrijzing van de Nederlandse bevolking maakt maatregelen noodzakelijk om de betaalbaarheid van de verzorgingsstaat te behouden. Nu staan naast elke gepensioneerde in Nederland vijf werknemers, maar in de komende drie decennia zal deze verhouding veranderen tot twee op vijf. In dezelfde periode zullen de inkomsten uit de Nederlandse gasbel sterk dalen. Het Centraal Planbureau heeft recent een rapport uitgebracht, waarin de gevolgen hiervan voor de overheidsfinancin tot 2040 worden doorgerekend (Noot 3). Doordat uitgaven voor de AOW en de zorg sterk zullen stijgen en de inkomsten onvoldoende stijgen, zal ongewijzigd beleid leiden tot een oplopende staatschuld en onhoudbare overheidsfinancin. Sparen voor de vergrijzing betekent volgens de CPB berekeningen dat het komende kabinet een fors structureel overschot op de overheidsbegroting tot stand moet brengen, dat vervolgens jaren moet worden vastgehouden tot de overheidsschuld is omgebogen in een positief vermogen. Zowel niets doen als de spaarvariant komt uiteindelijk neer op bezuinigingen, in anticipatie van de vergrijzing of afgedwongen wanneer de overheidsfinancin onhoudbaar worden. Voorkomen dat de overheidsfinancin onhoudbaar worden is beter dan genezen, en daarom zou het komende kabinet moeten zowel moeten sparen als maatregelen nemen die de kosten van de vergrijzing verkleinen. Globalisering, individualisering en vergrijzing zijn trends die met onzekerheden zijn omgeven, maar in alle scenarios is een verhoging van de arbeidsparticipatie in Nederland noodzakelijk. Hogere arbeidsparticipatie, in personen maar zeker ook in uren, verbetert de betaalbaarheid van de verzorgingsstaat en helpt langdurige inactiviteit onder bepaalde groepen te voorkomen. Afgedwongen aanpassing in slechte economische tijden is pijnlijker en mogelijk minder rechtvaardig dan een weloverwogen geleidelijke aanpassing, die mensen de mogelijkheid biedt zich tijdig voor te bereiden op veranderingen. Daarbij ondergraaft onzekerheid over de houdbaarheid van onze verzorgingsstaat het vertrouwen in de overheid, en daarmee het vertrouwen van mensen in de economische ontwikkeling. De vraag hoe groot de rol van de overheid in de voorziening van collectieve verzekeringen en inkomensherverdeling in toekomst moet zijn, is vooral een politieke keuze. In een recente studie heeft het Centraal Planbureau verschillende mogelijke toekomstrichtingen van de Nederlandse verzorgingsstaat geschetst, met hun voor- en nadelen (Noot 4). En variant, de gerichte verzorgingsstaat, gaat uit van flexibilisering van de arbeidsmarkt en een terugtredende overheid, en gaat daarmee in de richting van het Angelsaksische model. Door lagere uitkeringen en belastingen nemen de werkgelegenheid toe, maar ook de inkomensongelijkheid. Het belangrijkste risico is het ontstaan van een groep achterblijvers die door de armoedeval afhankelijk blijven van sociale voorzieningen. Een andere variant, de universele verzorgingsstaat, gaat ook uit van flexibilisering van de arbeidsmarkt, maar in combinatie met uitgebreide herverdeling en collectieve regelingen die gericht zijn op het vergroten van de participatie. Het behoud, of zelfs vergroten, van publieke sociale uitgaven wordt uitgeruild tegen minder privacy en keuzevrijheid, omdat een streng en activerend overheidsbeleid nodig is om de arbeidsdeelname hoog te houden. In deze variant gaat Nederland richting het Scandinavische model, dat tegenwoordig erg populair lijkt te zijn. Overigens gaan achter deze modellen ook weer grote verschillen tussen landen schuil. Een discussie over modellen kan daarom niet de discussie over specifieke maatregelen vervangen. Nederlanders hechten terecht sterk aan onze verzorgingsstaat, die onder druk zal komen van globalisering, individualisering en vergrijzing. Om de goede en sociale kanten van ons stelsel te behouden zijn hervormingen noodzakelijk. De hervormingen die ik voorstel hebben vooral betrekking op verhoging van de arbeidsparticipatie, wat niet van de ene op de andere dag zal gaan. Hierdoor, en om mensen in staat te stellen zich op de hervormingen voor te bereiden, is nu het moment om tot nieuwe hervormingen te besluiten. Mijn voorkeur gaat daarbij uit naar maatregelen die vooral zijn gericht op een verhoging van de arbeidsparticipatie. Noot 1: Sociaal en Cultureel Planbureau, De sociale staat van Nederland 2005, september 2005. Noot 2: SCP, 2005, Steun voor de verzorgingsstaat in de publieke opinie, 1970-2002, SCP publicatie 2005/3. Noot 3: CPB, Ageing and the Sustainability of Dutch Public Finances, 2006. Noot 4: Centraal Planbureau, Reinventing the welfare state, 2006.

Title: President Wellink's speech on 'Europe postponement means no cancellation'
text: President Wellink's speech on 'Europe postponement means no cancellation' Speech Date: 31 May 2006 Time: 09:17 hrs Location Odulphus Lyceum, Tilburg Speaker Dr. A.H.E.M. Wellink Jean Monnet said that no one can say today exactly what the structure of Europe will be tomorrow, because tomorrow's changes, brought about by today's changes, are unpredictable. Recent developments prove us right. Three years ago, at the invitation of Rector Korsten, I also gave a lecture on Europe. At the time, I could not have imagined that, partly because of the Dutch and French 'No' votes in the referendum on the European Constitution, the European project would have to be put on hold. In my contribution to this Masterclass, I reflect on what I consider to be the great success of the European integration project. In doing so, I will first sketch the historical perspective. I need this background to show that the current European challenges do not have to be insurmountable hurdles. In doing so, I will argue in favour of a consistent policy, without panic tactics. We'd better save that for the World Championship, which starts in a few days at our eastern neighbors. Historical perspective A large proportion of your pupils are probably less aware of the reasons for European cooperation. European integration began as a peace initiative. After the horrors of the Second World War, European politicians realised that a way had to be found not to tear Europe down again and again, but to rebuild it together. This also explains the solemn words of the Treaty establishing the European Coal and Steel Community, signed on 18 April 1951: 'Dear fellow Europeans, we must lay the foundations for a greater and closer community between the peoples who have long been divided by bloody struggles and lay the foundations for institutions capable of giving direction to a destiny that will henceforth be shared in the future'. This ideal of peace from the 1950s has not lost its importance today. The relatively recent bloodshed in the former Yugoslavia may serve as an illustration. The founding fathers of European cooperation assumed that peace is nurtured by mutual trust and solidarity. In turn, trust and solidarity are shaped and stimulated by integration. European cooperation began in 1951 with the establishment of the European Coal and Steel Community (ECSC), in which six countries  including the Netherlands  participated. It is no coincidence that it was precisely these products that were chosen: after all, coal and steel were the building blocks of the war industry. Moreover, coal, like oil today, was very important to the economy at the time. So the coal and steel industries were also of the utmost importance for Europe's recovery. Despite the success of the ECSC, a European Defence Community proved to be a bridge too far. From that moment on, the main focus has been on economic integration in the form of good trade relations within Europe and support for lagging regions. It is not surprising that economic integration turned out to be the prelude to European integration. After the Second World War, European cooperation was given a major boost by the Marshall Plan, with which the United States contributed financially to the reconstruction of Europe after 1948 (according to today's purchasing power of 105 billion dollars). The Marshall Plan was not pure charity. In addition to humanitarian reasons, strategic considerations also played a role. For example, the US wanted to prevent Western Europe, which had been reduced to rubble, from falling prey to communism. In addition, Europe was an important market for American exports. In short, security and solidarity were provided by economic means. The course of European integration The aim of the European Economic Community was to create a common market for all products and factors of production. It is not least thanks to the EEC that the Member States experienced great economic prosperity in the 1960s. From the beginning of the 1970s, the process of European integration stagnated. An important reason for this was the economic headwinds caused by the oil crises. Member states focused on their own problems and less on European cooperation. Another reason was the stubborn attitude of Charles de Gaulle who stretched Britain's accession process from 1961 to 1973. This caused a lot of tension between the Member States. De Gaulle was also opposed to further integration between the then member states and even wanted to reverse earlier integration steps. Although a large number of new Member States joined (Great Britain, Denmark, Ireland, Greece, Spain and Portugal), the European integration project was gaining momentum. The newspapers even coined the term 'Eurosclerosis'. At the same time, the member states realised the need for further European cooperation. For example, France's fear of having to play second fiddle to West Germany led to its rigid stance. West Germany had to seek rapprochement with its allies precisely because of their support for the reunification Ostpolitik. Furthermore, the economic and technological gap with Japan and the US was widening, and individual member states could not compete with such superpowers. International crises such as the Soviet occupation of Afghanistan and the Iranian revolution underscored this dwindling role of individual countries on the world stage and contributed to their readiness for deeper integration. The process of European integration was relaunched with the entry into force of the Single European Act in 1987. In this agreement, the Member States of the EEC agreed to remove the remaining barriers to the common market as provided for in 1957 by 31 December 1992 at the latest. The creation of the internal market, in which people, goods and services could move freely, naturally led Europe to a further deepening of integration. After 1992, there was still a major economic obstacle: exchange rates. The introduction of a single currency in the European Union would put an end to this. To achieve this, clear criteria were needed for factors that determine the value of a currency, such as the size of the government deficit, the inflation rate and interest rates. In 1992, the Heads of Government laid down these agreements in the Maastricht Treaty. The Maastricht criteria are intended to ensure that the participating countries are sufficiently similar in economic terms to be able to benefit from a common interest rate and exchange rate. Since 1 January 1999, the financial markets have been working with the euro as a book-entry currency. This was followed in 2002 by euro notes and coins, known as cash. The single currency thus became a fact. Of course, a country must not fall out of line even after it has been introduced. To this end, the fiscal rules are written in the Stability and Growth Pact. In spite of this Pact, the budgetary discipline of some countries is unfortunately in a bad state. Monetary union, in which a group of autonomous countries voluntarily decides to exchange their own currency for a common currency, is unique in the world. Without perhaps realising it every day, this is further proof that Europe has already achieved a great deal in terms of solidarity and mutual trust since the devastating Second World War. Enlargement of the EU Solidarity was also the driving force behind the European Union's next great project: the 2004 enlargement to the East. In the 1990s, the process of European integration received an important boost: the fall of the Iron Curtain. This last remnant of the Second World War had divided Europe for almost fifty years. After its disappearance, Europe was able to continue the search for the 'common destiny' together. With the accession of ten Eastern Bloc countries in May 2004, this historic and moral promise has been fulfilled. The economic and political stabilisation that will result from the integration of the entire European continent is invaluable, also for Dutch citizens. Not only because of the disappearance of the threat from the East that was so palpable for my generation. On a smaller scale, your recent exchange program with Polish colleague schools would have been unthinkable until recently. The financial consequences of enlargement have received a great deal of attention. Apart from the fact that the Dutch contribution has now been significantly reduced, this financial side is only a limited part of the story. The enlargement process also brings us economic benefits. As a result of the broadening of the internal market, the Dutch business community has more trade and investment opportunities. Another consequence of enlargement is migration. Due to the differences in wages, residents of the new Member States will emigrate to the rest of the EU. I don't expect this flow to be very extensive. Firstly, because full freedom of movement of persons will not be possible until 2011. Because income disparities are already smaller, fewer people will migrate. In addition, labour mobility in Europe appears to be low. For example, the expected large migration flows did not materialise after the accession of Spain and Portugal. Furthermore, the arrival of the proverbial Polish plumber also has advantages. They often fill low-skilled vacancies, which are difficult to fill in richer countries. Future challenges The EU's successes did not prevent a significant gap with its citizens from opening up unnoticed. After all, Europe was primarily shaped by the political will of a small number of direct stakeholders, such as the agricultural sector and the business community, supplemented by a select group with an interest in the European cause. In addition, the Brussels regulations are not very appealing due to their complexity and high technical content. However, as long as Europe was doing well, there was little reason for the people to stir. The Dutch and French 'No' votes in the referendum on the European Constitution inexorably revealed this gap. The text of the Constitution is to a large extent a consolidation of the existing legislation, supplemented by a recording of applicable case law. The truly constitutional articles were in the minority, and they too consisted largely of existing texts. The choice of the word "Constitution" was also less fortunate. People were taken by surprise by this document, which apparently would apply above the Dutch Constitution. The internet survey commissioned by Secretary of State Nicolai [NederlandinEuropa.nl, results published 19 May] also shows that the majority thinks that things were going too fast in Europe. Previous surveys have already shown that some voted against because of dissatisfaction with the state of affairs in their own country. Some politicians also did not hesitate to blame Europe for national problems. Incidentally, Europe does not stand still without a Constitution. As has been said, the Constitution is largely an amalgamation of existing treaties, which retain their validity. I am not advocating that the Constitution should simply be thrown in the rubbish bin. We should not conclude from the referendum result that the citizens are rejecting Europe. After all, Nicolai's survey shows that the majority of Nicolai still sees the usefulness of Europe. I can therefore understand President Barosso of the European Commission wanting to postpone a decision on the Constitution. He wants the Heads of Government to come up with a new political declaration in March 2007, around the celebration of the fiftieth anniversary of the Treaty of Rome. This declaration should address Europe's values and ambitions and how to achieve them. The debate on the ratification of the Constitution will then be reopened. It is up to the politicians to decide whether they want to continue with the Constitution as a whole, or whether they want to introduce the parts of it that are deemed most necessary. In any case, we must ensure that postponement does not become cancellation. That is why the coming period should be used to debate a number of sensitive issues. I will now deal with three of them. First administrative reforms, then citizen involvement, and finally Europe's geographical boundaries. Administrative reforms The objectives of the creation of the European Community were mainly internal, as reflected in the four freedoms (freedom of movement of persons, services, work and capital). In addition, the policy of reducing disadvantage in less-favoured areas and agricultural policy played a major role. The worldview has changed substantially under the influence of globalization. The emergence of new economies is striking. Other factors also play a role. Examples are demographic developments (ageing population), ideological shifts (such as the disappearance of the clear East-West division), technological progress (the internet) and energy supply (rising oil prices). Moreover, the EU is confronted with issues in the field of climate and the environment (greenhouse effect) that can no longer be tackled within Europe (let alone within the Netherlands). If Europe is to fulfil its potential to play an international role, it must respond appropriately and with one voice to these and other challenges of the 21st century. Europe's ability to act is determined by its governance model. However, this model was still largely based on a Community of six countries. That is why this model was overhauled in the run-up to the accession of the ten new Member States in 2004. A first attempt, the Treaty of Nice, was no more than a first step. More ambition was shown with the European Constitution signed on 29 October 2004. On a large number of subjects, the requirement for unanimous decision-making in the Council of Ministers has been replaced by qualified majority voting. As a result, an obstructionist would no longer be able to impede progress on its own. This is desperately needed; after all, in a Union of 25 or more Member States, there is a good chance that the unanimity requirement will lead to stagnation. The European Constitution would have raised the Council's decision-making capacity far beyond the level of the EU15. The influence of the large countries would increase slightly [8%], and that of countries such as the Netherlands would decrease [-7%]. Incidentally, the biggest shift here is due to the enlargement by ten countries and not to the possible changes made by the Constitution. Since the relinquishment of the right of veto entails a loss of sovereignty for the Member States, it is not surprising that there has been a strong protest against this. Nevertheless, decision-making in Europe must remain on the agenda to prevent further stagnation. Citizen involvement At the Laeken Summit in 2001, the Heads of Government gave new impetus to reducing the gap with citizens. While the Treaty of Nice, which has already been mentioned, brought few improvements, the Constitution took a major step in the right direction. The rejection of this is all the more regrettable, because it would have given an important boost to democratic legitimacy. Examples include more influence for the European Parliament, a better demarcation of European and national competences, the openness of Council meetings, a tightening of the principle of subsidiarity, the yellow card procedure with which Brussels could be reprimanded if it exceeded its powers, and the citizens' initiative, with which a subject can be put on the agenda in Brussels with a number of signatures. Although miracles should not be expected, these innovations could have helped to make Europe a living political movement in which citizens could identify. Surveys consistently show a positive basic attitude of citizens towards membership of the Union. This reinforces my confidence that the referendum result does not have to fundamentally change the future of Europe. In my opinion, the result has served as a starting signal for a stronger involvement of citizens in Europe. Better information provision is part of this. A survey conducted immediately after the referendum showed that the lack of information was an important reason for Dutch people to vote no (32%). For me, part of that information should be to highlight Europe's successes. For your pupils, a war within the EU may be almost unthinkable, but for my generation it is anything but. Furthermore, we sometimes forget how much our prosperity has increased in recent decades. Not only on a material level, but especially with regard to the intangible aspects. These include measures against discrimination, good working conditions, increased leisure time, greatly improved health care and attention to the environment. We must continue to bear this in mind, not least because otherwise our willingness to make sacrifices for the challenges of the EU in the 21st century will be diminished. Geographical expansion of the Union and the euro area The European project does not have to be finished after the current 25 countries have been enlarged to include Bulgaria and Romania and later possibly Turkey and Croatia. The EU is already in exploratory talks with Macedonia and countries in the Western Balkans. These processes may one day lead to accession and are already contributing to peace and security. Not only in those countries themselves, but also by reducing the threat of violence in our country. Following on from the quote from Monnet with which I began, it is perhaps better not to philosophize for too long about the ultimate geographical boundary of Europe. Our environment is so dynamic that it seems unwise to pin Europe down on a single course. Instead of formulating an end goal, it can also be emphasised that Europeans have common ground and common interests. If the Union denies access to potential candidates in advance, it is casting doubt on its own right to exist. However, with every subsequent expansion of the European house, we must first have completed the previous renovation. In this respect, Europe must learn from the complaint of many citizens that things have gone far too fast. The geographical enlargement of the Union will at some point be followed by the introduction of the euro. For example, the European Central Bank and the European Commission recently gave a positive opinion on Slovenia's adoption of the euro. Participation in the currency union will anchor the new Member States even more firmly in the common future of Europe. Moreover, we should not rush our accession to the currency union. After all, most of the new Member States started the transition to a market economy barely 15 years ago from a centrally planned economy and still have a long way to go. Conclusion Willy Brandt has already said that the history of the European Community is the history of its crises. We must therefore not be deterred by the current impasse. However, postponement must not mean cancellation. We need to make good use of the current period of reflection, for example by working towards greater citizen involvement. It is also appropriate to reflect on what we have already achieved, namely sixty years of peace and security. We should not worry too much about the EU's ultimate goal or its outer borders. It is better to increase our manageability and decisiveness, so that we can act adequately in the event of changes. There is still plenty to discuss about greater citizen involvement and greater governability and decisiveness, to which we can all make our contribution in the next forty-five minutes.
text_original: Speech president Wellink over 'Europa uitstel betekent geen afstel' Speech Datum 31 mei 2006 Tijd 09:17 uur Lokatie Odulphus Lyceum, Tilburg Spreker Dr. A.H.E.M. Wellink Jean Monnet zei dat niemand vandaag precies kan zeggen wat morgen de structuur van Europa kan zijn, omdat de veranderingen van morgen, teweeggebracht door de veranderingen van vandaag, onvoorspelbaar zijn. De ontwikkelingen van de laatste tijd bewijzen zijn gelijk. Drie jaar terug hield ik op uitnodiging van rector Korsten ook een lezing over Europa. Ik kon toen niet bevroeden dat onder andere door het Nederlandse en Franse Nee in het referendum over de Europese Grondwet, het project Europa pas op de plaats moest maken. In mijn bijdrage aan deze Masterclass sta ik stil bij het in mijn ogen grote succes van het Europese integratie project. Daarbij schets ik eerst het historisch perspectief. Ik heb deze achtergrond nodig om aanschouwelijk te maken dat de Europese uitdagingen van dit moment geen onoverkomelijke hordes hoeven te zijn. Ik zal daarbij pleiten voor een consistent beleid, zonder paniekvoetbal. Dat kunnen we beter bewaren voor het Wereldkampioenschap dat over een paar dagen bij onze oosterburen start. Historisch perspectief Een groot deel van uw leerlingen is zich waarschijnlijk minder goed bewust van het waarom van de Europese samenwerking. De Europese integratie is begonnen als vredesinitiatief. Na de verschrikkingen van de Tweede Wereldoorlog realiseerden Europese politici zich dat er een manier moest worden gevonden om Europa niet telkens weer af te breken maar juist gezamenlijk op te bouwen. Dat verklaart ook de plechtige woorden uit het Verdrag ter oprichting van de Europese Gemeenschap voor Kolen en Staal, dat op 18 april 1951 werd ondertekend: Beste mede-Europeanen, wij dienen de grondstenen te leggen voor een grotere en hechtere gemeenschap tussen de volkeren, die lange tijd door bloedige strijd verdeeld zijn geweest en de grondslagen te leggen voor instellingen die in staat zijn richting te geven aan een voortaan gezamenlijke bestemming.. Dit vredesideaal uit de jaren vijftig heeft heden ten dage nog niet aan belang ingeboet. Het relatief recente bloedvergieten in voormalig Joegoslavi, moge als illustratie dienen. De grondleggers van de Europese samenwerking gingen ervan uit dat vrede wordt gevoed door wederzijds vertrouwen en solidariteit. Op hun beurt worden vertrouwen en solidariteit vormgegeven en gestimuleerd door integratie. De Europese samenwerking begon in 1951 met de oprichting van de Europese Gemeenschap voor Kolen en Staal (de EGKS), waaraan zes landen  waaronder Nederland  deelnamen. Het is geen toeval dat juist deze producten werden gekozen: kolen en staal waren immers de bouwstenen van de oorlogsindustrie. Bovendien waren kolen, net als olie nu, destijds zeer belangrijk voor de economie. Dus ook voor het herstel van Europa was de kolen- en staalindustrie van het grootste belang. Ondanks het succes van de EGKS bleek een Europese Defensie Gemeenschap een brug te ver. Men heeft zich vanaf dat moment primair gericht op economische integratie in de vorm van goede handelsbetrekkingen binnen Europa en steun aan achterblijvende regios. Het is niet gek dat economische integratie de opmaat bleek voor Europese integratie. Na de Tweede Wereldoorlog kreeg de Europese samenwerking immers al een flinke zet door het Marshall Plan, waarmee de Verenigde Staten na 1948 financieel bijdroegen aan de wederopbouw van Europa (naar huidige koopkracht ter hoogte van 105 miljard dollar). Het Marshall Plan was geen pure liefdadigheid. Naast humanitaire redenen speelden namelijk ook strategische overwegingen een rol. Zo wilden de VS bijvoorbeeld voorkomen dat het in puin gelegde West Europa ten prooi zou vallen aan het communisme. Daarnaast was Europa een belangrijk afzetgebied voor Amerikaanse exportproducten. Kortom, veiligheid en solidariteit werden ingevuld met economische middelen. Het verloop van de Europese integratie De Europese Economische Gemeenschap had als doel de creatie van een gemeenschappelijke markt voor alle producten en productiefactoren. Het is niet in de laatste plaats dankzij de EEG dat de lidstaten in de jaren zestig grote economische bloei kende. Vanaf het begin van de jaren zeventig stagneerde het Europese integratieproces. Een belangrijke reden hiervoor was de economische tegenwind als gevolg van de oliecrises. Lidstaten concentreerden zich op hun eigen problemen en minder op Europese samenwerking. Een andere reden was de koppige houding van Charles de Gaulle die het toetredingsproces van Groot-Brittanni oprekte van 1961 tot 1973. Dit veroorzaakte veel spanningen tussen de lidstaten. De Gaulle was ook tegen verdere integratie tussen de toenmalige lidstaten en wilde zelfs eerder genomen integratiestappen terugdraaien. Hoewel een flink aantal nieuwe lidstaten toetraden (Groot-Brittanni, Denemarken, Ierland, Griekenland, Spanje en Portugal) was de vaart uit het Europese integratieproject. In de kranten verscheen zelfs de term Eurosclerose. Tegelijkertijd beseften de lidstaten dat verdere Europese samenwerking noodzakelijk was. Zo leidde de angst van Frankrijk tweede viool te moeten spelen achter West Duitsland, ertoe haar starre opstelling te verzachten. West Duitsland moest juist toenadering zoeken tot haar bondgenoten omwille van hun steun voor de op hereniging gerichte Ostpolitik. Verder werd de economische en technologische achterstand ten opzichte van Japan en de VS steeds groter en individuele lidstaten konden niet tegen zulke grootmachten op. Internationale crises zoals de Sovjet bezetting van Afghanistan en de Iraanse revolutie onderstreepten deze slinkende rol van de individuele landen op het wereldtoneel en droegen bij aan hun bereidheid tot verdergaande integratie. Het proces van Europese integratie kwam weer op gang met het inwerkingtreden van de Europese Akte in 1987. Daarin spraken de lidstaten van de EEG af de resterende belemmeringen voor de gemeenschappelijke markt zoals die in 1957 was voorzien, uiterlijk per 31 december 1992 te slechten. De totstandkoming van de interne markt, waarin personen, goederen en diensten zich vrij konden bewegen, bracht Europa als vanzelf bij een verdere verdieping van de integratie. Na 1992 restte er namelijk nog een belangrijke economische belemmering: de wisselkoersen. De invoering van n munt in de Europese Unie zou hieraan een eind maken. Om dit te bereiken, waren duidelijke criteria nodig voor factoren die de waarde van een munt bepalen, zoals de hoogte van het overheidstekort, het inflatiepercentage en de rente. Deze afspraken legde de regeringsleiders in 1992 vast in het Verdrag van Maastricht. De Maastricht criteria moeten waarborgen dat de deelnemende landen in economisch opzicht genoeg op elkaar lijken om te kunnen profiteren van een gezamenlijke rente en wisselkoers. Vanaf 1 januari 1999 werken de financile markten met de girale euro. In 2002 volgden de euromunten en biljetten, het zogenaamde chartale geld. De ene munt werd daarmee een feit. Uiteraard mag een land ook na invoering niet uit de pas gaan lopen. Hiertoe zijn de begrotingsregels in het Stabiliteit- en Groeipact geschreven. Ondanks dit Pact is het met de begrotingsdiscipline van sommige landen helaas slecht gesteld. De monetaire unie, waarin een groep autonome landen vrijwillig besluit de eigen munt in te ruilen voor een gemeenschappelijke munt, is uniek in de wereld. Zonder dat we het wellicht elke dag beseffen, is dit weer een bewijs dat Europa al erg veel heeft bereikt op het gebied van solidariteit en wederzijds vertrouwen sinds de verwoestende Tweede Wereldoorlog. Uitbreiding van de EU Solidariteit was ook de drijvende kracht achter het volgende grote project van de Europese Unie: de uitbreiding naar het Oosten van 2004. In de jaren negentig kreeg het Europese integratieproces namelijk een belangrijke impuls: het wegvallen van het IJzeren Gordijn. Dit laatste overblijfsel van de Tweede Wereldoorlog had Europa bijna vijftig jaar lang verdeeld. Na het wegvallen ervan, kon Europa de zoektocht naar de gezamenlijke bestemming ook echt gezamenlijk voortzetten. Met de toetreding van tien meest Oostbloklanden in mei 2004, is deze historische en morele belofte ingelost. De economische en politieke stabilisatie die uit de integratie van het gehele Europese continent voortkomt, is van onschatbare waarde, ook voor de Nederlandse burger. Niet alleen door het wegvallen van de dreiging van het Oosten die voor mijn generatie zo tastbaar was. Op kleinere schaal zou uw recente uitwisselings-programma met Poolse collega-scholen tot voor kort ondenkbaar zijn. De financile gevolgen van de uitbreiding hebben veel aandacht gekregen. Los van het feit dat de Nederlandse bijdrage inmiddels fors is teruggebracht, is deze financile kant maar een beperkt deel van het verhaal. Het uitbreidingsproces biedt ons namelijk ook economische voordelen. Door de verbreding van de interne markt heeft het Nederlandse bedrijfsleven meer handels- en investeringsmogelijkheden. Een ander gevolg van de uitbreiding is migratie. Door de verschillen in lonen zullen inwoners van de nieuwe lidstaten emigreren naar de rest van de EU. Ik verwacht niet dat deze stroom erg omvangrijk wordt. Ten eerste omdat volledig vrij verkeer van personen pas mogelijk is in 2011. Doordat de inkomensverschillen dan al geringer zijn, zullen minder mensen migreren. Daarnaast blijkt de arbeidsmobiliteit in Europa gering. Zo bleef de verwachte grote migratiestroom uit na de toetreding van Spanje en Portugal. Verder heeft de komst van de spreekwoordelijke Poolse loodgieter ook voordelen. Zij vervullen vaak laaggeschoolde vacatures, die in de rijkere landen moeilijk vervulbaar blijken. Toekomstige uitdagingen De successen van de EU verhinderden niet dat er ongemerkt een forse kloof met de burger ontstond. Europa werd namelijk primair gevormd vanuit de politieke wil van klein aantal direct belanghebbenden, bijvoorbeeld de landbouwsector en het bedrijfsleven, aangevuld met een select gezelschap met interesse voor de Europese zaak. Daar kwam nog bij dat de Brusselse regelgeving door de complexiteit en het hoge technische gehalte, weinig aansprekend is. Zolang het Europa voor de wind ging, was er voor de bevolking echter weinig reden zich te roeren. Het Nederlandse en Franse Nee in het referendum over de Europese Grondwet bracht deze kloof onverbiddelijk aan het licht. De tekst van de Grondwet is in belangrijke mate een consolidatie van de bestaande regelgeving, aangevuld met een vastlegging van geldende rechtspraak. De werkelijk grondwettelijke artikelen waren in de minderheid, en ook die bestonden voor een groot deel uit bestaande teksten. Ook de keuze voor het woord Grondwet was minder gelukkig. Mensen werden overvallen door dit document, dat kennelijk zou gelden boven de Nederlandse Grondwet.
