To this end, countries should assign high level policy makers for the job of Executive Director and need to grant their Director sufficient authority and leeway. After this in depth discussion of the Funds governance structure, let me again briefly restate my main points. I started by contending that it is important for the Fund to keep rapidly emerging economies closely involved with the IMF. To this end, the Fund needs to make sure that the participation of these economies remains a reflection of their role in the global economy and financial system. I subsequently argued that the Fund has recognized this challenge, leading to the encouraging reform agenda that was agreed at last weeks Annual Meetings. I fully support these reforms, even though the Netherlands would have been open to a more ambitious package in Singapore. My two words of caution concern the quota formulas, which should in my view continue to reflect the openness of economies, measured both in trade and in financial terms, and the discussion on one European seat in the Board, which is in my view highly premature. Concluding remarks This brings me towards the end of my remarks. I have argued that the Fund has in the past proven to be capable of adapting to a changing environment. This has always kept it a relevant institution, well-placed to promote international financial stability. I strongly belief that it again needs it adaptive capacity today, as it faces 1) the build-up of global imbalances, 2) the increasing size and complexity of the financial system and 3) the rapid rise of several emerging economies. These three challenges have a common denominator. They are all rooted in the process of economic and financial globalisation. Therefore, the Fund should not view the response to each of them in isolation, but rather address them simultaneously. In the end, improvement of the Funds governance structure is not enough. It has to be accompanied by improvement in the quality of surveillance, in particular by greater inclusion of developments in the financial sector. In a somewhat broader perspective, I think it is fair to say that globalisation and the current accelerated integration of the emerging world into the global economy and financial system provide the background against which all current discussions on the international financial architecture take place. Globalization does not only pose challenges to the IMF, but to all elements of the international financial system, as will undoubtedly come to the fore in the many panel discussions and workshops of this conference. Let me end by saying that I trust that the next two and a half days will stimulate fruitful discussion on these interesting issues.

Title: Speech president Wellink over Microfinance institutions, deposits and adequate prudential supervision
text: Speech president Wellink over Microfinance institutions, deposits and adequate prudential supervision Speech Datum 12 oktober 2006 Tijd 16:54 uur Lokatie Conferentie 'Promoting Inclusive Financial Systems' te Bazel Spreker Dr. A.H.E.M. Wellink, Voorzitter van het Bazel's Comite We are here to discuss ways to promote inclusive financial systems. This is important because well over three billion people do not have access to basic financial services such as credit, savings accounts and insurance. As microfinance offers such basic financial services, it is of prime importance. In this context, the microfinance industry must surely be impressed by the enormous success of the telecommunication industry. In Africa, for example, the number of mobile phone subscribers grew from 7.5 million in 1999 to almost 80 million in 2004. And experts believe this number will increase to 250 million over the next four years! Furthermore, people at all income levels are able to access cell phone services, either by owning or sharing a phone. Gender, age, and education do not seem to be barriers to access. Mobile phones and microfinance have much in common. In Bangladesh, for example, Grameen Bank offers microfinance to more than 100.000 telephone ladies. These ladies buy cell phones with loans and rent out airtime to people in their villages. Other microentrepreneurs are setting themselves up as text writers and interpreters for illiterate clients, so that even the very poor can use SMS text messages. My speech, however, is not about the latest developments in mobile phone technology impressive as they are but about microfinance institutions. Yesterday I belief Her Royal Highness Princes Maxima already discussed the role of national and international banks and how they may contribute to building inclusive financial systems. Therefore, I will focus only on microfinance institutions, and I will do so in my capacity as President of the Netherlands Central Bank and not as Chairman of the Basle Committee. There are two issues that I wish to address today. First, I will argue that microfinance institutions should widen their financial services, particularly by offering deposit accounts. Secondly, I will argue that deposit-taking by microfinance institutions requires adequate prudential supervision. The challenge for regulators and supervisors is how to accommodate these institutions that engage in deposit-taking. Unfortunately, I cannot give you a blueprint for a regulatory framework. But I can offer you some tentative ingredients that I personally believe to be important. Microfinance institutions need deposits to finance their micro credits Nowadays, more and more people in the microfinance industry are realising that broadening the set of financial services beyond credit can further improve the welfare of low-income households. In my view, offering deposit accounts is a particularly welcome development. Fortunately, many new initiatives are being taken in this area. An example close to my own experience concerns Child Saving International, an organisation supported by DNB. In India, around 70,000 children are learning to manage their own savings through school programs. Today, this concept is being implemented in more than ten countries. On a far larger scale, Bank Rakyat Indonesia manages the savings of about 25 million deposit-holders. This bank has attracted many low-income depositors by, for example, reducing minimum required balances and by creating an extensive network of close on 4,000 branches. Although individual deposits are small in absolute terms in 2003, the average deposit at Bank Rakyat was about 75 US dollars they can have a big impact on the lives of those holding a deposit. Until recently, many people believed that the very poor do not save. Evidence shows that even households below the poverty line wish to save and  more importantly  actually manage to do so. Why? Surveys show that poor households have several motives, e.g. for tuition fees, future consumption, and business working capital. But there are many saving constraints and those constraints are particularly relevant for poor households. They typically do not have access to the services of regular banks. Critical observers may say that saving constraints are unimportant because poor households can save informally. I disagree. Not because such opportunities do not exist, but because they have serious drawbacks. Without access to deposits, households save in various ways. For example, they may bury their money around the house, buy livestock, purchase jewellery or use informal money guards. But stashing money away at home leaves households vulnerable to theft. Moreover, there is no compensation for inflation. Livestock and jewellery are subject to another type of risk. When a community is hit by a crisis, local markets may become flooded with cows, chickens and jewellery, as households desperately try to generate income. Money guards can be very costly. A case study for India shows that such services can come at an annual interest rate on deposits of roughly minus 30 percent. So, informal savings are risky, costly and inefficient. There is also another important reason why informal savings are problematic. Without access to deposits, households simply save too little. Research suggests that access to deposits can increase the financial saving rate by 5-7 percentage points. More saving is good not only for the poor households themselves but also for financial institutions, as deposits can become a source of funding. In 2003, Grameen Bank, for example, held deposits equal to three-quarters of its loan portfolio. This means less dependency on external financing. One challenge for the microfinance industry is thus to create new products that stimulate poor people to save and meet their specific needs. A field study in the Philippines showed that savings can increase substantially when depositors choose to have limited access to their own deposits. Other customers may not need self-protection and fare better with more flexible accounts. Another challenge which I believe to be very important when savings accounts become more prominent is adequate prudential supervision and the protection of depositors. This brings me to the second issue that I wish to address. How can regulators and supervisors cope with microfinance institutions engaging in deposit-taking? Deposit-taking requires adequate prudential supervision Let me first further define the scope of my address. Firstly, I will not focus on banks but will deal explicitly with prudential supervision of microfinance institutions. Furthermore, I will stick to microfinance institutions in developing and emerging economies. This is where the majority of microfinance institutions operate and where microfinance is mainly practised. Secondly, there can be no doubt in my mind that a microfinance institution which raises deposits from the public to finance its micro credits should be subject to prudential supervision. If such a microfinance institution becomes insolvent, it will no longer be able to meet its obligations to its depositors. But then the question arises as to the kind of supervision. In thinking about these issues, it may not come as a surprise to you that I have looked to the Basel Core Principles for guidance. For those unfamiliar with these principles, they are a set of minimum standards for Effective Banking Supervision in all jurisdictions, issued by the Basel Committee in September 1997. They have presently been reviewed and were finalised last week in Merida, Mexico. In this process, participants expressed a desire for the Basel Committee to provide guidance and to identify good international supervisory practices in several areas, including microfinance. So what do the Core Principles tell us? They provide that The taking of deposits from the public is generally reserved for institutions that are licensed and subject to supervision as banks. I agree. However, and I quote from principle two, The word generally allows for the presence in some countries of non-banking financial institutions which may not be supervised in the same manner as banks but do take deposits and provide lending services, given these institutions collectively do not hold a significant proportion of deposits in a financial system. Examples of such institutions are credit unions and microfinance institutions. End of quote. In this spirit the IMF staff has recommended that allow me one final quote These (microfinance) institutions should be subject to a form of regulation and supervision commensurate to the type and size of their transactions, and which does not impose an excessive burden. Clearly, this leaves regulators and prudential supervisors with room for manoeuvre to make the supervisory regime proportional to the specific sort of institution wishing to attract deposits. Making prudential supervisory arrangements more proportional to deposit-taking microfinance institutions is not something to be done rashly or light-heartedly. It is important for microfinance institutions to maintain sufficient capital. Although the quality of the loan portfolios is generally high, it can potentially deteriorate very rapidly: when one borrower defaults on a loan, others may soon follow. Moreover, default risks may be correlated as microfinance institutions usually lend to a relatively homogenous group of people who depend on the regional economy. For these and other reasons supervisors need to understand well the unique risks of microfinance institutions when they apply the principle of proportionality. Let me explore some potential criteria when applying this principle. A starting point is the specific type of transactions effected by microfinance institutions. For instance, does the microfinance institution have enough experience and a local presence? Throughout the 1980s and 1990s, programs of NGOs and other non-bank financial institutions improved upon the original methodologies and bucked conventional wisdom about financing the poor. They have shown that the poor repay their loans and are willing and able to pay interest rates that cover the costs of providing the loans. Experience should count for something. Not only in terms of judging risk management systems or the fit and properness of management, but perhaps also in terms of a lower capital charge. Furthermore, if a microfinance institution has experience in the shape of a long historical presence, it might have administrative records consisting of repayment histories, client files and other personal information. This is important, because we must not forget that microfinance depends on customer relations more strongly than mainstream banking. A microfinance institution might be lacking economic capital but this may be compensated for by social capital. In other words, experience and trust. Let me continue along these lines. Another criterion might be the characteristics of micro depositors and micro debtors. This is not immaterial. For instance, there is plenty of evidence that groups have better repayment potential than individuals and that loans to women have been more successful than loans to men. These facts could be taken into account when assessing the risk profile of these institutions. To give you one last potential criterion, it is particularly relevant whether there are guarantees from sponsors, be they explicit commitments by an NGO or a more indirect backing by a government. Ideally, donors wishing to contribute to the development of microfinance could make means available for helping microfinance institutions meet their capital charge. And clearly, other criteria are conceivable. For instance, I have deliberately not gone into the size of deposits and credits. Microfinance is a comprehensive concept and we must not forget that the services covered by it may vary widely from one country to the next. In Latin America, the average deposit is about USD 250, much higher than the USD 75 of Bank Rakyat in Indonesia mentioned earlier. Any criteria based on the size of deposits or micro credit may therefore vary per country. But setting criteria should not tempt prudential supervisors to do away with flexibility. For instance, for some geographically remote microfinance institutions, the costs of prudential supervision may be prohibitively high. In such exceptional cases, one might consider flexible approaches to prudential supervision that balance social benefits and risks, as the alternative would be that the local poor have no access to microfinance at all. Other areas where flexibility might be desirable are reporting requirements and reporting frequency. Will a prudential regime tailored to microfinance institutions, in combination with more flexibility, work? And will it contribute to building inclusive financial systems? I have high hopes that it will. Experience with microfinance institutions in several African countries, which are already subject to prudential supervision, has shown that prudential supervision need not be disadvantageous. The very fact that supervision is being exercised seems to have enhanced the microfinance institutions legitimacy. It has also improved operational management, as microfinance institutions are required to meet higher standards of financial control and reporting, and has enabled them to offer a wider range of financial services. All these improvements have made it easier for microfinance institutions to access finance, allowing them to expand rapidly and serve more customers. Concluding remarks Microfinance is increasingly recognized as an effective tool in the fight against poverty and the building of inclusive financial systems. In my view, deposit-taking is a welcome development, as even the very poor are eager to save. Moreover, it can become an important funding source for microfinance institutions. In parallel with this development, the role of adequate prudential supervision will also gain in importance. Prudential supervision can contribute to inclusive financial systems by defining clear criteria for microfinance institutions wishing to take deposits and expand their services. Here, supervisors should seek a balance between creating opportunities for microfinance services on the one hand, while safeguarding the financial interests of depositors and the system on the other. I am the first to realise that what I have offered you today is at best a partial solution. If we truly wish to succeed in building inclusive financial systems, further contributions are desperately needed. Regulators and governments, in particular, need to develop legal and regulatory frameworks for microfinance, consumer protection, and the (financial) infrastructure. But together we can make a difference and set the right conditions for making financial systems more inclusive. Links Speech van H.K.H. Prinses Maxima der Nederlanden, uitgesproken op 11 oktober 2006

Title: President Wellink's speech on traffic jams on the financial highway
text: President Wellink's speech on traffic jams on the financial highway Speech Datum 13 november 2006 Time: 3:58 p.m. Location for the lecture series Leadership Panel, Economics Faculty Association, Groningen Speaker Dr. A.H.E.M. Wellink It is a great pleasure for me to be able to speak in front of an audience of Groningen economists. This faculty has produced one of the most important central bankers in history. Wim Duisenberg started his studies in economics here in 1954, then worked for several years as a research assistant and obtained his doctorate in economics. The Groningen years proved to be a good basis for a glittering career, culminating in the presidency of the European Central Bank. De Nederlandsche Bank therefore attaches great importance to the good relationship with this faculty. Many of our employees have studied here and one of them was recently appointed as a professor. Duisenberg has sometimes compared monetary policy to the operation of the accelerator pedal in a car. By accelerating, the economy is stimulated gradually, to a level where you have to let go of the accelerator again in order to reverse the risk of inflation in time. Today, however, I do not want to talk about monetary policy, but about the financial system in its entirety. As a central bank, we are only one of the road participants, albeit not an insignificant one. First of all, I will briefly dwell on some important trends in the system. Against this background, I will discuss current developments, such as ample liquidity and the so-called 'search for yield'. Finally, I will pay more specific attention to the recent developments around hedge funds and private equity houses. These investors have been in the spotlight lately. The negative image that is sometimes painted is too one-sided for my taste and needs to be nuanced. This does not alter the fact that there are risks involved. In recent months, the Dutch Central Bank has therefore conducted research into private equity and the involvement of financial institutions in this regard. I would like to comment briefly on some of the results of this study. Trends in the financial system If we hold the analogy with car traffic for a moment, the financial system looks more and more like an advanced road network with a number of busy junctions and ever faster cars. In recent decades, the system has undergone enormous development. Many countries have deregulated and liberalized their financial markets since the early 1970s, making capital flows easier to move between sectors and between economies. The traditional separation between banks and other financial institutions, such as insurers and investment funds, has begun to blur. National borders are losing their meaning, which means that there is more and more of a single global financial system. This process still has a long way to go, but the policy consequences have been visible for some time. For example, it has become increasingly important to coordinate supervision and regulations internationally. For banking supervision, this was already recognised in the 1970s, when the Basel Committee was established. For example, it includes agreements on minimum solvency requirements, in order to create a global level playing field for the globally operating banking sector. In a similar way, international agreements are being made for the supervisory framework for insurers: Solvency 2. And in other areas, such as payments or accounting rules, there is also increasing efforts to harmonise rules and standards. All of this has contributed to an unprecedented financial expansion. When I was a student, in the early 1960s, the combined balance sheet total of the Dutch banking system was about twenty billion euros, slightly less than the gross domestic product at the time. Now it's more than two thousand billion, four times our GDP. Financial services have become more accessible to businesses and broad sections of the population. Financial markets have grown sharply and become more liquid. In addition, the possibilities for managing and spreading risks have increased. This partly explains why the system has responded so resiliently to a series of setbacks in recent years, including the bursting of the dot-com bubble, accounting scandals, the September 11 attacks, and rising geopolitical tensions. The financial system has therefore developed rapidly and has improved in many respects. Yet the challenges have certainly not diminished. In the first place, the financial expertise and risk management of financial institutions is increasingly being called upon. This is also reflected in the changing attitude of the regulator. As all kinds of restrictions on financial institutions have been phased out, the emphasis in supervision has increasingly shifted to risk management. Institutions have therefore been given more leeway, but must be able to demonstrate that they have their risk management in order. This means a growing need for high-quality financial and economic knowledge. Initiatives by both universities and private institutions to get a top financial programme off the ground therefore deserve full support. In any case, the job market looks good for you! A second challenge is that the financial system as a whole is becoming increasingly complex. This is evidenced by the growth of derivatives trading, among other things. These instruments have the characteristic that they decouple risks from the underlying financial products. This has fundamental implications for the way we look at financial institutions. Banks are still at the heart of the system, but their traditional intermediation function is clearly changing. They remain the main providers of credit, but no longer keep all of them on their balance sheets. By means of securitisation, for example through credit derivatives, credit risks are made tradable and spread across various market participants. As a result, it becomes less clear where credit risks ultimately fall. It is even conceivable that these accumulate elsewhere in the economy and lead to imbalances. The challenge for us as central banks and financial stability institutions is to identify and monitor such risks. Excess liquidity and search for yield In recent years, substantial flows of money have flowed into the financial markets. These can be partly attributed to strong credit growth, for example in the mortgage market. Another cause is the approaching ageing of the population. In many industrialised countries, a large part of the population is in the phase of life in which they save a lot for old age, for example through pension funds and insurers. The abundance of liquidity is reflected in the low capital market interest rates and ultimately leads to lower investment returns. Investors are therefore looking for alternative routes that provide more returns. This phenomenon is now known as 'search for yield'. A popular route involves asset classes that are traditionally less in the spotlight because they are less accessible and riskier. Examples are investments in emerging economies, commodities or real estate. Of course, investors should take into account that the prospect of additional returns is also a reflection of additional risk. Moreover, these are often small, illiquid markets where price gouging easily arises with the risk of overvaluation and downward corrections. On the other hand, the additional capital inflows allow these markets to develop better, making them more accessible and transparent. A second route to generate additional returns is through leverage. The idea is simple: by supplementing the company's own investments with additional debt capital, a larger volume can be invested to compensate for the reduced margins. It should come from the length or from the width. Still, I feel a bit uncomfortable with this. After all, this 'profit multiplier' also works in reverse, so that in the event of setbacks, the losses are magnified. Moreover, leverage on a macro scale could be counterproductive, pumping even more liquidity into the financial system, ultimately putting even more pressure on returns. You also don't solve traffic jams by increasing the number of cars. Thus, what seems beneficial to an individual investor may turn out to be wrong for the system as a whole. In this context, it is also good to consider the role of financial innovation in creating leverage. As I mentioned, the securitisation of credit risk has taken off. In the first half of this year alone, the global market for credit derivatives grew by more than fifty percent, to a nominal outstanding amount of 26 trillion dollars. To put it in perspective, this is more than twice the volume of outstanding corporate bonds in the world. Banks and other debt lenders can use these instruments to trade credit risks, which ultimately result in them being borne by a large number of parties. If banks divest themselves of credit risk, this also creates room for them to issue and trade new loans. As long as other market parties are willing to invest in this, a credit expansion can take place in this way. It is interesting to ask whether the joint creation of leverage puts the system as a whole at risk. Suppose, for example, that there is a recession or that capital interest rates rise. In that case, the leverage can start acting as a 'loss multiplier'. With so many market parties involved, the picture of a chain collision on the financial highway soon emerges. It is difficult to make firm statements about the likelihood of such a scenario. For this, we simply have too little insight into the distribution of risks within the financial system and the way in which institutions deal with them. A wide spread reduces the vulnerability of individual parties, but also reduces the incentive to monitor risks to which one is only exposed to a limited extent. It may therefore well be the case that at the micro level, everyone manages their own risks adequately and thus becomes less sensitive to shocks, while the system as a whole becomes more vulnerable to a major correction. Top officials at leading institutions, such as Geithner of the New York Fed and Rajan of the IMF, have recently pointed out this potential paradox. Hedge funds en private equity Hedge funds and private equity funds play an important role in the search for yield process and the creation of leverage. These two categories are sometimes wrongly lumped together. Let me describe both briefly. Private equity is an investment in the equity of a non-listed company, often supplemented by debt capital. The investor is usually actively involved in the company's policy with the aim of getting rid of it after a number of years, for example through an IPO or a management buy-out. It can also happen that a listed company is bought by a private equity house, which then delists it from the stock exchange. The latter has recently happened at VNU and Vendex. Hedge funds engage in a wide range of activities, ranging from stocks to commodities and investments in emerging economies. Some hedge funds also invest directly in companies, but that's just one of many possibilities. Unlike private equity houses, such participations are usually limited to a small minority share. Characteristic of hedge funds is that they finance their activities largely with borrowed money. They also often run a high liquidity risk, by taking positions that have to be reduced at a loss in a short period of time in the event of setbacks. So they sail close to the wind, but sometimes take big risks and that sometimes goes badly wrong. The bankruptcy of the hedge fund LTCM in 1998 is well known, which even threatened a major financial crisis. And recently, the hedge fund Amaranth had to take a loss of six billion dollars in one week, two-thirds of the invested assets. Hedge funds and private equity investors are in many ways an enrichment of our financial system. They mobilise venture capital and are actively involved in the running of companies. This is a good fit for companies that need to restructure. Moreover, they are important pacesetters in the field of financial innovation, having contributed greatly to the development of the market for credit derivatives, for example. However, not everyone appears to be happy with these investors, as evidenced by the media attention in which emotions sometimes run high. This even includes terms such as locusts, wreckers and barbarians. I can well imagine that companies sometimes have mixed feelings about the activist stance of private equity investors. After all, they are explicitly involved in the course of events and are particularly attracted to companies that they believe are ripe for a strategic change of course. And it is simply the case that when a course is changed, opinions can differ considerably. This is not to say that the shareholders should always be right, but I think a good dialogue between management and investors is a good thing. I agree with Morris Tabaksblat, who recently pointed out once again that companies need to respond to the changing role of shareholders. Part of this is that the company must constantly ask itself what kind of shareholders suit it. In some cases, there may be advantages to abandoning the stock market listing. In this respect, we should not exaggerate the influence of private equity: of the 48 companies that were withdrawn from Euronext between 2001 and 2006, only 7 cases involved a private equity investment. So there are many good sides to the rise of private equity and hedge funds. But there are also points of attention. This concerns in the first place the turbulent growth of these activities. This is fine if the growth is driven by a wide range of profitable investment projects. It is different when the influx of capital is the driving force, in connection with the 'search for yield' phenomenon that I have just mentioned, especially if it boosts returns by means of additional leverage. A second point of attention is the non-transparent nature of investments in hedge funds and private equity. These institutions have hardly any reporting obligations and are not directly supervised. This makes it more difficult for investors to get a good idea of the return prospects and risk profile. In order to get a better grip on the possible risks associated with private equity, the Dutch Central Bank recently conducted a survey among banks, pension funds and insurers. A year and a half ago, we conducted a similar study on hedge funds, but for now I will focus mainly on private equity. For the study, various interviews were conducted with banks, institutional investors and other organisations. This is important, as these parties are involved in private equity in a variety of ways: For investors in private equity  mostly institutional investors  it is of course first and foremost important that a good return is achieved. In addition, private equity is seen as an opportunity to spread risks within the investment portfolio. It is important to note that the returns of private equity show a low correlation with those of other investments. The latter is certainly not obvious: in a recession, both listed equities and private equity are likely to perform poorly. After all, it will be difficult to sell an investment at a good price on the stock market or through a buy-out. Another risk associated with private equity investments is their limited tradability. Companies are not listed on the stock exchange and it usually takes a number of years before the investment can be disposed of. Banks are mainly involved as providers of debt capital and therefore contribute to leverage. They also benefit from fee and commission income. In general, banks try to transfer most of the credit risks to other parties, for example through syndication. In doing so, the loan is split into several tranches for which suitable buyers are sought. Part of the loan can also be securitised. The survey clearly shows that almost all those involved see ample liquidity and low capital market interest rates as driving forces behind the private equity market. This also includes the use of debt capital to increase returns through leverage. This came as no surprise to us. More worryingly, the degree of leverage is clearly increasing and in some cases is approaching the limits of what is acceptable. On top of that, lending is not only becoming more extensive, but also riskier. For example, repayment is increasingly being postponed until the end of the term. As a result, investments in private equity become more vulnerable to setbacks such as an economic recession or a turnaround in the interest rate environment. A particular point of attention is how much risk banks run as a result of their involvement in such transactions. The total exposure of banks is usually limited to less than one percent of their balance sheet total, while the credit risks of individual projects are usually reduced within a few months by placing them with other parties. Banks are therefore well aware of the risks. The results of our research are not isolated. We are also looking at developments in private equity in Europe within the ECB, having previously jointly mapped out the financial stability implications of hedge funds. International cooperation on these issues is important. These are global developments of which we in the Netherlands have only limited visibility. In addition, it is important to coordinate any policy measures with each other. Incidentally, I would be reluctant to introduce rules or direct supervision of hedge funds and private equity funds. These funds are a logical consequence of the deregulation process and, as I said earlier, an asset to our financial system. Moreover, regulation is ineffective insofar as it would create new entities that would take over the activities of hedge funds and private equity houses. A better starting point for policy is banks, pension funds and insurers, which are already under supervision. It is fine for these institutions to invest in private equity, as long as they have a clear view of the associated risks. This is not always easy, due to the opacity of private equity and the limited experience that most institutions have with it. On top of that, some parties have much more expertise than others, with the risk that risks accumulate in institutions that are least prepared for them. As a supervisor, it is therefore important to encourage institutions to strengthen their risk management in this regard. To this end, we are developing guiding principles for non-transparent investments, such as private equity and hedge funds, on which we will consult with the financial sector. For example, it is important that institutions have sufficient knowledge and experience in-house to make a good assessment of the risks of private equity, in relation to their own objectives and strategy. These risks are not only purely financial, but can also relate to integrity issues or the quality of the people directly involved in private equity projects. It is important for financial institutions to be well aware of who they are doing business with. Managing the risks associated with private equity - and also hedge funds - should therefore mainly be done through the institutions with which they do business and which are already supervised. This does not alter the fact that it would also be good to increase the transparency of private equity. As far as I'm concerned, the ball is mainly in the sector's court. A good starting point is the code of conduct of the Dutch Association of Private Equity and Venture Capital Companies, which will soon be tightened up. In any case, I think it is important that the provision of information to investors is properly regulated, so that they can make a realistic assessment of the return and the risk profile. In addition, it is of course important to keep a close eye on compliance with the code of conduct. Lock The financial highway has become busier and less clear, but it does lead to increasingly interesting travel destinations. If you want to be on the road, you must have sufficient driving skills and also be able to rely on your fellow road users. It is not our job as a central bank and supervisor to interfere too much in the route. We do, however, try to keep the road surface in optimal condition through efficient payment transactions, we carry out an MOT inspection with our supervision and we give speed advice with our monetary policy. And for emergencies, we have a guardrail on hand. But apart from that, everyone can chart their own course.
text_original: Speech president Wellink over Files op de financile snelweg Speech Datum 13 november 2006 Tijd 15:58 uur Lokatie Tgv de lezingenreeks Leadership Panel, Economische Faculteitsvereniging, Groningen Spreker Dr. A.H.E.M. Wellink Het is voor mij een groot genoegen te mogen spreken voor een publiek van Groningse economen. Deze faculteit heeft n van de belangrijkste centrale bankiers uit de geschiedenis voortgebracht. Wim Duisenberg begon hier in 1954 zijn economiestudie, was daarna enkele jaren werkzaam als wetenschappelijk medewerker en promoveerde tot doctor in de economische wetenschappen. De Groningse jaren bleken een goede basis voor een glanzende carrire met uiteindelijk als hoogtepunt het presidentschap van de Europese Centrale Bank. De Nederlandsche Bank hecht dan ook aan de goede band met deze faculteit. Veel van onze medewerkers hebben hier gestudeerd en n daarvan is kort geleden zelfs aangesteld als hoogleraar. Duisenberg heeft monetair beleid wel eens vergeleken met de bediening van het gaspedaal in een auto. Door gas te geven wordt de economie geleidelijk gestimuleerd, tot een niveau waarop je het gaspedaal weer moet loslaten om inflatiegevaar tijdig te keren. Vandaag wil ik het echter niet hebben over monetair beleid, maar over het financile stelsel in zijn volle breedte. Hier zijn we als centrale bank slechts n van de verkeersdeelnemers, zij het geen onbelangrijke. Ik zal allereerst kort stilstaan bij enkele belangrijke trends in het stelsel. Tegen deze achtergrond zal ik ingaan op actuele ontwikkelingen, zoals de ruime liquiditeit en de zogeheten 'search for yield'. Tot slot zal ik meer specifiek aandacht besteden aan de recente ontwikkelingen rond hedge funds en private equity-huizen. Deze investeerders staan de laatste tijd sterk in de belangstelling. Het negatieve beeld dat daarbij soms wordt geschetst is naar mijn smaak te eenzijdig en behoeft nuancering. Dit neemt niet weg dat er risico's aan kleven. De Nederlandsche Bank heeft daarom de afgelopen maanden onderzoek gedaan naar private equity en de betrokkenheid daarbij van financile instellingen. Ik zal kort ingaan op enkele uitkomsten van dit onderzoek. Trends in het financile stelsel Als we de analogie met het autoverkeer nog even vasthouden, dan lijkt het financile stelsel steeds meer op een geavanceerd wegennet met een aantal drukke knooppunten en steeds snellere auto's. De afgelopen decennia heeft het stelsel een enorme ontwikkeling doorgemaakt. Veel landen hebben sinds begin jaren zeventig hun financile markten gedereguleerd en geliberaliseerd, waardoor kapitaalstromen zich gemakkelijker zijn gaan bewegen tussen sectoren en tussen economien. De traditionele scheiding tussen banken en andere financile instellingen, zoals verzekeraars en beleggingsfondsen, is gaan vervagen. Landsgrenzen zijn hun betekenis aan het verliezen, waardoor steeds meer sprake is van n mondiaal financieel stelsel. Dit proces heeft nog een lange weg te gaan, maar de beleidsconsequenties zijn al geruime tijd zichtbaar. Zo is het steeds belangrijker geworden om toezicht en regelgeving internationaal af te stemmen. Voor het bankentoezicht werd dit al onderkend in de jaren zeventig, toen het Bazels Comit werd opgericht. Hierin worden bijvoorbeeld afspraken gemaakt over minimum solvabiliteitseisen, teneinde wereldwijd een gelijk speelveld te creren voor het mondiaal opererende bankwezen. Op soortgelijke wijze worden internationale afspraken gemaakt voor het toezichtraamwerk voor verzekeraars: Solvency 2. En ook op andere terreinen, zoals het betalingsverkeer of boekhoudregels, wordt in toenemende mate gewerkt aan harmonisatie van regels en standaarden. Dit alles heeft bijgedragen aan een ongekende financile expansie. Toen ik student was, begin jaren zestig, bedroeg het gezamenlijke balanstotaal van het Nederlandse bankwezen ongeveer twintig miljard euro, iets minder dan het toenmalige bruto binnenlands product. Nu is dat meer dan tweeduizend miljard, viermaal ons BBP. Financile dienstverlening is toegankelijker geworden voor het bedrijfsleven en brede lagen van de bevolking. Financile markten zijn fors gegroeid en meer liquide geworden. Bovendien zijn de mogelijkheden toegenomen om risicos te beheersen en te spreiden. Dit verklaart voor een deel waarom het stelsel de afgelopen jaren zo veerkrachtig heeft gereageerd op een reeks tegenslagen, waaronder het knappen van de dotcom-zeepbel, boekhoudschandalen, de aanslagen op 11 september en oplopende geopolitieke spanningen. Het financile systeem heeft dus een snelle ontwikkeling doorgemaakt en is in veel opzichten beter gaan functioneren. Toch zijn de uitdagingen er bepaald niet minder om geworden. In de eerste plaats wordt een steeds groter beroep gedaan op de financile expertise en het risicobeheer van financile instellingen. Dit komt ook tot uiting in de veranderende houding van de toezichthouder. Naarmate allerlei beperkingen voor financile instellingen zijn afgebouwd, is de nadruk in het toezicht steeds meer verschoven naar risicobeheersing. Instellingen hebben dus meer speelruimte gekregen, maar moeten wel kunnen aantonen dat ze hun risicobeheer op orde hebben. Dit betekent een groeiende behoefte aan hoogwaardige financieel-economische kennis. Initiatieven van zowel universiteiten als particuliere instellingen om een financile topopleiding van de grond te krijgen verdienen dan ook volle steun. In ieder geval ziet de arbeidsmarkt voor u er goed uit! Een tweede uitdaging is dat het financile stelsel als geheel steeds complexer wordt. Dit blijkt onder meer uit de groei van de derivatenhandel. Deze instrumenten hebben als kenmerk dat ze risico's loskoppelen van de onderliggende financile producten. Dit heeft fundamentele gevolgen voor de manier waarop we naar financile instellingen kijken. Banken vormen nog steeds de kern van het stelsel, maar hun traditionele intermediatiefunctie is duidelijk aan het veranderen. Ze blijven de belangrijkste verstrekkers van kredieten, maar houden deze niet meer allemaal op hun balans. Door middel van securitisatie, bijvoorbeeld via kredietderivaten, worden kredietrisico's verhandelbaar gemaakt en verspreid over diverse marktpartijen. Hierdoor wordt minder duidelijk waar kredietrisicos uiteindelijk neerslaan. Het is zelfs denkbaar dat deze zich elders in de economie ophopen en leiden tot onevenwichtigheden. De uitdaging voor ons als centrale banken en financile stabiliteitsinstellingen is om dergelijke risico's in kaart te brengen en te monitoren. Overliquiditeit en search for yield De afgelopen jaren zijn omvangrijke geldstromen naar de financile markten gevloeid. Deze kunnen deels worden toegeschreven aan de sterke kredietgroei, bijvoorbeeld op de hypotheekmarkt. Een andere oorzaak is de naderende vergrijzing. In veel industrielanden zit een groot deel van de bevolking in de levensfase waarin flink wordt gespaard voor de oude dag, onder andere via pensioenfondsen en verzekeraars. De overvloed aan liquiditeit komt tot uitdrukking in de lage kapitaalmarktrente en leidt uiteindelijk tot lagere beleggingsopbrengsten. Beleggers gaan daarom op zoek naar alternatieve routes die meer rendement opleveren. Dit verschijnsel staat inmiddels bekend als 'search for yield'. Een populaire route betreft beleggingscategorien die traditioneel minder in de belangstelling staan omdat ze minder toegankelijk en risicovoller zijn. Voorbeelden zijn investeringen in opkomende economien, grondstoffen of vastgoed. Uiteraard moeten beleggers daarbij incalculeren dat het vooruitzicht op extra rendement ook een weerspiegeling is van extra risico. Bovendien zijn dit veelal kleine, illiquide markten waar gemakkelijk prijsopdrijving ontstaat met kans op overwaardering en neerwaartse correcties. Daar staat tegenover dat deze markten zich door de extra kapitaalinstroom beter kunnen ontwikkelen, waardoor ze vanzelf toegankelijker en transparanter worden. Een tweede route om extra rendement te genereren is door middel van de hefboomwerking, oftewel 'leverage'. Het idee is simpel: door de eigen investeringen aan te vullen met extra vreemd vermogen kan een groter volume worden belegd, ter compensatie van de geslonken marges. Het moet uit de lengte of uit de breedte komen. Toch voel ik me hier al wat ongemakkelijker bij. Immers, deze 'winstvermenigvuldiger' werkt ook in omgekeerde richting, waardoor bij tegenvallers de verliezen worden uitvergroot. Bovendien zou de hefboomwerking op macroschaal wel eens contraproductief kunnen zijn: er wordt nog meer liquiditeit in het financile systeem gepompt, waardoor uiteindelijk de rendementen nog verder onder druk worden gezet. Je lost files ook niet op door uitbreiding van het aantal autos. Wat gunstig lijkt voor een individuele belegger, kan dus verkeerd uitpakken voor het systeem als geheel. In dit kader is het ook goed om stil te staan bij de rol van financile innovatie bij het creren van leverage. Zoals ik al aangaf, heeft de securitisatie van kredietrisico's een grote vlucht genomen. Alleen al in de eerste helft van dit jaar nam de markt voor kredietderivaten wereldwijd met ruim vijftig procent in omvang toe, tot een nominaal uitstaand bedrag van 26 biljoen dollar. Om het in perspectief te plaatsen: dit is meer dan tweemaal het volume van uitstaande bedrijfsobligaties in de wereld. Banken en andere vreemdvermogenverstrekkers kunnen met behulp van deze instrumenten kredietrisico's verhandelen waardoor deze uiteindelijk worden gedragen door een groot aantal partijen. Als banken kredietrisico afstoten schept dit voor hen bovendien ruimte om nieuwe leningen te verstrekken en te verhandelen. Zolang andere marktpartijen hierin willen investeren kan op die manier een kredietexpansie plaatsvinden. Interessant is de vraag of door het gezamenlijk creeren van leverage het systeem als geheel een risico loopt. Stel bijvoorbeeld dat er een recessie komt of dat de kapitaalrente gaat stijgen. In dat geval kan de hefboom gaan werken als een 'verliesvermenigvuldiger'. Met zoveel betrokken marktpartijen doemt dan al gauw het beeld op van een kettingbotsing op de financile snelweg. Het is moeilijk harde uitspraken te doen over de kans op een dergelijk scenario. Hiervoor hebben we simpelweg te weinig zicht op de verdeling van risicos binnen het financile systeem en de manier waarop instellingen hiermee omgaan. Een brede spreiding verkleint de kwetsbaarheid van individuele partijen, maar vermindert ook de prikkel om risicos de monitoren waaraan men slechts voor een beperkt deel is blootgesteld. Het zou daarom best zo kunnen zijn dat op microniveau iedereen zijn eigen risico's adequaat beheerst en daardoor minder gevoelig wordt voor schokken, terwijl het stelsel als geheel kwetsbaarder wordt voor een grote correctie. Topfunctionarissen van toonaangevende instellingen, zoals Geithner van de New York Fed en Rajan van het IMF, hebben onlangs gewezen op deze mogelijke paradox. Hedge funds en private equity In het 'search for yield'-proces en het creren van leverage spelen hedge funds en private equity-fondsen een belangrijke rol. Deze twee categorien worden soms ten onrechte over n kam geschoren. Laat ik beide kort beschrijven. Private equity is een investering in het eigen vermogen van een niet-beursgenoteerde onderneming, vaak aangevuld met vreemd vermogen. De investeerder is meestal actief betrokken bij het beleid van de onderneming met als doel deze na een aantal jaren weer van de hand te doen, bijvoorbeeld door een beursintroductie of een management buy-out. Ook kan het voorkomen dat een beursgenoteerde onderneming wordt gekocht door een private equity-huis, dat deze vervolgens van de beurs haalt. Dit laatste is recentelijk gebeurd bij VNU en Vendex. Hedge funds houden zich bezig met een breed scala van activiteiten, varirend van aandelen tot grondstoffen en investeringen in opkomende economien. Sommige hedge funds investeren ook direct in ondernemingen, maar dat is slechts n van de vele mogelijkheden. Anders dan bij private equity-huizen blijven dergelijke deelnemingen meestal beperkt tot een klein minderheidsaandeel. Kenmerkend voor hedge funds is dat ze hun activiteiten grotendeels financieren met geleend geld. Ook lopen ze vaak een groot liquiditeitsrisico, door posities in te nemen die bij tegenslagen in korte tijd met verlies moeten worden afgebouwd. Ze zeilen dus scherp aan de wind, maar nemen daarbij soms grote risico's en dat gaat wel eens goed mis. Bekend is het faillissement van het hedge fund LTCM in 1998 waardoor zelfs gevaar dreigde voor een grote financile crisis. En recentelijk moest het hedge fund Amaranth in n week een verlies incasseren van zes miljard dollar, tweederde van het belegde vermogen. Hedge funds en private equity-beleggers zijn in veel opzichten een verrijking van ons financile stelsel. Ze mobiliseren risicodragend kapitaal en houden zich actief bezig met het reilen en zeilen van ondernemingen. Dit past goed bij bedrijven die zich moeten herstructureren. Bovendien zijn ze belangrijke gangmakers op het terrein van financile innovatie, die bijvoorbeeld sterk hebben bijgedragen aan de ontwikkeling van de markt voor kredietderivaten. Toch blijkt niet iedereen gelukkig met deze beleggers, getuige de media-aandacht waarbij emoties soms hoog opspelen. Daarbij vallen zelfs termen als sprinkhanen, slopers en barbaren. Ik kan me best voorstellen dat ondernemingen soms gemengde gevoelens hebben bij de activistische houding van private equity-investeerders. Ze bemoeien zich immers nadrukkelijk met de gang van zaken en voelen zich vooral aangetrokken door bedrijven die in hun ogen rijp zijn voor een strategische koerswijziging. En het is nu eenmaal zo dat bij een koerswijziging de meningen flink kunnen verschillen. Daarmee wil ik niet zeggen dat de aandeelhouders altijd gelijk moeten krijgen, maar een goede dialoog tussen management en investeerders lijkt mij een goede zaak. Ik ben het eens met Morris Tabaksblat, die er onlangs nog eens op heeft gewezen dat ondernemingen moeten inspelen op de veranderende rol van aandeelhouders. Onderdeel daarvan is dat de onderneming zich voortdurend moet afvragen wat voor soort aandeelhouders bij haar past. In sommige gevallen kunnen er voordelen aan zitten om de beursnotering op te geven. Wat dat betreft moeten we de invloed van private equity trouwens niet overdrijven: van de 48 bedrijven die tussen 2001 en 2006 van Euronext zijn gehaald hebben slechts 7 gevallen betrekking op een private equity-investering. Er zitten dus veel goede kanten aan de opkomst van private equity en hedge funds. Maar er zijn ook aandachtspunten. Dit betreft in de eerste plaats de onstuimige groei van deze activiteiten. Dit is prima als de groei wordt gedreven door een ruim aanbod van rendabele investeringsprojecten. Anders wordt het als de toestroom van kapitaal de drijvende kracht is, in verband met het 'search for yield'-fenomeen dat ik zojuist al noemde, vooral als daarbij het rendement wordt opgekrikt door middel van extra leverage. Een tweede aandachtspunt is het intransparante karakter van beleggingen in hedge funds en private equity. Deze instellingen hebben nauwelijks rapportageverplichtingen en staan niet onder direct toezicht. Dit maakt het moeilijker voor investeerders om een goed beeld te krijgen van de rendementvooruitzichten en het risicoprofiel. Om meer grip te krijgen op de mogelijke risico's rond private equity heeft de Nederlandsche Bank onlangs een onderzoek uitgevoerd onder banken, pensioenfondsen en verzekeraars. Anderhalf jaar geleden hebben we een soortgelijk onderzoek uitgevoerd naar hedge funds, maar ik zal me nu vooral concentreren op private equity. Voor het onderzoek zijn diverse interviews gehouden met banken, institutionele beleggers en andere organisaties. Dit is belangrijk, aangezien deze partijen op uiteenlopende manieren zijn betrokken bij private equity: Voor investeerders in private equity  veelal institutionele beleggers  is het natuurlijk in de eerste plaats van belang dat een goed rendement wordt behaald. Daarnaast wordt private equity gezien als een mogelijkheid om binnen de beleggingsportefeuille risicos te spreiden. Hiervoor is van belang dat de opbrengsten van private equity een geringe correlatie vertonen met die van andere beleggingen. Dit laatste is zeker niet evident: in een recessie zullen waarschijnlijk zowel beursgenoteerde aandelen als private equity slecht renderen. Het zal dan immers lastig zijn om een investering tegen een goede prijs te verkopen op de beurs of via een buy-out. Een ander risico van private equity-beleggingen is de beperkte verhandelbaarheid. Bedrijven zijn niet beursgenoteerd en het duurt meestal een aantal jaren voordat de investering van de hand kan worden gedaan. Banken zijn vooral betrokken als verschaffers van vreemd vermogen en dragen daardoor bij aan de hefboomwerking. Verder profiteren zij van fee- en commissie-inkomsten. Doorgaans proberen banken de kredietrisico's grotendeels onder te brengen bij andere partijen, bijvoorbeeld via syndicering. Daarbij wordt de lening opgesplitst in verschillende tranches waarvoor geschikte kopers worden gezocht. Ook kan een deel van de lening worden gesecuritiseerd. Uit het onderzoek komt duidelijk naar voren dat vrijwel alle betrokkenen de ruime liquiditeit en lage kapitaalmarktrente zien als drijvende krachten achter de private equity-markt. Hierbij past ook het gebruik van vreemd vermogen om via de hefboomwerking de rendementen te verhogen. Dit was voor ons geen verrassing. Zorgelijker is dat de mate van leverage duidelijk toeneemt en in sommige gevallen de grenzen nadert van wat acceptabel is. Daar komt nog eens bij dat de kredietverlening niet alleen steeds omvangrijker, maar ook risicovoller wordt. Zo wordt in toenemende mate de aflossing uitgesteld tot het einde van de looptijd. Beleggingen in private equity worden hierdoor kwetsbaarder voor tegenslagen zoals een economische recessie of een omslag in het renteklimaat. Een speciaal aandachtspunt daarbij is hoeveel risico banken lopen als gevolg van hun betrokkenheid bij dergelijke transacties. De totale exposure van banken blijft meestal beperkt tot minder dan n procent van hun balanstotaal, terwijl de kredietrisicos van individuele projecten meestal binnen enkele maanden worden afgebouwd door deze bij andere partijen te plaatsen. Banken zijn zich dus goed bewust van de risico's. De uitkomsten van ons onderzoek staan niet op zichzelf. We zijn ook in ECB-verband aan het kijken naar ontwikkelingen rond private equity in Europa, nadat we eerder gezamenlijk de financile stabiliteitsimplicaties van hedge funds in kaart hebben gebracht. Internationale samenwerking bij dit soort onderwerpen is belangrijk. Het gaat om mondiale ontwikkelingen waarop wij in Nederland slechts beperkt zicht hebben. Bovendien is het belangrijk om eventuele beleidsmaatregelen onderling goed af te stemmen. Overigens zou ik terughoudend zijn met de invoering van regels of direct toezicht op hedge funds en private equity-fondsen. Deze fondsen zijn een logische consequentie van het dereguleringsproces en, zoals ik al eerder aangaf, een aanwinst voor ons financile stelsel. Bovendien is regulering ineffectief voorzover hierdoor weer nieuwe entiteiten zouden ontstaan die de activiteiten van hedge funds en private equity-huizen overnemen. Een beter aangrijpingspunt voor beleid zijn banken, pensioenfondsen en verzekeraars, die reeds onder toezicht staan. Het is prima dat deze instellingen investeren in private equity, mits ze de bijbehorende risico's goed in het vizier hebben. Dit is niet altijd gemakkelijk, vanwege de ondoorzichtigheid van private equity en de beperkte ervaring die de meeste instellingen hiermee hebben. Daar komt nog eens bij dat sommige partijen over veel meer expertise beschikken dan andere, met het gevaar dat risico's zich ophopen bij instellingen die daarop het slechtst zijn voorbereid. Als toezichthouder is het daarom belangrijk instellingen te prikkelen hun risicobeheer op dit punt te versterken. Hiervoor ontwikkelen we 'guiding principles' voor intransparante beleggingen, zoals private equity en hedge funds, waarover we overleg zullen voeren met de financile sector. Zo is het belangrijk dat instellingen voldoende kennis en ervaring in huis hebben om een goede inschatting te maken van de risico's van private equity, in relatie tot hun eigen doelstelling en strategie. Deze risico's liggen overigens niet alleen op puur financieel terrein maar kunnen bijvoorbeeld ook betrekking hebben op integriteitsvraagstukken of de kwaliteit van de personen die direct betrokken zijn bij private equity-projecten. Het is belangrijk dat financile instellingen zich goed bewust zijn met wie ze zaken doen. Beheersing van de risico's rond private equity - en ook hedge funds - zou dus vooral moeten via de instellingen waarmee zij zaken doen en die reeds onder toezicht staan. Dit neemt niet weg dat het ook goed zou zijn om de transparantie van private equity te vergroten. Daarvoor ligt de bal wat mij betreft vooral bij deze sector zelf. Een mooi vertrekpunt is de gedragscode van Nederlandse Vereniging van Participatiemaatschappijen die binnenkort wordt aangescherpt. Het lijkt me in ieder geval belangrijk dat daarin de informatievoorziening aan beleggers goed wordt geregeld, zodat deze een realistische beoordeling kunnen maken van het rendement en het risicoprofiel. Daarnaast is het natuurlijk belangrijk goed zicht te houden op naleving van de gedragscode. Slot De financile snelweg is drukker geworden en minder overzichtelijk, maar leidt wel tot steeds interessantere reisbestemmingen. Wie zich op de weg wil begeven moet over voldoende rijvaardigheid beschikken en bovendien kunnen vertrouwen op zijn medeweggebruikers. Het is niet onze taak als centrale bank en toezichthouder om ons teveel met de route te bemoeien. Wel proberen we door efficint betalingsverkeer het wegdek in optimale conditie te houden, voeren we met ons toezicht een APK-keuring uit en geven we met ons monetaire beleid snelheidsadviezen. En voor noodgevallen hebben we een vangrail achter de hand. Maar verder mag iedereen zijn eigen koers uitstippelen.

Title: President Wellink's speech on Globalisation and ageing: implications for the Dutch labour market
text: President Wellink's speech on Globalisation and ageing: implications for the Dutch labour market Speech Datum 14 november 2006 Time: 1:39 p.m. Location Meeting of the Foundation Real Estate Reporting Groningen-Assen, Groningen Speaker Dr. A.H.E.M. Wellink This afternoon I will speak about the implications of globalisation and ageing for the Dutch labour market. The specific consequences for the North are also discussed. But first, I would like to discuss the current state of affairs in the Dutch labour market with you. Current state of affairs Let me start with some figures on the growth of the Dutch economy. After the Dutch economy grew by an average of four percent per year in the second half of the 1990s, the average economic growth in the period from 2001 to 2003 was less than one percent per year. In 2004, growth picked up to two percent, only to fall back to one and a half percent in 2005. For this year and next, I foresee growth of about 3%. After a temporary hiccup in 2005, the economy is now really picking up steam. The recovery follows a traditional pattern. After first an increase in exports, business investment and private consumption are now following suit. This illustrates our dependence on global economic developments. The pick-up in economic growth is clearly noticeable on the labour market. For example, unemployment has already fallen one percentage point in the past year and the number of unfilled vacancies is increasing rapidly. At the turn of the century, the Dutch labour market underwent a similar development, which led to an overstrained labour market. Given the current dynamics, there is a risk that this will happen again. In recent years, the social partners have pursued a responsible policy, which has resulted in moderate wage developments. It is now important to extend this responsible policy. Assuming balanced ratios between profit and labour income, this means wage growth that remains below the sum of inflation and productivity growth. Seen from this macro sum, the current contract wage demands for next year do not appear excessive. However, I would like to make two comments on this. Firstly, some sectors are facing significant price erosion due to international competition. Wage differentiation between sectors is therefore unavoidable. Given the differences in labour productivity growth between sectors, wage differentiation is also justifiable. Secondly, there is a risk that substantial incidental wage increases will still result in irresponsible wage developments. Globalization: Implications for China's Rise Let me now turn to the implications of globalisation for the labour market. Globalisation means that economies are becoming increasingly interconnected. I have just mentioned the Netherlands' dependence on the world economy. Globalization reinforces this dependence. I will explain this by discussing the consequences of China's rise as an economic superpower. The rise of China is giving a huge supply boost to the global economy. China, for example, now accounts for 16 percent of total world production. In the early 1980s, this was less than 4 percent. In terms of output, China has now surpassed the euro area as the world's second largest economy after the US. The rise of China is clearly noticeable to everyone in the Netherlands. Textiles and electronics, for example, have become considerably cheaper in recent years, partly thanks to cheap Chinese production. On the other hand, the explosive growth of China's economy has pushed up the prices of raw materials and oil. Anyone who refuels regularly can tell you about this. On balance, however, the Dutch consumer benefits from the rise of China. According to recent research, Dutch families have saved an average of 300 euros per year in recent years due to cheap Chinese imports. The appreciation of the euro has also helped. This brings me to the question of whether the rise of China poses a threat to Dutch employment. To answer this question, we need to look at what China and the Netherlands respectively are relatively good at. China appears to be particularly good at producing and exporting clothing, shoes, toys and consumer electronics cheaply. The Netherlands, on the other hand, is relatively good at the production and export of flowers, dairy and food. Chinese exports therefore show little overlap with Dutch exports. The situation is different for a country such as Italy, which faces strong competition from China in the footwear and clothing sector. Italy is an example of a Western economy that, due to the rise of China, will have to focus less on industry and more on the service sector. This transition from an industrial to a service economy started in the Netherlands several decades ago. Examples include the restructuring of the textile and shipbuilding sectors. The service sector in the Netherlands now accounts for three-quarters of employment and that share is growing by half a percentage point per year, thanks in part to China. In this way, the Netherlands can better exploit its strong geographical position as a distribution centre for Europe due to the rise of China. The increase in Chinese exports, for example, creates a lot of activity for the transport sector. For example, 1000 trucks currently drive to and from Rotterdam every day with Chinese containers. According to a recent study by the Netherlands Bureau for Economic Policy Analysis, the rise of China has created about 15,000 jobs in the Dutch export sector. In addition, about 8,000 jobs have been created by the increased importance of the Netherlands as a distribution centre. In total, about 23,000 new jobs have been created. On the other hand, China's rise has been accompanied by job losses in some sectors. Consider, for example, the transfer of production from the Philips factory in Stadskanaal to China. It is difficult to quantify these job losses for the Netherlands as a whole. However, as I mentioned above, China is hardly a competitor of the Netherlands in terms of product specialisation. As a result, the total job losses are estimated to have been limited, and the rise of China is on balance beneficial for Dutch employment for the time being. However, this may change in the future if the educational attainment of the Chinese population increases. Like Japan in the past, China could then focus more on high-value industry and services. In order to withstand this potential competition, it is therefore essential to properly train our workforce. I have just noted that the Netherlands is increasingly transforming itself into a service economy. Some services are by nature location-specific, such as a hairdresser. However, other services are becoming less and less location-specific due to the possibilities of modern information technology. For example, a call center of a large company does not necessarily have to be located in the Randstad. On the contrary, it may well become more attractive for such service companies to establish themselves where office space is still relatively cheap, such as in the North. At the same time, it would also make it less necessary for young people from the North to move to the crowded Randstad for a job. The meritorious performance of the Dutch economy can therefore offer opportunities for strengthening the economic structure of the North, from which the real estate sector can also benefit. Higher labour participation and longer working week help to cope with ageing population Then there are the implications of an ageing population for the labour market. Like globalisation, the ageing population will change society. The ageing of the population is noticeable to everyone now that the baby boom generation is slowly retiring. However, the ageing of the population will be a permanent phenomenon, as life expectancy has structurally increased and the birth rate has fallen structurally. The development of the number of over-sixty-fives per 100 adult under-sixty-five is significant in this respect. In 2040, this indicator for the old-age pressure will be as high as 46, double the current 23. At the moment, the North is already slightly ahead of the rest of the Netherlands in terms of ageing. For example, the grey pressure in Groningen is currently 24, in Friesland 25 and in Drenthe even 27. Here the comparison with the American state of Florida comes to mind, where many retired Americans spend their old age because of the pleasant climate. Although the North cannot quite mirror Florida in terms of climate, the North does offer the desired peace and space for retirees. Some even speak of Drentheians in this context. The care needs of these pension migrants from the rest of the Netherlands can give the service sector in the North a boost. In this way, the ageing population also offers opportunities for the North. Compared to many other countries, the Netherlands has an excellent pension system. For example, every person over the age of sixty-five is entitled to an AOW benefit and often also to a supplementary pension through participation in a pension fund. Many pension funds ran into problems after the turn of the century due to the collapse of stock market prices. At the moment, almost all pension funds have put their house back in order. Although future indexation is often not yet guaranteed, supplementary pensions are age-proof in the sense that nominal pension entitlements are covered. The situation is different for the AOW. In contrast to supplementary pensions, the state pension is not financed by savings, but by levying state pension contributions on the income of working people. The increase in the number of AOWers per potential worker makes the AOW system vulnerable. This raises the question of what we can do to broaden support for the state pension. I will outline two options. Firstly, it would help if we could get more people into work. Less than two-thirds of the 100 adults under the age of 65 in the Netherlands are currently working. So there is room for improvement. Secondly, it would help if we worked a little longer. At 26 hours, the average Dutch working week is currently the shortest of all industrialised countries. So there is potential here too. A higher labour participation rate and a longer working week could significantly broaden the economic support base for the state pension. Let me illustrate this with a simple calculation. Imagine that the employment rate would immediately rise from the current 64 percent to 75 percent. Suppose that at the same time the average working week were to be extended by four hours to 30 hours with immediate effect. This would correspond to an increase in the labour supply with as many as one and a half million full-time jobs. This raises the question of how we can achieve such an increase in participation and an extension of the working week. Let me elaborate on that. I will start with increasing participation. In recent years, about 5% of all young people in school left school without a diploma. As a result, these drop-outs are not sufficiently qualified on the labour market, which means that they have to rely on social security more often. It is therefore very important that young people complete their education. Not only young people, but also older people in the Netherlands give the pipe to Maarten relatively early: on average, we retire at the age of 61 in the Netherlands. Although this is in line with the European average, people outside Europe often retire later: in the US at the age of 64 and in Japan at the age of 69. Because we retire so young in the Netherlands, only 15 out of every 100 women in the age group of 60 to 65 are currently working, and only 30 out of every 100 men - of which I am fortunate to be one myself. Since we are living longer and staying healthy longer, we could work a little longer. In my opinion, the transition of the Netherlands to a service economy, which I have just mentioned, also offers opportunities for people to participate in the labour process for longer. After all, the computer programmer working from the office chair suffers less from physical wear and tear than, for example, a bricklayer. Provided that this computer programmer is sufficiently trained during his working life, he can therefore also work longer. In the context of early retirement and pre-pension schemes, the government has recently taken measures to make early retirement less financially attractive. Recent research by the Dutch Central Bank (DNB) has shown that with the right financial incentives, older people can indeed be persuaded to work longer. An increase in the state pension age could also promote the participation of older people. Such a measure acts as a double-edged sword: on the one hand, the number of AOW recipients is decreasing, and on the other hand, the number of AOW premium payers is increasing. However, as we know, this is a very sensitive issue. The SER recently advised the incoming cabinet to 'develop a balanced policy to tackle the bottlenecks associated with the ageing population, in the areas of care, welfare and income'. Then there is the second option for broadening the economic base for the ageing population, namely the extension of the average working week. For example, the standard for a full-time working week could be set back to 40 hours. However, the short average working week in the Netherlands is also the downside of the large number of part-time workers. For example, no less than 75% of all Dutch women currently work part-time. Part-time work stems in part from the desire to make time for raising children. However, research shows that many women would like to work longer, but that this is simply not worthwhile because of high marginal tax rates and loss of childcare subsidies. In addition, it is often practically impossible to work more hours due to a lack of good before- and after-school care. The government has recently taken measures to make childcare financially attractive even when working longer, and to oblige schools to offer out-of-school care. These measures reduce the obstacles to working more, and can broaden the economic base for an ageing population. Suppose we do indeed succeed in increasing the labour supply through higher labour participation and a longer working week. The question then arises as to how this extra labour supply can be absorbed. First and foremost, this requires a flexible labour market, in which both employees and employers are prepared to respond to changing circumstances. Continuous retraining and further training during the career is essential in this respect. Secondly, it is important to make it more attractive for employers to keep older people in employment for longer. A targeted policy in this area can contribute to a cultural change: from sending older people into retirement as soon as possible to allowing older people to participate for as long as possible. Lock Dutch society will change as a result of globalisation and an ageing population. In my estimation, however, both developments offer opportunities to make better use of the Dutch labour potential. Globalisation contributes to the transition of the Netherlands to a service economy, making national production more knowledge-intensive. Provided that the Dutch labour force remains sufficiently qualified, this is more of an opportunity than a threat to employment. With the ageing population, the challenge lies mainly in increasing labour participation and extending the working week. With adequate childcare facilities and the right financial incentives, it should be possible to make better use of the Dutch labour potential. As explained above, globalisation and an ageing population can also offer specific opportunities for the North. If the North manages to capitalise on these opportunities, this may still be a reason for the national government to build the coveted suspension train in the future. With this, the travel time between the West and the North would hopefully finally be experienced as long as that between the North and the West!
text_original: Speech president Wellink over Globalisering en vergrijzing: implicaties voor de Nederlandse arbeidsmarkt Speech Datum 14 november 2006 Tijd 13:39 uur Lokatie Bijeenkomst van de Stichting Vastgoedrapportage Groningen-Assen, Groningen Spreker Dr. A.H.E.M. Wellink Vanmiddag zal ik spreken over de implicaties van globalisering en vergrijzing voor de Nederlandse arbeidsmarkt. Daarbij komen ook de specifieke gevolgen voor het Noorden aan bod. Maar eerst wil ik graag de actuele stand van zaken op de Nederlandse arbeidsmarkt met u doornemen. Actuele stand van zaken Laat ik beginnen met enkele cijfers over de groei van de Nederlandse economie. Nadat de Nederlandse economie in de tweede helft van de jaren negentig gemiddeld met vier procent per jaar groeide, bedroeg de gemiddelde economische groei in de periode van 2001 tot 2003 minder dan n procent per jaar. In 2004 trok de groei aan tot twee procent, om in 2005 weer terug te vallen tot anderhalf procent. Voor dit en volgend jaar voorzie ik een groei van ongeveer 3%. Na een tijdelijke hapering in 2005 komt de economie dus nu echt op stoom. Het herstel volgt daarbij een traditioneel patroon. Nadat eerst de exporten aantrokken, volgen nu de bedrijfsinvesteringen en de particuliere consumptie. Dit illustreert onze afhankelijkheid van de wereldwijde economische ontwikkelingen. Het aantrekken van de economische groei is goed merkbaar op de arbeidsmarkt. Zo is de werkloosheid in het afgelopen jaar al een procentpunt gedaald en neemt het aantal openstaande vacatures snel toe. Rond de eeuwwisseling heeft de Nederlandse arbeidsmarkt een soortgelijke ontwikkeling doorgemaakt, die toen leidde tot een overspannen arbeidsmarkt. Gezien de huidige dynamiek bestaat het risico dat dit weer gaat gebeuren. De afgelopen jaren hebben de sociale partners een verantwoord beleid gevoerd, dat in een gematigde loonontwikkeling heeft geresulteerd. Het is nu zaak dit verantwoorde beleid door te trekken. Uitgaande van evenwichtige verhoudingen tussen winst- en arbeidsinkomen, betekent dit een loonstijging die onder de som van de inflatie en de productiviteitsstijging blijft. Vanuit deze macrosom bezien, lijken de huidige contractlooneisen voor volgend jaar niet buitensporig. Hier wil ik echter wel twee kanttekeningen bij plaatsen. Ten eerste worden sommige sectoren door internationale concurrentie geconfronteerd met forse prijserosie. Loondifferentiatie tussen sectoren is dan ook onontkoombaar. Gezien de verschillen in arbeidsproductiviteitsgroei tussen sectoren is loondifferentiatie ook goed te rechtvaardigen. Ten tweede bestaat het risico dat door forse incidentele loonstijgingen alsnog een onverantwoorde loonontwikkeling resulteert. Globalisering: implicaties opkomst China Dan zal ik nu ingaan op de implicaties van globalisering voor de arbeidsmarkt. Globalisering houdt in dat economien in toenemende mate met elkaar verbonden raken. Ik noemde zojuist al de Nederlandse afhankelijkheid van de wereldeconomie.
