DNB is concerned with financial stability and trust. As the indexation component is an important part of a pension contract, we regularly present an estimate for the weighted average real funding level. That is the funding level if pension obligations are raised every year in line with expected price developments. Assuming 2% per cent annual indexation in the future this real funding estimate is now just over 100%. This is an average, meaning that some pension funds do better and others do worse. I would like to encourage pension funds to be transparent about their real funding ratio. The reason I promote this awareness is that there is a distinction between the objective of pension funds expressed in real terms and the regulatory constraint which is defined in nominal terms. To fulfil their indexation ambition in an affordable manner, pension funds generally develop a long-term investment strategy. The implementation of their strategy involves significant risks, for which the funds are remunerated. But as a result of these risks, their financial position is also subject to substantial volatility. The introduction of marked-to-market valuation gives a precise snap-shot of the funding position and thus highlights this volatility. Such valuation makes clear to what extent a difference in duration between liabilities and fixed income investments is a risk factor for pension funds. In reaction to that, some pension funds have gradually raised the average duration of their fixed income assets since 2004. Better matching of nominal liabilities of course helps to pass the solvency test but does not necessarily contribute to the realisation of indexation policy of the pension fund. It would be an unintended consequence of the new pension regulation if the nominal constraint was to be allegedly mistaken for the objective function. Pension funds should keep a clear view on the real world, within the nominal constraint set by the pension regulator. This illustrates the complicated trade-off between short term and long term objectives, on the one hand, and nominal versus indexed liabilities, on the other hand. All four dimensions are incorporated into the new Pension Act, but it is the challenge of the professionals in the industry to find the optimal solution under the specific circumstances they encounter. Long term uncertainties Fortunately, the financial position of pension funds has improved in the past few years. But even though most pension funds have now reduced or eliminated their solvency deficits, there is still a need to strengthen the sustainability of our old age provisions. This is due to a number of major uncertainties. One of these is related to the future changes in the economic structure. Labour will become scarcer compared to capital, while some sectors will grow and others will shrink. Through wage negotiations and labour mobility, among other factors, this could affect the pension system. For instance, tight labour market conditions in certain sectors may translate into upward pressure on wages. Our simulations show that if the rate of inflation is one percentage point higher on a permanent basis, the real funding ratio drops, on average, by five to ten percentage points relative to the baseline projection. Changes in economic structure may also give rise to increasing discontinuity risks during the pension accrual phase. These are risks that manifest themselves when companies go bankrupt or otherwise cease to exist and therefore need to be taken into account. Another uncertain factor is the development of asset returns. Since the Dutch second pillar is based on full funding, adequate returns are essential to secure the pension benefits. Structurally lower asset returns imply, on average, higher pension contributions and perhaps higher indexation cuts for pension scheme members. Specifically, in the event the equity risk premium turns out to be one percentage point lower than foreseen, pension contribution rates would in the long run have to be some five percentage points higher to deliver the same pension result. Increasing the allocation to bonds would imply a lower risk premium and lower return prospects, leading to higher average pension contributions. On the other hand, this would also provide pension plan members with greater certainty as to their pensions. The DNB Dutch Household Surveys, by the way, point out that the majority of respondents value security and are willing to pay for that. Raising the pensionable age in line with the increased life expectancy, for instance by two years, would also make for better controllability of pension liabilities. In periods of recovery, this would reduce the need for recourse to indexation cuts or contribution raises. Moreover, our simulations show that, in the long run, contribution rates could, on average, be one percentage point lower. All of these solutions need further consideration. The tools to do this are available. The Financial Assessment Framework can be used to determine the trade-off between risk, return and pricing. I do hope that this Academy is in the business of analysing all of this. The importance of the Academy There is a great opportunity for this Academy to exchange theory and practice, both nationally and internationally. To my knowledge there is no equivalent post-academic college which targets the pension and insurance professionals in the way the Netspar-UMBS Academy plans to. The approach is thematic, so the curriculum can easily track recent developments and bring cutting edge technologies to participants. Last, but not least, this Academy will prove to be a valuable network, bringing people together from different backgrounds, institutions and countries. If the Netspar-UMBS Academy succeeds in its mission, top lecturers, professionals and decision makers will regularly exchange thoughts here in the Netherlands, bringing pension thinking and education to a higher level. A key feature of the Academy is interactive learning. Case studies will probably determine the slope of the learning curve. As a pension supervisor I would be able to show ample practical experiences, but we are bound by confidentiality considerations. Nonetheless, DNB warmly supports this Academy and other initiatives to bring the pension debate to a higher level. Later this week DNB, Netspar and the International Organisation of Pension Supervisor will jointly co-host a two-day conference entitled Frontiers in pension finance and pension reform. The objective of this conference is to facilitate the dialogue between pension stakeholders on the implications of these frontiers for pension funds, supervisors and governments. I do hope to see many of you on Thursday and Friday at The Grand in Amsterdam. Let me finish by congratulating academic director Rob Bauer and all of you who contributed to the origination of this unique Academy. I wish you all the inspiration you need to accomplish your mission.

Title: Speech by Witteveen Managing Director: Challenges for the Dutch pension sector
text: Speech by Witteveen Managing Director: Challenges for the Dutch pension sector Speech Date: 16 april 2007 Time: 2:30 p.m. Location Kurhaus Hotel, Scheveningen - General meeting of members of the Association of Industry Pension Funds Speaker Mr. D. Witteveen, Director of the Dutch Central Bank "The pension fund is a unique and special institution that cannot go bankrupt; After all, the rights of participants can be curtailed." Legally, this may be correct, but also as a lawyer I say: I am happy to help dispel this fairy tale. Stamping by a pension fund is no less serious than the bankruptcy of an insurer or a bank. Today, I would like to emphasise once again that pensions are a social provision that should not be underestimated, and that they must be treated seriously. More than 8.5 million people have a pension benefit or pension entitlement. With pension assets of 680 billion euros, their financial "pension interest" is on average 80,000 euros per person. Within Europe, pensions are dealt with in different ways. In my opinion, the Netherlands has a very strong starting position. We, the Netherlands, can play a pioneering role in the reforms and adjustments that have been initiated in Europe. You, the Dutch pension sector and perhaps more broadly the Dutch financial sector, are facing major challenges in this regard. It is necessary to adapt to a rapidly changing environment. At the same time, this offers opportunities. The Netherlands has a very strong starting position within Europe Let me start with the rock-solid starting position of the Dutch pension sector. A system characterized by collectivity, risk sharing and efficient implementation. We have a solid system of supplementary pensions with a rich history. With pension assets amounting to approximately 130% of GDP, the Netherlands stands out from an international perspective. Pension administrators operate in an environment with a highly developed infrastructure and innovative service providers. The Netherlands has a highly trained staff with actuarial expertise and knowledge of asset management, risk management and fund administration. In addition, it will come as no surprise to me to mention this, the Netherlands has a modern supervisory framework that gives substance to a 'principle-based' approach. Just look at what we are doing in this area with the topic of hedge funds. The Netherlands has always been at the forefront of modernising supervision; of adapting to markets and pension developments. What do I see as characteristic innovations that put the Netherlands at the forefront of Europe? I will mention three of them. Firstly, the scope we offer to the use of internal models. Secondly, the application of the 'prudent person' principle: the Netherlands has virtually no investment restrictions. Thirdly, flexible recovery periods. As a supervisor, we think along with the pension institutions and provide tailor-made solutions. You experienced this yourself during the stock market crash at the beginning of this century: whereas according to the letter of the law you had a few months to recover and otherwise would have had to close or reinsure, we as a regulator have given you more time. In the end, the financial position of the funds was quickly restored. The modern Dutch supervisory framework contributes to the sustainability and resilience of our pension system. It increases the security of the pension for the participants and it increases the predictability of the pension burden for the entrepreneurs who run less competitive risk with those securities. I would also like to point out a few advantages of the consultation culture in the Dutch pension environment (there are of course also disadvantages): we can and want to talk about the price and quality of pensions. And that's what we do. You also invest in strengthening your professionalism as a director. That will come back after my presentation. 'Pension fund governance' is high on the policy agendas. And rightly so, because improving and strengthening governance is something you do for a reason. Keith Ambachtsheer argues that, on average, an institution with good governance yields a significantly higher pension result per euro saved in the fund, compared to an institution with poor governance. In my experience, there is a world to be won. If, by strengthening governance, all pension funds manage to reduce administration costs by moving from their own to the average cost level and then even to the level of 'best practice', then we will not be doing anything new, but it will yield a lot. To illustrate: recent DNB research shows that there is a wide spread in the administration costs of pension providers. While the most expensive category has operating expenses of 1.2% of total assets, this percentage is only 0.1% for the cheapest category. To give you an idea of what the difference in costs of 0.5% could make to pension benefits if that cost difference were to continue to occur year after year: a cost saving of 0.5% of total assets could lead to more than 10% higher pension benefits over the entire term, or a lower contribution of the same order of magnitude (and not both at the same time). Dynamism in Europe offers opportunities With its many comparative advantages, the Netherlands is an excellent base for pension services within Europe. However, maintaining this starting position in a free European pension market cannot be taken for granted. This brings me to the second part of my contribution: the challenges facing European Member States and the opportunities they offer you. We are faced with the challenge of responding to the dynamics within the European pension sector. I see two developments at the root of this. Firstly, Europe's ageing societies. Secondly, the impact of the European Pensions Directive. Ageing population makes pensions a growth market First of all, the ageing population. In the coming decades, almost all European member states will see an increase in life expectancy combined with lower fertility rates. This is not a new phenomenon. The question is what we know about the ageing population and to what extent this knowledge is in the past and will be included in the funding for the future. Living longer means  if we no longer want to continue working  significantly higher pension costs. However, with an adequate calculation of mortality tables, the problem is well known. The political choice that countries face is whether this knowledge will also be incorporated into the prize. If pension costs are perceived as too high, the solution does not lie in opportunistically using, for example, outdated mortality tables, unrealistic expected returns or high discount rates. I will come back to that in a moment. An ageing society is a particular challenge for countries where pension systems are largely funded on a pay-as-you-go basis. In response to the ageing population, these countries are currently reforming their pension systems. In France, Germany and southern Europe, for example, pay-as-you-go financing through the public budget is gradually, sometimes partially, replaced by capital formation invested in the financial markets. In Germany, there is also a shift from pension reservation on the company's balance sheet to funded funds outside the companies. The ageing population and the transition to funded systems offer opportunities for the Dutch pension sector if we want to make use of them. In Western Europe, the market for the administration of occupational pension provisions is expected to grow from more than 7 trillion euros now to more than 16 trillion euros in 2015. This will be accompanied by an increasing demand for the administrative implementation of the underlying schemes, the management of the pension capital and the insurance of the related pension risks. These are all parts of the pension business that can be used to create jobs, often of high quality. Pension Funds Directive enables cross-border implementation Pension administrators can benefit from this growth market. This brings me to the second development that poses challenges for the Dutch pension sector: the Pension Funds Directive. This Directive allows for the cross-border administration of pension schemes. Companies can now host their pension schemes anywhere in Europe. But a pan-European pension fund, which bundles the local pension schemes of all employees of a multinational in Europe, is also a possibility. It offers the Dutch pension sector the opportunity, for those who want it, to play a role in the field of cross-border services in order to achieve cost advantages through economies of scale, also for the Dutch participant. The Netherlands has the potential to play a significant role in the European pension market. We really have something additional: 'proven technology' and pension institutions that others don't have. The 10 or 25 largest Dutch pension organisations are probably able to serve foreign customers, provided that there is room to do so. That does not necessarily mean that all these funds choose to do so, but they should at least be able to make this consideration. The challenge is to get the Dutch pension sector to take advantage of the opportunities on the European market, without compromising the essential features of the Dutch system. Scale is becoming increasingly important With the Pension Funds Directive, the European Commission has taken the first step towards a European internal market for occupational retirement provision. This leads to more competition between pension providers. And that brings me to the third part of my contribution: the importance of scale. Increasing competition makes cost efficiency, and therefore economies of scale, an even more important factor for pension funds. This effect is reinforced by the trend towards greater transparency. Scale really does matter. DNB research shows a wide spread in the level of execution costs without a direct relationship to the investment results; In fact, the difference between the fund with the lowest and the highest execution costs amounts to more than a factor of 10. I already told you at the beginning of my speech that implementation costs can mean a lot for the outcome for participants. The challenge is to reduce the spread in cost levels. This challenge goes beyond just thinking about the scale of a fund as a whole. I see a pension fund as a unique collection of ordinary activities and products, which can be outsourced to a large extent. Think of asset management or administration. The optimal scale differs per activity. A pension fund does not necessarily have the optimal scale for every activity and is therefore more likely to outsource some activities than others. But beware; Neither the expertise requirement nor the function of the board of directors to be "in control" can be outsourced. Fund managers also need to understand what they are doing when outsourcing. It cannot be the case that outsourcing all activities and processes means that the pension fund is de facto only managed by external parties and the directors are no longer 'in control'. DNB will not allow this either. Let's face it; In general, you carry out your tasks with a lot of commitment and you take the necessary expertise and professionalism seriously. That is also expected of you. After all, you derive your raison d'etre as a pension fund from the added value for your participants. A pension fund must remain affordable for all stakeholders compared to the alternatives. A pension fund with high administration costs has some explaining to do. Therefore, be transparent and ensure good, understandable accountability to the participants. It may well be that this fund provides tailor-made solutions and puts a lot of effort into personal contact with the participants, which means that the costs are higher than with comparable other funds. Be transparent about this so that all stakeholders have the opportunity to have an opinion on it. A deliberate choice for small-scale can be deliberate, but then all stakeholders must also have sufficient insight into the costs and benefits of this choice. Economies of scale can be achieved through mergers or cooperation between pension funds. Signals from the sector, at the moment especially from company pension funds, point to an increasing need for cooperation in order to achieve the desired scale. The road back to an industry-wide pension fund has already been taken a few times. This seems to me to be a positive development. We must ensure that such initiatives are not hampered by laws and regulations. Although the strong industry-like boundaries are logically explainable from a historical perspective, we must be careful that they do not form obstacles to being able to move with the needs of society. Those of you who have followed my debates over the past few years know that this is not the first time I have said this. Importance of an adequate price In addition to economies of scale, adequate pricing is crucial for the continuity of the pension fund and the sustainability of the pension scheme. Offering a pension below cost price is not a basis for sustainable business operations. This is the case in the Netherlands and also in Europe. The Pension Funds Directive is an opportunity for many countries to take serious action to ensure a competitive position in the market for occupational pension provision. Ireland and Luxembourg are striking examples. But Belgium is also making progress. Following the implementation of the Pension Funds Directive, Belgium has created a new legal framework for pension institutions. Meetings have been organised to put Belgium on the map. This illustrates that Europe is still working and is working; And that's good. At the same time, it is clear that you cannot continue to live on your achievements. This is also known as the Law of the Braking Lead. Nevertheless, the profiling of Member States deserves a further analysis, starting from the old Dutch saying: 'what you get from afar is tasty'. Let me say a few words about Belgium. In the media, you have been extensively informed about the way in which Belgium is strengthening its competitive position. The focus was on the Belgian supervisory requirements without being worked out in detail. It is therefore similar to the sale of a car, of which only a general leaflet is available, without the technical specifications. What does Belgium have that the Netherlands doesn't? It's hard to say. In part, the Belgian legal and supervisory framework still needs to be worked out and in part it is the same as in the Netherlands. Incidentally, there is no misunderstanding: I have no doubt that what the IMF  paraphased Dutch supervision is world-class  says about Dutch supervision can also be achieved by other member states, including Belgium. Nevertheless, a number of comments can be made on what is clear about the Belgian supervisory framework. For example, a pension fund in Belgium can consult with the Belgian regulator about the discount rate to be applied. Perhaps some of you will now say: 'Ah, Belgium is therefore advantageous because of the acceptance of a high discount rate in the determination of pension liabilities'. But is that so? The Belgian approach with a combination of flexibility, customization and marketing looks attractive. But it is questionable whether this approach promotes a good pension product. I once put myself in the position of a CFO of a company, that of a participant and that of a negotiator. In all three situations, I would not feel comfortable with the situation in Belgium. By using a higher discount rate  and therefore lower technical provisions  there is a greater chance that a situation of under-coverage will occur in Belgium. This, in turn, leads to a greater risk of an additional payment obligation on the part of the sponsor to be imposed by the Belgian regulator. I will first put myself in the position of a CFO, as far as that still works for me. I wouldn't be happy. Not only because this can put pressure on the cost structure, but also because according to current accounting rules, this risk must be reflected in the company's balance sheet and income statement. Moreover, this risk will arise mainly in times of economic hardship, so that the obligation to make additional payments will be pro-cyclical. To the extent that the sponsor is unable to meet the obligation, the pension participant also suffers. This bears the residual risks. Then it turns out that cheap can be expensive. The participant should also be careful not to compare apples and oranges. A 'Dutch' pension has, among other things, a different indexation structure than a 'Belgian' pension. And the special feature of the Pension Fund Directive is that a 'Belgian' pension can be administered in the Netherlands and a 'Dutch' pension in Belgium. In my imaginary role as CFO, I would have a lot of sympathy for my colleagues who are satisfied with the negotiators who have renegotiated the pension scheme into an arrangement at the intersection of DB and collective DC with a long-term stable contribution combined with a decent chance of indexation. And finally, the negotiator: what are they up against? If this person wants to have a Dutch scheme administered by a foreign pension institution, where the quality of the pension deteriorates by, for example, working with a high discount rate, he or she will run into two crucial parts of the Pensions Act. First, the consistency requirement applies to the relevant scheme. This requirement means that there must be consistency between expectations raised, financing and the realisation of conditional allowances. In concrete terms, this means that the pension institution also has to deal with the indexation matrix and that it cannot be the case that the contribution associated with the scheme will be lower if expectations remain unchanged. Secondly, the information provisions of the Pensions Act continue to apply. These, like the consistency requirement, are part of social and labour law. Foreign pension institutions that administer a Dutch scheme must also inform participants about, among other things, the amount of the expected indexation and the uncertainty surrounding it. The future indexation label will also apply to these pension institutions. This means that the pension quality offered is transparent. Or, in terms of another old Holland saying: "all value is for money". For the participants, quality is predictability and certainty. And for the employers, actually, too. That is why I am pleased with the FTK. And that is why this modern supervisory framework is also appreciated within and outside Europe. The FTK is an instrument to achieve adequate pension pricing and prevents the need to repair a shock afterwards. Of course, the FTK is by no means sacred nor perfect, but it is the best yet. The fact that it will continue to develop and adapt in the future does not change that. The FTK is an instrument to give substance to the 'prudent person principle'. We use the market price for this. Why? Because in the Netherlands we don't want to pay too high, but also not too low a price for pensions; It has to be a realistic price. With the FTK, you are prepared for pension risks. In other words, the FTK encourages pension funds to find an optimal balance between risk, return and transparency. It thus offers you a head start in Europe. It is not in the interest of the participants for countries to compete with each other on those supervisory requirements that offer a certain level of protection to pension participants. Of course, healthy competition between regulators that leads to better quality, accessibility and efficiency is a good thing. So do we. See, for example, the recovery period applicable to pension funds providing cross-border services. The Directive requires "fully funded at all times", for which the Dutch legislator has adopted a consistent and sensible approach. Consistent because we do the same to domestic and foreign pension funds. This is sensible because in the Netherlands we steer ex ante to prevent problems. Of course, that is no guarantee that a fund will never run into problems. But we have learned from the financial crisis at the beginning of this century, and have gained experience that it is better to steer ex ante to prevent problems than to correct them ex post. Giving funds some time to strengthen their financial position through recovery plans is "in the best interest of all". But a 'race to the bottom' cannot be in the interest of the participant. That is why DNB believes that rapid progress is needed to arrive at adequate European supervisory standards and methodologies that are in the interest of participants and contribute to pensions that remain affordable. It would also be good if we could avoid the tempting trap of a pro-cyclical premium regime at European level. In addition, for the Netherlands, I would like to protect you from long litigation after disappointing results. You and I are not waiting for a "Pension Loss Foundation" that will haunt your institution and you in person for decades with claims worth millions. Importance of good marketing of the Netherlands as a centre of pension services As far as competition is concerned, I have also looked with a slight smile at the marketing efforts of the various Member States. Belgium is sending the Prime Minister, Verhofstadt, to Switzerland to give a presentation on the attractiveness of Belgium as a location for pension funds. Ireland has a government agency where someone is working full-time to promote Ireland as a business location and attract financial institutions. And Luxembourg has a major conference on European pensions opened by Prime Minister in the presence of the Grand Duke of Luxembourg. At first glance, the Netherlands seems to be lagging behind in terms of visibility at major conferences and positive image in pension-oriented media. I don't think it's the Dutch thing to travel with a delegation of, for example, Balkenende, Bos, Donner, Borgdorff, Prins and Sibbing, Noordman and Van Popta, Sluimers, Wellink and I, whether or not with a member of the royal family, city and country to sell the Netherlands. At the same time, the Netherlands does have a strong case and that should be enough. If all goes well, we should hear our strengths in the media, based on the adage: "if you are satisfied, tell others; If you have any complaints, please tell us". Together, we need to project a positive image nationally and internationally. Above all, come to us, and also to the ministries, with your problems. Clearly identify the bottlenecks you encounter that are preventing you from achieving your European ambitions; that hinder you from taking advantage of the opportunities that have arisen. The door is always open and, very Dutch, the coffee is ready. Fence We have a lot to be proud of. Let's prevent the Law of the Inhibitory Lead from applying to the Netherlands. You are faced with the challenge of strengthening the future-proofing of our well-developed pension sector. This offers you opportunities in a European pension market that is emerging. Scale and an adequate price are crucial prerequisites for this. The FTK and your experience offer you a head start. I am confident that you are up to the challenge. The pension sector, you, has shown in recent years that it has an impressive ability to adapt. With its comparative advantages, the Netherlands is an excellently situated centre of pension knowledge and services within Europe. With a proactive attitude of all stakeholders, the Netherlands can consolidate, strengthen and expand its position. This is not a complex activity. After all, by analogy with an old Dutch proverb: "good goods, praise themselves".
text_original: Speech directeur Witteveen: Uitdagingen voor de Nederlandse pensioensector Speech Datum 16 april 2007 Tijd 14:30 uur Lokatie Kurhaus Hotel, Scheveningen - Algemene ledenvergadering Vereniging van Bedrijfstakpensioenfondsen Spreker Mr. D. Witteveen, directeur van de Nederlandsche Bank Het pensioenfonds is een unieke en bijzondere instelling die niet failliet kan gaan; er kan immers worden gekort op de rechten van deelnemers. Juridisch mag dit juist zijn, maar ook als jurist zeg ik: dit sprookje help ik graag de wereld uit. Afstempelen door een pensioenfonds is niet minder erg dan een faillissement van een verzekeraar of een bank. Vandaag wil ik nog eens benadrukken dat pensioen een niet te onderschatten maatschappelijke voorziening is waarmee serieus moet worden omgegaan. Ruim 8,5 miljoen mensen hebben een pensioenuitkering of pensioenaanspraak. Met een pensioenvermogen van 680 miljard euro, is hun financile pensioenbelang gemiddeld 80.000 euro per persoon. Binnen Europa wordt op verschillende manieren met pensioen omgegaan. Mijns inziens heeft Nederland een ijzersterke uitgangspositie. Wij, Nederland, kunnen een voortrekkersrol vervullen bij de in gang gezette hervormingen en aanpassingen in Europa. U, de Nederlandse pensioensector en wellicht breder de Nederlandse financile sector, staan daarbij wel voor grote uitdagingen. Er moet worden aangepast aan een sterk veranderende omgeving. Tegelijkertijd biedt dit kansen. Nederland heeft ijzersterke uitgangspositie binnen Europa Laat ik beginnen met de ijzersterke uitgangspositie van de Nederlandse pensioensector. Een systeem gekenmerkt door collectiviteit, risicodeling en een efficinte uitvoering. We hebben een solide stelsel van aanvullende pensioenen met een rijke historie. Met een pensioenvermogen van circa 130% van het BBP onderscheidt Nederland zich in internationaal perspectief. Pensioenuitvoerders opereren daarbij in een omgeving met een sterk ontwikkelde infrastructuur en innovatieve dienstverleners. Nederland beschikt over hoog opgeleid personeel met actuarile expertise en kennis van vermogensbeheer, risicobeheer en fondsenadministratie. Daarnaast, het zal niet verbazen dat ik dit memoreer, kent Nederland een modern toezichtkader dat invulling geeft aan een principle based benadering. Zie ook maar wat we op dit vlak doen met het thema hedge-funds. Nederland heeft altijd vooropgelopen met de modernisering van toezicht; van het meebewegen met markten en pensioenontwikkelingen. Wat zie ik als kenmerkende vernieuwingen, waardoor Nederland zich in de voorhoede bevindt binnen Europa? Ik noem u er drie. Ten eerste de ruimte die wij bieden aan het gebruik van interne modellen. Ten tweede toepassing van het prudent person principe: Nederland kent vrijwel geen beleggingsrestricties. Ten derde de flexibele hersteltermijnen. Als toezichthouder denken we mee met de pensioeninstellingen en leveren maatwerk. U heeft dit zelf ervaren tijdens de beurscrash begin deze eeuw: waar u volgens de letter van de wet een paar maanden de tijd had om te herstellen en anders had moeten sluiten of herverzekeren, hebben wij als toezichthouder u langer de tijd gegeven. Uiteindelijk heeft het herstel van de financile positie van de fondsen snel plaatsgevonden. Het moderne Nederlandse toezichtkader levert een bijdrage aan de houdbaarheid en de veerkracht van ons pensioenstelsel. Het verhoogt de zekerheid van het pensioen voor de deelnemers en het vergroot de voorspelbaarheid van de pensioenlast voor de ondernemers die met die zekerheden minder concurrentierisico lopen. Voorts wijs ik op een paar voordelen van de overlegcultuur in de Nederlandse pensioenomgeving (er zijn natuurlijk ook wel nadelen): we kunnen en willen praten over prijs en kwaliteit van pensioen. En dat doen we ook. U investeert bovendien in het versterken van uw professionaliteit als bestuurder. Dat komt n mijn presentatie nog terug. Pension fund governance staat hoog op de beleidsagendas. En terecht, want het verbeteren en versterken van governance doet u niet voor niets. Keith Ambachtsheer betoogd dat een instelling met een goede governance gemiddeld genomen een aanzienlijk hoger pensioenresultaat per in het fonds gespaarde euro oplevert, ten opzichte van een instelling met een slechte governance. In mijn beleving is een wereld te winnen. Als alle pensioenfondsen door het versterken van de governance weten te bewerkstelligen dat de uitvoeringskosten dalen door van het eigen naar het gemiddelde kostenniveau te bewegen en vervolgens zelfs naar het niveau van de best practice, dan doen we niets nieuws maar het levert wel een hoop op. Ter illustratie: recent DNB-onderzoek toont aan dat sprake is van een grote spreiding in de uitvoeringskosten van pensioenverstrekkers. Waar de duurste categorie bedrijfskosten heeft van 1,2% van de totale activa, is dit percentage voor de goedkoopste categorie slechts 0,1%. Om u een indruk te geven wat het verschil in kosten van 0,5% kan uitmaken voor de pensioenuitkeringen als dat kostenverschil zich jaar in jaar uit zou blijven voordoen: een kostenbesparing van 0,5% van de totale activa kan leiden tot meer dan 10% hogere pensioenuitkering gedurende de hele looptijd ofwel een lagere premie in dezelfde orde van grootte (en niet allebei tegelijk). Dynamiek in Europa biedt kansen Met zijn vele comparatieve voordelen is Nederland binnen Europa een uitstekende uitvalsbasis voor pensioendienstverlening. Het behouden van deze uitgangspositie in een vrije Europese pensioenmarkt is echter niet vanzelfsprekend. Daarmee kom ik bij het tweede onderdeel van mijn bijdrage: de uitdagingen waar Europese lidstaten voor staan en de kansen die deze u bieden. Wij staan voor de uitdaging in te spelen op de dynamiek binnen de Europese pensioensector. Ik zie twee ontwikkelingen die daaraan ten grondslag liggen. Ten eerste de vergrijzende Europese samenlevingen. Ten tweede de impact van de Europese Pensioenrichtlijn. Vergrijzing maakt pensioen een groeimarkt Allereerst de vergrijzing. De komende decennia is in vrijwel alle Europese lidstaten sprake van een toenemende levensverwachting in combinatie met lagere vruchtbaarheidscijfers. Dit is geen nieuw fenomeen. De vraag is wat we weten over de vergrijzing en in hoeverre deze kennis in het verleden is en voor de toekomst wordt meegenomen in de bekostiging. Langer leven betekent  als we niet langer willen doorwerken  fors hogere pensioenkosten. Bij een adequate calculatie van sterftetabellen is het probleem evenwel bekend. De politieke keuze waar landen voor staan is of deze kennis ook wordt verwerkt in de prijs. Als de pensioenkosten als te hoog worden ervaren, ligt de oplossing in ieder geval niet in het opportunistisch gebruikmaken van bijvoorbeeld verouderde sterftetabellen, onrealistische verwachte rendementen of hoge disconteringsvoeten. Ik kom daar straks nog op terug. Een vergrijzende samenleving is in het bijzonder een uitdaging voor landen waar het pensioenstelsel grotendeels op omslagbasis wordt gefinancierd. Als reactie op de vergrijzing hervormen deze landen momenteel hun pensioensysteem. Zo wordt in Frankrijk, Duitsland en Zuid-Europa de omslagfinanciering via de overheidsbegroting geleidelijk, soms deels, vervangen door kapitaalvorming die wordt belegd op de financile markten. In Duitsland vindt ook een verschuiving plaats van pensioenreservering op de bedrijfsbalans naar kapitaaldekking buiten de ondernemingen. De vergrijzing en de overgang naar kapitaaldekkingsystemen bieden  als we er tenminste gebruik van willen maken  kansen voor de Nederlandse pensioensector. Binnen West-Europa wordt de komende jaren een groei voorzien van de markt voor uitvoering van bedrijfspensioenvoorzieningen van ruim 7 biljoen euro nu tot ruim 16 biljoen euro in 2015. Dit zal gepaard gaan met een toenemende vraag naar de administratieve uitvoering van de achterliggende regelingen, het beheer van het pensioenkapitaal en het verzekeren van de gerelateerde pensioenrisicos. Allemaal onderdelen van het pensioenbedrijf waarmee, vaak hoogwaardige, werkgelegenheid kan worden gerealiseerd. Pensioenfondsenrichtlijn maakt grensoverschrijdende uitvoering mogelijk Pensioenuitvoerders kunnen profiteren van deze groeimarkt. Daarmee kom ik op de tweede ontwikkeling die de Nederlandse pensioensector voor uitdagingen stelt: de Pensioenfondsenrichtlijn. Deze richtlijn maakt grensoverschrijdende uitvoering van pensioenregelingen mogelijk. Ondernemingen kunnen nu hun pensioenregelingen overal in Europa onderbrengen. Maar ook een pan-Europees pensioenfonds, dat de lokale pensioenregelingen van alle werknemers van een multinational in Europa bundelt, behoort tot de mogelijkheden. Het biedt de Nederlandse pensioensector de kans, voor wie het wil, mee te spelen op het terrein van grensoverschrijdende dienstverlening om zo, ook voor de Nederlandse deelnemer, kostenvoordelen door schaalgrootte te behalen. Nederland heeft de potentie om een rol van betekenis te spelen op de Europese pensioenmarkt. We hebben echt iets additioneels: proven technology en pensioeninstellingen die anderen niet hebben. De 10 of de 25 grootste Nederlandse pensioenorganisaties zijn vast in staat om buitenlandse klanten te bedienen, mits die ruimte er zou zijn. Dat hoeft niet te betekenen dat al deze fondsen daar voor kiezen, maar ze zouden ten minste deze overweging moeten kunnen maken. De uitdaging is om de Nederlandse pensioensector de kansen op de Europese markt te laten benutten, zonder af te doen aan de wezenskenmerken van het Nederlandse stelsel. Schaalgrootte wordt steeds belangrijker Met de Pensioenfondsenrichtlijn heeft de Europese Commissie de eerste stap gezet op weg naar een Europese interne markt voor bedrijfspensioenvoorziening. Dit leidt tot meer concurrentie tussen pensioenaanbieders. En daarmee kom ik op het derde onderdeel van mijn bijdrage: het belang van schaalgrootte. Toenemende concurrentie maakt kostenefficintie, en dus schaalgrootte, een nog belangrijker factor voor pensioenfondsen. Dit effect wordt versterkt door de trend van meer transparantie. Schaalgrootte doet er ook echt toe. Uit DNB-onderzoek blijkt een grote spreiding in het niveau van uitvoeringskosten zonder directe relatie met de beleggingsresultaten; het verschil tussen het fonds met de laagste en de hoogste uitvoeringskosten loopt zelfs op tot meer dan een factor 10. Dat uitvoeringskosten veel voor de uitkomst voor deelnemers kan betekenen heb ik u aan het begin van mijn speech al verteld. De uitdaging is om de spreiding in kostenniveaus te verkleinen. Deze uitdaging gaat verder dan alleen nadenken over de schaalgrootte van een fonds als geheel. Ik zie een pensioenfonds als een unieke verzameling van gewone activiteiten en producten, die in belangrijke mate kunnen worden uitbesteed. Denk aan vermogensbeheer of administratie. De optimale schaalgrootte verschilt daarbij per activiteit. Een pensioenfonds heeft niet vanzelfsprekend de optimale schaalgrootte voor elke activiteit en zal daarom sommige activiteiten eerder uitbesteden dan andere. Maar let op; de deskundigheidseis noch de functie van het bestuur van het in control zijn, is uit te besteden. Fondsbestuurders moeten ook bij uitbesteden wel begrijpen waar ze mee bezig zijn. Het kan niet zo zijn dat het uitbesteden van alle activiteiten en processen ertoe leidt dat het pensioenfonds de facto alleen nog wordt gestuurd door externe partijen en de bestuurders niet langer in control zijn. DNB zal dit ook niet toelaten. Laten we wel zijn; in het algemeen voert u uw taken met veel betrokkenheid uit en u neemt de benodigde expertise en professionaliteit serieus. Dat wordt ook van u verwacht. U ontleent uw bestaansrecht als pensioenfonds immers aan de toegevoegde waarde voor uw deelnemers. Een pensioenfonds moet betaalbaar blijven voor alle belanghebbenden ten opzichte van de alternatieven. Een pensioenfonds met hoge uitvoeringskosten heeft wat uit te leggen. Wees daarom transparant en draag zorg voor een goede, begrijpelijke verantwoording naar de deelnemers. Het kan best zijn dat dit fonds maatwerk levert en veel werk maakt van persoonlijk contact met de deelnemers, waardoor de kosten hoger liggen dan bij vergelijkbare andere fondsen. Wees daar transparant over zodat alle belanghebbenden de mogelijkheid krijgen om er een oordeel over te hebben. Een bewuste keuze voor kleinschaligheid kan weloverwogen zijn, maar dan moeten alle belanghebbenden ook voldoende inzicht hebben in de kosten en in de baten van deze keuze. Schaalgrootte kan worden bereikt door fusies of samenwerking tussen pensioenfondsen. Signalen uit de sector, op dit moment met name van ondernemingspensioenfondsen, wijzen op een toenemende behoefte aan samenwerking om de gewenste schaalgrootte te bereiken. De weg terug naar een bedrijfstakpensioenfonds is al een paar keer ingeslagen. Dit lijkt mij een positieve ontwikkeling. We moeten er voor waken dat dergelijke initiatieven niet worden belemmerd door wet- en regelgeving. Hoewel de sterke bedrijfstakachtige grenzen vanuit historisch perspectief logisch verklaarbaar zijn, moeten we oppassen dat deze geen belemmeringen vormen voor het kunnen meebewegen met de behoefte in de samenleving. Degene die de afgelopen jaren debatten van mij hebben gevolgd, weten dat ik dit niet voor het eerst zeg. Belang van een adequate prijs Naast schaalgrootte is een adequate prijsvorming cruciaal voor de continuteit van het pensioenfonds en de houdbaarheid van de pensioenregeling. Het onder de kostprijs aanbieden van een pensioen is geen basis voor een duurzame bedrijfsvoering. Dat is in Nederland zo en ook in Europa. De Pensioenfondsenrichtlijn is voor veel landen aanleiding om serieus werk te maken van een goede concurrentiepositie op de markt voor bedrijfspensioenvoorzieningen. Ierland en Luxemburg zijn aansprekende voorbeelden. Maar ook Belgi timmert aan de weg. Belgi heeft naar aanleiding van de implementatie van de Pensioenfondsenrichtlijn een nieuw juridisch raamwerk voor pensioeninstellingen in het leven geroepen. Tot Zwitserland zijn bijeenkomsten georganiseerd om Belgi goed op de kaart te zetten. Dit illustreert dat Europa nog steeds effect heeft en werkt; en dat is goed. Tegelijkertijd is duidelijk dat je niet op je verworvenheden kan blijven teren. Dit wordt ook wel de Wet van de remmende voorsprong genoemd. Toch verdient de profilering van lidstaten een nadere analyse met als vetrekpunt het oud-Hollands gezegde: wat je van ver haalt is lekker. Laat ik eens kort stilstaan bij Belgi. In de media bent u uitgebreid deelgenoot gemaakt van wijze waarop Belgi haar concurrentiepositie verstevigt. Daarbij stonden de Belgische toezichteisen centraal zonder dat deze al precies zijn uitgewerkt. Het lijkt daarmee op de verkoop van een auto, waarvan alleen een algemene folder beschikbaar is, zonder de technische specificaties. Wat heeft Belgi dat Nederland niet heeft? Dat is lastig te zeggen. Voor een deel moet het Belgische wettelijk en toezichtkader nog worden uitgewerkt en voor een deel is het hetzelfde als in Nederland. Overigens geen misverstand: ik heb geen twijfel dat wat het IMF  geparafaseerd Nederlands toezicht is van wereldklasse  zegt over het Nederlandse toezicht ook door andere lidstaten, ook door Belgi, kan worden gerealiseerd. Toch kan een aantal kanttekeningen worden geplaatst op datgene wat wel duidelijk is van het Belgische toezichtkader. Zo kan een pensioenfonds in Belgi in overleg treden met de Belgische toezichthouder over de te hanteren disconteringsvoet. Wellicht zullen sommigen van u nu zeggen: Aha, Belgi is dus voordelig vanwege de acceptatie van een hoge disconteringsvoet bij de vaststelling van pensioenverplichtingen. Maar is dat zo? De Belgische aanpak met een combinatie van flexibiliteit, maatwerk en marketing oogt aantrekkelijk. Maar het is de vraag of deze aanpak een goed pensioenproduct bevordert. Ik heb me eens verplaatst in de positie van een CFO van een onderneming, die van een deelnemer en die van een onderhandelaar. In alle drie de situaties zou ik me niet comfortabel voelen bij de situatie in Belgi. Door gebruik te maken van een hogere disconteringsvoet  en daarmee lagere technische voorzieningen - bestaat in Belgi een grotere kans dat zich een situatie van onderdekking voordoet. Dit leidt op zijn beurt tot een groter risico van een door de Belgische toezichthouder op te leggen bijstortingsverplichting van de sponsor. Ik verplaats mij eerst eens in de positie van een CFO, voor zover dat mij nog goed afgaat. Ik zou niet blij zijn. Niet alleen omdat dit de kostenstructuur onder druk kan plaatsen, maar ook omdat dit risico volgens de huidige boekhoudregels tot uitdrukking moet komen in de balans en resultatenrekening van de onderneming. Bovendien zal dit risico zich vooral voordoen in tijden van economische tegenspoed, zodat de bijstortingsverplichting procyclisch zal uitpakken. Voor zover de sponsor de verplichting niet kan nakomen, gaat ook de pensioendeelnemer erop achteruit. Deze draagt de residuele risico's. Dan blijkt goedkoop wel eens duurkoop te kunnen zijn. De deelnemer moet ook opletten dat er geen appels met peren worden vergeleken. Een Nederlands pensioen heeft onder meer een andere indexatie structuur dan een Belgisch. En het bijzondere van de pensioenfondsrichtlijn is dat in Nederland een Belgisch en in Belgi ook een Nederlands pensioen kan worden uitgevoerd. In mijn denkbeeldige rol van CFO zou ik veel begrip hebben voor mijn collegas die tevreden zijn met de onderhandelaars die de pensioenregeling hebben heronderhandeld naar een regeling op het snijvlak van DB en collectief DC met een langjarige stabiele premie in combinatie met een behoorlijke kans op indexatie. En tot slot de onderhandelaar: waar loopt deze tegenaan? Als deze persoon een Nederlandse regeling wil laten uitvoeren door een buitenlandse pensioeninstelling, waarbij de pensioenkwaliteit achteruit gaat door bijvoorbeeld te werken met een hoge disconteringsvoet, loopt hij aan tegen twee cruciale onderdelen van de Pensioenwet. Ten eerste is de consistentie-eis op de desbetreffende regeling van toepassing. Deze eis houdt in dat er sprake moet zijn van consistentie tussen gewekte verwachtingen, financiering en het realiseren van voorwaardelijke toeslagen. Concreet betekent dit dat de pensioensinstelling ook te maken heeft met de indexatiematrix en dat het niet zo kan zijn dat de premie die bij de regeling hoort bij ongewijzigde gewekte verwachtingen lager zal uitvallen. Ten tweede blijven de informatiebepalingen van de Pensioenwet van toepassing. Deze behoren, net als de consistentie-eis, tot het sociaal- en arbeidsrecht. Ook buitenlandse pensioeninstellingen die een Nederlandse regeling uitvoeren dienen de deelnemers te informeren over onder meer de hoogte van de te verwachten indexatie en onzekerheid daaromtrent. Het toekomstige indexatielabel zal ook van toepassing zijn op deze pensioeninstellingen. Daarmee is de geboden pensioenkwaliteit transparant. Of, in termen van opnieuw een oud-Holland gezegde: alle waar is naar zijn geld. Kwaliteit is voor de deelnemers voorspelbaarheid en zekerheid. En voor de werkgevers eigenlijk ook. Daarom ben ik blij met het FTK. En daarom wordt dit moderne toezichtkader ook gewaardeerd binnen en buiten Europa. Het FTK is een instrument om te komen tot een adequate beprijzing van pensioen en voorkomt dat achteraf een schok moet worden gerepareerd. Natuurlijk, het FTK is zeker niet heilig noch perfect, maar het is wel het beste tot nu toe. Dat het in de toekomst verder zal ontwikkelen en dat het zal worden aangepast, doet daar niets aan af. Het FTK is een instrument om handen en voeten te geven aan het prudent person principle. We maken daarbij gebruik van de marktprijs. Waarom? Omdat we in Nederland niet een te hoge, maar ook geen te lage prijs voor pensioen willen betalen; het moet een realistische prijs zijn. Met het FTK bent u voorbereid op pensioenrisicos. Anders gezegd, het FTK stimuleert pensioenfondsen om een optimaal evenwicht te vinden tussen risico, rendement en transparantie. Het biedt u daarmee een voorsprong in Europa. Het is niet in het belang van de deelnemers als landen elkaar beconcurreren op die toezichteisen die de pensioenparticipanten een zekere bescherming bieden. Natuurlijk, gezonde concurrentie tussen toezichthouders die leidt tot een betere kwaliteit, toegankelijkheid en efficintie, juist goed. Wij doen dat ook. Zie bijvoorbeeld de herstelperiode die geldt voor pensioenfondsen met grensoverschrijdende dienstverlening.De richtlijn eist fully funded at all times, waarvoor de Nederlandse wetgever een consistente en verstandige benadering heeft gekozen. Consistent omdat we naar binnenlandse en buitenlandse pensioenfondsen hetzelfde doen. Verstandig omdat we in Nederland ex ante sturen op het voorkomen van problemen. Dat is natuurlijk geen garantie dat een fonds nooit in de problemen komt. Maar we hebben geleerd van de financile crisis begin deze eeuw, en de ervaring opgedaan dat je beter ex ante kunt sturen op het voorkomen dan ex post corrigeren van problemen. Fondsen even de tijd geven om de financile positie weer te versterken, via herstelplannen, is in the best interest of all. Maar een race to the bottom op kan niet in het belang zijn van de deelnemer. Daarom vind DNB snel voortgang nodig is om tot Europese adequate toezichtstandaarden en methodieken te komen die in het belang zijn van deelnemers n bijdragen aan pensioen dat betaalbaar blijft. Het zou ook goed zijn als we op Europees niveau de verleidelijke valkuil van een procyclisch premieregime zouden weten te vermijden. Voor Nederland komt daar bij dat ik u graag wil behoeden voor lange processen na tegenvallende resultaten. U en ik zitten niet te wachten op een Stichting Pensioenverlies die uw instelling en u in persoon tientallen jaren achtervolgt met miljoenenclaims. Belang van een goede marketing van Nederland als centrum van pensioendienstverlening Wat betreft de concurrentieslag heb ik overigens met een lichte glimlach gekeken naar de marketing-inspanningen van de verschillende lidstaten. Belgi vaardigt de premier, Verhofstadt, af om in Zwitserland een presentatie te houden over de aantrekkelijkheid van Belgi als vestigingsplaats voor pensioenfondsen. Ierland heeft een overheidsinstantie waar iemand zich fulltime bezighoudt met de promotie van Ierland als vestigingsplaats en het aantrekken van financile instellingen. En Luxemburg laat een grote conferentie over Europese pensioenen openen door premier in de aanwezigheid van de Groothertog van Luxemburg. Nederland lijkt op het eerste gezicht achter te blijven wat betreft de zichtbaarheid op grote congressen en positieve uitstraling in op pensioen gerichte media. Het is denk ik niet des Nederlands om met een delegatie van bijvoorbeeld Balkenende, Bos, Donner, Borgdorff, Prins en Sibbing, Noordman en Van Popta, Sluimers, Wellink en ik al of niet met een lid van het koninklijk huis, stad en land af te reizen om Nederland te verkopen. Tegelijkertijd heeft Nederland wel een sterke casus en dat zou eigenlijk genoeg moeten zijn. Als het goed is zouden we onze sterke punten in de media moeten horen, vanuit het adagium: bent u tevreden, zeg het anderen; heeft u klachten, zeg het ons. Gezamenlijk moeten we nationaal en internationaal een positief beeld uitdragen. Kom vooral naar ons, en ook de ministeries, toe met uw problemen. Benoem helder de knelpunten waar u tegen aanloopt en die uw Europese ambities verhinderen; die u belemmeren om de ontstane kansen te benutten. De deur staat altijd open en, heel Nederlands, de koffie staat klaar. Afsluiting We hebben veel om trots op te zijn. Laten we voorkomen dat de Wet van de remmende voorsprong van toepassing is op Nederland. U staat voor de uitdaging om de toekomstbestendigheid van onze goed ontwikkelde pensioensector te versterken. Dat biedt u kansen in een Europese pensioenmarkt die ontstaat. Schaalgrootte en een adequate prijs zijn daarbij cruciale randvoorwaarden. Het FTK en uw ervaring bieden u daarbij een voorsprong. Ik ben ervan overtuigd dat u de uitdagingen aankunt. De pensioensector, u, heeft de afgelopen jaren laten zien over een indrukwekkende aanpassingskracht te beschikken. Met de comparatieve voordelen is Nederland binnen Europa een uitstekend gesitueerd centrum van pensioenkennis en -dienstverlening. Met een pro-actieve opstelling van alle stakeholders, kan Nederland zijn positie consolideren, versterken en uitbouwen. Dit is geen complexe activiteit. Immers, naar analogie van een oud-Hollands spreekwoord: goede waar, prijst zichzelf.

Title: Speech directeur Witteveen: Two challenges for a cross-sectoral approach to supervising Islamic financial institutions: Risk transparency and consistent regulatory standards
text: Speech directeur Witteveen: Two challenges for a cross-sectoral approach to supervising Islamic financial institutions: Risk transparency and consistent regulatory standards Speech Datum 15 mei 2007 Tijd 13:00 uur Lokatie 4th IFSB summit, Dubai Spreker Mr. D. Witteveen, directeur van de Nederlandsche Bank Introduction It is a pleasure and an honour to be invited by the Islamic Financial Services Board (IFSB) and to speak at its 4th summit on the need for a cross-sectoral approach to the supervision of Islamic financial services. So far we have heard about the experiences of our fellow regulators with multiple and cross-sectoral approaches towards the supervision of Islamic financial services. Two developments are important for regulators. First, the Islamic financial services industry is expanding rapidly worldwide, both in Muslim and non-Muslim countries. Each with their own challenges. A few countries have an encompassing Islamic financial sector, whilst others have a dual system. Second, financial innovation and the ongoing integration of financial sectors have made Islamic financial systems and products more complex. Against this background, two key challenges for regulators and supervisors of Islamic financial services are to quantify risks adequately and to foster consistency of regulatory standards and practices. Developments Islamic finance is booming business, although the rapid growth of the last ten years has to be maintained for the next ten years. The estimated yearly growth rate of 15 percent and current assets in excess of US 300 billion underscores the growing role of Islamic finance in the global financial sector (note 1). The increased variety and sophistication of Islamic financial services has enhanced convergence between Islamic finance and conventional finance. However, differences remain. Islamic finance has a long and rich history. One of the well-known sharia principles the prohibition on Riba, i.e. the prohibition of interest or any unjustified rewards, is based on the Quran (note 2). Comparable principles can also be found in the Old Testament and the Torah. Riba and other sharia principles strongly influence the design of Islamic financial products and forming a distinctive feature of Islamic finance. Another difference is that Islamic financial products are subject to a sharia approval process. Given different religious schools of thought, there is no uniform application of these sharia principles across the world. This complicates matters. Islamic financial institutions generally have their own sharia boards which provide advice and guidance on the design of financial products and services. Different interpretations may result in the rejection of a financial product by one board and acceptance by another and, in the end, contracts for similar financial products may diverge (note 3). A second development is the changing financial landscape. Financial innovation has boosted the variety and complexity of financial products, diffusing the boundaries between financial sectors. Take the emergence of financial conglomerates: in the Islamic financial sector there are financial conglomerates combining banks and securities firm which is quite logic given the background. Those in Europe tend to combine banks and insurance companies, where deregulation was the catalyst for the emergence of financial conglomerates. Consequences So what are the consequences of the diverse sharia interpretations and the increasing complexity of financial products? I believe that different sharia interpretations pose a serious challenge in any financial system where consistency, standardisation and clarity are essential for robust contracts and efficient market operations. A lack of standardisation makes it difficult for regulators and consumers to define and understand contracts (note 4). Moreover, comparisons between Islamic and conventional financial products may be misleading and may even result in false expectations about specific financial products. Suppose you are one of the lucky owners of the latest Mercedes McLaren SLR with over 600 brake horsepower. And you accelerate within 3.6 seconds from 0 to 60 miles per hour. When you hit the brakes at this speed, you expect that you will stop at least as quickly. Whether they are made of ceramic or hardened steel, should not matter. We now turn to the financial sector. Take for example an 'Islamic mortgage', more familiar as the Islamic home purchase plan. It may be offered as either an Ijara or a diminishing Musharaka contract. These two contracts have different ownership terms. Under the Ijara, contract ownership is transferred to the consumer at the end of the agreement, whereas under the diminishing Musharaka ownership is transferred gradually. If the financial firm goes bankrupt, the consumer risks losing all or part of the property depending on the contract. Consumers may not be fully aware of this, especially in non-Muslim countries. Again, if you hit the brakes you expect that the car stops. If you take on a mortgage, you trust that you acquire property rights independent of the contract. The lack of uniformity has far-reaching consequences. It is more difficult for economic agents to fathom contracts and to understand the risk-profile. As a result, consumers and investors are less able to make informed decisions and risks may be priced incorrectly. This will lead to a suboptimal allocation of resources. In addition, the sector may not be able to take appropriate risk mitigation measures and regulators may be less able to carry out effective and efficient supervision to protect the interests of consumers. Given the increasing complexity and hybrid nature of Islamic financial products, understanding the underlying risks of these products is likely to represent a growing challenge. Consistency of treatment is not only important across product lines, but also across sectors. Regulators in most Muslim countries have adopted a sectoral approach towards the supervision of banks, securities firms and insurance companies (takaful operators)(note5). While this approach has the advantage of tailor-made solutions to sectoral developments, it may result in different treatments of financial services. As set out by the Joint Forum, it is therefore important to address sectoral issues at an early stage in the policy development process in order to minimise differences in regulatory approaches (note 6). Having said this, I would like to note that a cross-sectoral approach to the supervision of Islamic financial institutions is desirable but may not necessarily be required in every instance. But I am more positive in this respect than other speakers this morning. Nevertheless, banking and securities firms' supervisors rightly have a different focus in setting capital requirements. After all, investment account holders at securities firms participate in losses as well as profits, whereas demand deposit holders are at least partly protected by a guarantee. Challenges In my view, risk analysis at financial firms is the basis for addressing the increasing complexity of Islamic financial products. The first challenge is to break down Islamic financial products into their various components so that the underlying risks can be clearly quantified. In this way, appropriate risk-mitigating measures could be put in place to minimise risks of financial incidents. Fortunately, we are better equipped than ten to fifteen years ago to work out complex calculations, identify underlying correlations, model financial instruments and pinpoint the most substantial risks. For me the positive note is that we can develop instruments to treat similar products in a similar way and to treat different products relative to their differences. But we should not disregard the past. Although a financial product may be new, its basic parts and their associated risks may be well-known. In the end, the risk analysis performed by financial institutions should be the basis for risk-based supervision. Allow me to elaborate. Financial supervision should have the same aim as financial firms' own risk management: to minimise the risk of incidents, thereby fostering public confidence in the financial sector. A stable financial sector promotes an efficient allocation of resources and a country's economic development. In a risk-orientated supervisory framework, the supervisor's stance focuses on an institution's inherent financial and organisational soundness. The supervisor directs its resources and instruments to those areas where the net risks, being the gross risks corrected for an institution's internal risk mitigation measures, are largest. In this way, combining with a principle based approach, the supervisor is able to deploy its resources as effectively as possible. This approach is not new. In recent years we have witnessed a widespread shift towards risk-based supervision and steps to a more principle based approach. Note that a risk-based approach cannot take away all risks, nor should it aim to. An environment that values risk-taking and entrepreneurship contributes to a country's economic growth. The risk-taking behaviour of the Dutch East India Company, founded in 1602, resulted in the first-ever multinational corporation. The flourishing Asian trade brought huge profits and wealth to the Netherlands. Key to the success was that the Dutch businessmen were well aware of the huge risks; approximately one out of three vessels did not return. But through risk-sharing, the merchants were able to spread the financial losses of wrecked vessels and the gains on those ships that returned provided ample compensation. Again a positive note, not only the most modern and sophisticated developments are interesting, but the available approaches from the past are useful and interesting as well. A second challenge for regulators and the IFSB is to develop a cross-sectoral approach towards the supervision of Islamic finance that advances the consistency with supervision of conventional financial institutions. Most Muslim countries have a dual system with both Islamic and conventional financial institutions. In some but not all Muslim countries, the authorities apply an integrated approach towards both types of institutions (note 7). Integrated supervision, in our case within the central bank, is helpful. Moreover, Islamic finance has an increasing market share in non-Muslim countries. Again the challenge for regulators is to foster consistency between the supervision of both types of financial instruments. Principles on risk-based capital requirements, fair value accounting, transparency and corporate governance developed by various standard setting bodies like the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision BCBS), the International Organization of Securities Commissions (IOSCO) and the International Association of Insurance Supervisors (IAIS) serve as excellent points. As you all know, the IFSB and the Accounting and Auditing Organization for Islamic Institutions (AAOIFI) have already made much progress. Concluding remarks The aim of a cross-sectoral approach to the supervision of Islamic financial services should be to minimise the risk of financial incidents. The challenge is to reveal the underlying risk profile of complex and hybrid Islamic financial products. And than, sometimes differences become similarities. For example, Takaful companies will have a 'risk profile' similar to a mutual insurer. The risk analysis of financial institutions should be the point of departure. With the latest techniques available, Islamic financial institutions can quantify the risks of Islamic financial products. A better understanding of risks makes it possible for institutions and regulators alike to implement an effective and efficient risk-based supervisory framework. In this context, increased risk transparency can support an optimal allocation of resources. A lot of the work, expertise and experience at the Joint Forum are dedicated to achieve an effective and efficient risk-based supervisory framework and as such I am looking forward to cooperate with the IFSB. Our cross-sectoral experience could be useful for the work of the IFSB. Last but not least, when regulators develop policies, the challenge is to foster consistency between the supervision of Islamic and conventional financial services. Much work has been done by various standard-setting bodies. The diminishing difference between Islamic and conventional financial products makes it easier to match Islamic finance to the recently developed standards. Ultimately, regulators should provide the same level of protection and confidence to market participants and public. With respect to the different sharia interpretations, the IFSB can promote consistency by providing guidance. To conclude, development goes with time. So, whilst Islamic finance is pouring, the coming year will show more convergence between the standards in Islamic and conventional finance. As it took more ten to fifteen years to reach the present  from imperfect convergence to much convergence concerning sectoral supervisory standards  I am looking forward for the next ten to fifteen years. Notes 1. KPMG, 2007, Making the transition from niche to mainstream. 2. Yunis, H., 2007, New products, new challenges, Financial Regulator, 11 (4), pp. 53-56. 3. Bhambra, H., 2007, Regulating Islamic finance, Financial Regulator, 11 (4), pp. 49-52. 4. Ibidem Bhambra, 2007. 5. Zaher, T.S. and M.K. Hassan, 2001, A comparative literature survey of Islamic finance and banking, Financial Markets, institutions & instruments, 10 (4), pp. 184-190. 6. Joint Forum, 2006, Regulatory and market differences: issues and observations, p.2 7. Ibidem Zaher and Hassan, 2001.

Title: Speech president Wellink over 'No globalisation without innovation'
text: Speech president Wellink over 'No globalisation without innovation' Speech Datum 4 juni 2007 Tijd 16:30 uur Lokatie Buenos Aires, Central Bank of Argentina Spreker Dr. A.H.E.M. Wellink Introduction I grew up in a small Dutch village. Although it was not in a polder, to me the world seemed flat. It took several years before I saw mountains for the first time and realised that the world is not flat. The generation of my grandchildren misses this kind of experience. Flying long-distance at early age is no longer exceptional in the more prosperous parts of the world. The world has changed dramatically in the course of decades. Information technology has brought us many new opportunities, in particular mobility of people, goods and ideas. Ill discuss technological progress, and what it means for the macro economy in general, and for monetary policy in particular. Globalisation is driven by technological change There are at least four manifestations of technological change that have dramatically reshaped the world over the past decades: What we see in major cities are people from all over the world. What lies behind this is cheap and fast air traffic. Competition is a driving force. So is technology, which makes air transportation more efficient, and management skills that allow for splitting up the market in high yielding business-class tickets and low cost fares. What we see are cheap imports from China everywhere in the Western world. What lies behind this are low transportation costs thanks to the cargo container. The cargo container can move non-fragile goods for about 1% of retail value to anywhere in the world. In the pre-container era, shipping costs used to be between 10 and 20% of retail value. [i] Apart from low transportation costs, additional factors are needed to explain the surge in Asian products in Western markets. In particular the catch-up of Asian economies is creating new trading opportunities. What we see is offshoring of labour-intensive production to low-wage countries. What lies behind this is that new technologies allow the production process to be unbundled. Production sites are located far from target markets, both in manufacturing and in the service industry. The share of offshored inputs in GDP can reach up to12%, as in Canada and the Netherlands. [ii] What we see is low-skilled labour in the West feeling a cold wind of competition from cheap labour from Asia and Central and Eastern Europe . At the same time, wages for high-skilled labour are on the increase. What lies behind this is skill-biased technology. Automation lowers demand for low-skilled workers, since computers offer a substitute. But computers can also amplify natural advantages of high-skilled labour, as complements to labour. A talented professional can serve a much larger customer base due to new ICT opportunities. Financial engineering and management skills also tend to favour high-skilled labour. These are just examples, illustrating that there would be no global economy without new technology. Technology has always been the driving force for change. This was the case when the invention of the printing press in the 15th century boosted the diffusion of ideas; and it is still the case in todays world, where ideas are spreading much faster than twenty years ago thanks to the internet. Macro-economic consequences Technological change has brought the world prosperity. In recent years, output growth has been at levels not seen since the early 70s. Not just Western economies are growing fast. China and India are integrating in the world economy at full speed. China s average productivity growth over the last ten years was close to 10%. Average productivity growth in emerging and developing countries has also increased, to 5% last year. [iii] Despite a recent pick-up, productivity growth in Latin America is lagging that in other emerging markets. Although technology is a source of welfare, it can also have negative side-effects. For instance, the unprecedented speed at which ideas are passed between people is a key achievement of the ICT revolution. But it also allows bad ideas to travel fast, such as religious fundamentalism. I feel some sympathy for those who fear rapid technological change. But whether we like it or not, we cant stop technological progress. Like toothpaste, once its out of the tube, it is hard to get it back in again. The challenge is to make sure that new technologies bring change for the better. There are winners and losers from technological change, at least in relative terms. The developing world at large is benefiting from recent developments. However, some areas are losing out. On the losing end are areas that lack connections to the container-handling network and the internet. This applies to areas that lack crucial infrastructure, be it reliable electricity and roads, or the rule of law. In the Western world, job security has diminished, not just for blue-collar workers. These days, services in ICT and other high-tech sectors are offshored to low-income countries. But the number of offshored jobs is still very modest compared to the total number of jobs lost and created. In the Netherlands , roughly 9.000 jobs are offshored each year, whereas the annual number of job destruction and creation is above 800.000. [iv] Since the ICT revolution is skill-biased, it favours high- over low-skilled labour. Fortunately, higher income inequality between high- and low-skilled workers does not necessarily imply that low-skilled workers are worse off. The IMF has shown that recent trends have increased the size of the pie. Cheaper inputs have lifted output and overall labour compensation by about 6% in real terms in advanced economies over the last 25 years. [v] And all consumers benefit from lower prices. To keep labour market effects in check, employability is a key policy issue. Flexible employees can adapt to new circumstances that technology brings about. Governments can offer a helping hand by improving education, and by providing a social security system that encourages people to move from one job to another. In some countries, social security schemes may be so generous that they deter efforts to seek new employment. But the slogan the lower, the better goes much too far. In Latin America , for instance, social security schemes alleviate income inequality. If the benefits of economic growth are widely shared, support for economic reform can be expected to be broader than otherwise. Monetary policy The challenge for monetary policy is to adapt to the new environment. Fortunately, central banks have much more room for manoeuvre now than they had when Arthur Burns was appointed as Fed Chairman by President Richard Nixon back in 1970 with the words: [quote] I respect his independence; however, I hope that independently he will conclude that my views are the ones that should be followed [unquote]. Also downward pressure on inflation by cheap imports from low-income countries has made central bankers life in the Western world a bit easier than in the past. Prices for clothes and big ticket items such as cars and personal computers have declined. Computers became a lot cheaper if one takes into account quality improvements. The overall downward pressure on inflation has allowed for lower monetary policy interest rates, at least in the short term. In the longer term, the real equilibrium interest rate might rise. This would be the case if the world would have moved to a permanently higher trend rate of productivity growth. The jury is still out on whether this is true. Other things equal, a higher real equilibrium interest rate implies that monetary policy interest rates also have to move to a higher level, consistent with the new equilibrium. So, a major issue is to determine the trend rate of productivity growth. From a monetary policy point of view the question can be rephrased as: What is the level of growth at which the economy can operate without generating higher inflation? It is always difficult to determine the speed limits of an economy, but in times of change this is even more challenging. One development makes it particularly hard. That is the move from an industrial to a post-industrial society. In the 1950s, 30% of the US labour force was employed in manufacturing. Now the number is 10%. We have moved to a service oriented society. In the service industry, capacity utilisation cannot be measured by counting idle capacity in factories. Besides, productivity growth can only be estimated in an imprecise way. Usually, total factor productivity is used as the key measure. It is determined as a residual: productivity growth is the increase in value added that cannot be explained by the volume of inputs used. This measure is very rough. All in all, potential output and its growth rate is more difficult to determine than it was in an industrial economy. Uncertainty about potential output translates into uncertainty about the output gap between potential and actual output. It has always been tricky to base monetary policy on output gaps. Research by Orphanides suggests that the Great Inflation was to a large extent due to mismeasurement of potential output and the output gap. [vi] It appears virtually impossible to determine output gaps in real time. They can only be measured in a reliable way ex post, with the benefit of hindsight. Life can only be understood backwards, but it must be lived forewards as the Danish philosopher Kierkegaard said. This is certainly true for monetary policy, with its medium term objectives. How to cope with this? Ive learnt a couple of things since I thought the world was flat. One is that the objectives of monetary policy should be modest. Fine-tuning economic growth has always been a too ambitious goal in a world with long and variable lags in monetary transmission. A clear focus on low and stable inflation can safeguard central banks against the temptation of activism. Given current uncertainties, monetary authorities must be particularly cautious in interpreting the output gap. They have to remain firm in reaction to actual inflation and other relatively reliable indicators of inflation risks, such as excessive wage growth.
