As a side remark, I add that, in theory, capital account liberalisation and trade openness warrant a sharper focus of monetary policy on price stability rather than output stabilisation. [vii] International capital mobility, as well as broader access to financial markets, creates new opportunities for households to smooth consumption over the years. Free international trade allows for specialisation in domestic production. As a result, it might be possible to disentangle consumption and production to a higher extent than in the past. In other words, households can cushion changes in production without intervention by the central bank. I would like to conclude with a warning. A focus on price stability is more complicated than it sounds. Low and stable consumer price inflation is no reason for complacency. In spite of consumer price stability, asset price inflation may signal underlying imbalances, such as an overoptimistic risk assessment by financial market participants that keeps long-term interest rates at unwarranted low levels. Monetary policymakers must be forward-looking, and assess possible divergences between real and nominal factors in the area of monetary aggregates, credit and asset markets. How this should be done in practice is a difficult question that deserves further elaboration. I wont answer it now. Time is running out. Sometimes it is better to stop before one has finished. Notes [i] J. Bradford DeLong (2006) The box that changed the world, Project Syndicate. [ii] IMF (Spring 2007) World Economic Outlook. [iii] Productivity is measured as real GDP divided by working age population. Source: IMF (Spring 2007) World Economic Outlook. [iv] Numbers are averages over 2001-2005. Source: Dutch Ministry of Economic Affairs (2005) Visie op verplaatsing. [v] IMF (Spring 2007) World Economic Outlook. [vi] Athanasios Orphanides (2003) The quest for prosperity without inflation, Journal of Monetary Economics, Vol. 50, nr. 3. [vii] Assaf Razin and Prakash Loungani (2006) Globalization and equilibrium inflation-output tradeoffs, NBER Working Paper nr. 11641.

Title: Speech by director Schilder 'The contribution of pension management to stability'
text: Speech by director Schilder 'The contribution of pension management to stability' Speech Datum 13 september 2007 Time: 2:55 p.m. Location DNB meeting for directors of pension funds, Apeldoorn Speaker Prof. dr. A. Schilder, director of the Dutch Central Bank There is a lot of change in the pension world, but some things remain the same. For example, social partners, fund managers and regulators are jointly responsible for the financial soundness of our pension system. The social partners are responsible for the content of the scheme, you implement this scheme and DNB ensures that the agreements are complied with. This will remain the case under the Pensions Act. What is new, however, is the modernisation of prudential supervision. These include the introduction of market valuation of liabilities and investments, risk-sensitive solvency requirements and an important place for risk management through continuity analysis. In short, the new pension law provides a solid basis for looking to the future with confidence. But, although a good law is an important condition for success, it offers no guarantees. Ultimately, success depends in part on how you deal with the uncertainties that the future brings. Speaking of uncertainties: these are turbulent times in the financial markets. The past few weeks have once again illustrated that the mood in financial markets can change quickly and that the resulting losses can be large. What started with payment problems in a small segment of the U.S. mortgage market grew into a financial shock with a major impact. Globally, stock prices plummeted and liquidity problems arose in both the US and Europe, forcing European and US central banks to make additional liquidity available to financial institutions. Of course, developments in the financial markets also affect pension funds. Between mid-July and mid-August, the sector's average funding ratio fell by more than 12 percentage points, from around 159% to around 146%. This means that approximately 50 billion euros in buffers have been lost in one month, almost a tenth of the total Dutch pension assets. By the way, this is not an abnormal fluctuation. Over the past 10 years, the absolute change in 1 in 4 quarters was more than 10% funding ratio points. It is unlikely that the shock has fully worn off yet. We know from previous experience that shocks can linger for some time. Due to the 'perfect storm' of simultaneously falling capital market interest rates and share prices at the beginning of this century, the average funding ratio fell from 200% at the end of the 1990s to 120% in 2003. This 'perfect storm' has therefore largely wiped out the substantial buffer in a period of 3 years. This puts the current funding ratio into perspective. If we want to be able to absorb the same blow again, we should not think that we are well within the current 150%. All these experiences underline how important it is to take risks into account. This afternoon, I would like to discuss with you some of the conclusions we can draw from this: Firstly, pension funds should not focus their policy on daily exchange rates, but on the long term. Second: Within a long-term perspective, indexation plays a major role. It is recommended to pay attention to the actual funding ratio in your financial set-up. Thirdly, risk management is crucial for a good pension provision. The continuity analyses you need to develop are an indispensable tool for gaining insight into these risks. Pension policy should not be focused on daily exchange rates but on the long term..... Let me start with the first theme. When we started organizing this day in the spring, we thought that everyone would be comfortable today. Especially compared to the previous DNB retirement days. At that time, the financial position of the sector was still precarious and many of you were still working on recovery plans. The recovery then went much faster than expected and we were on average back in the right quadrant this spring. However, the current volatility shows that we should not count ourselves rich too quickly on the basis of short-term developments. This does not mean that we should be restless now. It does, however, show that you are well advised to focus your policy on the long term. The starting point for such a long-term policy is: prevention is better than cure. After all, the essence of a good pension scheme is a stable standard of living before and after retirement. This requires both a reasonably stable pension contribution and a benefit with sufficient prospect of indexation. The challenge for pension funds is to achieve this combination through a balanced distribution of benefits and burdens over time and among all stakeholders. Ideally, the long-term policy is reflected in the premiums. The recent volatility in financial markets illustrates that it is undesirable to allow the premium to be influenced too much by the issues of the day. In the recent past, we have seen the consequences of such policies. In the 1990s, for example, total premium income averaged only 6% of the wage bill. This was below the cost-covering level, but was considered possible due to the high real investment returns and ample financial position. As a result, labor was relatively cheap, which contributed to the overheating of the economy. Due to the aforementioned 'perfect storm', the premium had to be doubled in a short period of time to 12% of the wage bill. As a result, the recovery of the economy was relatively slower. A policy in which premiums are aligned with the current funding ratio therefore leads to pro-cyclical premium changes. Our pension system would then become a source of macroeconomic distortions. With hindsight, we can say that if premiums had been at a cost-covering level in the mid-1990s, the average funding ratio in 2003 would have been about 12% higher and would have been around 130%. We would have had less low premiums in the mid-1990s in a time of prosperity, but perhaps also fewer premium increases and indexation reductions between 2002-2005 in a time of adversity. In short, a good long-term policy avoids rapid premium adjustments in the event of changes in the funding ratio and thus limits pro-cyclical effects. One option offered by the Pensions Act is to use a cushioned contribution. Moreover, by building up sufficient financial space in good times, substantial premium increases and indexation reductions in bad times can be avoided. And then you stay away from those pesky recovery plans. These buffers have the advantage that they do not represent dead money, but also generate income that can be used to make indexation possible. This is an important source of funding, because the Dutch system does not require a reservation for indexation as long as it is conditional. This importance can be illustrated by looking at indexation in bad case scenarios. For an average Dutch pension fund with a funding ratio between 100% and 160%, every 10%-point increase in the funding ratio means a 10% increase in the expected indexation in bad times by 10%. ...... and has an eye for real liabilities (real funding ratio) This brings me to the second theme. A policy aimed at the long term also includes attention to indexation. After all, inflation can seriously erode the purchasing power of pension entitlements in the long run. On average, a 65-year-old lives another 15 to 20 years. If no indexation is done over that period, real income will fall by a quarter to a third at an inflation rate of 2% per year. Someone who turns 100 will see their purchasing power halved without indexation. Indexation is also of great importance for employees. After all, the vast majority of employees nowadays participate in an average pay scheme with conditional indexation. After 40 years of accrual, approximately one-third of the accrued pension entitlements consist of cumulative indexation at 2% annual indexation. From this point of view, indexation is therefore of great importance for the purchasing power of pensions in the long term. However, the nominal funding ratio from the Pensions Act does not provide direct insight into the extent to which pension funds can meet their indexation ambitions. For example, a funding ratio of 130 to 140% sounds generous, but depending on the age structure, it is equal to a real funding ratio of only 100%. This would be just enough for pensions that retain their value, i.e. without any room to deal with unforeseen circumstances. Since pension funds broadly endorse the importance of indexation, the real funding ratio provides a better insight into the actual financial position of the pension fund. Moreover, taking into account indexation objectives, it becomes clear that, under normal circumstances, the legal requirements should actually form the lower limit of what you are heading for as a pension fund. A target with regard to the actual funding ratio would therefore not be out of place in the financial set-up. This is not mandatory, but it is an opinion from a regulator who is also a central banker and, in that capacity, does not like pro-cyclical indexation cuts or contribution changes, nor pension rights that are eroded by inflation. Risk management is crucial for a good pension provision Inflation risk brings me to my third theme. What the world will look like in the long term is and remains uncertain. That's not a bad thing, but it's something to keep in mind. The purpose of the continuity analysis is to provide insight into the financial development of the fund in favourable and less favourable circumstances. In addition, the continuity analysis provides a picture of the steering power of the various policy instruments in these circumstances. Whereas the actual funding ratio reflects the current state of affairs, the continuity analysis provides useful information about the possible development of the financial position in the future. A good continuity analysis is indispensable for you to gain insight into the consequences of unforeseen circumstances before they occur. This offers the opportunity to chart a good course at an early stage and to make adjustments where necessary. I have just signed the policy rule on continuity analysis, which is intended as a tool for the funds. In addition, the continuity analysis provides important information for the indexation label. This label provides participants with insight into the expected indexation and the uncertainty surrounding it. The Pensions Act stipulates that participants are entitled to this information. In that context, you must provide information about the expected indexation and risk before 1 April 2008, i.e. in six months' time. This will require a lot of work from you in the coming months. Although this is not yet mandatory, you can base this information on a continuity analysis. I would therefore urge you to start the continuity analysis as soon as possible. Your risk management and therefore your participants will benefit. This allows us to maintain a high quality of the Dutch pension system. Relationship with Holland Financial Centre That brings me to the end of my speech. I would like to dwell on the relationship between what I have said and the Holland Financial Centre initiative. I am a director of this foundation and therefore closely involved. This initiative is intended to put the Netherlands on the map as an internationally competitive financial centre. A lot of attention is paid to the pension sector. One of the propositions about this sector is that just being good is not enough. This must also be propagated. I am happy to endorse this. One of the strengths of the Dutch pension sector is the management of risks so that a good and fairly secure pension can be realised at low and predictable costs. In line with the conclusions of the Holland Financial Centre, this strength may also be propagated as such. The risk-based approach of the Dutch pension system is an advantage compared to many other systems, because the high costs of repairs, which often fall at the wrong time, can be avoided. The seemingly high costs in the Netherlands are not so bad when the costs of repair afterwards are also taken into account. I therefore do not believe that many pension funds are considering leaving the Netherlands because of the supervisory requirements. Not only because it means that the benefits of making it mandatory will no longer apply. But also, because the costs of long-term pension schemes are not determined by the supervisory regime, but by the nature of the agreed agreements, as recently indicated by Minister Donner. These costs must be paid, whatever the form of supervision. Nevertheless, in order to prevent supervision from becoming a motive in the competition for pension funds, it is necessary to standardise supervisory requirements in Europe. DNB is committed to this internationally. This is in line with the strengths of the Dutch supervisory regime. After all, it is not about the cost of pension, but about the distribution of those costs over time. Risk management is crucial in this regard. And that is precisely one of the strengths of our pension sector and the new pension law. Downloads Presentations at DNB Pension Afternoon 13 September 2007 (PPT, 451.5 kB)
text_original: Speech directeur Schilder 'De bijdrage van pensioenbestuur aan stabiliteit' Speech Datum 13 september 2007 Tijd 14:55 uur Lokatie DNB-bijeenkomst voor bestuurders van pensioenfondsen, Apeldoorn Spreker Prof. dr. A. Schilder, directeur van de Nederlandsche Bank In de pensioenwereld is veel in beweging, maar sommige dingen blijven hetzelfde. Zo zijn sociale partners, fondsbestuurders en toezichthouder gezamenlijk verantwoordelijk voor de financile soliditeit van ons pensioenstelsel. Sociale partners gaan over de inhoud van de regeling, u voert deze regeling uit en DNB ziet erop toe dat de afspraken worden nagekomen. Dit blijft zo onder de pensioenwet. Nieuw daarentegen is de modernisering van het prudentieel toezicht. Hierbij valt te denken aan de invoering van marktwaardering van verplichtingen en beleggingen, risicogevoelige solvabiliteitseisen en een belangrijke plaats voor risicobeheersing via de continuteitsanalyse. Kortom, de nieuwe pensioenwet biedt een solide basis om de toekomst met vertrouwen tegemoet te zien. Maar, hoewel een goede wet een belangrijke voorwaarde is voor succes, biedt het geen garanties. Uiteindelijk hangt het welslagen mede af van de wijze waarop u om gaat met de onzekerheden die de toekomst brengt. Over onzekerheden gesproken: het zijn roerige tijden op de financile markten. De afgelopen weken hebben weer eens gellustreerd dat de stemming op financile markten snel kan omslaan en dat de daaruit voortvloeiende verliezen groot kunnen zijn. Wat begon met betalingsproblemen op een klein segment van de Amerikaanse hypotheekmarkt, groeide uit tot een financile schok met grote impact. Wereldwijd gingen de aandelenkoersen onderuit en zowel in de VS als in Europa ontstonden liquiditeitsproblemen, waardoor de Europese en Amerikaanse centrale banken zich genoodzaakt zagen om extra liquiditeit beschikbaar te stellen aan financile instellingen. De ontwikkelingen op de financile markten treffen uiteraard ook pensioenfondsen. De gemiddelde dekkingsgraad van de sector daalde tussen medio juli en medio augustus met ruim 12%-punten, van circa 159% naar circa 146%. Dit betekent dat in n maand tijd circa 50 miljard aan buffers verloren is, bijna een tiende van het totale Nederlandse pensioenvermogen. Dit is overigens geen abnormale fluctuatie. In de afgelopen 10 jaar bedroeg de absolute mutatie in 1 op de 4 kwartalen meer dan 10% dekkingsgraadpunten. Het is niet waarschijnlijk dat de schok nu al volledig is uitgewerkt. Uit eerdere ervaringen weten we dat schokken enige tijd kunnen na-ijlen. Door de perfect storm van gelijktijdig dalende kapitaalmarktrentes en aandelenkoersen aan het begin van deze eeuw, daalde de gemiddelde dekkingsgraad van 200% eind jaren 90 naar 120% in 2003. Deze perfect storm heeft in een periode van 3 jaar de forse buffer dus voor een groot deel weggevaagd. Dit plaatst de huidige dekkingsgraad in perspectief. Willen we een zelfde klap opnieuw kunnen opvangen, dan moeten we niet denken dat we er bij de huidige 150% ruim bij zitten. Al deze ervaringen onderstrepen hoe belangrijk het is om rekening te houden met risicos. Vanmiddag wil ik met u een aantal conclusies bespreken die we hieruit kunnen trekken: Ten eerste: Pensioenfondsen moeten hun beleid niet richten op dagkoersen, maar op de lange termijn. Ten tweede: Binnen een lange termijnperspectief speelt indexatie een grote rol. Aandacht voor de rele dekkingsgraad in uw financile opzet verdient daarbij aanbeveling. Ten derde: Risicobeheersing is cruciaal voor een goede pensioenvoorziening. De door u te ontwikkelen continuteitsanalyses zijn een onmisbaar instrument om inzicht te krijgen in deze risicos. Pensioenbeleid moet niet gericht zijn op dagkoersen maar op de lange termijn..... Laat ik beginnen met het eerste thema. Toen we in het voorjaar met de organisatie van deze dag begonnen, dachten we dat iedereen er vandaag comfortabel bij zou zitten. Zeker in vergelijking met de vorige DNB-pensioendagen. Toen was de financile positie van de sector nog precair en waren velen van u nog druk in de weer met herstelplannen. Het herstel ging vervolgens veel sneller dan verwacht en we zaten dit voorjaar gemiddeld genomen weer in het goede kwadrant. De huidige volatiliteit leert echter dat we ons niet te snel rijk moeten rekenen op basis van korte termijn-ontwikkelingen. Dit betekent overigens ook niet dat we nu onrustig moeten worden. Het toont echter wel aan dat u er goed aan doet uw beleid op de lange termijn te richten. Het uitgangspunt bij een dergelijk lange termijn beleid luidt: voorkomen is beter dan genezen. De essentie van een goede pensioenregeling is immers een stabiele levensstandaard voor en na pensionering. Dit vereist zowel een redelijke stabiele pensioenpremie als een uitkering met voldoende uitzicht op indexatie. De uitdaging voor pensioenfondsen is om deze combinatie te realiseren door een evenwichtige verdeling van lusten en lasten over de tijd en over alle belanghebbenden. Het lange termijn beleid komt idealiter tot uitdrukking in de premiestelling. De recente volatiliteit op financile markten illustreert dat het ongewenst is om de premie te veel te laten benvloeden door de waan van de dag. In het recente verleden hebben we de consequenties van dergelijk beleid kunnen ervaren. Zo lagen de totale premie-inkomsten in de jaren 90 gemiddeld genomen slechts op 6% van de loonsom. Dit was onder kostprijsdekkend niveau maar werd mogelijk geacht door de hoge rele beleggingsrendementen en ruime financile positie. Arbeid was hierdoor relatief goedkoop hetgeen bijdroeg aan de oververhitting van de economie. Door de al eerder genoemde perfect storm moest vervolgens de premie in korte tijd worden verdubbeld tot 12% van de loonsom. Hierdoor verliep het herstel van de economie relatief minder snel. Een beleid waarin premies worden afgestemd op de actuele dekkingsgraad, leidt dus tot procyclische premiemutaties. Ons pensioenstelsel zou dan een bron van macro-economische verstoringen worden. Met de kennis achteraf kunnen we stellen dat als de premies midden jaren 90 op kostendekkend niveau hadden gelegen, de gemiddelde dekkingsgraad in 2003 circa 12% hoger was geweest en was uitgekomen rond 130%. We hadden dan minder lage premies gehad midden jaren 90 in een tijd van voorspoed maar wellicht ook minder premieverhogingen en indexatiekortingen tussen 2002-2005 in een tijd van tegenspoed. Kortom, een goed lange termijn beleid vermijdt snelle premieaanpassingen bij wijzigingen in de dekkingsgraad en beperkt zo procyclische effecten. Een mogelijkheid die pensioenwet daartoe biedt is om een gedempte premie te gebruiken. Door bovendien in goede tijden voldoende financile ruimte op te bouwen, kunnen forse premieverhogingen en indexatiekortingen in slechte tijden worden voorkomen. En dan blijft u uit de buurt van die vervelende herstelplannen. Deze buffers hebben trouwens als voordeel dat zij geen dood geld vertegenwoordigen, maar ook inkomsten genereren die gebruikt kunnen worden om indexatie mogelijk te maken. Dit is een belangrijke financieringsbron, omdat het Nederlandse stelsel geen reservering eist voor indexatie zolang deze voorwaardelijk is. Dit belang kan worden gellustreerd door te kijken naar de indexatie in slechte scenarios. Voor een gemiddeld Nederlands pensioenfonds met een dekkingsgraad tussen 100% en 160% betekent iedere 10%-punt stijging van de dekkingsgraad een toename van de verwachte indexatie in slechte tijden met 10%. ...en heeft oog voor rele verplichtingen (rele dekkingsgraad) Dit brengt mij bij het tweede thema. Bij een beleid gericht op de lange termijn hoort ook aandacht voor indexatie. Inflatie kan immers de koopkracht van de pensioenaanspraken op termijn behoorlijk uithollen. Een 65-jarige leeft gemiddeld nog 15 tot 20 jaar. Als over die periode niet wordt gendexeerd daalt het rele inkomen bij een inflatie van 2% per jaar met een kwart tot een derde. Iemand die 100 wordt ziet zijn koopkracht halveren zonder indexatie. Ook voor werknemers is indexatie van groot belang. Verreweg de meeste werknemers nemen tegenwoordig immers deel aan een middelloonregeling met voorwaardelijke indexatie. Na 40 jaar opbouw bestaat bij jaarlijkse indexatie met 2% ongeveer een derde van de opgebouwde pensioenaanspraken uit cumulatieve indexatie. Indexatie is dus vanuit die optiek van groot belang voor de koopkracht van pensioenen op lange termijn. De nominale dekkingsgraad uit de pensioenwet biedt echter niet direct inzicht in hoeverre pensioenfondsen aan hun indexatie-ambities kunnen voldoen. Zo klinkt een dekkingsgraad van 130 tot 140% ruim, maar is deze, afhankelijk van de leeftijdsopbouw, gelijk aan een rele dekkingsgraad van slechts 100%. Dit zou precies voldoende zijn voor waardevaste pensioenen, dus zonder ruimte om onvoorziene omstandigheden op te vangen. Aangezien pensioenfondsen het belang van indexatie breed onderschrijven, biedt de rele dekkingsgraad een beter inzicht in de werkelijke financile positie van het pensioenfonds. Rekening houdend met indexatiedoelstellingen, wordt bovendien duidelijk dat de wettelijke eisen onder normale omstandigheden eigenlijk de ondergrens zouden moeten vormen van waar je als pensioenfonds op koerst. Een doelstelling met betrekking tot de rele dekkingsgraad zou dan ook niet misstaan in de financile opzet. Dit is niet verplicht, maar wel een advies van een toezichthouder die ook centrale bankier is en vanuit die hoedanigheid niet van procyclische indexatiekortingen of premiemutaties houdt, noch van pensioenrechten die door inflatie worden uitgehold. Risicobeheersing is cruciaal voor een goede pensioenvoorziening Het inflatierisico brengt mij bij mijn derde thema. Hoe de wereld er op lange termijn uit ziet is en blijft onzeker. Dat is niet erg, maar wel iets om rekening mee te houden. De continuteitsanalyse is bedoeld om inzicht te geven in de financile ontwikkeling van het fonds in gunstige en minder gunstige omstandigheden. Daarbij biedt de continuteitsanalyse een beeld over de sturingskracht van de verschillende beleidsinstrumenten in die omstandigheden. Waar de rele dekkingsgraad de actuele stand van zaken weer geeft, levert de continuteitsanalyse zinvolle informatie over de mogelijke ontwikkeling van financile positie in de toekomst. Een goede continuteitsanalyse is voor u onmisbaar om inzicht te krijgen in de consequenties van onvoorziene omstandigheden voordat deze zich voordoen. Dit biedt de mogelijkheid om reeds in een vroeg stadium een goede koers uit te stippelen en waar nodig bij te sturen. Zojuist heb ik de beleidsregel continuteitsanalyse getekend en deze is bedoeld als hulpmiddel voor de fondsen. Daarnaast levert de continuteitsanalyse belangrijke informatie op voor het indexatielabel. Dit label biedt deelnemers inzicht in de verwachte indexatie en de onzekerheid daaromheen. In de pensioenwet is vastgelegd dat deelnemers recht hebben op deze informatie. In dat kader moet u voor 1 april 2008, dus al over een half jaar, informatie aanleveren over de verwachte indexatie en risico. Dit vergt van u de komende maanden nog flink wat werk. Hoewel dat nog niet verplicht is, kunt u deze informatie op een continuteitsanalyse baseren. Ik zou u dan ook willen aansporen om snel een begin te maken met de continuteitsanalyse. Uw risicobeheersing en daarmee uw deelnemers worden er beter van. Hierdoor kunnen we de kwaliteit van het Nederlandse pensioenstelsel hoog houden. Relatie met Holland Financial Centre Hiermee kom ik aan het slot van mijn betoog. Graag wil ik nog even stilstaan bij de relatie tussen hetgeen ik heb gezegd en het initiatief Holland Financial Centre. Ik ben bestuurder van deze stichting en dus nauw betrokken. Dit initiatief is bedoeld om Nederland als internationaal concurrerend financieel centrum op de kaart te zetten. Daarbij wordt veel aandacht besteed aan de pensioensector. En van de stellingen over deze sector is dat goed zijn alleen niet voldoende is. Dit moet ook worden uitgedragen. Ik sluit mij hier graag bij aan. En van de sterke punten van de Nederlandse pensioensector is het beheersen van risicos waardoor een goed en vrij zeker pensioen tegen lage en voorspelbare kosten kan worden gerealiseerd. Hierbij past, in lijn met de conclusies van het Holland Financial Centre, dat deze kracht ook als zodanig mag worden uitgedragen. De risicogebaseerde aanpak van Nederlandse pensioenstelsel is in vergelijking met veel andere stelsels een voordeel, omdat de hoge kosten van reparatie achteraf, die vaak op het verkeerde moment vallen, achterwege kunnen blijven. De op het eerste gezicht hoog lijkende kosten in Nederland vallen bij nader inzien mee wanneer ook de kosten van herstel achteraf worden meegewogen. Ik geloof dan ook niet dat veel pensioenfondsen overwegen om Nederland te verlaten vanwege de toezichteisen. Niet alleen, omdat daarmee de voordelen van de verplichtstelling vervallen. Maar ook, omdat de kosten van pensioenregelingen op lange termijn niet worden bepaald door het toezichtregime, maar door de aard van de overeengekomen afspraken, zoals ook recent is aangegeven door minister Donner. Die kosten moeten worden betaald, hoe het toezicht er ook uit ziet. Om niettemin te vermijden dat toezicht een motief wordt in de concurrentiestrijd voor pensioenfondsen is uniformering van toezichteisen in Europa nodig. DNB zet zich hier internationaal voor in. Hierbij wordt aangesloten bij de sterke punten in het Nederlandse toezichtsregime. Het gaat immers niet om de kosten van pensioen, maar om de verdeling van die kosten over de tijd. Risicobeheersing is daarbij cruciaal. En dat is nu net n van de sterke punten van onze pensioensector en de nieuwe pensioenwet. Title: Speech directeur Brouwer 'Ageing & Financing Pension Fund Contracts: Why it is wise to share the risks'
text: Speech directeur Brouwer 'Ageing & Financing Pension Fund Contracts: Why it is wise to share the risks' Speech Datum 27 september 2007 Tijd 13:53 uur Lokatie ABP Conference Pension Diversity and Solidarity in Europe, Heerlen Spreker Drs. H. Brouwer, directeur van de Nederlandsche Bank The ageing of population has triggered intense debate on the sustainability of pension arrangements in many countries. As a result, we have witnessed reforms that typically include less generous pension arrangements. In many countries, policymakers stress the importance of increased funding rather than relying on a pay-as-you-go system, not in the least to reduce explicit and implicit fiscal liabilities. Most of the recent debates and reforms concern the second pillar pension provision. However, in 2004 the US government proposed to reform Social Security, which is the first pillar old age income arrangement. Initiated by President Roosevelt in the 30s as part of his New Deal, it provides the major part of the average American households retirement income. The US government proposed to replace part of this unfunded, defined benefit arrangement by a system of privately funded individual accounts, arguing that future demographic developments make more funding inevitable. I discuss some lessons learned from the US discussion and apply these for Europe. I focus on three interrelated questions. First: Should European countries switch to a more funded system? Second: If they do so, what will be the implications for the financial system and households risk profile? Finally and most importantly: How can retirement savings be organised? I will argue that a crucial element for a feasible pension system is collective risk sharing and that pension funds are very suitable instruments for doing so. The case for funding Let me begin with the first question: Is there a case for greater funding in Europe? Note that the US proposals are about funding the first pillar, even though America is much less affected by ageing than Europe. On top of that American households hold on average more or less the equivalent of their annual incomes as savings in second pillar pension arrangements. Compare this situation with European countries like Germany, France and Italy, where both the first and the second pillar are on a pay-as-you-go basis, with virtually no long-term savings as a result. Combined with much gloomier demographic projections one would think the case for funding is much more pressing for Europe than for the US. It was Paul Samuelson - the Nobel Prize winner - who compared pay-as-you-go pension schemes with Ponzi games [- in Dutch we call them piramide spel -] as early as 1967. He considered them an asset by that time: The beauty of social insurance is that it is actuarially unsoundAlways there are more youths than old folks in a growing populationA growing nation is the greatest Ponzi game ever contrived. But now, precisely that basic condition is no longer met. Population pyramids are turning top heavy, leaving an increasingly smaller base. Standard and Poors calculated the consequences of the status quo: by 2030 European government bonds would be rated non investment grade. To me, the question therefore is not whether European countries should switch to more funding but rather what would be the most suitable way for doing this? Consequences of greater funding This brings me to the second question: What will be the consequences of greater funding for households and financial markets? Let me start with households risk exposure. In a funded system - by definition - household wealth and retirement income is subject to fluctuations on financial markets. In other words: through their pension savings, households bear investment risk. Obviously pay-as-you-go arrangements are not directly affected by market sentiment, but they are sensitive to other risk, like fiscal and political risk. I would define this risk as the possibility that the next generation goes back on previous promises. Political risk in a pay-as-you-go system increases in an ageing society. Should we therefore conclude that wed better completely rely on funding? I wouldnt advocate that either for the following reasons. Rights in a pay-as-you-go system can be seen as claims on the next generations human capital. Since human capital is not tradable in financial markets, holding such claims provides households with an important possibility to diversify risk. Therefore, a combination of systems, pay-as-you-go and capital based, enables households to spread the risk between market and political risk, which makes a mixed system probably the optimal one. Roughly, this could be achieved by keeping the basic pension arrangement - the first pillar  on a pay-as-you-go basis and fund the work-related second pillar. As it happens, this is the situation in the Netherlands. Here, the pay-as-you-go first pillar provides half of the average retirement income; the other half comes from the funded second and third pillar, mostly from pension funds. This is only an example and by no means meant to be prescriptive. In any case, there seems to be a growing consensus that the optimal proportion between pay-as-you-go and funding lies - under normal circumstances - somewhere in the 40-60 range, depending on the specific situation in a country. To appreciate the discussion it is important to recognize that European policymakers dont have the opportunity to build up a pension system from scratch. They have inherited the outcome of decisions and commitments made by their predecessors. This brings me to transition costs. Obviously switching to more funding will generate transition costs and somebody has to pay for them. Either current workers will pay more but receive less from a pay-as-you-go system which is partly phased out, or current pensioners will receive less than they had hoped for, or the bill will be split between the two. Because transition costs will be sizable, the only feasible way of switching into more capital funding is doing it gradually and in a intergenerational fair way. Yet there is another argument for gradual change, which is related to capital markets. Today, pension funds in the OECD countries hold 12 percent of world financial assets. Imagine that households of all OECD countries would have saved on average one year gross earnings as Americans have. In that hypothetical situation pension funds would hold a quarter of world financial assets! This experiment of thought gives a rough indication of the potential demand for capital investments that future retirement savings can bring about. Let me therefore mention three possible consequences of greater funding. First, population ageing in itself makes labour scarce and therefore capital relatively abundant. A trend to greater funding will create additional supply of capital and demand for assets which may cause an upward price pressure on assets and subsequently lower returns on investment. This will make adequate old-age-income savings much harder. Second, the size of countries pension assets and the deepness of their capital markets are positively correlated. This suggests that Says law  each supply will create its own demand - applies also to capital markets. In that case, the extra supply of capital could increase the potential production and therefore enhance growth. Lastly, one would also expect that more funding will elicit greater demand for various new financial products. After all, there will be a desire and need to hedge against various kinds of risks. How should we organize the retirement savings? I argued that the case for funding is more pressing for European countries like Germany, France and Italy than for the United States. Switching to more funding is inevitable for countries that rely almost completely on pay-as-you-go systems. I also indicated that more funding will have consequences for the risk exposure of households, while the additional savings will have implications for financial markets as well. But there still remains one major question to answer: What is the best way to organize retirement savings? Like proposed in the United States, many countries have chosen to promote funding by means of individual accounts. Individual accounts have two clear advantages. First: they can provide a maximum of free choice. In theory individuals are able to tailor their pension savings to their preferences and personal circumstances. In contrast, for a long time the choice of a pension funds member looked more like the choice Henry Ford gave his costumers: You can have them in all colours as long as its black. Now, choice possibilities are getting introduced little by little, for instance by trading in survivor or partner pensions. The second advantage of organizing savings in individual accounts is transparency. Compare for instance the simplicity of the financial statement of your mutual fund investments with that of your pension fund. Almost everybody understands the first, few understand the latter. But individual accounts come with a cost. To achieve it one has to preclude any kind of collective risk sharing. And to me that looks like throwing away the baby with the bathwater. In fact retirement savings and retirement income have to deal with four major risks: longevity risk, inflation risk, interest rate risk and investment risk. Let me give you some examples how risk sharing  for instance in pension funds  can mitigate these risks. First longevity risk. The difference between ex-ante en ex-post risks plays an important role here. Let me explain this a bit more. If I knew  god forbid  the date of my death, there would be no point in joining a collective arrangement, since I would exactly know how much I have to save to keep me out of dire straits in  hopefully  old age. But since I dont know, diversifying away longevity risk in a pool of people that face the same limitation means an important improvement in income certainty. Whereas the life-expectancy of individuals is uncertain, this is also the case for the whole generation. In contrast to the first - which can be cancelled out - the latter is a one-sided risk: it affects everybody in the same way. Thats why it is also called macro longevity risk. In handling macro longevity risk it appears that pension funds enjoy some flexibility. Since macro longevity risk evolves very gradual, a pension fund has enough time to adjust its provisioning or premium with every new actuarial projection. Next to longevity risk, other important risks to pensions are inflation and interest rate risk. Probably only few people in the Netherlands realize that their pension fund not only provides them with management service for savings and investments but also  after retirement - with a life long annuity in more or less real terms. I say more or less, because recently the inflation indexation became conditional to the financial health of the pension fund. But compare that to an owner of an individual account. At retirement age, savings have to be converted into an annuity, at least partly. This will happen at the then prevailing market interest rate, hence high rates mean high retirement income and low rates mean low income. Consequently, there is substantial exposure to interest rate risk at that moment in time. In addition, most annuities are sold in nominal terms, which leave - at an age of 85 - only two thirds of the initial purchasing power if inflation is 2 percent. Last but not least there is investment risk. Pension funds appear to be very efficient entities to bear investment risk. With their big asset holdings, they have access to investment categories and opportunities, like private equity, commodities or big infrastructural projects. This widens the scope for diversification, hence mitigates risk. Moreover, pension funds can buy tailor-made products, for instance for hedging purposes. This is of course all beyond the reach of most individuals. There is yet another aspect to investment risk I want to mention: the same investment strategy can in fact yield very different results. As it happens, in real life there is no such thing as a long-term average investment return. This is merely a statistical construction, where the mean depends on your point of entry and exit in the investment scheme. Moreover, the last years before retirement significantly determine the outcome. Let me illustrate that point. Imagine you and your three year older brother both saved for retirement in an individual account and employed the same investment strategy, for simplicitys sake the American stock index. You earned the same; you paid the same, so everything is equal except your age. After 40 years of work your brother retired in 2000 and you, being younger, retired in 2003. In this case your brother would receive a pension which is two and a half times larger than yours. Of course, this example refers to the very extreme case of the dotcom crisis, but nevertheless, it provides an idea of the magnitude in possible outcomes. Pension funds can help smooth away these differences. This is not to say that pension funds dont run investment risks that can have a bearing on participants. By the way, Dutch pension funds emerged reasonably well from the turmoil on the financial markets a few years ago. But in general the combined decline of stocks and interest rates took a heavy toll on pension funds balance sheets, all over the world. In many countries therefore the conclusion was reached that the old fashioned defined benefit pension fund is not sustainable anymore. New accounting rules added extra weight to this argument. Many pension experts are quiet impressed by the rather creative shift to a more hybrid system the Dutch pension system managed to make. The introduction of an average earnings system together with conditional indexing created a system lying somewhere in between defined benefit and defined contribution. Also the experiment with collective defined contribution earned a lot of approval, precisely because the benefits of risk sharing are preserved. Besides their excellent risk sharing properties there are other arguments in favour of pension funds. Pension funds enhance efficiency in two ways. First pension funds are able to provide pensions at low costs. This is in contrast with individual accounts notoriously bad track records, which are well documented for countries like the United States, United Kingdom and Canada. Second, research by De Nederlandsche Bank found, that Dutch pension funds follow, on average, a rebalancing investment strategy. In order to keep the asset mix constant this basically means buying shares in declining markets and selling shares in booming markets. Of course for pursuing this policy, pension funds need to have sufficient reserves, but by doing so they contribute to the stability of the financial system. The last remark I want to add concerns human nature. Since behavioural economics gave us real people of flesh and blood instead of rationally acting agents, the insight grew that one can actually be overloaded by choice and information. Especially in the field of pensions  which is complicated and where the consequences materialise only in a far distant future  behavioural studies show that many people either dont understand, thus put decisions off, or are simply not interested. The ones that do act, prove to be very sensitive to the presentation of the information, are prone to advertising or simply follow rules of thumb without really understanding the underlying risk. Indeed: asset management is a real profession and individual learning costs are high. I would hope that all the years spent in university would render some results. So in my eyes, delegating these decisions to pension fund professionals is simply a matter of efficient division of labour. Should we make participation mandatory? If pension funds can be superior instruments for collective risk sharing, the logical next question has to be: how can it be arranged? Parts of the answer lie in the fact that people are mandated to enrol. In the Netherlands accepting a job almost always goes together with the membership of the accompanying pension fund. But this lack of freedom of choice is increasingly questioned. Lets put this into perspective with the American experience. President Bushs reform proposal is presented as an important cornerstone of his vision of an ownership society. The assumption is that it is crucial to give individuals more control over, and responsibility for, their own health care and pension provisions. On the other hand, The Commission to Strengthen Social Security, the advisory commission to the president, has noted the lessons from behaviour finance very well. According to the proposal Americans can only choose from three or four investment categories. A default option is provided in case people find it difficult to decide. Everybody gets automatically enrolled with the possibility of opting out. Joining is further encouraged by substantial tax benefits. In other words: every possible means is used to push Americans gently in the right direction. By giving them as little actual choice as possible the proposal acknowledges the necessity of protecting people against their own behaviour. Hence to me, the difference with mandatory enrolment becomes very subtle indeed. Robert Pozen, who was a member of that Commission, phrased it in a recent interview differently. He pointed to the strong cultural preferences in the Anglo Saxon world which make mandatory enrolment, at least in the second pillar, unfeasible. According to him, having automatic enrolment with opting-out possibility is then the next best thing. In Continental Europe, the preferences may be different and I think the cultural barrier to mandatory enrolment may not be that high. By the way, the other side of the same cultural coin is that if things go wrong Europeans are more likely to claim public support as well. After all, the purpose of pension arrangements is providing a sufficient old age income and mandatory participation helps a lot to achieve this goal. Moreover it prevents calculating or myopic individuals to speculate that eventually they will be bailed out by social security. Of course if you direct people towards a pension fund, you have to deliver the goods. In other words: the corporate governance of pension funds has to be state of the art and there has to be strong supervision in place. In that regard, I cant put it better than Keith Ambachtsheer, who gave in one of his letters the following argument for Why the Dutch are leading the way. He mentioned the confluence of three elements: the culture of integrative thinking and consensus building, the compactness of our country  only the national government is responsible - and leadership, both in the regulatory as well in the research field. Conclusion Let me summarize and conclude. The case for more funding of the pension provision is much more pressing for European countries than for the United States. Countries like Germany, Italy and France are almost completely dependent on pay-as-you-go systems while the demographic projections are gloomy. In organizing new pension arrangements collective solutions, like pension funds, are much more suitable than individual accounts. They are efficient and have very good risk sharing properties. Moreover, the average household seems insufficiently prepared to make good investment decisions. The efficiency of the collective solution is facilitated in a major way by making participation mandatory. This necessitates good supervision and a well thought-through corporate governance structure. At first sight individual accounts may appear the easiest way to achieve more funding. But let us not discard the benefits of collective risk sharing too easily, even if it might feel at the moment like rowing upstream. I am quite convinced that the collective solution is most appropriate for Europe. Not just because mandatory participation will be accepted much easier by Europeans, but also because it facilitates a collective solution, which in these areas is most efficient. Therefore, lets work on the collective solution and preserve the benefits of collective risk sharing instead of putting our efforts in optimising the suboptimal in individual accounts arrangements.

Title: Speech president Wellink over 'Financial turmoil and an integrated model for supervision'
text: Speech president Wellink over 'Financial turmoil and an integrated model for supervision' Speech Datum 28 september 2007 Tijd 09:30 uur Lokatie Central bank, Montenegro Spreker Dr. A.H.E.M. Wellink Introduction I would like to thank the Central bank of Montenegro for inviting me to this conference. Now that Montenegro and the Netherlands are in the same constituency in the IMF and the World Bank our ties have already strengthened. It is only three months ago that I visited this beautiful country. At that time, I had the privilege to meet with the Montenegrin government and Mr. Ljubisa Krgovic. But I also visited the University of Podgorica where I talked with students about the future of their country. I was touched by their enthusiasm for Europe and the idea of European integration. I very much share this enthusiasm and optimism which have faded somewhat over the years, including in my own country. Often Europe now is only associated with over regulation and bureaucracy. I am very glad that some of these students will pay a visit to the Netherlands at the end of this year. And I am sure that they will help in moving Montenegro towards successful membership of the European Union. I trust this will also be the case for some other countries around this table. I will address two topics that are somewhat interrelated. First I will go into the recent turmoil in financial markets. I will try to put this turbulence into some perspective, while of course it is still far too early to draw any definitive conclusions. In addition, I will touch upon the supervisory arrangements in the Netherlands. We have introduced a so called 'Twin Peak' model, where the prudential supervision of financial institutions is consolidated at the central bank, while conduct-of-business supervision is performed by the financial market authority. A three stage crisis Three important elements can be identified that contributed to the recent financial markets stress. The first and in a sense the most 'real' one is the higher than expected increase in the delinquency rates on US sub-prime mortgages. The second factor is an upward shift in the perception of risk, which triggered a process of re-assessing and re-pricing, especially in the structured credit market. The third factor is the increased uncertainty as to which parties are most severely affected. The interaction between them resulted in a malfunctioning of the inter bank money markets. The increased delinquencies on sub-prime mortgage in the US remind us of a typical boom-bust cycle. The continuing increase in house prices in the US since 1991 reinforced itself as it fed into the expectations of buyers. This mechanism, referred to as price-to-price feedback, can result in irrational price increases. In the last couple of years it became progressively clear that the continued price increase could not go on for ever. For example, Robert Shiller showed that US house prices had risen only 0.4% annually in real terms between 1890 and 2004, thereby pointing-out that the strong price increase since the early nineties was unlikely to continue. In addition, a survey held in April 2006 showed that a large part of mortgage lenders in de US expected house prices to fall. At the same time, these lenders continued to sell highly risky mortgages, in terms of loan-to-value and loan-to-income ratios. These were often made even more attractive by teaser elements, such as interest-free periods. This created the possibility to postpone payments, but only pushed-up delinquencies when interest rates were to be reset. Extending mortgage loans under such loose conditions would probably have been more constrained if related credit risks could not have been transferred so easily to financial markets. The losses in the sub-prime market acted as trigger to a process of re-assessing and re-pricing credit-related risk on a much larger scale. The downgrading of assets backed by sub-prime mortgages made market participants wary about the risks of structured products in which they had often been parcelled. This change in risk-perception is reflected in the large increase in spreads for structured products across the whole credit spectrum. These increasing spreads implied a capital loss, setting in motion a series of sometimes self-reinforcing mechanisms. Margin calls by banks that had extended credit to non-bank financial institutions, such as hedge funds, sometimes forced these institutions to liquidate their assets. This further pushed down other asset prices and triggered the unwinding of trades that were set-up under the historic assumption of market tranquillity, such as Yen carry-trades. One striking aspect here is that emerging markets have not been under much pressure, clearly reflecting improved fundamentals. The emergence of large losses, not only in the US, but also at banks in Germany, created great uncertainty about the size and distribution of losses. In the asset baked commercial paper market this was amplified by uncertainty about the value of underlying assets in so called conduits, thereby making it increasingly difficult to roll-over short-term paper. This made them tap bank credit lines for liquidity, thereby further increasing liquidity pressure in the inter bank money market, that was also already suffering from increased counterparty uncertainty and liquidity hoarding. The culmination of these effects eventually led to liquidity shortages in money markets, prompting central banks world-wide to injected liquidity. All in all, the process of re-pricing risk and losses in the sub-prime market increased counterparty risk to such a level that money markets dried-up. The first two events, delinquencies in the sub-prime market and an underestimation of risk in general, were on the radar of many institutions and central banks around the globe. Indeed, my own central bank had pointed to these risks in our financial stability report. The unwinding towards a global liquidity crisis was nevertheless somewhat of a surprise. Factors underlying the resent unrest and some initial lessons So let me now put the recent events in some perspective by trying to answer the question what underlying factors have contributed to this turbulence? Although it is too early for making definitive assessments, at least two factors have played a role; 1) financial innovation and 2) over-optimism about risks and the value of assets. Let me start with financial innovation. Recent years have shown an enormous growth in especially structured credit and new derivative products such as credit default swaps, sometimes combined in new complex financial instruments. Complex or not, in essence all these new instruments serve one main purpose: they make risks tradable. Or at least they make it possible to transfer risks off banks balance sheets. Indeed, the originate-to-distribute model has developed into a major source of income for banks. These new products have opened-up a range of new hedging possibilities and very much enriched our financial system. It is good that risk is transferable, if this leads to a situation where risks end up with investors who can best bear them. In addition, risks can to some extent be evened-out, through the bundling of uncorrelated risks. Moreover, risk redistributing in itself can be a good thing. A constellation where a certain risk impacts on a lot of parties a little bit, might be preferable over a situation where one party is affected a lot. This is what insurance is all about. Although the recent financial innovations have an overall positive impact on the functioning of the financial system, the current circumstances unfortunately show that they can have important drawbacks. One drawback is that the complexity of new instruments makes it often difficult to correctly measure the underlying risk. This is not strange if one imagines that measuring risk is predicting the future. We, central bankers, only know too well difficult this is. We often have trouble predicting something fairly straightforward, such as a countries GDP. Measuring the value of a CDO, based on income streams from different sources over a thirty year horizon might be even harder to do. Measuring risk is also complicated by the short history of these products. It will be interesting to see how recent data will show up in the models. Another difficulty, stemming from the tradability of risk, is that it creates uncertainty about what parties are bearing which risks. This has become very clear during recent events. In this sense, the current turmoil is really different from other crises, such as the LTCM or emerging market crises. Then, it was quite clear who were in trouble and why. To some extent this increased uncertainty could be a lasting feature of our financial system. A third difficulty in measuring risk of, especially, complex instruments is their vulnerability to liquidity risk. As we have witnessed, the difference between mark-to-market and mark-to-model can become very large if markets dry-up. Here is am important lesson to learn. The apparent vulnerability of markets to liquidity shortages in combination with the increased dependency of banks and other financial institutions on these markets have induced risks that were not foreseen. At least not to this extent. Therefore, more effort should be directed in trying to capture liquidity risks. Stress tests should probably make different assumptions about the possibility to sell assets under stress. In addition, the transparency about contingent liabilities of banks should be enhanced. The Basel committee will surely put some effort into these subjects over the coming period. In addition, the progressive adoption by many banks of the originate-to-distribute business model has increased the distance between the end-investor and the debtor and has thereby complicated the monitoring of risks. The firm extending credit in the first place is no longer the one directly suffering from default of a debtor. Often this is a third party, investing in securitised loans. For these investors, it is essential that transparency is increased on the models used by the originator and the rating agency assessing the risk. Moreover, the tough lesson of todays turbulence is that a sole reliance on ratings is insufficient. The second factor central to the recent turbulence has been the over-optimistic behaviour of many market participants, fed by ample liquidity, competition and search for yield. A clear sign of this was the steady decline of credit spreads on almost all financial instruments since 2002. Central banks and other authorities have warned early on for the risk of missprising. At the same time, return-seeking investors used new financial products to take on even larger risks especially by leveraging their positions. This made them vulnerable to a decline in the underlying value of assets. Indeed, deleveraging this mechanism has been one of the drivers of the current adjustment. The current process of risk re-assessment is in itself a positive development that helps to correct imbalances built-up in the financial system. Such periods are inherent to financial markets. Ever since financial markets exist there have been episodes of re-assessing and re-pricing risk. The expectation of market participants about risk or the price of financial assets is often a reflection of their most recent experience. Long periods of stability can result in an underestimation of risks and an overestimation of the value of assets. Such overly optimistic expectations will be corrected one day. That being said, we should be careful in not letting a period of over-optimism be followed by a sentiment of over-pessimism. Financial markets can be subject to overshooting both ways. Although the coming period will not be easy for banks, we can be glad about the timing of the turbulence. We have experienced years of strong world-wide economic growth, which enabled the financial system to create substantial buffers. Even though we cannot prevent episodes of rebalancing in the financial system, public authorities can sometimes shield the public from its excesses. The ones losing most from deteriorated credit monitoring in the US sub-prime market are customers that were allowed to borrow large amounts of money to buy a house when they could not really afford it. This is, however, not a matter of direct concern to financial stability, but of good conduct-of-business. The terms under which mortgages were extended show some features of miss-selling. Public authorities do have a responsibility in preventing this. They should urge banks and other institutions to secure proper borrower documentation and should set limits to the amount of mortgage credit to be extended. Also in the Nederlands households have shown a tendency to increase the loan-to-value and loan-to-income ratios of their mortgages. Because we, the central bank and the Dutch ministry of finance, were of the opinion that this could put households in a vulnerable position, we facilitated a stricter code of conduct on mortgage lending that is owned by the industry itself. The Twin Peak model Let me now finally turn to our set-up of supervision. In the Netherlands, we call this model the Twin Peak model. That is because it involves only two supervisory institutions and both cover all financial firms. We, the central bank, are also the prudential supervisor for banks, pension funds, insurance companies and securities firms. This, combined with our responsibility for oversight of payment and settlement systems, monetary policy and monitoring of financial markets underpins our overarching responsibility as guardian of financial stability. The second peak is the supervision on the conduct-of-business of the same large group of financial institutions. This is carried-out by my colleagues of the financial market authority. The division between conduct-of-business and prudential supervision is useful, as there can be conflicts of interest between then. Here, I would especially emphasise the advantages of combining prudential supervision with the more traditional tasks of a central bank. Our Twin Peak model was established in 2004, so we do have some experience. The combination of prudential supervision and central banking has certain advantages. It facilitates the interaction of knowledge about the macro economy and monetary transmission and about the position of the financial institutions within this environment. This improves both supervision and macroeconomic analysis as it gives a better understanding of the system-wide implications of potential risks in financial institutions. From a financial stability perspective, there is a large difference between knowing that one bank is prone to a certain risk or that the system as a whole is. In addition, this bundling of knowledge also improves the understanding of how the behaviour of financial institutions interacts with the real economy. For example, increased risk-oriented regulation, such as Basel II and Solvency II, might induce some pro-cycality with respect to the behaviour of financial institutions. And vice-versa, developments in the real economy are deemed to influence financial institutions. If it is possible to take such aspects into account in prudential policies, they can be more stabilising. Another advantage is that knowledge about new financial instruments is naturally available within the financial markets division of the central bank. Sharing this knowledge with prudential supervisors can lead to a better understanding of potential uncertainties for individual firms. The combination of supervision of banks, pension funds, insurance companies and securities firms also has some important advantages. Also here there are synergies from bundling knowledge. The increased dependency of all financial sectors on the well-functioning of financial markets has increased such synergies. A good understanding of markets and new financial products is thus an asset to the execution of supervisory tasks. In addition, it enhances the quality and scope of stress-tests, as it helps to assess the impact from a certain stress situation on the system as a whole. This gives us a fairly comprehensive insight into the financial stability impact of a certain stress scenarios. The combination of cross-sector supervision and central banking not only enhances the synergies of knowledge and expertise, it is also helpful on a more operational level. It gives us a particular broad set of possible policy instruments. This is especially helpful when guarding financial stability. Looking back at the policy measures aimed at improving financial stability, they often concerned issues that have both prudential, system and macroeconomic aspects. An example is the aforementioned Code on mortgages lending. Another is the preparation of business continuity planning, which involves both financial institutions and financial infrastructure. Next to these advantages under stable circumstances, I think that our Twin Peak model has proved its use in the recent period of stress. In such a period, it is especially important to be able to act quickly and to be fully informed. Being the prudential cross sector supervisor, we were able to quickly assess the impact on Dutch institution and sectors. In addition, we could combine this assessment with very up-to-date information from our financial markets and payment system departments. This combination is especially valuable when market liquidity is under stress. The decisions of a central bank regarding the terms under which it makes additional liquidity available have a bearing on the condition of individual banks. The aim is of course to inject liquidity in such a way that it solves the liquidity problems of healthy, solvable banks. Setting the right conditions can be a rather delicate task, especially in a turbulent situation. Our institutional set up allows a continuous monitoring and timely acting if needed, and the interaction between macro and financial sector liquidity conditions. Combining the different views within one institution gave us a first picture of the potential impact of the current turbulence on financial stability as a whole. This picture becomes clearer as the turmoil evolves and is generally reflected in the analysis presented in the first part of my speech. This analysis is still premature and further work needs to be done as developments further unfold, but I hope you found it interesting.

Title: Speech directeur Brouwer 'The integration of the European continent through economic cooperation'
text: Speech directeur Brouwer 'The integration of the European continent through economic cooperation' Speech Datum 11 oktober 2007 Tijd 13:53 uur Lokatie IV Joint High-Level Eurosystem  Bank of Russia Seminar, Moscow, Russian Federation Spreker Drs. H. Brouwer, directeur van de Nederlandsche Bank It is a great pleasure for me to have the opportunity to talk to you about EU enlargement and economic cooperation at large. During the last two decades, the face of the European continent has changed completely. Given how much has changed over a short time-span, I will today resist the temptation to predict the future of European integration. Instead, I will touch upon the evolution of the EU, and that what might help us today to enhance economic cooperation on the European continent. The European integration project was created to bring lasting peace and stability after World War II. This is achieved through economic cooperation between a heterogeneous group of countries. The foundation was laid in 1951, when six countries agreed to form the European Coal and Steel Community. Six years later, the Treaty of Rome created the forerunner of today's EU: the European Economic Community, often referred to as the Common Market. The idea behind the Common Market was simple: free movement of people and capital, and free mobility of goods and services across borders. Europes Economic Integration The Common Market soon attracted more countries and the original group of six expanded in several steps to the number of fifteen in 1995. With the exception of Norway and Switzerland, Western Europe was then united in the Economic Community. The end of the Cold war marked the beginning of a new era, leading to further enlargement to Central and Eastern Europe. Today the EU has increased to 27 countries, and encompasses almost half a billion people. Despite some feelings of enlargement fatigue, negotiations with candidate countries like Croatia, Macedonia and Turkey about possible EU membership are taking place. European economic cooperation is a success. It has enabled the creation of a single currency and has also brought other tangible gains. Today EU citizens have the right to live, work, study or retire in the EU country of their choice. Consumers benefit from a wider range of products and services at higher quality and lower prices. Businesses enjoy the access to a domestic market of almost 500 million people and can operate under a common set of rules. According to estimates of the European Commission, over the period 1992-2006 the gains of the EU single market amounted to 2.2% of EU GDP and 2.75 million extra jobs. Despite the success of economic integration, we should not forget that there is ample room for improvement. To mention one clear cut example, the Common Agricultural Policy absorbs 42% of the EU budget and is far from efficient. The EU should always keep in mind that enlargement has implication for the rest of the European continent. This is particularly true for our largest neighbour, Russia. In 2004 we expected that the accession of Central and Eastern European countries would not only provide stability and prosperity to the accession countries, but would also prove to be beneficial for Russia. The substitution of ten different sets of national trade rules and customs duties in favour of a single harmonised EU framework would reduce the overhead costs of Russian companies and facilitate their activities in the New Member States (NMS). What we see, however, is that the relative importance of Russia as a trading partner for the New Member States has decreased. In 1996, 8.5% of the NMS total trade was with Russia, whereas in 2006 it decreased to 6.2%. The competitive position of Russian companies has decreased; free movement of goods, services and capital within the EU has reinforced the strong position of EU companies in the NMS. Also practicalities like the implementation of a visa regime, high technical, sanitary and environmental standards are frustrating economic cooperation. For both Russia and the EU it is a challenge to overcome these problems. However, I believe that the necessary ingredients for improvement are already present and it is to these I now turn. EU and Russia: a relation of interdependence The first basic ingredient of economic cooperation is to recognise the degree of interdependence. The EU is Russias most important trading partner and its significance is growing. In 1996 the EU accounted for 46% of Russias total trade, whereas today this has amounted to more than 55%. Russia is the largest country on the European continent and the 4th most important non-EU trading partner. Despite its decreasing role as a trading partner with the NMS, Russia has become more important for the euro area. In 1996, 3% of total euro area trade was with Russia, whereas in 2006 this had doubled to 6%. The interdepence is especially evident regarding energy products. Russia is a major supplier of energy products and the EU receives the bulk of Russias energy exports. To put it in numbers, two thirds of Russias total oil and gas exports was destined for the EU, which constitutes around 25% of the EU's oil and gas consumption. EU exports to Russia are more diversified, with machinery and electronic equipment being the most important product categories. The second ingredient stems from the rapid integration of financial markets. Financial links between Russia and the EU are well-established. Loans, which are an important source of foreign capital flows to Russia, are mainly funded by European banks (Note 1). Albeit foreign direct investment in Russia is relatively low, the EU accounted for more than 70% of total FDI flows in 2006. Given the strong financial ties, cooperation on an international level is essential to safeguard the financial system and maintain financial stability. Over the past few years, the Eurosystem and the Bank of Russia have put this into practice in various ways. Todays high level dialogue is an example. But even more important are projects like the two year training programme on banking supervision(Note 2). Between 2003-2005 around 1500 Russian participants were trained in standards and methods of risk-based supervision. Russian managers conducted study visits to central banks and supervision authorities in the EU to gain experience of the practical implementation of banking supervision. The third ingredient is political will. Both the EU and Russia acknowledge that cooperation is necessary. I think that President Putin put it well in his letter to commemorate the 50th anniversary of the Treaties of Rome when he wrote: 'the full unity of our continent can never be achieved until Russia, as the largest European state, becomes an integral part of the European process'. And on the EU side, Commissioner Mandelson has stated: 'In the twentieth century our enduring goal must be a deep partnership built around far-reaching economic integration embracing the European continent, including Russia'. Lessons for cooperation There is a common goal, but as the expression goes, a goal without a plan is just a wish. I believe the basis for such a plan is already in place. As to the three key ingredients: First, I see considerable scope for Russia and the EU to further exploit the economic gains that come from closer economic cooperation through trade and investment. Trade and investment relationships between Russia and the EU can both be broadened and deepened. Membership of the WTO facilitates this process. WTO accession will anchor Russia into the world trading system, providing transparency and further global integration. Despite some potential short term costs, mutual acceptance of common rules of the game is beneficial to all parties in the long run. As soon as Russias WTO membership is accomplished, the EU and Russia can develop the Common Economic Space and reap the full benefits of economic cooperation. Second, I see that there is mutual political will to achieve cooperation. Both Russia and the EU have explicitly expressed this on various occasions. This opportunity must be seized and the only possibility to transform will into action is through dialogue. There currently are a number of fora in place to facilitate this dialogue. For example: the Northern Dimension, the Black Sea cooperation initiative, the energy dialogue, and various business dialogues like the Industrialists Round Table and NGOs initiatives, to name just a few. Third, I see the need for Russia and the EU to cooperate on issues regarding global financial markets. Cooperation on financial issues can and should be strengthened. Lets conclude by stressing the role of central banks in this respect. The Bank of Russia and the eurosystem can intensify the relationship through exchanging best practices in the field of supervision and the conduct of monetary policy. I, therefore, support the second project training programme that is in the pipeline. The focus will most likely be on internal audit and banking supervision. Training in these fields and an exchange of best practices will contribute directly to the quality of supervision and thereby to the stability of the financial system. De Nederlandsche Bank, being fully responsible for financial prudential supervision, will gladly contribute to this project. The evolution of the EU showed us that economic forces are strong enough to build and maintain stability between a heterogeneous group of countries. And because it is beneficial to both Russia and the EU, I strongly believe that economic cooperation can once again facilitate closer integration of the European continent. Notes: Note 1: Among BIS reporting banks in 2006 almost 84% of the outstanding loans were held by EU banks. Although this number has dropped from 98% in 1996, it is substantial. Note 2: This two year training programme is part of TACIS, the EUs Technical Assistance programme for CIS countries.

Title: Speech by director Schilder 'Challenges for company pension funds in a sustainable pension system'
text: Speech by director Schilder 'Challenges for company pension funds in a sustainable pension system' Speech Datum 8 november 2007 Time: 11:30 a.m. Location Circus Theatre Scheveningen Speaker Prof. dr. A. Schilder, director of the Dutch Central Bank It is a pleasure for me to be here again. Again, because six years ago, in 2001, I was also a guest speaker at your annual conference. The theme at the time was the increasing governance requirements of pension funds. This is a subject that I would like to draw attention to again today. But in the meantime, a lot has changed around us. We have survived the crisis of 2001-2002 and have barely recovered from it, when a new period of financial turbulence arrives. That is why I would like to talk to you today about the theme that we at DNB are committed to together with you, namely the sustainability of our Dutch pension system. As a pension fund manager, you have a pivotal role in this system. It is clear that you hold the key to a carefree old age for many Dutch people. Participation in work-related pensions is more than 90% here. This is much higher than in other European countries. In this way, the pension sector manages the most important financial asset of working Dutch people. Dutch pension savings in the second pillar amount to approximately 700 billion euros, or 140% of the Gross National Product.
