Title: President Wellink's speech 'The credit crisis and financial literacy'
text: President Wellink's speech 'The credit crisis and financial literacy' Speech Date: 21 april 2009 Time: 10:30 a.m. Location Annual Congress HBO Council Speaker Dr. A.H.E.M. Wellink, President of the Dutch Central Bank Introduction More than half of adults in Pakistan are unable to read and write a simple sentence about their everyday lives with comprehension. In a number of countries, especially West African, the percentage of illiterate people is even higher. As you can imagine, this makes the daily lives of those involved enormously more difficult. In addition, it hampers macroeconomic development. In the more developed countries, illiteracy on this scale is fortunately a ghost of the past. Financial literacy, on the other hand, falls short here as well. Basic financial knowledge needed to make responsible financial decisions is often insufficient. Think, for example, of being able to deal with concepts such as interest rates or inflation. Of course, not everyone needs to become a financial expert. Some choices are very complex. Above all, it is important that people are cautious, that they are well informed and that they try to get as complete a picture as possible of the risks involved in decisions. This is also relevant from a macroeconomic point of view. A major reason for the emergence of the current crisis was that American households, often with limited creditworthiness, took out risky mortgage loans. The problems that arose in this sub-prime mortgage market developed into a global financial and economic crisis. The crisis has highlighted important challenges. I will discuss this, and in particular the importance of financial literacy. Innovation and supervision There has been a wave of innovation in the financial sector in recent years. New complex products were developed at breakneck speed. Among other things, they made it possible to resell loan portfolios more easily. These kinds of innovations played an important role in the creation of the crisis. The speed of innovation was so high that in retrospect we can say that supervisors, regulators and risk managers of banks have not been able to keep up sufficiently. As a result, an isolated problem in the subprime market in the U.S. could grow into a global crisis. The crisis has made it clear that laws, regulations and supervision will have to be tightened. However, we must not lose sight of the fact that innovation remains a necessary condition for progress. It's about finding the right balance. The new financial products that were at the origin of the crisis also offered advantages. If loans become more tradable, the risk can be taken over by those who can - and want to - bear it best. We should not throw the baby out with the bathwater. Trust Financial innovation has reduced the insight into the exact place where risks ultimately precipitate. When losses arose, this created persistent doubts about the quality of banks' loan portfolios and hidden liabilities. As a result, confidence in the financial world eroded rapidly. A few years ago, it was difficult to imagine the scenario that has unfolded, with a complete drying up of liquidity and a simultaneous collapse of almost all financial markets. The real economy is also affected by the loss of confidence. Consumers are becoming more reluctant to make purchases due to the ominous news. Companies are investing less. The deteriorating outlook for companies, in turn, is exacerbating the problems at banks. As economies worldwide have become increasingly intertwined, these reinforcing mechanisms play a role worldwide. A sudden drop in demand reached all corners of the global economy at lightning speed. From the supplier of the German car industry in Eastern Europe to the Asian producers of consumer goods. Restoring confidence will play a key role in overcoming the crisis. Many measures taken by the authorities contribute to this. For example, hundreds of billions were injected into financial institutions by governments worldwide and guarantee funds were created to ensure the stability of the financial system. Central banks cut interest rates sharply and provided liquidity support. The Importance of Financial Literacy The crisis has also shown that households are vulnerable and sometimes invest in products whose risks they do not fully understand. This has played a role in the US subprime market in particular. Here, a group of homebuyers with limited credit ratings bought risky mortgage products. These mortgages often had a low and fixed interest rate for the first few years. After this, the interest rate was variable, which in practice meant a sharp increase in the monthly costs. This put many subprime homeowners in trouble. At the end of 2007, the number of subprime mortgages for which interest rates could vary over the term accounted for only 7% of the total. Still, this segment accounted for 40% of foreclosure sales. In practice, financiers and intermediaries have not always met the requirements of the duty of care. This raises questions about the integrity of their actions. The duty of care requires that the risks of financial products are made as transparent as possible. This is no mean feat. For example, a Dutch study from 2006 found that a person would have to read 41 documents totalling 398 pages to be able to fully understand all the terms and conditions of an investment mortgage. But providing insight is not the same as confronting someone with endless amounts of pages. All this does not alter the fact that households also bear responsibility for their own financial choices. And research shows that the financial knowledge and skills of households are often seriously lacking. This applies to both developing and developed countries. A lot of research has been done on this, especially in the US, and this conclusion emerges consistently. DNB research among 1500 Dutch households has shown that a significant part of the Dutch population does not have sufficient basic knowledge in areas such as interest rates, inflation and investments. Knowledge that is of great importance for making well-considered financial choices. An example of a question we asked to measure knowledge about interest rates and inflation was: suppose the interest rate on your savings account is 1% per year and the inflation rate is equal to 2% per year. Would you be able to buy more, exactly the same or less after 1 year than today with the money in the account? Another question was: suppose you have EUR 100 in a savings account and the interest rate is 20% per year and you never withdraw money or interest. How much would you have in the savings account after five years: more than EUR 200, exactly EUR 200 or less than EUR 200? Of the five questions we asked in this area, only 40% answered all of them correctly. Less than 20% of those surveyed answered the correct answer to more than six of the eight questions about investments. For example, only 60% of respondents gave the correct answer to the question of whether the statement "Stocks are normally riskier than bonds" is true. A lack of financial literacy among households has become a bigger problem due to deregulation and financial innovation. Not only has the number of products to choose from increased significantly. If you go to a comparison site on the internet to search for a mortgage, you can choose from more than 8 mortgage types on the first page, ranging from an interest-only to a life investment mortgage. But households have also increasingly started to behave like asset managers. In the Netherlands, both the debt and the wealth of households have risen sharply relative to their income over the past decade. Whereas in 1997 the total mortgage debt was equal to the total Dutch household income, at the end of 2008 it was twice as high. On the other hand, total wealth increased from four to six and a half times income. This does not include pension assets. The increase is mainly due to the increased wealth of households in their own homes. With this increase in debt and wealth, the financial risks faced by households have increased. As a result, the importance of making the right financial decisions has increased. Of course, having sufficient financial knowledge and skills is primarily important for households themselves. Research indicates a strong correlation between financial literacy and the size of their wealth. More financial knowledge goes hand in hand with greater participation in the stock market and better planning of retirement. Moreover, the problems in the sub-prime market in the United States have made it clear that financial literacy also has macroeconomic relevance. When households take irresponsible financial risks that then lead to defaults at the same time, this causes a significant shock to the financial system. Policy Financial education and training of the public are high on the agenda worldwide. This is also being worked on in the Netherlands. For example, DNB participates in CentIQ. This platform was set up by the Ministry of Finance in collaboration with other governments and parties from the financial sector, information and consumer organisations and science. CentIQ conducted a survey among high school students last year. The results don't lie. One-third of young people engage in risky financial behaviour; They are in debt and playing for money. Two-thirds of young people find it difficult to manage money. More than half of all young people believe that their parents did not teach them the value of money. 'What you learn when you're young is what you do when you're old'. Of course, improving financial literacy starts with education. But education also plays a key role in this. DNB is doing its bit. In our visitor centre, pupils and students can get acquainted with the world of money, gold and the economy. We receive 10 to 15 thousand visitors here every year. At the moment, the interactive exhibition 'Money and your life!' can also be admired there. Especially for students between the ages of 12 and 16. In addition, we issue lesson plans for secondary schools. The lesson plan on the credit crisis in particular proved to be extremely popular. Of these, no less than 13,000 were ordered. At first glance, secondary education seems to be the right place for improving financial education. However, it plays at all levels. For example, DNB supports Aflatoun, an organisation that focuses specifically on improving the financial skills of children from the age of six. In developing countries, but also in the Netherlands. But higher education also has a role to play here. Through teacher training courses, but also by offering top-notch courses that train professionals for the financial sector. Finally Ladies and gentlemen, you are here today to exchange views on 'shaping innovation' in higher professional education. The speed at which changes in the economy and society are taking place makes this theme very challenging. I wish you every success today.
text_original: Speech president Wellink 'De kredietcrisis en financile geletterdheid' Speech Datum 21 april 2009 Tijd 10:30 uur Lokatie Jaarcongres HBO-raad Spreker Dr. A.H.E.M. Wellink, president van de Nederlandsche Bank Inleiding Meer dan de helft van de volwassenen in Pakistan is niet in staat een simpele zin over hun alledaagse leven met begrip te lezen en te schrijven. In een aantal, vooral West-Afrikaanse, landen ligt het percentage ongeletterden nog hoger. U kunt zich voorstellen dat het dagelijkse leven van de betrokkenen hierdoor enorm wordt bemoeilijkt. Bovendien belemmert het de macro-economische ontwikkeling. In de meer ontwikkelde landen is ongeletterdheid op deze schaal gelukkig een spook uit het verleden. Financile geletterdheid daarentegen schiet ook hier tekort. Basale financile kennis die nodig is om verantwoorde financile beslissingen te kunnen nemen is dikwijls onvoldoende. Denk bijvoorbeeld aan het kunnen omgaan met begrippen als rente of inflatie. Natuurlijk hoeft niet iedereen financieel expert te worden. Sommige keuzes zijn erg complex. Het gaat er bovenal om dat mensen behoedzaam zijn, zich goed laten voorlichten en de risico's rond beslissingen zo volledig mogelijk in beeld proberen te krijgen. Dit is ook macro-economisch relevant. Een belangrijke aanleiding van het ontstaan van de huidige crisis was dat Amerikaanse huishoudens, vaak met beperkte kredietwaardigheid, risicovolle hypotheekleningen zijn aangegaan. De problemen die op deze sub-prime hypotheekmarkt ontstonden ontwikkelden zich tot een wereldwijde financile en economische crisis. De crisis heeft belangrijke uitdagingen aan het licht gebracht. Ik ga hierop in, en in het bijzonder op het belang van financile geletterdheid. Innovatie en toezicht Er heeft de laatste jaren een innovatiegolf in de financile sector plaatsgevonden. Nieuwe complexe producten werden in sneltreinvaart ontwikkeld. Ze maakten het onder andere mogelijk dat leningportefeuilles makkelijker konden worden doorverkocht. Dit soort innovaties speelde een belangrijke rol bij het ontstaan van de crisis. De snelheid van innovatie lag namelijk zo hoog dat we achteraf kunnen stellen dat toezichthouders, regelgevers en risicomanagers van banken het onvoldoende hebben kunnen bijbenen. Hierdoor kon een gesoleerd probleem op de subprime markt in de VS uitgroeien tot een wereldwijde crisis. De crisis heeft duidelijk gemaakt dat wet- en regelgeving en toezicht zullen moeten worden aangescherpt. Hierbij moeten we echter niet uit het oog verliezen dat innovatie een noodzakelijke voorwaarde blijft voor vooruitgang. Het gaat om het vinden van de juiste balans. De nieuwe financile producten die aan de wieg van de crisis stonden boden ook voordelen. Als leningen beter verhandelbaar worden kan het risico worden overgenomen door degene die dat het beste kan - en wil - dragen. We moeten het kind niet met het badwater weggooien. Vertrouwen Door de financile innovatie is het inzicht in de precieze plaats waar risico's uiteindelijk neerslaan verminderd. Toen er verliezen ontstonden creerde dit een aanhoudende twijfel over de kwaliteit van de kredietportefeuilles en verborgen verplichtingen van banken. Hierdoor erodeerde het vertrouwen in de financile wereld razendsnel. Het scenario dat zich heeft voltrokken, met een volledige opdroging van de liquiditeit en simultaan inzakken van vrijwel alle financile markten, was enkele jaren geleden moeilijk voor te stellen. Ook de rele economie wordt geraakt door het verlies van vertrouwen. Consumenten worden door het onheilspellende nieuws terughoudender met aankopen. Bedrijven investeren minder. De verslechterde vooruitzichten voor bedrijven versterken op hun beurt weer de problemen bij banken. Doordat de economien wereldwijd steeds verder vervlochten zijn geraakt, spelen deze versterkende mechanismen wereldwijd. Een plotselinge vraaguitval bereikte razendsnel alle uithoeken van de wereldeconomie. Van de toeleverancier van de Duitse auto-industrie in Oost-Europa tot de Aziatische producenten van consumentengoederen. Bij het overwinnen van de crisis zal vertrouwensherstel een hoofdrol spelen. Veel maatregelen die de autoriteiten hebben genomen dragen hieraan bij. Zo werden door overheden wereldwijd honderden miljarden genjecteerd in financile instellingen en werden garantiefondsen in het leven geroepen om de stabiliteit van het financile stelsel te waarborgen. Centrale banken verlaagden de rentetarieven fors en gaven liquiditeitssteun. Het belang van financile geletterdheid De crisis heeft ook laten zien dat huishoudens kwetsbaar zijn en soms in producten stappen waarvan ze de risicos niet goed overzien. Dit heeft in het bijzonder een rol gespeeld op de Amerikaanse subprime markt. Hier kocht een groep huizenkopers met beperkte kredietwaardigheid riskante hypotheekproducten. Deze hypotheken hadden de eerste paar jaar vaak een lage en vaste rente. Hierna was de rente variabel, wat in de praktijk een fikse stijging van de maandlasten betekende. Dit bracht veel subprime-huizenbezitters in de problemen. Het aantal subprime hypotheken waarbij de rente over de looptijd kon variren vormde eind 2007 slechts 7% van het totaal. Toch was dit segment verantwoordelijk voor 40% van de executieverkopen. Financiers en tussenpersonen hebben in de praktijk niet altijd voldaan aan de eisen die de zorgplicht hen stelt. Dit roept dan ook vragen op rondom de integriteit van hun handelen. De zorgplicht dwingt ertoe dat risicos van financile producten zo inzichtelijk mogelijk worden gemaakt. Dit is geen sinecure. Uit een Nederlands onderzoek uit 2006 bleek bijvoorbeeld dat iemand 41 documenten van in totaal 398 paginas zou moeten lezen om volledig kennis te kunnen nemen van alle voorwaarden van een beleggingshypotheek. Maar inzichtelijk maken is toch iets anders dan iemand met eindeloze hoeveelheden bladzijden confronteren. Dit alles neemt niet weg dat huishoudens ook zelf verantwoordelijkheid dragen voor hun financile keuzes. En de financile kennis en kunde van huishoudens schiet vaak ernstig tekort, zo blijkt uit onderzoek. Dit geldt zowel voor ontwikkelingslanden als voor ontwikkelde landen. Vooral in de VS is hiernaar veel onderzoek gedaan, en deze conclusie komt consistent naar voren. Uit DNB-onderzoek onder 1500 Nederlandse huishoudens is gebleken dat ook een belangrijk deel van de Nederlandse bevolking niet in voldoende mate beschikt over basale kennis op gebieden als rente, inflatie en beleggingen. Kennis die voor het maken van weloverwogen financile keuzes van groot belang is. Een voorbeeld van een vraag die we stelden om kennis over rente en inflatie te meten was: veronderstel dat de rente op uw spaarrekening 1% per jaar is en de inflatie is gelijk aan 2% per jaar. Zou u dan na 1 jaar meer, precies hetzelfde of minder kunnen kopen dan vandaag met het geld op de rekening? Een andere vraag was: veronderstel dat u EUR 100 op een spaarrekening hebt en de rente is 20% per jaar en u neemt nooit geld of rente op. Hoeveel zou u dan na vijf jaar op de spaarrekening hebben: meer dan EUR 200, precies EUR 200 of minder dan EUR 200? Op de vijf vragen die we op dit terrein stelden bleek slechts 40% op alle vragen het juiste antwoord te geven. Op de vragen over beleggingen gaf nog geen 20% van de ondervraagden op meer dan zes van de acht vragen het juiste antwoord. Zo gaf bijvoorbeeld slechts 60% van de respondenten het goede antwoord op de vraag of de stelling 'Aandelen zijn normaal gesproken risicovoller dan obligaties' waar is. Een gebrek aan financile geletterdheid bij huishoudens is door deregulering en financile innovatie een groter probleem geworden. Niet alleen is het aantal producten waaruit gekozen kan worden sterk toegenomen. Wie naar een vergelijkingssite op internet gaat om een hypotheek te zoeken kan op de eerste pagina al kiezen uit meer dan 8 hypotheekvormen, varirend van een aflossingsvrije tot levens-beleggingshypotheek. Maar ook zijn huishoudens zich steeds meer als vermogensbeheerder gaan gedragen. In Nederland is het laatste decennium zowel de schuld als het vermogen van huishoudens sterk toegenomen ten opzichte van hun inkomen. Was de totale hypotheekschuld in 1997 gelijk aan het totale Nederlandse gezinsinkomen, eind 2008 lag deze twee keer zo hoog. Daartegenover nam het totale vermogen toe van vier tot zesenhalf keer het inkomen. Hierbij is het pensioenvermogen niet meegerekend. De toename komt vooral door de gestegen vermogens van huishoudens in hun eigen woning. Met deze toegenomen schulden en vermogens zijn de financile risico's die huishoudens lopen groter geworden. Het belang van het maken van de juiste financile beslissingen is daardoor toegenomen. Het beschikken over voldoende financile kennis en vaardigheden is natuurlijk in eerste instantie van belang voor huishoudens zelf. Onderzoek wijst op een sterke samenhang tussen financile geletterdheid en de omvang van hun vermogen. Meer financile kennis gaat daarbij samen met een grotere participatie op de aandelenmarkt en een betere planning van het pensioen. Bovendien hebben de problemen op de sub-prime markt in de Verenigde Staten duidelijk gemaakt dat financile geletterdheid ook macro-economische relevantie heeft. Wanneer huishoudens onverantwoorde financile risico's nemen die vervolgens tegelijkertijd tot wanbetalingen leiden, zorgt dat voor een forse schok voor het financile systeem. Beleid Financile voorlichting en training van het publiek staan wereldwijd hoog op de agenda. Ook in Nederland wordt hier werk van gemaakt. Zo neemt DNB deel aan CentIQ. Dit platform is opgezet door het ministerie van Financin in samenwerking met andere overheden en partijen uit de financile sector, voorlichtings- en consumentenorganisaties en de wetenschap. CentIQ heeft vorig jaar onderzoek gedaan onder middelbare scholieren. De resultaten liegen er niet om. Eenderde van de jongeren vertoont risicovol financieel gedrag; ze hebben schulden en spelen om geld. Tweederde van de jongeren vindt het moeilijk om met geld om te gaan. Ruim de helft van alle jongeren is van mening dat hun ouders hun de waarde van geld niet goed heeft bijgebracht. 'Jong geleerd is oud gedaan'. Het verbeteren van financile geletterdheid begint natuurlijk bij de opvoeding. Maar ook het onderwijs speelt hierbij een hoofdrol. DNB draagt haar steentje bij. In ons bezoekerscentrum kunnen scholieren en studenten kennis maken met de wereld van geld, goud en economie. We ontvangen hier jaarlijks 10 tot 15 duizend bezoekers. Op dit moment is daar ook de interactieve tentoonstelling 'Geld en je leven!' te bewonderen. Speciaal voor leerlingen tussen de 12 en de 16 jaar. Daarnaast geven we lesbrieven uit voor middelbare scholen. Vooral de lesbrief over de kredietcrisis bleek enorm populair. Hiervan werden er maar liefst 13.000 besteld. In eerste instantie lijkt het middelbaar onderwijs de aangewezen plek voor het verbeteren van financile educatie. Het speelt echter op alle niveau's. DNB ondersteunt bijvoorbeeld Aflatoun, een organisatie die zich speciaal richt op het verbeteren van financile vaardigheden van kinderen vanaf zes jaar. In ontwikkelingslanden, maar ook in Nederland. Maar ook het Hoger Onderwijs heeft hier een rol. Via de lerarenopleidingen, maar ook door topopleidingen te bieden die professionals opleiden voor de financile sector. Tot slot Dames en heren, u bent hier vandaag bij elkaar om van gedachten te wisselen over 'vormgeven aan vernieuwing' in het HBO. De snelheid waarmee veranderingen in de economie en de maatschappij zich voltrekken maakt dit thema zeer uitdagend. Ik wens u hierbij vandaag veel succes toe.

Title: Speech by director Kellermann: 'More attention to prudence'
text: Speech by director Kellermann: 'More attention to prudence' Speech Date: 23 april 2009 Time: 4:15 p.m. Location 11th PBM symposium Pension in Motion, Kurhaus Scheveningen Speaker Mr. A.J. Kellermann, Director of the Dutch Central Bank Louis XIV, the Sun King, set up a pension fund for the artists of the French Opera in 1698. The pension scheme not only took into account the intensive work of the ballet dancers, but also a healthy turnover of performers. Ballet dancers retired at the age of 40 and the singers on their 50th birthday. Of course, such an arrangement implies a considerable financial burden. As a result, there was regularly a deficit in the pension fund's coffers. To make up for this shortfall, a benefit performance was organized. An elegant way to shape a recovery plan. Recovery plans are therefore timeless. After the golden era for pension funds in the 1990s, the tide seems to have turned since the start of this millennium. The first pension crisis of 2002-2003 already had a major impact on our retirement provisions. The current financial crisis is leaving deep scars at an unprecedented speed. Since the start of the credit crisis in mid-2007, the investments of Dutch pension funds have been written down by roughly 150 billion euros. That is an amount of 25,000 euros per employee. At the same time, the present value of future pension benefits has increased by the same amount. On balance, this scissor movement has led to a sharp drop in the funding ratio. In mid-2007 it was still at the perfectly acceptable level of 150%; In the first months of this year, the average coverage rate of the sector fluctuated between 90 and 95%. Until recently, no one could have imagined that such percentages would be possible in the Netherlands. Fortunately, we see that pension funds, the government and the regulator are tackling the current problems energetically. Most pension funds were on time with the submission of their recovery plans. Our first impressions of the content of all these plans are certainly encouraging, although there will certainly be a lot of discussion before they are all approved. If we return to the financial position for a moment, we know that a funding shortfall does not immediately cause a pension fund to pay problems. At the same time, it is also true that a pension fund cannot pay out more than is available for a long time. In the interests of solidarity, this is acceptable to a certain extent. However, due to the ageing of the population, it is becoming less and less possible to rely on young people to guarantee the pensions of the elderly. That is a fact that we will have to take into account. Anyone who enters into an employment contract with an employer is automatically and compulsorily affiliated to the pension scheme of the company in question. This is a pension commitment that is formulated as the accrual of an entitlement to a future benefit. This commitment is implemented by a pension fund in the form of a foundation, without external shareholders. In the absence of shareholders, pension fund members ultimately bear the risk themselves. In the event of a funding shortfall, and after all other options have been exhausted, the discount scheme will come into effect at some point in time, reducing existing entitlements and rights. With a view to a balanced representation of interests, it is better to use this emergency measure in the event of structural undercoverage than to pass on an unpaid bill to the future. This makes it  and this is sometimes forgotten  a measure that contributes to the long-term sustainability of the pension system. In this way, the law protects (future) pensioners and contributors against increasing funding shortfalls and risks. Because the effect on confidence is difficult to estimate, a drastic measure such as curtailment should be used with the greatest possible caution. The dilemma that arises here is that, on the one hand, it is necessary to prevent pension funds from making cuts too quickly, while we may just be at the lowest point of a crisis. In that case, the retrospective cuts would not have been necessary. On the other hand, necessary measures cannot be postponed for too long. Certainly not if interest rates continue to fall or remain low for a long time; the Japan scenario. In our opinion, the chosen approach is appropriate to the current crisis. For the time being, cuts are not on the agenda in the vast majority of cases and pension funds will be given sufficient time to prepare for the serious measures that will have to be taken if recovery is not forthcoming. However, the future is uncertain and that is why we need to keep a grip on things. In mid-2010, the situation will be thoroughly re-evaluated and DNB will advise on whether it is justifiable to wait any longer before implementing emergency measures. Of course, all this does not affect the responsibility of pension fund boards to formulate their own policy that does justice to a balanced distribution of burdens and benefits among the various stakeholders. In my opinion, part of that responsibility is to inform the members of the pension fund of the possible consequences of the current crisis for their pension accrual or benefit. This is necessary to make it possible for participants to adjust to potentially lower pension prospects. In this way, one can deliberately reduce consumption patterns, increase free savings or, for example, choose to retire later. The latter indicates that it makes more sense than ever for people to continue to invest in themselves. Many people remain healthy and vital in old age. They can continue to work in their jobs or even start building a new career. Transparency is also essential to maintain support for the collective Dutch system. Pensions are pre-eminently a service that can be organised collectively. After all, pensions are provided on the basis of collective agreements between employers' organisations and trade unions. Subsequently, these agreements are implemented by the collective in the interest of the collective. It is well known that this leads to significant economies of scale and opportunities to share risks. After all, both effects increase welfare. If we look at today's propositions, solidarity is certainly not over and there is plenty of reason to take advantage of the possibilities for scaling up and even increase them. Openness is needed with regard to the financial position and the underlying risks. Discounting against the current yield curve is essential to have a good picture of the pension fund's actual financial position and the risks that are locked up in the balance sheet. Moreover, the FTK seems to contain an ambivalence on this point. The funding ratio is assessed on the basis of a certainty measure of 97.5%. Such a measure is acceptable because there is the discount instrument. However, if it turns out that in the event of substantial funding shortages, the implementation of a discount is not seen as a regular instrument, a higher degree of certainty is apparently considered desirable. In other words, if some degree of uncertainty in the obligations is not desirable, I think we should consider the possible implications for the FTF. Transparency on the risks is also needed with regard to the distribution of shocks as they occur in the future. Making agreements in advance about this division prevents the need for periodic new negotiations about the distribution of the benefits and burdens. Without such agreements, sooner or later there will be unnecessary tension on the system. This brings us to the expectations for the Dutch pension system. It is necessary to reassess the principles of our defined benefit system. The benefits for individuals and society need to be re-emphasised. In addition, it is desirable to review the financial structure of the funds. Until the 1990s, the management of a pension fund was dominated by prudence. The financing was used on the cautious side, which allowed pension funds to fall back on substantial implicit reserves. Then, in the 1990s, the stock market entered a prolonged boom and the impression of a free lunch arose. Pension rights were extended and at the same time contributions were reduced to below the cost-covering level. In fact, the money was spent twice: a reversal of the cautious pension logic of the previous period. In addition, interest rates showed a trend of decline, which also ate into the implicit buffers. The principle that pension funds invest in shares and other real assets is fine. After all, the supply of risk capital stimulates economic growth and any higher returns can be used to build up buffers and to link pensions to prices or wages. But the current and previous pension crises show that the associated risks should not be underestimated. For example, let's take a look at the stock markets. At the end of this year, the leading MSCI World Equity Index will be celebrating its 40th anniversary. Since its inception, this index has experienced 4 tumbles that are greater than the 25% decline on which the FTK is based. Two of these events occurred in the last 7 years. We have just completed the biggest drop of almost 44% as a result of the credit crisis. When the internet bubble burst, prices fell by about 30%. Furthermore, the OPEC oil embargo in October 1973 led to a sharp drop in the share price of 39% and the first Gulf War sent shockwaves through the stock markets of minus 26%. Since the FTK assumes a certainty measure of 97.5%, a decline of more than 25% should only have occurred once in the last 40 years. I think this is a reason to take a closer look at the adequacy of the parameters in the FTK, but also at the question of whether there are not too many open risks in the financing of our pensions. In addition to a realistic assessment, it is important that pension funds are able to bear the risks. It has recently become clear that control by means of premium adjustments and limitation of indexation is not sufficient in all circumstances to absorb large fluctuations in the funding ratio. This may mean that we will have to strive for structurally higher buffers, for example by reserving the excess returns on investments much more to absorb setbacks. It is also possible that pension fund balance sheets will be made more balanced. [Sheet 8] In principle, there are two ways to achieve this. After all, more matching between assets and liabilities can take place through adjustments to investments or liabilities. In the former, risks are transferred through the capital market; The second is about the possibility of explicitly assigning more risks  both plus and minus  to the participants. Such a shift, in which the emphasis will be on the provision of good information to the participants, is only attractive to young people. Older people benefit from a stable and predictable pension result. Let me end with the observation that, even after recent developments, the Dutch pension system is still one of the best in the world. The intrinsic value that the system offers will become clear again in the near future if all stakeholders jointly take care of the necessary repair work. This is not in the form of a benefit performance as with the French Opera, but in essence there is not much difference either. Everyone will have to do their part to make the recovery a reality. This collective approach is one of the core values of the Dutch system: many parties are involved in the pension debate and just as many feel responsible for achieving a good result. After the recovery process has been completed, I am sure that our retirement provision will be even more firmly grounded in our society than before. Financial care for the elderly is optimally accompanied by risk-taking by pension funds. In my opinion, more attention should be paid to prudence in the financial structure of these funds. The credit crisis has brought us all back down to earth, and in that respect, every disadvantage has its advantage. Downloads Powerpoint 'More attention to prudence' (PPT, 112.5 kB)
text_original: Speech directeur Kellermann 'Meer aandacht voor prudentie' Speech Datum 23 april 2009 Tijd 16:15 uur Lokatie 11e PBM symposium Pensioen in beweging, Kurhaus Scheveningen Spreker Mr. A.J. Kellermann, directeur van de Nederlandsche Bank Louis XIV, de zonnekoning, richtte in 1698 een pensioenfonds op voor de artiesten van de Franse Opera. De pensioenregeling hield niet alleen rekening met het intensieve werk van de balletdansers, maar ook met een gezond verloop van artiesten. Balletdansers gingen op 40 jarige leeftijd met pensioen en de zangers op hun 50-ste verjaardag. Een dergelijke regeling impliceert natuurlijk een behoorlijke financile last. Regelmatig was er dan ook een tekort in de kas van het pensioenfonds. Om dit tekort aan te vullen werd dan een benefietvoorstelling georganiseerd. Een elegante manier om een herstelplan vorm te geven. Herstelplannen zijn dus van alle tijden. Na het gouden tijdperk voor de pensioenfondsen in de jaren 1990 lijkt sinds de start van dit millennium het tij gekeerd. De eerste pensioencrisis van 2002-2003 had al een grote impact op onze oudedagsvoorzieningen. De huidige financile crisis laat ongekend snel, diepe sporen na. Vanaf de start van de kredietcrisis medio 2007 zijn de beleggingen van Nederlandse pensioenfondsen met grofweg 150 miljard euro afgewaardeerd. Dat is een bedrag van 25.000 euro per werknemer. Gelijkertijd is de contante waarde van de toekomstige pensioenuitkeringen met eenzelfde bedrag toegenomen. Deze schaarbeweging heeft per saldo geleid tot een fikse daling van de dekkingsgraad. Lag deze medio 2007 nog op het alleszins acceptabele niveau van 150%; in de eerste maanden van dit jaar fluctueerde het gemiddelde dekkingspercentage van de sector tussen de 90 en 95%. Niemand kon tot voor kort vermoeden dat dergelijke percentages in Nederland mogelijk zijn. Gelukkig zien we dat pensioenfondsen, de overheid en de toezichthouder de huidige problematiek voortvarend aanpakken. De meeste pensioenfondsen waren mooi op tijd met het indienen van hun herstelplan. Onze eerste indrukken van de inhoud van al deze plannen zijn zonder meer bemoedigend al zal er zeker nog heel wat discussie volgen voor dat ze allemaal zijn goedgekeurd. Als we even terugkeren naar de financile positie dan weten we dat een dekkingstekort een pensioenfonds niet direct in betalingsproblemen brengt. Tegelijkertijd is het ook zo dat een pensioenfonds niet langdurig meer kan uitkeren dan er beschikbaar is. Met het oog op solidariteit is dit tot op zekere hoogte acceptabel. Echter, door de vergrijzing kan steeds minder een beroep worden gedaan op de jongeren om de pensioenen van de ouderen te garanderen. Dat is een gegeven waarmee wij rekening zullen moeten houden. Wie een arbeidscontract sluit met een werkgever neemt daarmee automatisch en verplicht deel aan de pensioenregeling van de betreffende onderneming. Het gaat daarbij om een pensioentoezegging die is geformuleerd als het opbouwen van een aanspraak op een toekomstige uitkering. Die toezegging wordt uitgevoerd door een pensioenfonds in de vorm van een stichting, zonder externe aandeelhouders. Omdat aandeelhouders ontbreken dragen pensioenfondsdeelnemers uiteindelijk zelf risico. In geval van een dekkingstekort, en nadat alle andere opties zijn benut, treedt op enig moment de kortingsregeling in werking waarbij bestaande aanspraken en rechten worden verminderd. Met het oog op een evenwichtige belangenbehartiging is het inzetten van deze noodmaatregel bij structurele onderdekking beter dan een onbetaalde rekening door te schuiven naar de toekomst. Daarmee is het  en dat wordt nog wel eens vergeten  een maatregel die bijdraagt aan de duurzaamheid van het pensioenstelsel op lange termijn. De wet beschermt op die manier de (toekomstige) pensioengerechtigden en premiebetalers tegen oplopende financieringstekorten en risicos. Omdat het effect op het vertrouwen moeilijk is in te schatten dient een ingrijpende maatregel als korten met de grootst mogelijke voorzichtigheid te worden ingezet. Het dilemma dat hierbij speelt is dat enerzijds moet worden voorkomen dat pensioenfondsen te snel tot korten overgaan, terwijl we misschien net op het dieptepunt van een crisis zitten. In dat geval was het korten achteraf niet nodig geweest. Anderzijds kunnen noodzakelijke maatregelen niet te lang worden uitgesteld. Zeker niet als de rente verder blijft dalen of langdurig laag blijft; het Japan scenario. De gekozen aanpak past naar onze mening bij de huidige crisis. Korten is voorlopig in verreweg de meeste gevallen niet aan de orde en pensioenfondsen krijgen voldoende tijd om zich voor te bereiden op de serieuze maatregelen die genomen moeten worden als herstel uitblijft. De toekomst is echter onzeker en daarom is het nodig dat we grip op de zaak houden. Medio 2010 wordt de situatie opnieuw grondig gevalueerd en zal DNB adviseren of langer wachten met het doorvoeren van noodmaatregelen verantwoord is. Dit alles laat natuurlijk onverlet de eigen verantwoordelijk van pensioenfondsbesturen om hun eigen beleid te formuleren dat recht doet aan een evenwichtige verdeling van lasten en lusten over de verschillende belanghebbenden. Onderdeel van die verantwoordelijkheid is mijn inziens dat de deelnemers in het pensioenfonds op de hoogte worden gebracht van de mogelijke gevolgen van de huidige crisis voor hun pensioenopbouw of uitkering. Dit is nodig om het voor deelnemers mogelijk te maken zich aan te passen aan wellicht lagere pensioenvooruitzichten. Op deze manier kan men weloverwogen het consumptiepatroon verlagen, de vrije besparingen opvoeren of er bijvoorbeeld voor kiezen later met pensioen te gaan. Dit laatste geeft overigens aan dat het meer dan ooit zinvol is dat mensen in zichzelf blijven investeren. Veel mensen blijven gezond en vitaal op oudere leeftijd. Ze kunnen blijven werken in hun baan of zelfs starten met een nieuwe carrire op te bouwen. Transparantie is bovendien essentieel om het draagvlak voor het collectieve Nederlandse stelsel te behouden. Pensioen is bij uitstek een collectief te organiseren dienst. Pensioenen worden immers verstrekt op basis van collectieve afspraken tussen werkgeversorganisaties en vakbonden. Vervolgens worden deze afspraken uitgevoerd door het collectief in het belang van het collectief. Het is genoegzaam bekend dat dit leidt tot significante schaalvoordelen en mogelijkheden om risicos delen. Beide effecten zijn immers welvaartsverhogend. Als we kijken naar de stellingen van vandaag dan is solidariteit dus zeker niet uit en is er genoeg aanleiding om de mogelijkheden tot schaalvergroting te benutten en zelfs te vergroten. Openheid is nodig met betrekking tot de financile positie en de onderliggende risicos. De discontering tegen de actuele rentecurve is essentieel om een goed beeld te hebben op de werkelijke financile positie van het pensioenfonds en die risicos die zitten opgesloten in de balans. Op dit punt lijkt het FTK overigens een ambivalentie te bevatten. De dekkingsgraad wordt getoetst op een zekerheidsmaat van 97,5%. Een dergelijke maatstaf is acceptabel omdat er het kortingsinstrument is. Echter als zou blijken dat in geval van forse dekkingstekorten het doorvoeren van korting niet wordt gezien ziet als een regulier instrument, wordt blijkbaar een hogere mate van zekerheid wenselijk gevonden. Anders gezegd, als enige mate van onzekerheid in de verplichtingen niet wenselijk is, zouden we mijn inziens na moeten denken over de mogelijke implicaties voor het FTK. Transparantie over de risicos is ook nodig met betrekking tot de verdeling van schokken zoals deze zich in de toekomst voordoen. Het op voorhand afspraken maken over deze verdeling voorkomt dat periodiek nieuwe onderhandelingen nodig zijn over de verdeling van de lusten en de lasten. Zonder dergelijke afspraken komt er vroeg of laat onnodig veel spanning op het stelsel. Hiermee komen we aan bij de verwachtingen voor het Nederlandse pensioenstelsel. Het is nodig de uitgangspunten van ons defined benefit systeem opnieuw te toetsen. De voordelen voor individu en samenleving moeten opnieuw over het voetlicht worden gebracht. Daarnaast is het wenselijk de financile opzet van de fondsen tegen het licht te houden. Tot aan jaren 90 van de vorige eeuw stond het besturen van een pensioenfonds in het teken van prudentie. De financiering werd aan de voorzichtige kant ingezet waardoor pensioenfondsen konden terugvallen op omvangrijke impliciete reserves. Vervolgens kwam de aandelenmarkt in de jaren 90 in een langdurige hausse terecht en ontstond de indruk van een free lunch. Pensioenrechten werden verruimd en gelijktijdig werden premies verlaagd tot onder kostendekkend niveau. Daarmee werd het geld in feite twee keer uitgegeven: een omdraaiing van de voorzichtige pensioenlogica uit de periode daarvoor. Bovendien liet de rente een trendmatige daling zien waardoor de impliciete buffers eveneens werden opgegeten. Het principe dat pensioenfondsen in aandelen en andere zakelijke waarden beleggen is prima. Het aanbod van risicodragend kapitaal is immers stimulerend voor de economische groei en de eventueel hogere rendementen kunnen worden gebruikt om buffers op te bouwen en de pensioenen te koppelen aan prijzen of lonen. Maar de huidige en de vorige pensioencrisis laten zien dat de bijbehorende risicos niet moeten worden onderschat. Laten we bijvoorbeeld eens kijken naar de aandelenmarkten. De toonaangevende MSCI Wereldaandelenindex bestaat eind dit jaar precies 40 jaar. Sinds de start heeft deze index 4 keer een tuimeling meegemaakt die groter is dan de 25%-daling waar het FTK op is gestoeld. Twee van deze gebeurtenissen vielen in de afgelopen 7 jaar. De grootste daling van bijna 44% als gevolg van de kredietcrisis hebben we net achter de rug. Bij het uiteenspatten van de internetbubble gingen de koersen zon 30% omlaag. Verder was het olie-embargo van OPEC in oktober 1973 aanleiding tot forse koersdaling van 39% en bracht de eerste Golfoorlog een schokgolf teweeg op de beurzen van minus 26%. Aangezien het FTK uitgaat van een zekerheidsmaatstaf van 97,5% zou een daling van meer dan 25% maar n keer in de afgelopen 40 jaar mogen zijn opgetreden. Dit is denk ik aanleiding om nog eens goed te kijken naar de toereikendheid van de parameters in het FTK, maar ook naar de vraag of er niet teveel open risicos zitten in de financiering van onze pensioenen. Naast een realistische inschatting is het zaak dat pensioenfondsen de risicos kunnen dragen. Het is recentelijk duidelijk geworden dat sturing via premieaanpassingen en beperking van indexatietoekenning niet onder alle omstandigheden voldoende is om grote schommelingen in de dekkingsgraad op te vangen. Dit kan betekenen dat we structureel hogere buffers moeten gaan nastreven bijvoorbeeld door de overrendementen op de beleggingen veel meer te reserveren voor het opvangen van tegenvallers. Ook is mogelijk dat pensioenfondsbalansen evenwichtiger worden gemaakt. [Sheet 8] Hiertoe staan in beginsel twee wegen open. Meer matching tussen activa en passiva kan immers lopen via aanpassing van de beleggingen of van de verplichtingen. Bij het eerste worden risicos via de kapitaalmarkt overgedragen; bij het tweede gaat het om de mogelijkheid om meer risicos - zowel plus als min  expliciet bij de deelnemers weg te leggen. Een dergelijke verschuiving, waarbij de nadruk komt te liggen op een goede informatievoorziening aan de deelnemers, is overigens alleen voor jongeren aantrekkelijk. Ouderen zijn gebaat bij een stabiel en voorspelbaar pensioenresultaat. Laat ik eindigen met de constatering dat het Nederlandse pensioenstelsel zelfs na de recente ontwikkelingen nog altijd tot de beste in de wereld behoort. De intrinsieke waarde die het stelsel biedt wordt de komende tijd weer duidelijk als alle belanghebbenden gezamenlijk zorgdragen voor de benodigde herstelwerkzaamheden. Dit is dan niet in de vorm van een benefietvoorstelling zoals bij de Franse Opera, maar in de kern is er ook niet veel verschil. Een ieder zal zijn steentje moeten bijdragen om het herstel te realiseren. Deze collectieve aanpak is een van de kernwaarden van het Nederlandse stelsel: veel partijen zijn betrokken bij het pensioendebat en even zoveel voelen zich verantwoordelijk om tot een goed resultaat te komen. Nadat het herstelproces is afgerond ben ik er zeker van dat onze oudedagsvoorziening nog steviger dan voorheen is gefundeerd in onze samenleving. Waarbij de financile zorg voor ouderen optimaal gepaard gaat met het nemen van risicos door pensioenfondsen. Daarbij past mijn inziens dan wel weer meer aandacht voor prudentie in de financile opzet van die fondsen. De kredietcrisis heeft ons allen weer met beide voeten op de grond gezet, wat dat betreft heeft inderdaad elk nadeel zijn voordeel. Title: Speech directeur Brouwer 'Supervisory issues in a changing financial landscape'
text: Speech directeur Brouwer 'Supervisory issues in a changing financial landscape' Speech Datum 14 mei 2009 Tijd 14:35 uur Lokatie Studentensymposium aan de Universiteit Tilburg Spreker Drs. H. Brouwer, directeur van de Nederlandsche Bank I am glad to be here, speaking in front of this student audience. As students, you have the 'privilege' of being on the sidelines during the most severe financial crisis in decades. My guess is that most of you do not face substantial downside risks in terms of investments. Besides, I suppose the only credit related issue that is of real interest to you is the student credit facility IBG (Informatie Beheer Groep) in Groningen. However, you certainly benefit from the positive side: you get to witness the best possible test of economic and financial theory in real life. This seminar, titled A new financial world will surely give you an opportunity to disentangle and understand the crisis from different points of view. In my contribution, I will give you some supervisory insights in the period before, during and after the crisis. This approach is useful, because before we can envision a new financial world, we should determine what went wrong in the old one. First of all, I will explain my view on how the initial problems concentrated in the subprime market ended in a worldwide crisis. Second, I will focus on the toolkit that governments and policymakers used during the crisis. And finally, I will demonstrate the main challenges DNB faces as a prudential supervisor. Let me start with an old cliche, that history is repeating itself. Proof can be seen in our own past with the 17th centurys tulip mania. The more expensive the tulip bulbs became, the more people viewed them as smart investments. At the peak of the tulip mania, tulip bulbs sold for more than 10 times the annual income of a skilled craftsman. All good things come to an end: in 1637, the bubble burst and the price of a tulip bulb ended lower than the price of a common onion. Only recently, at the start of the current decade, the dotcom bubble burst. An important common feature of bubble markets is that they are characterized by periods of optimism and hence too much credit. Predictably, we have also observed these features in the build-up to the crisis. On the one hand, the supply of credit was too large. We had years with low interest rates. To increase investment returns and spread risks, new financial products were invented. The underlying idea was to increase leverage: achieve maximum turnover with minimum equity. In addition, over the years, banks shifted their business model away from 'originate to hold' to the more profitable 'originate to distribute'. Financial products sold by a bank were packaged and sold on to any investor willing to pay, the so-called securitization of assets. In principle, the idea of securitization is to spread risks over more parties. However, securitization also stimulated banks to take more risks. As these activities were often off-balance sheet, the banks real leverage could be further increased. On the other hand, credit demand increased too. In the US, the demand for credit exploded in the past decade, with seven credit cards per person being the rule rather than the exception. We have also seen this in the Netherlands where household debt and its associated risks have risen. For example, while so-called 'interest only' mortgages were introduced as recently as in the mid-nineties, by 2008 about 40% of all contracts were financed by interest only mortgages. And another 30% of all mortgages had a kind of hybrid structure, where at least part of the debt is financed by an interest only mortgage. What is really worrying is that roughly 45% of the borrowers do not realise that they may still have debt at maturity. Both supply and demand of credit grew rapidly, thus reinforcing each other as in many other bubbles. Myopic behaviour on both the supply and the demand side led to an excessively low risk premium. What was unique, however, was the trigger of the subsequent downturn. The initial losses on the subprime market were quite small on a world scale. Historically this would not have seemed like an immediate problem as not every bubble collapse results in a crisis. So, what went wrong? My answer is that risks did not end up with those who were most capable of bearing them, but with those who were keenest to take them on. When the initial problems arose, financial institutions and markets were so interconnected that the collapse of just a small part of the economy did ultimately trigger a systemic crisis. I think the main underlying cause lies in the shortcomings in the risk management of financial institutions. Generally speaking, risk management did not keep pace with financial innovations. Risk management proved to be inadequate in several aspects. For instance, banks used inadequate measures to contain leverage and maturity mismatches on their balance sheets. In addition, ill-designed compensation schemes gave the wrong incentives. Specifically, these schemes did not fully take into account all the risks. In particular traders had incentives to take risks beyond the radar screen of bank managers. In the subsequent crisis, however, these risks became painfully clear. As Warren Buffet puts it: only when the tide goes out you do discover who has been swimming naked. Another important way risk management was inadequate is probably of the most interest to you as econometricians. I think that financial institutions trusted too much in the existing risk models without a critical evaluation of the underlying assumptions. For example, most models assume a normal distribution. However, in the financial sector, risk is often characterized by fat tails. To illustrate, according to a normal distribution, a 7% fall in stocks on one day happens only once in 300.000 years. In reality, this has happened 48 times in the past 100 years! I would say that in risk management 'the devil is in the tail'. Additionally, in times of crisis, correlations between events tend to go to 100%. Therefore, a model that uses correlations that have been observed in 'normal' times tends to underestimate tailrisks. And let me give a final example to illustrate that anyone can fall into the trap of over-reliance on models. In 1998, the hedge fund 'Long Term Capital Management' went bankrupt, almost dragging down the financial system. Founders of this hedge fund were- among others- Robert Merton and Myron Scholes. These two economists had just won the Nobel Price in economics. As I have already argued, the initial write-downs on the US subprime market triggered a crisis on a global scale. Clearly, problems in the financial sector were like a snowball rolling downhill, growing with every twist and turn. Then, in no time at all, the snowball grew to encompass nearly all other economic actors. As a result, the initial snow flake leads to a number of different phases in the crisis. Policymakers- in the Netherlands too- reacted accordingly, making use of the toolkit of instruments at their disposal. The common element among these instruments is that they are focused on restoring confidence in the financial sector. Here, I will briefly discuss the four main categories of financial sector rescue/support measures taken thus far: (i) the guarantee of deposits (ii) the guarantee of debt (iii) the guarantee of distressed assets and (iv) the capital injections. The first form of general support from most authorities was raising the deposit guarantee scheme. Small depositors constitute the cornerstone of trust in the financial system. A modern economy does not work without people having trust in their banking system. Besides, small depositors are not capable of monitoring banks. In order to maintain this trust, at least part of their money should be guaranteed. Trust is also very important for other bank debt issuance. In line with European agreements, Dutch authorities guaranteed newly issued banking debt in the beginning of October. The goal was to secure the functioning of the financial system. Third, back-up facilities were installed to partially cover the risks of banks' securitized portfolios. In public discussions and the media it is often said that this facility is specifically meant for toxic assets. For me, toxic means that debt is doomed not to be paid back. Subprime mortgages are a good example in this respect. However, most back-up facilities are meant for distressed assets. These assets suffer from a lack of market liquidity rather than from underlying problems, a case in point being the Alt-A mortgage portfolio of ING in the US. Fourth, governments aimed to maintain the solvency ratios of financial institutions at the levels deemed necessary by the supervisors. In October, the State fully acquired the Dutch share of Fortis, including ABN AMRO. In addition, the government has committed itself to make capital available to each financial enterprise in the Netherlands that is fundamentally sound and viable. EUR 20 billion was immediately available. As of today, three institutions, Aegon, ING and SNS, have made use of this facility. So, the point that I would like to make here is that authorities focused on more than one instrument to be most effective. The variability inherent in the toolbox of all responsible authorities has been on display. Dutch authorities are no exception. Especially the combination of capital injections and guarantees of distressed assets has been essential. In that case, both sides of the balance sheet are strengthened. I have discussed the period up to the crisis and our crisis management tools. The question remains how we can prevent such crises in the future and make our financial system more resilient. I will now address some important challenges we face as a supervisor. First of all, the crisis demonstrates that the amount of loss-absorbing capital of banks was too low. To save the functioning of the banking system, governments had to step in on a global scale. The best way to prevent this in the future would be to raise capital standards. An immediate increase in capital requirements would however worsen the economic downturn. The regulatory framework for banks implemented in 2008, Basel II, offers a good starting position to reconsider capital requirements. In this framework, capital requirements are risk oriented. That is, banks with higher risks have to pay the price by holding more capital. However, risk-weightings have become increasingly subtle and complex, to the point that banks may comply fully with the risk-weighted capital requirements and yet still be highly leveraged. Therefore, we would like to have a simple leverage ratio as an additional measure. Such a simple ratio would counterbalance the sophisticated and complex risk-based supervisory framework. In addition, banks need to perform better stress tests that are forward looking and show the specific weaknesses for banks in extreme scenarios, allowing banks to anticipate possible future events. A second important challenge for supervisors is to take better account of macro developments with systemic consequences in an institutions supervision. Systemic risks were underestimated and insufficiently converted into regulatory requirements at the micro level. That is, financial institutions were examined separately rather than as part of a complex system. Recent European initiatives are aimed at incorporating systemic effects by diminishing procyclicality in banking. Procyclicality is the possibility that regulatory actions amplify the economic cycle. The main goal is to realise a system in which buffers are built up in good times in order to strengthen resistance to economic downturns. Valuation of the bank balance sheet as a whole is also an important issue. I think that fair value accounting is the best method we have, as it reveals the true financial position of a bank. At the same time we have seen that, in times of crisis, fair value accounting can work procyclically, sometimes forcing institutions to sell assets in illiquid markets. Policymakers at the international level have an important task in making this accounting method less procyclical. What the crisis also made clear is that all these challenges are not restricted to national boundaries. In other words, we need to reconsider the scale of supervision. In the past decade, cross-border banking has strongly increased. In 2004, more than half of M&A activity in Europe was across national borders. In contrast, supervision focused too much on the national level. Therefore, supervisors need to address issues of cooperation. One advantage of the crisis is that it has created a political willingness to implement some necessary changes. In Europe, a high level expert group chaired by Mr. Jaques de Larosiere, former Managing Director of the IMF, has advised on the organisation of financial supervision. Among his main recommendations is that European supervisory practices need to be harmonised. In addition, colleges of supervisors of cross border groups need more bite. Redefining the scope of supervision is another important challenge. The G20 recently asked for adequate supervision for all financial institutions, specifically aiming at hedge funds. Insight into and monitoring of this sector currently run only via their interactions with institutions which are subject to direct supervision. It seems wise to consider whether unregulated institutions should fall under a more direct form of supervision. However, we cannot expect to work miracles and achieve absolute safety by only widening the scope of supervision and simply regulating more types of institutions. In the end, there will always be new unregulated entities where risks will concentrate. As a supervisor, we should set the regulatory framework and corresponding principles ex ante, not an exhaustive list of dos and donts. I discussed with you some supervisory insights from before, during and after the crisis. I argued that problems on the subprime market were simply the trigger. Weak risk management was the underlying weakness that escalated the initial bubble to a global crisis. During the crisis authorities- including the Dutch- deployed their whole toolkit of instruments to be most effective. In addition to crisis management, it is of vital importance for supervisors to focus on the prevention of future crises. More specifically, I addressed some important challenges in the near future, ranging from higher capital to better micro and macro risk management and international cooperation. To conclude, the aim for supervisors is that risks should be correctly priced and that the price of risk be paid by those earning the rewards for risk. We are not tasked with the goal of avoiding bubbles at all costs. However, what we do want to avoid in future financial markets is that a bursting bubble triggers a systemic crisis on this scale. I hope that these supervisory insights sharpen your vision and that this financial crisis will help us and you to prevent such crises in the future.

Title: Speech directeur Hoogduin 'Payment innovation in a European landscape'
text: Speech directeur Hoogduin 'Payment innovation in a European landscape' Speech Datum 26 mei 2009 Tijd 09:00 uur Lokatie DNB-ECB conference Retail payments: integration and innovation, Frankfurt Spreker Prof. dr. L.H. Hoogduin, directeur van de Nederlandsche Bank Ladies and gentlemen, It is a great pleasure to welcome you all on the second day of the joint DNB-ECB-conference on retail payments. I hope you all enjoyed yesterdays program about the integration of the retail payments markets. Today, we will focus on the second theme of this conference: payment innovations. There are three points I would like to make: Payment innovations are important for social welfare, Successful adoption of a payment innovation depends on bringing both buyers and sellers on board, and Payment innovators inEurope: Please join forces! Let me introduce my first message 'payment innovations are important for social welfare' by sharing some of my own payment experiences with you. Last month I bought a car. I paid for it by means of a so-called 'urgent payment', using Internet banking from home. With just a few simple mouse clicks I transferred my money to the account of my car dealer. Paying for my very first car was a completely different experience. Back then you had to go to your bank for an urgent payment. The payment was costly, in terms of both time and money. To begin with I had to go to the bank in person. And secondly, the fee was considerable, because it included a clerks labour costs. Many car buyers probably opted for cash in order to avoid such a fee, but I preferred the safety of an urgent payment. This personal experience illustrates some of the social benefits of payment innovations for society: they make life easier and safer for consumers and retailers and they reduce payment costs. In addition, they also enhance economic welfare by stimulating trade. Not only can money be transferred much faster, consumers can also make unplanned purchase decisions using payment cards or effect cross-border purchases using online payment methods. In general, innovations are one of the key driving forces behind economic growth. During the past decades many economists have studied the relationship between innovation, productivity growth and economic welfare. They have found that productivity growth leads to more economic welfare and that innovation is one of the driving forces behind productivity growth. Estimated elasticities between expenditures on R&D and productivity growth at the firm level indicate that 1% more expenditure on R&D leads to 0.1 to 0.2% additional productivity growth. That sounds like a rather good investment to me. Investing in innovation in payments also leads to productivity gains. Cost studies, such as those conducted byDNBor the one presented yesterday by Olaf Gresvik forNorway, show that electronic payments are cheaper than paper-based payments. Several years ago,DNBcalculated the costs saved by substituting payment cards for cash. The results revealed that the increased use of payment cards reduced the costs of retail payments by 6% between 1990 and 2004. The development of electronic payment instruments has been driven by several factors, a crucial one being the rapid development of IT in the second half of the 20th century, which paved the way for electronic payment instruments for both point-of-sale payments and remote payments. Credit cards and debit cards were introduced for payments in shops, gas stations, hotels and restaurants. Now mobile and contactless payments are starting to take off at points of sale. For regular remote payments, such as rent or utility payments, electronic payment methods were introduced which included direct debits and electronic credit transfers. In theNetherlands, these have quite successfully replaced paper-based payments. The advent of electronic credit transfers brings me to a second important factor leading to payment innovation, the Internet. The Internet has drastically changed the way consumers and businesses buy, and pay for, goods and services. Within a decade or so, transferring money via Internet banking has become common practice in many countries. Moreover, on-line applications, such as electronic billing, are now a reality in some countries and underway in many others. The Internet has also led to the advent of an entirely new sales channel for sellers, allowing them to sell their goods and services to people all over the world. This new on-line sales channel has stimulated the development of new payment instruments. In theNetherlands, the Internet payment solution iDEAL has provided consumers and web retailers with a safe and user-friendly way of using Internet banking for their on-line purchases in web shops, because consumers are directly linked to the on-line banking website of their own bank. Other countries likeGermanyandAustriahave their own Internet payment solutions. A global Internet payment solution was introduced earlier by Paypal. All these payment innovations have in some way contributed to the social welfare of buyers and sellers. They have led to cost savings, they have brought buyers and sellers more user-friendly payment instruments, they have increased safety and, last but not least, they have stimulated trade. We dont know yet whether these most recent innovations will be successful. But lets look at some past successes to see what made them so attractive in the eyes of both buyers and sellers and try to learn from them. This brings me to my second message: Successful adoption of a payment innovation depends on bringing both buyers and sellers on board. Several research papers in the conference program deal with adoption issues in payments. They focus on adoption mechanisms in two-sided markets, that is markets with two demand sides, in which both buyers and sellers are required to pay with a particular payment instrument. An important result from this research field is that the use of payment instruments on one side of the market correlates positively with acceptance on the other side. That means that payment instruments should have features which make them attractive to both consumers and retailers. Payment instruments which score well on the following four aspects, namely added value, simplicity, safety and pricing, by comparison to existing payment instruments, stand a good chance of being used on a large scale. Lets start by looking at the first factor: added value. Internet banking has enabled consumers to make payments or use other banking services from behind a computer anywhere in the world, 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. That is highly convenient, especially for people who lack the time or are unable to visit their bank during regular opening hours. Payment cards are used widely because people no longer need to worry whether they are carrying enough cash to buy what they want. This feature is attractive to both consumers, and retailers. Secondly, simplicity is one of the keys to a successful adoption. New payment instruments should be easy to obtain, install and use, since most consumers and retailers dont want to spend much time learning how to use them. Nor are they keen to install complicated hardware and software. In this respect, payment service providers could perhaps pay more attention to the needs of small enterprises. In theNetherlands, card acceptance used to be fairly low among small retailers, even when costs went down. Apparently, small retailers found card acceptance too cumbersome, and got lost in the wilderness of offers from banks, telecom companies and terminal suppliers. In order to increase card acceptance, banks, telecom companies and payment service providers have developed smart debit card packages, tailored specifically to small retailers. These packages provide low-cost all-in-one solutions, including a contract for a payment terminal, a broadband Internet connection, and often a contract with an acquiring bank as well. Some consumers may feel insecure about their ability to use a new payment instrument. Take, for instance, the less-educated, the elderly and people with a physical disability. As a central banker, responsible for the accessibility of the payment system, I would like to ask payment innovators to think of these groups of people when developing new payment instruments. This is especially important if, eventually, all consumers and retailers are compelled to use the new payment instrument because banks no longer support the old one. Then it is key that the new payment instrument can be used by every buyer or seller, or in other words, every one of us. Investing time and money to develop a payment instrument that is suitable for everyone is not only preferable from a moral point of view, but from a commercial one as well. Fewer adjustments may be needed afterwards if innovators take the needs of vulnerable groups into account at an early stage of development. The period during which banks and businesses incur double costs for supporting both the legacy and the new payment infrastructure could then be shortened considerably. Another important adoption issue concerns safety. The adoption of a payment innovation will depend on how buyers and sellers perceive its level of safety compared to existing payment instruments. Therefore, I highly appreciate the investment made by payment innovators and sellers to enhance the safety of payment cards and Internet banking. In theNetherlands, payment card fraud at the point of sale and ATMs has increased in recent years. Retailers have now agreed with banks to switch to the safer EMV payment technology faster than was originally planned. I realise it may be challenging to offer payment instruments that are both safe and easy to use and to strike the right balance between stricter safety measures and user-friendliness. On the one hand, one doesnt wish to scare off buyers and sellers with complicated and costly safety measures. On the other, however, buyers and sellers are sometimes the weakest link in the payment chain and one would like to see them protect themselves more adequately against criminals. It is important that banks continue to invest in safety and in consumer information about safe usage, so that both consumers and retailers can make safe and efficient payment choices. A final issue I would like to raise concerns payment fees. I know this is a very delicate topic.In order to provide an incentive for both buyers and sellers to use a new payment instrument, banks may need to charge them both user-friendly fees. You may wonder what I mean by user-friendly fees. I believe user-friendly fees should reflect the differences in costs of the different payment instruments for both buyers and sellers. That way, both buyers and sellers will benefit financially from adopting a cost-effective innovation, and both will be stimulated to use it. Let me elaborate. In general, payment innovations enhance cost efficiency, which implies that the costs of a payment, based on the innovation, are lower than the costs of a payment made through an existing instrument. Pricing payment instruments in a way that reflects differences in costs will ensure that a new payment instrument is attractive to buyers and sellers alike. If the new payment instrument is always the cheapest available to both buyers and sellers, they will both be stimulated to use or accept it any time, and the adoption of the new payment instrument may run smoothly and rapidly. Research among Dutch consumers and retailers has shown that if Dutch consumers have to pay for a payment instrument, they will often opt for an alternative that is free of charge, even if they appreciate the features of the priced payment instrument more. Moreover, we have found that lowering debit card charges leads to a higher acceptance rate of debit cards, a continuing increase in the number of debit card payments and a higher level of cost efficiency. It may be challenging for banks to stimulate the adoption of a payment instrument in this way.In retail payments, buyers rarely pay for their payment behaviour; it is the sellers which shoulder the bulk of the costs. So, at first sight, buyers may think they are worse off if they have to start paying for their payments. However, eventually they may actually be better off. Transparent pricing, with the payment innovation representing the cheapest payment instrument, provides both buyers and sellers with incentives to adjust their payment and acceptance behaviour and reduces payment costs for society. In the end, buyers will benefit from these social cost savings through lower consumer prices. Now that we have discussed the conditions which may determine whether an innovation will be adopted on a large scale or not, I would like to look ahead and think about innovation in the future. My third and last message is addressed to payment innovators active inEurope: Please join forces! Innovation is a creative process. It can take quite a while before the final specifications of a payment innovation have crystallised. Waiting until every country or bank is ready for innovation may hold up its development for years. This may prove harmful to the innovation, because it may turn out to be past its sell-by date before it is even born. Therefore, I would like to encourage communities with ideas for something new to start developing, to experiment, to learn and to share their experiences with their European counterparts. This can be done in a competitive environment. I would be in favour of having leading players inEuropedevelop open standards together and welcome other interested players to join this initiative when they are ready. In theNetherlands, three banks took such an approach when developing iDEAL, the Dutch e-payment solution. Other banks joined in at a later stage. iDEAL has become a great success. I fully support standardisation at the European level. Too many variations in one basic type of payment innovation cannot be efficient and could cause all of them to fail. I realise that developing new payment innovations in a European context will be much more challenging than it used to be in national markets. Payment habits differ considerably among countries. In some countries, people may be ready for a payment innovation, whereas elsewhere people may actually be quite content with the existing options. In addition, coordinating the development and introduction of an innovation has become much more complex, because of the increased number of parties involved. Despite the complexity, the European Payments Council successfully managed to develop the standards for the SEPA credit transfer and the SEPA direct debit, and to draw up the SEPA cards framework. The next, and perhaps even bigger, challenge is to work on future European payment solutions such as e-payments and mobile payments. Each country has its own ideas and wishes as to the best specifications for a payment instrument. Finding compromises acceptable to all countries that could form the basis for a European payment solution is challenging and time-consuming. To be honest, this is a reason for concern. But perhaps it is even more of a concern to the banking community itself. Buyers and sellers inEuropemay not wait patiently for a European payment solution developed by the banking community. If non-bank payment service providers or global players in payments come up with a suitable payment solution first, this solution might be chosen rather than one developed by the European banking community. Incidentally, this solution may be equally beneficial from a social welfare point of view, provided that sound standards are maintained for safety and reliability. Public authorities, including central banks support payment innovation. The best way of doing so is by providing a regulatory framework that ensures safety and gives plenty of opportunities for new initiatives. Ladies and gentlemen, I am coming to the end of my speech. Payment innovations are highly important. I have much faith in the innovative power of banks, card associations and payment service providers. And I am confident that they, too, will come up with new payment innovations and instruments in the future. Payment innovators, keep in mind that for a successful adoption, you will have to focus on the future needs of both European buyers and sellers. I fully understand that innovating in a European landscape presents quite a challenge. But I trust that we will see new initiatives flourish in our market in the future. I thank you all very much for your attention and I wish you a pleasant and fruitful second conference day.

Title: Speech by director Hoogduin 'More efficient and safer debit card payments in Europe'
