text: Speech by director Hoogduin 'More efficient and safer debit card payments in Europe' Speech Date: May 27, 2009 Time: 10:30 a.m. Location On the occasion of the signing of the 'Further Agreement on the Payment Covenant', Amsterdam Speaker Prof.dr. L.H. Hoogduin, Director of the Dutch Central Bank Today is a historic day in the Dutch payment system. With the agreement to be signed soon, we are taking a big step towards debit cards on a European market. In the longer term, I am convinced that debit card payments in SEPA will be even more efficient and secure than is already the case. In the Netherlands, we now have one brand for debit cards in stores. In the integrated European payments market, there will be more. In the Netherlands, we now have about ten players from which retailers can purchase their debit card services. On the European market, this will be a multiple. With nearly 1.8 billion debit card payments in 2008, the Dutch are a pretty tough people. But we are still a relatively small player in Europe. Across the EU, around 17 billion debit cards were used in 2008, currently with mainly local brands in protected markets. But soon with international, widely accepted brands. In SEPA, European banks no longer have to rely on purely national processors, but can also have their currently national payment transactions processed in other countries. That's when economies of scale become possible. In combination with the increased market forces and the better breeding ground for innovations, all parties in the European payments market will ultimately benefit. In the long run, yes. In the last century, a British economist quoted more often said: 'in the long run we're all dead'. Here, too, the costs come before the benefit. 'What's in it for us now?', we want to know. SEPA is a logical follow-up to the euro. Further European integration will increase the efficiency of the European payment system. But how good is it for the Netherlands? The current Dutch payment system is already well and efficiently regulated. Also compared to other countries. It is logical that market parties are concerned that we may lose the efficiency achieved by the Dutch payment system. We must therefore carefully move towards payment on a European basis. These concerns of consumers and businesses have been addressed in the Social Dialogue on the Payment System. Such as the concerns about the retention of the Transfer Service. A service that most other countries don't know. The Dutch banks have a solution to be able to continue to offer this service in SEPA. Another example is the concern about the security of a European debt collection. Here, too, banks have found solutions to limit the risks after consultation with the Consumers' Association. Concerns have also been expressed about loss of efficiency in debit card transactions, with fewer choices and higher rates. Banks and point-of-sale institutions have been discussing this for almost a year now. The agreement did not come naturally. It was even stuck for a while. At the beginning of this year, DNB was asked to mediate. Given the expected benefits, it is definitely worth it for us to try to pull it loose. That wasn't easy. But all the greater is the satisfaction of the agreement to be ratified today. It is a special agreement. It is unique that stakeholders are talking to each other in this way to make payment transactions more efficient and safer for society. In that respect, the Dutch model can serve as an example for other countries that are switching to SEPA. With such a drastic transition, it is even more true that market parties can do a number of things better together. It is a special agreement because it will help shape the European payment market from the Netherlands. While retaining existing ones and with the prospect of much more efficiency. Pin, pin, pin. For a while, that was the slogan to promote debit cards. First for large amounts as a substitute for payment cheques. When they were off the market, as a safe substitute for the large cash payments. And now we have a campaign called 'small amount of debit cards allowed'. Debit cards are now also used as a substitute for small cash payments. Because it is precisely there that a lot of efficiency can still be achieved. The road to a 'cashless society' seems long to me. I don't think we'll get there either. What is clear is that it is becoming more and more 'less cash'. This agreement contains the agreement that point-of-sale institutions and banks will develop plans in the coming years for the further promotion of debit card payments in SEPA as well. Debit cards must also remain secure. The criminals grow along with the efficiency. For criminals, debit card fraud is also an interesting substitute for counterfeiting and theft of cash. Skimming causes a lot of problems for consumers, retailers and banks. It can undermine confidence in electronic payments. It is not for nothing that security campaigns are being conducted more and more often. It is therefore gratifying that this agreement will accelerate the use of much safer chip technology. I would like to offer my sincere congratulations to the banks and the Chamber as a whole. But I would also like to call on them immediately after the champagne to get to work on the agreements. All the smoother and faster the Netherlands will be able to switch to European payments. It is possible that in five years' time - when SEPA is already well under way - we will also be able to reap the first fruits of the larger European payments market.
text_original: Speech directeur Hoogduin 'Efficinter en veiliger pinnen in Europa' Speech Datum 27 mei 2009 Tijd 10:30 uur Lokatie Ter gelegenheid van de ondertekening 'Nadere Overeenkomst bij Convenant betalingsverkeer', Amsterdam Spreker Prof.dr. L.H. Hoogduin, directeur van de Nederlandsche Bank Vandaag is een historische dag in het Nederlandse betalingsverkeer. Met het zo direct te ondertekenen akkoord zetten we een flinke stap naar pinnen op een Europese markt. Pinnen in SEPA zal naar mijn overtuiging op langere termijn nog efficinter en veiliger zal zijn dan nu al het geval is. In Nederland hebben we nu n merk voor het pinnen in de winkels. Op de gentegreerde Europese betaalmarkt zullen dat er meer zijn. In Nederland hebben we nu zon tien spelers waarvan de winkeliers hun pindiensten kunnen afnemen. Op de Europese markt zal dat een veelvoud zijn. Met bijna 1,8 miljard pinbetalingen in 2008 zijn de Nederlanders een behoorlijk pinnig volkje. Maar Europees zijn we toch een relatief kleine speler. In de hele EU werd in 2008 ongeveer 17 miljard keer gepind, Nu nog met voornamelijk lokale merken in afgeschermde markten. Maar straks met internationale, breed geaccepteerde merken. Europese banken zijn in SEPA niet langer aangewezen op de puur nationale processors, maar kunnen hun nu nog nationale betalingsverkeer ook in andere landen laten verwerken. Dn worden schaalvoordelen mogelijk. In combinatie met de verhoogde marktwerking en de betere voedingsbodem voor innovaties gaan uiteindelijk alle partijen van de Europese betaalmarkt profiteren. Op lange termijn dat wel. Een recent weer wat vaker aangehaalde Britse econoom zei in de vorige eeuw al eens: 'in the long run were all dead'. De kosten gaan ook hier voor de baet uit. 'Whats in it for us now?', willen we weten. SEPA is een logisch vervolg op de euro. Verdere Europese integratie zal de efficintie van het Europese betalingsverkeer verhogen. Maar hoe goed is het voor Nederland? Het huidige Nederlandse betalingsverkeer is al goed en efficint geregeld. Ook in vergelijking met andere landen. Logisch dat marktpartijen bezorgd zijn dat we de bereikte efficintie van het Nederlandse betalingsverkeer kunnen verliezen. We moeten dan ook zorgvuldig overgaan naar betalen op Europese leest. In het Maatschappelijk Overleg Betalingsverkeer zijn die zorgen van consumenten en bedrijven geadresseerd. Zoals de zorgen over het behoud van de Overstapservice. Een service die de meeste andere landen niet kennen. De Nederlandse banken hebben een oplossing om die service ook in SEPA aan te kunnen blijven bieden. Ander voorbeeld is de zorg over de veiligheid van een Europese incasso. Ook hier hebben banken na overleg met de Consumentenbond oplossingen gevonden om de risicos te beperken. Ook zijn de zorgen geuit over verlies van efficintie in het pinverkeer, met minder keuzes en hogere tarieven. Hierover waren banken en toonbankinstellingen nu bijna een jaar in gesprek. Het akkoord kwam er dan ook niet vanzelf. Het zat zelfs even vast. Begin van dit jaar werd DNB gevraagd te bemiddelen. Gezien de verwachte voordelen, voor ons alleszins de moeite waard te proberen het los te trekken. Dat was niet eenvoudig. Maar des te groter is de voldoening van het vandaag te bekrachtigen akkoord. Het is een bijzonder akkoord. Het is uniek dat stakeholders zo met elkaar in gesprek zijn om betalingsverkeer maatschappelijk efficinter en veiliger te maken. Wat dat betreft kan het Nederlandse model best als voorbeeld dienen voor andere landen die overgaan naar SEPA. Bij zon ingrijpende overgang geldt nog meer dat marktpartijen een aantal zaken beter samen kunnen doen. Het is een bijzonder akkoord omdat het gaat meehelpen die Europese betaalmarkt vanuit Nederland gestalte te geven. Mt behoud van bestaande en met uitzicht op veel meer efficintie. Pin, pin, pin. Dat was een tijd de slagzin om pinnen te promoten. Eerst voor grote bedragen als substituut voor betaalcheques. Toen die van de markt waren, als veilig substituut voor de grote contante betalingen. En nu hebben we als campagne  klein bedrag pinnen mag. Pinnen nu ook als substituut voor de kleine contante betalingen. Want juist dr is nog veel efficintie te behalen. De weg naar een 'cashless society' lijkt me lang. Ik denk ook niet dat we daar uitkomen. Duidelijk is wel dat het steeds meer less cash wordt. Dit akkoord bevat de afspraak dat toonbankinstellingen en de banken de komende jaren plannen uitwerken voor het ook in SEPA verder promoten van het pinnen. Pinnen moet ook veilig blijven. De criminelen groeien mee in de efficintie. Voor criminelen is pinpasfraude ook een interessant substituut voor namaak en diefstal van contant geld. Skimmen geeft consument, winkelier en bank veel problemen. Het kan het vertrouwen in het elektronisch betalen ondermijnen. Niet voor niets worden steeds vaker veiligheidscampagnes gevoerd. Het is dan ook verheugend dat dit akkoord het gebruik van veel veiliger chiptechnologie gaat versnellen. Ik wil de banken en de gezamenlijke van deze plaats hartelijk feliciteren met dit bereikte resultaat. Maar ik wil ze ook meteen oproepen na de champagne direct aan de slag te gaan om de afspraken te verwezenlijken. Des te soepeler en sneller kan Nederland dan over naar Europees betalen. Mogelijk kunnen we over vijf jaar - als SEPA al aardig op stoom is - ook al de eerste vruchten plukken van de grotere Europese betaalmarkt.

Title: Speech directeur Brouwer 'Macroprudential supervision: from concept to practice'
text: Speech directeur Brouwer 'Macroprudential supervision: from concept to practice' Speech Datum 4 september 2009 Tijd 09:08 uur Lokatie 28th Suerf Colloquium, Utrecht Spreker Drs. H. Brouwer, directeur van de Nederlandsche Bank I'm of course delighted to be here at this 28th Suerf Colloquium. The interaction between academics and practitioners is now more important than ever. As the darkest clouds over the economy seem to be lifting, and the first sunbeams are breaking through, we have to make important decisions about the future design of the financial landscape. There are many questions and uncertainties about the specific characteristics of the new financial system. Not in the least because of the massive public interventions that have taken place. However, we all agree about one thing. The new financial system has to become more stable. Hence, this colloquium on 'The quest for stability' could not be more topica. As an executive board member of the Dutch central bank, I have covered the central banking part of the institution for many years, before taking up responsibility for banking supervision at the start of this year. Hence, I should be in a good position to reflect today on the interface between these two areas. The place where macro and micro come together. That is, the so-called macroprudential approach. A rather new and difficult term, which even my up-to-date Microsoft spell checker still does not recognize. So in order to avoid confusion, I will first clarify this concept a bit more, before going into its practical implications. What is the macroprudential approach The word 'macroprudential0 is today on everyones lips. Yet, the concept remains somewhat ambiguous. What do we mean when we say that we need a macroprudential approach? What is the difference with microprudential supervision? And what are the benefits of macroprudential supervision and regulation? Although it is easy to extend this list of questions, it is not always easy to answer them. First, I have to point out that, although the current financial crisis has illustrated the importance of macroprudential supervision, the concept itself dates back to much earlier. The Bank for International Settlements used the term already in the late 1970s. It realized that focusing supervision exclusively on individual institutions is not sufficient to ensure financial stability. However, it was just since the start of this century that efforts were made by Andrew Crockett and Claudio Borio (BIS) to define the concept more precisely. Basically, they described the concept by comparing micro and macro prudential supervision. I will do the same here. Microprudential supervision tries to limit the distress of individual institutions. Think about supervision of banks like Rabobank or ING. In this case, the ultimate objective is to safeguard the stability of the institution and the interests of investors and depositors. Macroprudential supervision on the other hand aims to limit the risk to the financial system. So instead of looking just at Rabobank, ING or any other individual institution in isolation, we look at the system as a whole. The ultimate objective of this approach is to limit the probability and severity of financial crises, mainly in terms of costs to GDP. It is useful to illustrate this with an example. Compare the financial system with a complex machine. For instance an aeroplane. Although a plane is much easier to navigate than our financial system, this analogy will fit my purpose. Since the safety of a plane is essential, each individual part, like the engine or wing, is monitored on a regular basis. Besides this, the parts of a plane need to satisfy strict quality requirements. Note that the main concern here is the functioning of the individual components. This is the microprudential dimension. Now, forget about the individual parts and try to take a macroprudential perspective. Since our ultimate objective is to prevent a crash, we need a broader view than just focusing on the individual elements. We want to assure that there are no vulnerabilities in the technical infrastructure of the plane. We want to give special attention to very crucial, systemically relevant parts that have little back-up and could by themselves cause a crash. And we definitely want to analyze in detail and high frequency the weather conditions. Thus, a macroprudential approach asks for a broader, more system-oriented perspective. Emergence of macroprudential perspective in supervision Now that we have some idea of what the macroprudential approach actually is, it is not difficult to imagine why it has been in the lime light for some time, and why, with this crisis, it is back on centre stage. Basically, a few forceful trends have amplified the move towards a macroprudential approach. First we have witnessed a wave of financial liberalization and globalization since the 1980s. Booming international trade has been accompanied by a rapid increase in cross-border financing. Financial institutions responded to these developments by spreading their wings and transforming themselves into global players. At the same time, with the benefit of new computer technologies, financial institutions drove many new innovations. More recently, this process of financial integration and innovation experienced a huge acceleration. The wide-spread use of collateralized debt products and credit default swaps are just two examples of this. Over the years, these structural changes increased the efficiency of international capital flows, and of financial markets more generally. However, they also contributed to periods of market turbulence, asset bubbles and financial crises. The financial system has become far more complex. It is like we have exchanged a manageable one-propeller plane for a large high-speed jumbo jet  or perhaps even a stealth fighter, hard to detect on the radar. A second trend has to due with the size and complexity of financial institutions. A number of institutions have become so important that they can be considered as systemically relevant. Not only due to their large balance sheets but also since they may dominate a particular market or are deeply embedded in the financial system. Ex post, an example to illustrate this is the demise of Lehman Brothers. This bank was so important to the financial system that its failure caused a financial earthquake. Its role in the global financial system was like the control stick, or one of the wings of the airplane. When troubles arise in these crucial parts it is extremely difficult to prevent a crash. Thus, the emergence of a larger, more integrated and complex financial system as well as the emergence of larger and more interconnected financial institutions need a macroprudential approach to mitigate systemic risks. Finally, the focus on the macroprudential approach can be explained by the substantial economic costs of financial crises. Since the financial system has become more interconnected and complex, the impact of a crisis has increased dramatically. I think it is not necessary to elaborate on this since we all see and feel the impact of the crisis we are in today. Without a doubt, in the run-up to the crisis, the macroprudential approach was certainly in the picture and early warnings were given by financial stability institutions, including my own central bank. But clearly, an adequate and effective macroprudential framework has been lacking. Practical implications The dramatic impact of this crisis has brought the discussion on macroprudential oversight back to the fore. Although we are still investigating the black box, most experts agree about one thing: the macroprudential approach to supervision should become more important and better anchored. The challenge now is to put these ideas into practice. So, for the remaining part of my speech, let me elaborate on the practical implications of a macroprudential approach. We can distinguish two broad categories when we practice macroprudential supervision. That is, rules and discretionary policies. The rule-based approach can be built through automatic stabilizers that aim to limit system-wide risks, ex-ante. The construction of countercyclical capital buffers by the Basel Committee is an example of this. However, the difficulty to assess cycles makes it dangerous to rely purely on automatic mechanisms, that cannot be precisely calibrated. An autopilot for our financial system is certainly useful, but we also want to be able to adjust the course manually. Therefore, we need discretionary judgement and intervention. Yet, several issues have to be addressed to implement a proper discretionary macroprudential approach. I will focus on the institutional setting, the macroprudential monitoring and follow-up, and the role of financial stability in legislation. Institutional setting First, the institutional setting. What is the best institutional architecture for a macroprudential approach? Should we have a separate central bank and prudential supervisor? Or should we merge the two as we have done in the Netherlands? This question has been subject to heated debate for years now. But the crisis has shed new light on the answer. We have learned again that macroeconomic and financial imbalances can closely interact. So it is of great importance that we incorporate the macroeconomic dimension in our prudential framework. Since central banks have an analytical advantage in judging the business cycle, monitoring financial markets and the payment system, it makes sense to give them a pivotal role in assessing financial stability. Moreover, we should ensure intensive interaction between macro- and microprudential supervision. In my view, the first and most logical step is to bring both disciplines close together, ideally under one roof. Just the simple fact that colleagues in both fields can easily grab a cup of coffee together can make a difference. I think DNB already has taken some important steps in this direction. In 2004 we merged with the Pension and Insurance Supervisory authority. This brought prudential supervision of all relevant financial players within one organization. From then on we not only supervised individual institutions, but also focused on cross-sectoral risks. To make the most of this new set up, we simultaneously established a financial stability division. Monitoring The main objective of this division is to play a coordinating role in preserving financial stability. For that reason, we have to map risks in our financial system continuously. An important instrument in monitoring the financial system is macro stress testing. The forward-looking nature of this tool gives supervisors and institutions insight into broader vulnerabilities and the impact of shocks. From the macroprudential perspective, stress tests disclose possible behaviour responses of firms that are often at the heart of systemic risk. At DNB, we conduct these macro stress-tests on a regular basis. In my view this tool is an indispensable part of the overall macroprudential framework. Macroprudential analysis often finds it way in financial stability reports, in DNBs case called the financial stability overview. This semi-annual report analyses the condition of the Dutch financial sector and is used internally by microprudential supervisors. We also publish a shorter version with more aggregate information for the general public. Financial stability reports are an important macroprudential tool in the sense that they increase the awareness of vulnerabilities in the financial system. However, I think that they have more potential and should be enhanced. By saying this, I do not refer to the analysis as such, but I am talking in particular about the follow-up. Some financial stability reports that were published before the crisis were shockingly accurate. Take for example our own financial stability report of March 2007. This edition contains a stress scenario that assumes a complete dry up of interbank funding. In the earlier overviews, we had pointed at the rapid increase of leverage, the vulnerabilities of the credit risk transfer model, and the risks of a sudden and sharp adjustment. These warnings were not exclusively given by DNB. Other central banks, the ECB included, and the IMF signalled the same risks in their financial stability reports. We have to acknowledge that, although there were signs that imbalances were building up, no, or only limited concrete policy actions were taken. It is like signalling dangerous thunderstorms on the flight route but not altering course. If we want to make the macroprudential approach work, we have to find a strategy for mitigating the risks that we identify. Translating warnings into policy Hence, the discretionary approach to macroprudential supervision requires a translation of judgements into concrete risk mitigating policies. There are several difficulties in doing this. For instance, it is difficult to signal the building up of imbalances on a timely basis, also because we need to have some comfort about observed weaknesses and about the probability of related risks materializing. In an international context, efforts are currently being made by the IMF and the FSB to develop a quantitative method to monitor systemic risks continuously. These so-called early warning exercises have risen to the top of the policy agenda. However, even when we are certain about specific vulnerabilities, it is hard to convince private or, for that matter, public agents of the need to alter their behaviour. It is not easy to take away the punch bowl at a party, especially when the party is just starting. The IMF has extensive experience with policy recommendations that are not lived up to. Related to this, how transparent can we be regarding imbalances and risks without creating a self-fulfilling prophecy? In other words, how do you communicate about risks when the environment is already vulnerable without precipitating the crisis? So although we have definitely made progress in developing our macroprudential monitoring framework, we need to think seriously about how we should use it. In this regard, continuing development of macroprudential policy instruments is crucial. I think the use of discretionary adjustments to capital ratios, provisions and margin requirements are a good starting point. However, in contrast to monetary policy that clearly has its own instrument; it is difficult to identify a distinct effective set of discretionary macroprudential tools. In fact, I think the search for effective macroprudential instruments is one of the greatest challenges for central bankers and supervisors in the near future. In the meantime, we should continue to make efforts to ensure that the expertise of macro and microprudential supervisors comes together. It is important that this interaction takes place on the basis of mutual trust, confidentiality and understanding. This is why at DNB we have internal financial stability reports that give concrete guidance and policy recommendations. We enhanced the process of horizontal interactions within the organisation by working with multidisciplinary teams that bring micro and macro expertise together around specific themes or cases. In the European context as well, steps have been taken to enhance the macroprudential approach. Financial stability in legislation Finally, I want to say a few words on anchoring financial stability in legislation. It is evident that the financial system has become far more complex than it used to be several decades ago. Many new players have arrived and financial institutions have become increasingly interconnected. Central bankers have a difficult task in guarding the stability of this complex financial system. The ongoing crisis stresses the need to improve our macroprudential instruments. In the same vein, we should create the necessary legal basis to allow a successful implementation of this macroprudential approach. If we want to be able to act quickly in case of stress, we need a legal backing. This is something that is currently being evaluated at European level by the commission. But also within our national boundaries, financial stability should get a firmer anchor. Most relevant laws, like the central banking law in this country, offer sufficient room during normal times. However, they give little ability to intervene in case of an emergency. We do not want to pass through a thunderstorm for the reason that we cannot change course since we then would cross forbidden territory. And we do not want a public organisation to violate the law either. If we take the macroprudential approach seriously, authorities should give priority to this issue. Right now we have the momentum to address difficult questions like shareholders rights, insolvency laws, mandatory information sharing by non-regulated entities, and so on. This is one important step we have to take in our quest for stability. Summing up Let me summarize the status of our flight today. There is common agreement of the need for an enhanced macroprudential approach for supervision. However, putting this noble ambition into practice is not easy. Several issues have to be addressed to make the concept workable. We need to strengthen the mutual understanding between micro and macroprudential supervisors. In addition we have to ensure that signalled risks are followed up by concrete policy actions. One way to realize this is by revising the instrumental and organisational setup, both on a national basis and globally. Another key priority for authorities today is to ensure that the financial stability mandate is better embedded in the relevant legislation. Although there are many other issues that have to be addressed, these are a good starting point. Of course, we should not have the illusion that with these changes we can prevent any future crisis. But we would already have accomplished a lot if such unfortunate event results in a smooth landing.

Title: Speech by director Kellermann: 'Pension policy one year after the collapse of Lehman Brothers'
text: Speech Director Kellermann 'Governance in microfinance' Speech Datum 29 september 2009 Time: 3:48 p.m. Location De Nederlandsche Bank, Amsterdam Speaker Mr. A.J. Kellermann, Director of the Dutch Central Bank It is a particular pleasure for me to speak with you about governance in microfinance. A special occasion, as we celebrate the fifth anniversary of WorldGranny, as well as the appointment of Her Royal Highness, Princess Maxima as UN Advocate for Accessible Finance in Developing Countries! As you know, World Granny has been committed to the empowerment of the elderly for the past 5 years by giving them a place in development policy. This ambition can be strengthened by paying attention to governance within microfinance institutions. We will discuss this in more detail in the panel discussion, but for now I would like to briefly outline the importance that De Nederlandsche Bank attaches to this subject. The current financial crisis has made it very clear that good governance is an essential part of well-functioning financial companies, including microfinance institutions  but I will go into that in a moment. First of all, it is important to get a clearer picture of the concept of governance. In short, good governance is a precondition for controlled business operations. This means that the organization is set up in such a way that risks are managed and set goals are achieved. This means that risks must be identified and measures must be put in place to control them. An adequate management environment is important in this respect, for example with regard to the organisational structure, information and communication provision and organisational culture What does that mean for financial institutions? In the first place, that the right checks and balances are in place in the organization. And that in addition, directors and, where applicable, supervisory directors or other internal supervisors must be competent and reliable. Expertise says something about knowledge and experience, but also about behaviour. Does a director have solid knowledge of the field and the organization, experience in leading a complex institution and does he not behave like a sun king? Reliability is reflected in integrity: does the director act in good conscience, even if local legal standards are complied with? And, good governance also means that undesirable incentives, for example through rewards, must be prevented. That warnings from people in the company are heeded. And that attention is paid to what the culture is like in the company in the first place. Are dissenting opinions allowed? The culture in a company, the behaviour of individual directors, is of great importance in this respect. And what does this mean for the governance of microfinance institutions? In principle, they would have to comply with the same high rules for governance as with 'ordinary' banks, insurers and pension funds, as well as with rules that need to be tightened further. Consider, for example, managing reputational risk in the case of unsustainable investments. But also the risk that pension administration or asset management in general is outsourced without adequate control. You could even argue that the very institutions that have such a drastic effect on the lives of millions of people should have checks and balances even more than other financial institutions to safeguard the trust placed in them. This is particularly true for micro-pensions, given the long-term nature of these schemes. So there seems to be a raison d'etre for supervision and regulation of microfinance institutions in general and micro-pension institutions in particular, partly to allow these institutions to grow in the important work they do. However, supervisory requirements are often complex and far-reaching. Microfinance institutions may be faced with rules that are disproportionate to the type and size of the transactions they make. As DNB President Wellink put it in his speech A Balancing act in progress of 6 May 2009, supervisors must find the right balance between stability on the one hand and access to financial services on the other. Overly strict regulations defeat the purpose of microfinance. You cannot, and perhaps don't need, impose rules on proportional interest representation, internal supervision, prevention of model dependencies and expertise in general on a group of fishermen in India who each set aside some money for their old age. In the first instance, exchange projects, such as the conference organised by WorldGranny in May last year and working visits to India, in which DNB participated, will help to exchange experiences/good practices. In addition, related regulations in a country will often play an important role in mitigating these types of governance risks, for example by means of anti-fraud provisions. Nevertheless, it is obvious to draw up some kind of requirements, for example about the way in which the board is controlled in its actions. Or the way in which continuing education within micro-pension initiatives, such as those developed by NGOs, Self Help Groups and cooperatives, is shaped to ensure the required expertise. Of course, the specific requirements must be adapted to the nature of microcredit institutions, but on the basis of clear criteria. This kind of thinking forms a good basis for the admittedly modest discussion on supervision and microfinance institutions that is already taking place internationally, for example in the Basel Committee. After all, it is a small step towards supervision of microfinance institutions by the DSOs of this world. The importance of microfinance institutions is growing, as evidenced by the estimated 35 million people worldwide who have already taken out micro-life insurance for their retirement provision. As more and more interests are involved in the decisions that these companies make, it may be logical that the functioning of a company is also looked at from the public sector. However, that is a discussion that may be held in the panel or else at a future meeting of WorldGranny. It is important to have a good understanding of how, for example, an insurance sector comes about and where the parallels with our own experiences lie.
text_original: Speech directeur Kellermann 'Pensioenbeleid n jaar na de ondergang van Lehman Brothers' Speech Datum 17 september 2009 Tijd 15:00 uur Lokatie Jaarlijkse DNB-bijeenkomst voor pensioenfondsbestuurders, Apeldoorn Spreker Mr. A.J. Kellermann, directeur van de Nederlandsche Bank Een jaar geleden ging Lehman Brothers ten onder en werd de wereld getroffen door een diepe vertrouwens- en beurscrisis. Sindsdien is er veel gebeurd. Het zal daarom geen verrassing zijn dat ik met u wil terugkijken op een roerige periode in het pensioendomein. Gemiddeld genomen is de dekkingsgraad van Nederlandse pensioenfondsen in 2008 met 50 procentpunt gedaald. Grofweg de helft hiervan komt voort uit een daling van de waarde van de beleggingen. De andere helft is het gevolg van de rentedaling op de waarde van de verplichtingen. De daling van de dekkingsgraad komt overeen met een verslechtering van de financile positie met circa 220 miljard euro voor de sector als geheel. Dit is bijna negen keer het jaarlijkse premievolume en tweederde deel van wat de Nederlanders op de spaarrekening hebben staan. Nu past bij een dergelijk getal natuurlijk enige nuancering. Iedereen heeft vermogensverlies ondervonden als gevolg van de crisis. Pensioenfondsen blijven dan niet buiten schot. Het verlies kan bovendien geleidelijk weer teruglopen als de beurzen zich herstellen. Zo is de afgelopen maanden de gemiddelde dekkingsgraad weer opgelopen tot het niveau dat hoort bij het minimaal vereist eigen vermogen. Dit is een gemiddelde. Individuele fondsen staan er beter of slechter voor. Bovendien is herstel geen wetmatigheid. De volatiliteit die we hebben gezien kan weer terugkeren als blijkt dat echte groei nog lang op zich laat wachten. De dekkingsgraad fluctueert, afhankelijk van het beleggingsbeleid, met de schommelingen op de financile markten. Daarom is het zinvol dit beleggingsbeleid eens onder de loep te nemen. Tegen de achtergrond van de kredietcrisis heeft DNB het beleggingsbeleid op verschillende manieren geanalyseerd. Dit onderzoek is onlangs afgerond. Het onderzoek is gebaseerd op een sectorbrede analyse van toezichtgegevens, de herstelplannen en de toezichtervaringen over de afgelopen jaren. Verder is bij een willekeurige dwarsdoorsnede van de pensioensector een inventarisatie gemaakt van de manier waarop de feitelijke beleggingen tot stand komen. Het onderzoek is uitgevoerd in een periode van grote turbulentie op de financile markten waarin de meeste beleggers vermogensverlies hebben geleden. Het is daarom goed om te benadrukken dat we het beleid van pensioenfondsen hebben beoordeeld tegen die achtergrond. Daartoe is getracht onderscheid te maken tussen externe omstandigheden waar pensioenfondsen geen invloed op hebben en factoren die wel binnen de invloedssfeer liggen. In het onderzoek is vervolgens gekeken naar de beleggingsstrategie, de vertaling van beleid naar daadwerkelijke beleggingen en de risicobeheersing. Het onderzoek wijst uit dat bij een aantal pensioenfondsen de risicos waaraan zij in hun beleggingsbeleid blootstaan worden onderschat. Die risicos hebben niet alleen te maken met externe factoren en met de gekozen strategische financile opzet. Ze hangen voor een deel ook samen met zaken als een actief beleggingsbeleid, complexe derivatentransacties of uitbesteding van activiteiten. Op dit moment treedt DNB nog niet in detail naar buiten met haar bevindingen. Ik wil graag de commissie Frijns de ruimte geven haar eigen onderzoek te doen. Wel heb ik de commissie Frijns een geanonimiseerde versie van onze studie ter inzage geven. Ook hebben we de koepels ingelicht over onze bevindingen. We gaan de discussie niet uit de weg en het is de ambitie om in overleg met de sector te kijken waar zo nodig dingen kunnen worden aangescherpt. Dit is geen eenvoudige klus want het beleggingsbeleid van pensioenfondsen is laveren tussen het invullen van een rele ambitie enerzijds en het vermijden van structurele onderdekking anderzijds. Overigens zijn we bij het onderzoek soms ook positief verrast. Er zijn pensioenfondsen die een adequate risicobeheersing hebben opgetuigd en die de staartrisicos van hun financile opzet goed op het netvlies hebben. Het risicobeheer is in die gevallen in overeenstemming met het risicoprofiel. We hebben ook pensioenfondsen gesproken die investeringen links hebben laten liggen omdat de voor- en nadelen onvoldoende konden worden gewogen. Dit is een goede zaak want uiteindelijk slaan de risicos neer bij de belanghebbenden van het pensioenfonds, dus de sponsoren en deelnemers. Een observatie die ik in dit verband wil maken is dat rondom de herstelplannen enige weerstand bestond om het onderwerp korten van pensioenrechten aan te roeren. Let wel, ook DNB ziet het korten van opgebouwde pensioenrechten als laatste noodmaatregel. Daar is geen misverstand over. We constateren alleen dat bij de huidige financile opzet van sommige fondsen het denkbaar is dat korten op enig moment nodig is. Dit voorkomt dat de ingegane pensioenen worden doorbetaald ten laste van de aanspraken van actieve deelnemers en zo het pensioenvermogen wordt uitgehold. Het is wat dat betreft van belang dat de deelnemers van de mogelijkheid tot korten op de hoogte zijn en eventueel daar op kunnen anticiperen. Ik reken het tot uw taak die boodschap aan deelnemers over te brengen en zie dat her en der hieraan wordt gewerkt. Naast het beleid van pensioenfondsen is het wenselijk om het toezichtkader te evalueren. Het FTK heeft naar mijn mening bijgedragen aan het transparant maken van risicos en het stimuleren van goed risicobeheer. Toch zitten in het toezichtkader elementen die het nemen van risico wat eenzijdig belonen. Dit wil zeggen dat de nadelen van het nemen van risicos minder zwaar doorwegen dan de voordelen. Dit komt op verschillende plekken terug in het FTK, zoals bij de gedempte kostendekkende premie en bij de berekening van het vereiste eigen vermogen. Daarnaast zal er bij de evaluatie van het FTK veel aandacht zijn voor het thema marktwaardering en de gevolgen voor het beleid van pensioenfondsen. Ik ga op deze elementen afzonderlijk in. Neem de onzekere risicopremies op zakelijke waarden. Deze worden in de gedempte kostendekkende premie ingecalculeerd alsof ze met zekerheid worden gehaald. Op papier is het daarom aantrekkelijk om veel risico te nemen. Bij de berekening van de gedempte premie ontstaat de opmerkelijke relatie dat door het nemen van risico de kostendekkende premie omlaag kan. De kosten van het pensioen worden echter niet bepaald door de verwachte rendementen maar door de realisaties. Het gevolg van te optimistische rendementsverwachtingen en te lage premies is dat de kans op tegenvallers wordt vergroot en de kans op meevallers juist wordt verkleind. Dit betekent dat in de toekomst hogere inhaalpremies nodig zijn om hetzelfde pensioen te financieren. Goedkoop wordt dan uiteindelijk duurkoop. Dit is niet in het belang van de deelnemers. Een ander punt is het vereiste eigen vermogen. We hebben in Nederland voor een model gekozen dat naar 97,5% zekerheid streeft. Dit betekent dat de buffers niet in alle gevallen toereikend zijn. Zoals ik in de inleiding heb gezegd is in 2008 op macroniveau een verlies geleden dat veel groter is dan de vereiste buffer. Dit kan natuurlijk een speling van het lot zijn. Toch is ook hier een nadere analyse nodig. Sommige risicofactoren worden bijvoorbeeld in het geheel niet meegenomen bij de berekening van de buffer. Denk aan liquiditeitsrisicos en aan concentratierisicos. Andere risicofactoren worden wellicht onderschat en diversificatievoordelen op hun beurt overschat. Dit komt in de evaluatie van het FTK zeker terug. Dit alles betekent dat niet alleen bij de pensioenfondsen maar ook in het toezichtkader meer aandacht nodig is voor de beleggingsrisicos bezien vanuit de totale financile opzet van een pensioenfonds. Het beleggingsonderzoek dat we hebben uitgevoerd suggereert dat daarbij een analyse op hoofdlijnen niet volstaat. Er is ook aandacht nodig voor de implementatie van het beleggingsbeleid. Dit kan deels worden verbeterd door het FTK op onderdelen aan te passen. Maar het is ook gewenst om doeltreffender en specifieker op te kunnen treden met betrekking tot geconstateerde tekortkomingen. Een ander thema, dat bij de evaluatie een prominente rol krijgt, is de gevolgen van marktwaardering voor het beleid van pensioenfondsen. Hier is de laatste tijd al veel over gezegd in de sfeer dat die regels pensioenfondsen dwingen om te sturen op dagkoersen. DNB is niet doof voor deze kritiek. Pensioenfondsen zijn verplichtingen aangegaan voor een lange termijn en de taak van het bestuur is om het evenwicht tussen de verplichtingen en de bezittingen over een dito lange periode te beheren. Dit zonder dat de strategie te veel wordt afgeleid door de 'witte ruis' van de dag tot dag fluctuaties op financile markten. Wat dit betreft hebben we eind vorig jaar serieus gekeken naar mogelijke verstoringen in de swapmarkt. Achteraf was het niet nodig, maar DNB had binnen het huidige kader kunnen besluiten een correctie toe te passen. We zijn daar alert op. Een verdergaande optie, die door sommigen naar voren wordt gebracht, is middeling van de rente die wordt gebruikt voor het disconteren van de verplichtingen. Dit leidt tot demping van de volatiliteit van de verplichtingen. Wanneer de rente over een lange periode wordt gemiddeld, in dit kader is een termijn van 7 jaar naar voren gebracht, komen trendmatige rentebewegingen echter pas vertraagd tot uiting in de dekkingsgraad. Dit leidt ertoe dat de besluitvorming achter de feiten aan gaat lopen en het doel voorbij wordt geschoten. Dit komt omdat de verandering in de dekkingsgraad niet alleen door de actuele rente wordt bepaald maar ook door de rentes uit een ver verleden die uit de berekening van het voortschrijdende gemiddelde vallen. Dergelijke effecten verminderen het zicht op de risicos die pensioenfondsen lopen. Zoals gezegd is na de val van Lehman Brothers veel gebeurd. Het is goed om dit diepgaand te analyseren. Maar ik wil natuurlijk ook graag met u vooruit kijken. Herstel van de buffers is een belangrijke voorwaarde voor de duurzaamheid van het Nederlandse pensioensysteem. Naast het vermogen om nieuwe schokken op te vangen kunnen de extra rendementen die over de buffer worden gehaald worden aangewend voor indexatie. Als de buffers zijn hersteld heeft een ieder hier profijt van. Ook de consequenties van de volatiliteit in dekkingsgraden kunnen verder worden beperkt door aan te sturen op de opbouw van hogere buffers in goede tijden. Dat de dekkingsgraad inmiddels weer is opgelopen tot iets boven het minimaal vereiste niveau wil daarom nog niet zeggen dat achterover leunen alweer op zijn plaats is. Pensioenfondsen kunnen er niet op vertrouwen dat herstel automatisch optreedt en aanhoudt. De toekomst is en blijft - helaas - onzeker. Het is zaak om door te groeien tot een niveau boven het vereist eigen vermogen en daarbij op te passen voor een optimistische handelwijze en voor te rooskleurige aannames. Een eerste beslissing die zich in dat verband aandient is die omtrent de indexatie. Inflatiecorrectie is belangrijk maar creert ook een dilemma omdat een indexatietoekenning op het herstel drukt. De omgeving waarbinnen pensioenfondsen opereren is complex en de belangen van de verschillende stakeholders moeten zorgvuldig worden gewogen. De pensioensector kent wat dat betreft zijn eigen dynamiek. Dat is overigens ook wat deze sector zo bijzonder maakt. De komende tijd staat in het teken van herstel maar ook in het teken van evaluatie en toekomstgericht denken. Dit proces is gebaseerd op onderling vertrouwen en resultaatgerichtheid. Ik ben blij dat Minister Donner verschillende initiatieven op de rails heeft gezet om onze pensioenvoorzieningen aan een duurzaamheidtest te onderwerpen. Medio volgend jaar zal er op basis van de uitkomsten van die processen een brede discussie plaatshebben. We moeten ons daarbij nog beter dan in het verleden voorbereiden op nieuwe gevaren die vroeg of laat op ons afkomen. De crisis heeft aan het licht gebracht dat de risicos die pensioenfondsen lopen worden onderschat. Ik wil u graag behoeden voor te veel optimisme. Niet omdat ik van nature pessimistisch ben. In tegendeel. Het streven is dat u zodanig veel ruimte bouwt in uw financile opzet dat u, na de recente moeilijke periode, zo nu en dan ook weer eens een keer een meevaller kunt melden. Ik wens u dat van harte toe.

Title: Speech Director Kellermann 'Governance in microfinance'
Subtitle: Het is mij een bijzonder genoegen om met u te mogen spreken over 'governance in microfinance'. Een bijzondere gelegenheid, daar wij het vijfjarig bestaan van WorldGranny vieren, alsook de benoeming van Hare Koninklijke Hoogheid, Prinses Mxima als VN Pleitbezorgster voor toegankelijke financiering in ontwikkelinglanden!
text: Speech Director Kellermann 'Governance in microfinance' Speech Datum 29 september 2009 Time: 3:48 p.m. Location De Nederlandsche Bank, Amsterdam Speaker Mr. A.J. Kellermann, Director of the Dutch Central Bank It is a particular pleasure for me to speak with you about governance in microfinance. A special occasion, as we celebrate the fifth anniversary of WorldGranny, as well as the appointment of Her Royal Highness, Princess Maxima as UN Advocate for Accessible Finance in Developing Countries! As you know, World Granny has been committed to the empowerment of the elderly for the past 5 years by giving them a place in development policy. This ambition can be strengthened by paying attention to governance within microfinance institutions. We will discuss this in more detail in the panel discussion, but for now I would like to briefly outline the importance that De Nederlandsche Bank attaches to this subject. The current financial crisis has made it very clear that good governance is an essential part of well-functioning financial companies, including microfinance institutions  but I will go into that in a moment. First of all, it is important to get a clearer picture of the concept of governance. In short, good governance is a precondition for controlled business operations. This means that the organization is set up in such a way that risks are managed and set goals are achieved. This means that risks must be identified and measures must be put in place to control them. An adequate management environment is important in this respect, for example with regard to the organisational structure, information and communication provision and organisational culture What does that mean for financial institutions? In the first place, that the right checks and balances are in place in the organization. And that in addition, directors and, where applicable, supervisory directors or other internal supervisors must be competent and reliable. Expertise says something about knowledge and experience, but also about behaviour. Does a director have solid knowledge of the field and the organization, experience in leading a complex institution and does he not behave like a sun king? Reliability is reflected in integrity: does the director act in good conscience, even if local legal standards are complied with? And, good governance also means that undesirable incentives, for example through rewards, must be prevented. That warnings from people in the company are heeded. And that attention is paid to what the culture is like in the company in the first place. Are dissenting opinions allowed? The culture in a company, the behaviour of individual directors, is of great importance in this respect. And what does this mean for the governance of microfinance institutions? In principle, they would have to comply with the same high rules for governance as with 'ordinary' banks, insurers and pension funds, as well as with rules that need to be tightened further. Consider, for example, managing reputational risk in the case of unsustainable investments. But also the risk that pension administration or asset management in general is outsourced without adequate control. You could even argue that the very institutions that have such a drastic effect on the lives of millions of people should have checks and balances even more than other financial institutions to safeguard the trust placed in them. This is particularly true for micro-pensions, given the long-term nature of these schemes. So there seems to be a raison d'etre for supervision and regulation of microfinance institutions in general and micro-pension institutions in particular, partly to allow these institutions to grow in the important work they do. However, supervisory requirements are often complex and far-reaching. Microfinance institutions may be faced with rules that are disproportionate to the type and size of the transactions they make. As DNB President Wellink put it in his speech A Balancing act in progress of 6 May 2009, supervisors must find the right balance between stability on the one hand and access to financial services on the other. Overly strict regulations defeat the purpose of microfinance. You cannot, and perhaps don't need, impose rules on proportional interest representation, internal supervision, prevention of model dependencies and expertise in general on a group of fishermen in India who each set aside some money for their old age. In the first instance, exchange projects, such as the conference organised by WorldGranny in May last year and working visits to India, in which DNB participated, will help to exchange experiences/good practices. In addition, related regulations in a country will often play an important role in mitigating these types of governance risks, for example by means of anti-fraud provisions. Nevertheless, it is obvious to draw up some kind of requirements, for example about the way in which the board is controlled in its actions. Or the way in which continuing education within micro-pension initiatives, such as those developed by NGOs, Self Help Groups and cooperatives, is shaped to ensure the required expertise. Of course, the specific requirements must be adapted to the nature of microcredit institutions, but on the basis of clear criteria. This kind of thinking forms a good basis for the admittedly modest discussion on supervision and microfinance institutions that is already taking place internationally, for example in the Basel Committee. After all, it is a small step towards supervision of microfinance institutions by the DSOs of this world. The importance of microfinance institutions is growing, as evidenced by the estimated 35 million people worldwide who have already taken out micro-life insurance for their retirement provision. As more and more interests are involved in the decisions that these companies make, it may be logical that the functioning of a company is also looked at from the public sector. However, that is a discussion that may be held in the panel or else at a future meeting of WorldGranny. It is important to have a good understanding of how, for example, an insurance sector comes about and where the parallels with our own experiences lie.
text_original: Speech directeur Kellermann 'Governance in microfinance' Speech Datum 29 september 2009 Tijd 15:48 uur Lokatie De Nederlandsche Bank, Amsterdam Spreker Mr. A.J. Kellermann, directeur van de Nederlandsche Bank Het is mij een bijzonder genoegen om met u te mogen spreken over 'governance in microfinance'. Een bijzondere gelegenheid, daar wij het vijfjarig bestaan van WorldGranny vieren, alsook de benoeming van Hare Koninklijke Hoogheid, Prinses Mxima als VN Pleitbezorgster voor toegankelijke financiering in ontwikkelinglanden! Zoals u weet heeft World Granny zich de afgelopen 5 jaar ingezet voor de empowerment van ouderen door hen een plek in het ontwikkelingsbeleid te geven. Dit streven kan versterkt worden door aandacht te geven aan governance binnen microfinancieringsinstelligen. In de paneldiscussie zullen we hierover dieper van gedachten wisselen, maar voor nu wil ik graag kort het belang schetsen dat De Nederlandsche Bank hecht aan dit onderwerp. De huidige financile crisis heeft bijzonder duidelijk gemaakt dat een goede governance een essentieel onderdeel is van goed functionerende financile ondernemingen, waar microfinancieringsinstellingen ook onder vallen  maar daar ga ik dadelijk specifiek op in. Allereerst is van belang om een scherper beeld te krijgen van het begrip 'governance'. Kort gezegd is goede governance een randvoorwaarde voor een beheerste bedrijfsvoering. Dit houdt in dat de organisatie zo is ingericht dat risicos worden beheerst en gestelde doelen worden bereikt. Dat betekent dat risicos moeten zijn gedentificeerd en maatregelen zijn ingericht om deze te beheersen. Daarbij is een adequate beheersomgeving van belang, bijvoorbeeld voor wat betreft de organisatiestructuur, informatie- en communicatievoorziening en de organisatiecultuur Wat betekent dat voor financile instellingen? In de eerste plaats dat de juiste checks and balances in de organisatie aanwezig zijn. En dat daarnaast bestuurders en waar van toepassing commissarissen of andere interne toezichthouders, deskundig en betrouwbaar moeten zijn. Deskundigheid zegt iets over kennis en ervaring, maar ook over gedrag. Heeft een bestuurder degelijke kennis van het vakgebied en de organisatie, ervaring met het leiden van een complexe instelling en gedraagt hij zich niet als een zonnekoning? Betrouwbaarheid vindt zijn weerslag in integriteit: handelt de bestuurder naar eer en geweten, ook als lokale, wettelijke normen nageleefd worden? En, een goede governance betekent ook dat ongewenste prikkels, bijvoorbeeld door beloningen, voorkomen moeten worden. Dat waarschuwingen van mensen in de onderneming ter harte worden genomen. En dat er aandacht is voor hoe de cultuur berhaupt in de onderneming is. Zijn afwijkende meningen toegestaan? De cultuur in een onderneming, het gedrag van individuele bestuurders, is daarbij van groot belang. En wat betekent dit vervolgens voor de governance van microfinancieringsinstellingen? In principe zouden zij moeten voldoen aan dezelfde hoge regels voor governance als bij 'gewone' banken, verzekeraars en pensioenfondsen n aan verder aan te scherpen regels. Denk bijvoorbeeld aan het beheersen van reputatierisico in geval van niet-duurzame beleggingen. Maar ook aan het risico dat de pensioenadministratie of het vermogensbeheer in het algemeen uitbesteed wordt zonder dat er toereikende controle op is. Je kunt er zelfs voor pleiten dat juist die instellingen die zon ingrijpend effect hebben op het leven van miljoenen mensen, nog meer dan andere financile instellingen 'checks and balances' dienen te hebben om het aan hen gegeven vertrouwen te borgen. Dit geldt in het bijzonder voor micro-pensioenen, gelet op het lange-termijn karakter van deze regelingen. Er lijkt dus een bestaansrecht te zijn voor toezicht en regulering van microfinancieringsinstellingen in het algemeen en micro-pensioeninstellingen in het bijzonder, mede om deze instellingen te laten groeien in het belangrijke werk dat ze doen. Maar, toezichteisen zijn vaak complex en ingrijpend. Microfinancieringsinstellingen kunnen geconfronteerd worden met regels die niet in verhouding staan tot het type en de omvang van de transacties die ze doen. Zoals DNB-president Wellink het verwoordde in zijn speech A Balancing act in progress van 6 mei 2009, moeten toezichthouders de juiste balans vinden tussen stabiliteit enerzijds en toegang tot financile diensten anderzijds. Te strenge regelgeving streeft het doel van microfinanciering voorbij. Aan een groep vissers in India die elk wat geld opzij zetten voor hun oude dag, kun je geen regels opleggen over evenredige belangenvertegenwoordiging, intern toezicht, voorkomen van 'model dependencies' en deskundigheid in het algemeen, en misschien is dat ook niet nodig. In eerste instantie zullen uitwisselingsprojecten, zoals de vorig jaar mei door WorldGranny georganiseerde conferentie en werkbezoeken in India, waaraan DNB deelnam, helpen om ervaringen / 'good practices' uit te wisselen. Daarnaast zal vaak aanverwante regelgeving in een land een belangrijke rol spelen om dit soort governancerisicos te ondervangen, bijvoorbeeld door middel van anti-fraude bepalingen. Toch ligt het voor de hand om iets van eisen op te stellen, bijvoorbeeld over de manier waarop het bestuur gecontroleerd wordt in zijn handelen. Of de manier waarop permanente educatie binnen micropensioeninitiatieven, zoals ontplooid door NGO's, Self Help Groups en coperaties, wordt vormgegeven om de vereiste deskundigheid te waarborgen. Vanzelfsprekend moeten de specifieke eisen aangepast worden aan de aard van microkredietinstellingen, maar wel op basis van duidelijke criteria. Dit soort gedachten vormt een goede basis voor de, weliswaar bescheiden, discussie over toezicht en microfinancieringsinstellingen die al internationaal gevoerd wordt, bijvoorbeeld in het Bazels Comit. Want, het is immers een kleine stap naar toezicht op microfinancieringsinstellingen door de DNBs van deze wereld. Het belang van microfinancieringsinstellingen groeit, getuige de naar schatting 35 miljoen mensen wereldwijd die al een micro-levensverzekering hebben afgesloten voor hun oudedagsvoorziening. Naarmate meer en meer belangen zijn gemoeid met de beslissingen die deze ondernemingen nemen, kan het logisch zijn dat ook vanuit de publieke sector wordt gekeken naar het functioneren van een onderneming. Dat is echter een discussie die wellicht in het panel of anders op een volgende bijeenkomst van WorldGranny kan worden gevoerd. Van belang daarbij is een goed besef te hebben van hoe bijvoorbeeld een verzekeringsector tot stand komt en waar de parallellen met onze eigen ervaringen zitten.

Title: Speech directeur Hoogduin 'M&A and Private Equity in a post-crisis era'
text: Speech directeur Hoogduin 'M&A and Private Equity in a post-crisis era' Speech Datum 28 oktober 2009 Tijd 13:28 uur Lokatie Mergermarket Benelux M&A and Private Equity Forum Spreker Prof.dr. L.H. Hoogduin, directeur van de Nederlandsche Bank These are challenging times, not only for M&A and private equity but also for my business of central banking. Be assured though that my presence here is not because I am looking for a potential buyer. In my view, M&A and private equity are valuable to growth and innovation. These activities can play an important role in the process of economic recovery through restructuring and the creation of synergies, bringing distressed companies back to life, increasing efficiency, and implementing new strategies. These might prove valuable characteristics on our way out of the worst recession since World War II. However, the sector has not been spared in this financial crisis. Many companies are too busy trying to survive to be thinking about takeovers. Of course the developments in European corporate bond markets have not helped either. Private equity managers as well need to divide their attention, more than before, between restructuring portfolio companies and searching for attractive takeover candidates. But more importantly, leveraged loan markets virtually closed down, bringing private equity markets to a near stand-still, even though most managers have idle capital on hand. Over the past few months we have seen M&A activity gaining traction. But private equity does not yet seem to be able to reap the benefits of green shoots in the markets. Besides the pace of economic recovery, much will depend on the revival of leveraged loan markets in the short to medium term. I will start the introduction to this Forum by arguing that this crisis might be less unique than often argued. Its consequences are nevertheless severe and despite encouraging signs, it is too early to assume that the crisis is over as we are still confronted with many uncertainties. Going forward, adjustments to the regulatory framework have to be made. Some will have a positive impact on M&A and private equity activity, others will not. However, it is safe to say that we most likely will not see pre-crisis leverage levels returning in the foreseeable future. This creates ample opportunities for investors who truly know how to create value, while at the same time posing challenges for those strategies that have been highly dependent on the use of high leverage and a favourable macroeconomic climate. We have witnessed the worst crisis in living memory. The feedback loops between the financial sector and the real economy remind us of economic history lessons about the Great Depression. Many comparisons to earlier crisis episodes have been made, but this one seems to be unique in many ways. Or, in other words, this time is different. At least, so it seems. In my view, the worst mistake we can make, is to let our vision be clouded by details and fail to see the forest for the trees. Indeed, this time is not so different at all. The bigger picture remains the same, with at the root a debt fuelled boom. Policy interest rates worldwide were structurally at low levels. The result was abundant liquidity, the building up of excessive leverage in the financial system and a pressing search for yield. The ingredients of innovation and globalisation made this process all the more explosive. We all know the subsequent, dramatic course of events. Stock markets collapsed, risk premia exploded, financial icons left the stage, and governments worldwide had to intervene in the financial sector on an unprecedented scale, severely disrupting public finances. This crisis has proven once again that when the skies ahead seem bright, credit is provided readily. Unfortunately, when the tide turns, it tends to be withdrawn brutally. With highly indebted households, companies and governments, there was an accident waiting to happen. M&A and private equity markets crashed in the same pile-up as the wider financial markets and the economy. So where are we now? At first glance, the recent stock market rally and tightening spreads are comforting. The same is true for bank profits over the first half of 2009. The key question confronting us, is whether these signals are signs of a permanent, sustainable recovery, or merely of a temporary upswing. I realise that central bankers have the reputation of being downers at the party; in the words of former central banker McChesney Martin, they tend to take away the punch bowl when the party is getting started. Such an accusation can hardly be made these days, as central banks are providing punch so generously, that we all run the risk of getting addicted to it. The only reason we might be accused of being downers, is that we are not joining the party where the end of the financial crisis is being celebrated. I would argue that, despite positive signs, we are just not there yet. History teaches us that recessions resulting from a financial crisis, and especially from bank crises, tend to be deeper and last longer. In addition, part of the current upswing can be explained by unprecedented macroeconomic stimulus and financial sector support measures. Exits out of these measures call for careful consideration and are surrounded by risks of timing errors. With respect to bank profits, a closer look at the numbers suggests that not all of them might prove sustainable, especially those stemming from one-off capital market gains. Indeed, the traditional banking business still showed declining profits, and further losses on loans might have to be absorbed. Especially developments in commercial real estate markets call for caution. On top of that, securitisation markets are still impaired. In sum, there is reason for cautious optimism, but we have to keep in mind that economic recovery is still fragile. Going forward, it is of the essence that we take the lessons of this crisis to heart. The obvious challenge is to translate these lessons into policy actions that make the financial system more fail-safe, but at the same time do not unduly hamper financial innovation and growth. Let me emphasise that these lessons are by no means simple, and that our ambitions can only be modest. After all, a financial system where failures are fully ruled out is not tenable, nor is it desirable. That being said, many changes to the regulatory framework will be made. Some of them will put a constraint on buyout activity, while others will have a positive impact. First of all, we cannot allow systemic gaps in the supervisory framework. Many of the risks that have materialised were built up outside the scope of supervision. For instance, hedge funds have become important players in some systematically relevant markets. Although this type of investors did not cause the crisis, they did play a role by reinforcing the procyclicality of financial markets. In order to fix the existing gaps, the European Commission is working on a proposal for a Directive to put all European alternative investment fund managers under some form of oversight. These include hedge funds, but also private equity managers, although probably not to the same extent. At this point the question if private equity needs to be supervised, is merely rhetoric, as there will be a Directive. The issue now is what exact shape and form this oversight will take. With respect to private equity, the proposed guideline mainly aims at increasing transparency in the sector. This might actually be a good thing, as many myths about the sector exist, and not all of them that favourable. More transparency and insight in what PE managers actually do and how they operate might positively influence the perception about the sector. The second lesson is that the capital base and liquidity position of many financial institutions have not been sufficient to navigate through this crisis. Furthermore, the accumulation of the excessive debt levels that I referred to before could not be prevented. With that, the rules that were in place tended to work out procyclically. To address these issues numerous policy initiatives have been developed. Some might not be implemented, but others definitely will be. It is obvious that the amount and the quality of regulatory capital should be increased, and that the introduction of a cyclical capital buffer will help in smoothing economic swings. However, these measures will be carefully timed, as many banks are still in the process of deleveraging and we clearly do not want to risk hampering the recovery. Of similar importance is the strengthening of the liquidity base. I am sure that all present here today know of financial institutions that were confronted with a liquidity squeeze while having adequate levels of capital. Reviving securitisation markets is another issue that is high on the international agenda of policymakers. Complex securitised products contributed significantly to the collapse of the system. Nevertheless, securitisation markets have become an important, indispensable part of the financial system. They have the ability to spread risks to well-positioned investors and provide for an important source of funding. As such, these markets can contribute to economic recovery. Several sets of policy measures are currently under consideration to address the structural weaknesses of these markets, revealed by the crisis. For example, the IMF and the Bank for International Settlements have come up with several proposals to bring securitisation back to life without threatening financial stability. A central feature of the proposed measures is that they are aimed at regaining investors confidence. Let me mention a few of them. First of all, complexity has to be reduced. Deal structures have become so complicated that even the math-wizards who designed them did not seem to have a full understanding of the risks, let alone the investors. Complexity could be reduced by an increased standardisation of structures, based on a smaller number of tranches. Secondly, also in this market, transparency should be enhanced, including standardised disclosure of asset-level data. It has become almost impossible to conduct a proper credit analysis of a securitised product, even for a more traditional one. Thirdly, ratings of securitised products have to be improved. The adverse effects of over-reliance on rating agencies have been discussed widely. This calls for both new regulatory rules relating to rating agencies and an improvement of rating methodologies. Finally, and possibly most importantly, incentives of originators and arrangers have to be better aligned. A promising method, associated with the necessary complexities, are tranche retention requirements, where the originators keep a skin in the game. Different approaches are currently being assessed to accomplish this. In short, there will be significant changes in the regulatory field. And these changes will have an impact on M&A activity and private equity markets. Needless to say, measures that are aimed at addressing capital buffers and liquidity management will cause risk-bearing capital to become more expensive. This is likely to have some impact on the availability and pricing of leveraged loans. On the other hand, initiatives to revive securitisation markets will have a positive effect on leveraged loan markets, which have been a key driver for the rapid acceleration of the buyout sector. However, the ample supply of low cost, covenant-lite debt we saw during the pre-crisis era is not likely to return any time soon, nor should it. By no means does this imply that leveraged loan markets should be banished. We simply do not want to return to the leverage levels we have seen in the recent past. The proposed measures are aimed at creating a more fail-safe financial system, and reducing the likelihood of a debt-fuelled boom from occurring. Capital markets will only revive to the fullest if trust in the system is restored. The proposed policy initiatives are indispensable for achieving this. So, it is safe to say that buyout activity will be different in the post crisis era. Not only banks, but also those who are active in buyout markets, will have to pay more attention to prudent risk management, especially with respect to the use of leverage. I do not see excessive debt levels against very low prices and almost no covenants returning in the foreseeable future. In fact, we should make sure they wont. In any case, I would not be surprised to witness a significant reduction in deal size when private equity managers start investing again, at least for the time being. This offers both challenges and opportunities for the sector. It also points to the need for some soul searching to what extent M&A transactions in general, and buyouts in particular, have truly created value and have made companies more efficient. How much of the superior returns generated in earlier years can be attributed to operational excellence and strategic vision? What percentage of the deals was successful because of the overall improvement in macro economic conditions, balance sheet engineering, and multiple expansion? These are obviously open questions, but the coming period will provide us with some of the answers. There will be companies that have been taken over during the boom years of M&A and private equity, especially the highly leveraged ones, that will simply not make it through the downturn. And, going forward, less sophisticated investors lacking true sector expertise and value creating capabilities will often not find it profitable to make acquisitions. This changed environment does however offer opportunities for investors that do know how to create value. The crisis might have a cleansing effect on M&A and private equity markets, leaving a less crowded, more professional sector. Its a typical case of the survival of the fittest and creative destruction. For some of those investors, the future might be a promising one.

Title: Speech by Paul Hilbers 'The future of the financial sector: two themes on the road to financial stability'
text: Speech by Paul Hilbers 'The future of the financial sector: two themes on the road to financial stability' Speech Datum 5 november 2009 Time: 15:13 hrs Lokatie Ernst & Young seminar 'Eye on Banking' Speaker Paul Hilbers, Division Director of Supervision Policy at the Dutch Central Bank I would like to go through two themes with you. Firstly, the supervisory reforms: what is the state of play in Basel and Brussels, and what are we doing at home? And secondly, what is the right exit route for government support? Supervisory reforms What will change in supervision? The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, commissioned by the G20, is currently working hard to tighten up the Basel II framework. The crisis has shown that banks need a higher level and quality of capital to absorb unexpected shocks. Firstly, the scope of the risks: some securitisations and trading book activities did not have sufficient capital funding. This will be repaired. Next, we need a solid capital base to cover these risks. The way to achieve this is by strengthening the quality of core capital. Moreover, in order to safeguard the level playing field, it is important that everyone uses the same definition. In addition, we aim to make the capital framework less pro-cyclical. This is easier said than done. Banks simply respond to a deteriorating creditworthiness of their customers by being more cautious about their lending, and this strengthens the business cycle. This is inherent in banking. But we can ensure that the capital framework amplifies this effect as little as possible. To this end, we are working on a system of countercyclical buffers, which ensure that capital or provisions are built up in good times, so that they can be used in bad times. The Basel Committee is currently working on translating this principle into concrete proposals. We want to do that in such a way that they can be applied in different national accounting and supervisory environments. Finally, the risk-weighted capital framework should be complemented by a non-risk-weighted measure. This measure should set a limit to the build-up of excessive leverage, which is one of the causes of the crisis. The measure should be simple, transparent and should take into account differences in accounting methods. It is expected that we will be able to start a Quantitative Impact Study early next year, in which the effects of the various policy options will be calculated. You will, of course, be involved in this. This will be an exciting period as it will show what the different policy options will mean in concrete terms for individual banks. But whatever we do, the changes will be made in such a way that they do not hinder the fledgling recovery. Strengthening capital is necessary for the creation of a robust banking system, but it is not enough. Equally important is a strong liquidity base. Banks around the world got into trouble because they were unable to generate enough liquidity under great stress. The Basel Committee is working on a new framework for liquidity supervision. This will be new for many countries, but not for you, because we have had liquidity supervision for many years. This will not mean, however, that everything will remain the same for Dutch banks in this area. In addition to raising the bar for capital and liquidity, the requirements for the risk management and governance of institutions will also increase. Risk management at banks needs to be improved. The complicated mathematical models that banks used to manage risk created a false sense of certainty: risk managers did not sufficiently realize that models are simply a simplified representation of reality. They are based on past data and assumptions, such as liquid markets, that do not hold true in crisis conditions. These models are therefore insufficient: they need to be supplemented more than before with stress tests, which provide insight into how a bank's financial situation behaves in a crisis scenario. Good risk management is therefore important, but risk awareness should not be limited to the experts of the risk management department. What is needed is a cultural change, in which knowledge and awareness of risks is widely supported within the organisation, and especially within the boards of directors: directors must know and understand the risks to which their bank is exposed.
